{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542424+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9983acdd24bab7573598cbe43c588211e9e1d72227253d0cb43782e29ec19a49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.934554+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9983bb71479d5fe3407b5abdca469c8032a54700e423ae3ee63ca959617abcbe","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:closure of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] For $2\le|S|\le3$ let

{"assumptions":["Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension","Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible","Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418611+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_99a13816dfad50d260100b726c1812dec833cb5ab9500c5108e4748d4cdc77db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Auditor's check: a proof that constructs 'a' weak solution and then calls it 'the' solution — or that computes shock speeds from Rankine-Hugoniot without verifying admissibility — is incomplete; check Oleinik's chord condition at every jump (for convex flux: the state must jump DOWN as x increases).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)","M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)","the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.562774+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation / random matrix theory","id":"claim_99cacf9752b7e70bfc79fa5a079c62ca089650407d9a61a19b42983a5a0f9318","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \\sum_{i=1}^M \\lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\\Sigma$, and let $M/n \\to c \\in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \\Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\\lambda_i \\breve m_F(\\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} m_F(\\lambda + i\\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \\int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Writing $\\operatorname{Im} \\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\pi f(\\lambda)$ and $\\operatorname{Re} \\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\pi H_f(\\lambda)$, $H_f(x) = \\pi^{-1} \\mathrm{PV}\\!\\int f(t)/(t - x)\\,dt$, the oracle reads $\\tilde d_i = \\lambda_i / \\big[(\\pi c \\lambda_i f(\\lambda_i))^2 + (1 - c - \\pi c \\lambda_i H_f(\\lambda_i))^2\\big]$. Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\\kappa(x) = \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \\lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j \\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j H_\\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\\kappa(x) = -\\tfrac{3x}{10\\pi} + \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5\\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\\log\\big|\\tfrac{\\sqrt5 - x}{\\sqrt5 + x}\\big|$. The resulting estimator $\\hat\\Sigma = \\sum_i \\tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The tilt is fixed, mu > 0, and 0 < sigma^2 < infinity.","m_n-n mu = O(1), with positive conditioning probability.","D is finite; tau is interior or is the finite-variance boundary tilt."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363251+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_99cd88c428f59ebc94e94fede1acb1357418317ec5a93a6518270b0d72a3d2f1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved mean-conditioning case of Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Let w_j >= 0, w_0 > 0, Phi(z) = sum_{j>=0} w_j z^j, and rho be its radius of convergence. Choose a fixed tau in (0,rho], with Phi(tau) < infinity, and define pi_j = w_j tau^j/Phi(tau), mu = sum j pi_j > 0, and sigma^2 = sum (j-mu)^2 pi_j in (0,infinity). Allow either tau < rho, or tau = rho with finite sigma^2. Let integers m_n satisfy m_n - n mu = O(1), and restrict to feasible sizes. Draw (Y_1,...,Y_n) with probability proportional to product_i w_{Y_i}, conditional on sum_i Y_i = m_n, and put N_d = number of i with Y_i = d. For any fixed finite set D of nonnegative integers, ((N_d-n pi_d)/sqrt(n))_{d in D} converges in distribution to a centered multivariate Gaussian vector. Its diagonal covariance is V_dd = pi_d(1-pi_d) - (d-mu)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2; for distinct d,e its covariance is V_de = -pi_d pi_e - (d-mu)(e-mu)pi_d pi_e/sigma^2. Degenerate Gaussian coordinates are allowed. In Janson's parameters, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), lambda = mu, and nu = lim_{t upward to rho} Psi(t), so the two cases are 0 < lambda < nu and lambda = nu with finite variance. The stronger O(1) centering hypothesis is explicit here; mere convergence m_n/n -> lambda is not being asserted to justify centering by the fixed law pi. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:42:39.077695+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_99d0309b697d8047602eaa18a2648c7871cb9153900bd62de68b3851ce305e8d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}),\, n \geq 1$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ be rooted compact resistance metric spaces.

{"assumptions":["F Borel probability on nonempty compact K","n positive integer","Fixed sum n*mean(F)","Empty-set convention retained"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T17:26:31.084900+00:00","domain":"probability; convex geometry; complete mixability","id":"claim_99f23514ee0c313c4719b9ab5616e47048c75001b78f28645430ffbc5b25337f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Independently checked proof (PASS w667 and w668): C003 v1. Let F be a probability on nonempty compact K subset R^d with mean mu and n>=1. Let Z be the n-tuples in K^n whose sum is n*mu. Then F is n-CM iff for every continuous real f on K, integral f dF <= max over Z of average_i f(x_i). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.169730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_99fc324bece9ac5c0cf4065dcf5816bdcb53f70c26792a97673c6368f28626bc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 69 (generalized budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the set $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:incr.p}.
For $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and a generalized ``budget'' function $f \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, let
$\Adm(q_0;p,f)$
denote the set of progressively measurable control processes $(b,\sigma)$, with $\sigma \ge 0$,
satisfying
    \beq
    \bbE\bigg[
    (b_t)^2 + \frac{tp'(t)}{p(t)} (\sigma_t-1)^2
    \bigg]
    \le f(t)\eeq
for all $t \in [q_0,1]$. Then let
	\[
    \cM(q_0;p,f) = \bigg\{
        \mu(q_* = q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0) : (b,\sigma)
        \in \Adm(q_0;p,f)
    \bigg\}\,,
\]
where we recall from \eqref{e:control.problems.endpoint.measures} that $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$ denotes the law of $X(1)$ where $X$ is given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with parameters $(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$. (Note that in order to accommodate controls $(b,\sigma)$ where the budget constraint is only satisfied in the averaged sense of condition~\ref{it:4.1}, we allow $f$ to map into $[0,+\infty)$. On the other hand, all classes of measures that we will represent using Definition~\ref{d:X.adm} will have $q_* = q_0$ and $\zeta = \delta_0$, so we will set these parameters in the definition.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:02:08.102392+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a072c71ac7ba6a6ea460f310c21b4b66e6c90c6ce2c4ca72b40d74d9f5bc52c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] For $i=1,\ldots,n$, let $F_i\in C^{1,2}(\R_+\times\R)$.  For each $T<\infty$, suppose that
$$
    |F_i(t,x)|+|\mathcal G F_i(t,x)|
    \le
    K_{i,T}(1+|x|^{r_{i,T}}),
    \qquad
    0\le t\le T,\quad x\in\R,
$$
for some $K_{i,T}<\infty$ and $r_{i,T}\ge0$, and assume that $x\longmapsto\mathcal G F_i(t,x)$
is non-decreasing for almost every $t\ge0$. Let $\rho\in\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$.  Suppose that for all
$i=1,\ldots,n$ and $\theta\in\{\rho_i,\sigma_i\}$, the family 
   $ \left\{
        F_i(t\wedge\theta,X_{t\wedge\theta})
        :t\ge0
    \right\}$
is uniformly integrable, then
$$
    \E[F_i(\sigma_i,X_{\sigma_i})]
    \ge
    \E[F_i(\rho_i,X_{\rho_i})],
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$
If the uniform-integrability condition holds for every
$\rho\in\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$, then $\sigma$ maximizes
$$
    \rho
    \longmapsto
    \E\!\left[
        \sum_{i=1}^n F_i(\rho_i,X_{\rho_i})
    \right]
$$
over $\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:19.983624+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a08686ba50e409f354635c6f6cd16b155730f2ddd597b843dbd528461b76e34","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Introthm 2 (Markov chains with a strictly positive transition density) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\XX$ be a set, $\XXA$ a $\sigma$-algebra on $\XX$ and $\lambda$ a
$\sigma$-finite measure on $(\XX,\XXA)$. Let $p : \XX \to (0,\infty)$ be measurable
with $\int_{\XX} p \dd\lambda = 1$ and let $\pi(A) := \int_{A} p \dd\lambda$ be the
target. Let
\[
  \tau : \XX\times\XX \to [0,\infty), \qquad (x,y) \longmapsto \tau(y \mid x),
\]
be $\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable with $\int_{\XX}\tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) = 1$
for every $x \in \XX$, and let $T$ be the Markov kernel
$T(A \mid x) := \int_{A}\tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y)$. Assume
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item \emph{(invariance)} $\displaystyle\int_{\XX}\tau(y \mid x)\,p(x)\,\lambda(\dd x) = p(y)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $y \in \XX$;
  \item \emph{(positivity)} $\tau(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y) \in \XX\times\XX$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and for every initial
distribution $\mu$ on $(\XX,\XXA)$,
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\ \sup_{A \in \XXA}\bigl| (T^{n}\circ\mu)(A) - \pi(A) \bigr| = 0 .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.961606+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a0ed5bf760729c612bf8d7e8875ae75b38e6a3024f1ae5a7928790100fb8a1f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] A Cartan geometry $(q:\mathcal{P}\to M,\omega)$ of type $(\operatorname{Euc}(n),O(n))$ canonically determines a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$ by

$$

\[
\mathcal{P}\longrightarrow \mathcal{F}_{g}(M),
\qquad
u\mapsto\big(\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{1}),\ldots,\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{n})\big),
\]
is an isomorphism of $O(n)$-principal fiber bundles over $M$.

\[
(e_1,\ldots,e_n)\cdot A
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i A_{i1},

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.495231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a373311faced9b1e270a6dbf43f9089e656bc02abaa3d735fb9068f7c3b3f5b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Loewner coordinate change in angular coordinate of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In angular (trigonometric) coordinates, suppose $\gamma(0) = \theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and let the marked points be $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n \in \mathbb{C}$. Let $\gamma(t)$ be the curve generated by the deterministic Loewner chain:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta_t}{2} \right), \qquad \dot{\theta}_t = b\left( \theta_t ; h_t(\theta_1), \ldots, h_t(\theta_n) \right),
\end{equation}
with initial condition $h_0(z) = z$ and $\theta_0 = \theta$, where $b : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth vector field.

Let $\tau : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{H}$ be a conformal map defined on a neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ of $\theta$ such that $\gamma[0,T] \subset \mathcal{N}$ and $\tau(\partial \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbb{R}) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Define the image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) := \tau(\gamma(t))$ for $t \in [0, T]$, and let $\widetilde{h}_t$ denote the conformal map associated with $\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]$.

Define the conformal coordinate change
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}.
\]

Then the image conformal map $\widetilde{h}_t(z)$ satisfies the evolution equation:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t \widetilde{h}_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{\widetilde{h}_t(z) - \widetilde{\theta}_t}{2} \right) \cdot \left[ \Psi_t'(\theta_t) \right]^2, \qquad \widetilde{h}_0(z) = z,
\end{equation}
where the new driving function is
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}(\theta_t) = \Psi_t(\theta_t), \quad \widetilde{\theta}_0 = \tau(\theta).
\]

Moreover, the curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t)$ is parameterized so that its unit disk capacity satisfies
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{hcap}(\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]) = 2 \sigma(t), \qquad \text{where} \quad \sigma(t) := \int_0^t \left| \Psi_s'(\theta_s) \right|^2 \, ds.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["u >= 0 on R^n x [0,T)","u continuous on R^n x [0,T), C^2_1 on R^n x (0,T)","u solves the heat equation on R^n x (0,T)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105607+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_9a5bad18bd9d3e1275fd6476bf5a6345e55dbed91dc58935fdaa7c480ad81ddc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T\\in(0,\\infty]$ and let $u\\ge0$ be continuous on $\\mathbb R^n\\times[0,T)$, of class $C^2_1$ on $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$, and satisfy $u_t-\\Delta u=0$ in $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$. Then, with $\\Phi(x,t)=(4\\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$, $u(x,t)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\Phi(x-y,t)u(y,0)\\,dy$ for all $x\\in\\mathbb R^n$ and $0<t<T$; in particular $\\int e^{-|y|^2/(4t)}u(y,0)dy<\\infty$ for every $t<T$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:41:54.355200+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9aaede87faba3c6bcefc72cacece90390f3c908874428eba6dafaea1245c3656","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem UFCLT_smoothed_Lip of arXiv:2412.01635, 'On the Weak Convergence of the Function-Indexed Sequential Empirical Process and its Smoot'] (Asymptotic equicontinuity under Lipschitz condition)\\

Let $ \psi $ be a  nondecreasing Young function with $ \limsup_{x,y \to \infty} \psi(x) \psi(y) / \psi(c x y) < \infty $ for some constant $c$ and $ \| \cdot \|_{L_1} \le \| \cdot \|_{L_\psi} $. Assume that $\mathbb Z_n^s(A,f) $, $ (A,f) \in \mathcal A \times \mathcal F $, is separable for all $n$, and suppose that the following assumptions hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] There is some constant $ C_1 $ such that for all $ A, B \in \mathcal A $ and $n \in \mathbb N,$
\[
\sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \| \mathbb{Z}_n^s(A,f) - \mathbb{Z}_n^s(B,f) \|_{L_\psi} \le C_1 \sqrt{\lambda(A \triangle B )}.
\]
\item[(ii)] There is some constant $C_2 $ such that for all $f, g \in \mathcal F $ and $n \in \mathbb N,$
\[
\sup_{A \in \mathcal A} \| \mathbb{Z}_n^s(A,f) - \mathbb{Z}_n^s(A,g) \|_{L_\psi} \le C_2 \rho(f,g).
\]
\item[(iii)] The covering numbers of $ \mathcal A \times \mathcal{F} $ satisfy 
\[
\int_0^{\Delta_s} \psi^{-1}( N(\mathcal A \times \mathcal{F}, \tau_s, \varepsilon/2 )) \, d \varepsilon < \infty.  
\]
\end{itemize}
Then for any $ \varepsilon > 0 $ there exists $ \eta = \eta( \varepsilon ) > 0 $ such that
\[
\E{ \sup_{\tau_s((A,f),(B,g)) < \eta} | {\mathbb{Z}}_n^s(A,f) - {\mathbb{Z}}_n^s( B,g) |} < \varepsilon
\]
which implies (equation DEF:AEC of the paper), such that fidi-convergence of $\mathbb Z_n^s$ implies its weak convergence in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal A \times \mathcal F)$.

In particular, if $ \mathcal A \times \mathcal{F} $ is a polynomial class, i.e., $ N(\mathcal A \times \mathcal{F}, \tau_s, \varepsilon ) = O( \varepsilon^{-a} ) $, for some $a>0$, and $ \psi(x) = x^p$ with $ p > \max(a,1) $, then (iii) holds and there exists a continuous version $ \tilde{\mathbb Z}_n^s $ of $ \mathbb{Z}_n^s $ with almost all sample paths lying in the space $ \mathcal C_u(\mathcal A \times \mathcal F; \mathbb R ) $ of bounded and uniformly continuous functions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.035658+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b16ad6ed73035a95f72e6903e4bfc91c2a7410527d305a6c2b124653cd7979c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 13 (Exact linearity of the separatrix; cf.\
Paper~III, Prop.~5.1) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Under \textup{(S1)--(S4)}, a distribution lies in the separatrix
if and only if it annihilates every normal direction:
\[
\pi\in\Sigma\iff\langle\pi,\mathbf n_\nu\rangle=0\ \ \forall\nu
\iff\langle\pi|_O,\mathbf d_O\rangle=0\ \ \text{for every orbit }O,
\]
and explicitly, on the whole simplex,
\[
\Sigma
=\Bigl\{\pi\in\Delta_{m-1}:\
\sqrt{\kappa(z)}\,\pi_z=\sqrt{\kappa(\sigma(z))}\,\pi_{\sigma(z)}\
\text{for every orbit}\Bigr\},
\]
with the weights of neutral sites unconstrained. Note that the
linear form of the condition already covers the boundary strata: if
one of $\pi_z,\pi_{\sigma(z)}$ vanishes so does the other, so no
orbit can carry mass at a single site --- which is how Paper~III's
ratio condition, stated only on orbits of positive mass, is
subsumed here. Equivalently:
$\Sigma$ is the intersection of the simplex with a linear subspace
of $\mathbb R^m$ of codimension $r=n_{\mathrm{pair}}$; the
interior part $\Sigma^\circ$, which the spherical
picture below uses, is the corresponding relatively open subset. We
write
\[
\Sigma^\circ:=\Sigma\cap\Delta^\circ_{m-1}
\]
throughout, and keep the distinction firmly: the \emph{algebraic}
statements of this section hold on $\Sigma\subseteq\Delta_{m-1}$,
closed simplex included, while every \emph{Riemannian} statement ---
distances, geodesics, isometries, Hessians --- is made on
$\Sigma^\circ\subseteq\Delta^\circ_{m-1}$, where the Fisher--Rao
metric is defined.
This recovers, through the orbit collapse, the affine characterisation
of the separatrix obtained in Paper~III, and prepares it for the
spherical representation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b1afa08cb1432c416d963cee443bdd6994471bd1a5eb173411bb5775883801e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ribbon-record of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] A rooted orthogonal-Weingarten ribbon record $\Gamma$ of degree $m$
consists of the dart set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$; its coefficient boxes and
color labels; perfect matchings $p,q,r$ giving the row,
coefficient-column, and rooted trace wiring; all local wedge and
direct/cross signs; the distinguished root boundary; and the following
orthogonal-Weingarten path data.

Partition the darts into the independent Haar-color classes
$\mathscr H_\Gamma$ (there is one class when all entries come from one
Haar matrix).  If $a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma$ contains $m_a$ coefficient
occurrences, put $k_a=2m_a$, so it has $2k_a=4m_a$ darts, and denote by
$p_a,q_a$ the restrictions of $p,q$.  The rooted dart order chooses a
deterministic relabelling $\sigma_a$ with
$\sigma_a\cdot e_{k_a}=p_a$, where
\[
 e_k=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\ldots,\{2k-1,2k\}\},
\]
and put
$\mathfrak m_a=\sigma_a^{-1}\cdot q_a\in\mathcal P_2(2k_a)$.
The orthogonal Weingarten graph has vertex set
$\bigsqcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal P_2(2j)$.  At level $j$ it has a solid arrow
\[
 \mathfrak n\longrightarrow(i,2j-1)\cdot\mathfrak n,
 \qquad 1\le i<2j-1,
\]
and it has a dashed arrow
$\mathfrak n\dashrightarrow\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ when
$\{2j-1,2j\}\in\mathfrak n$, where $\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ is
obtained by deleting that pair.  The record chooses, for every $a$, one
\emph{individual} path $\gamma_a$ from $\mathfrak m_a$ to the empty
pairing.  It uses exactly $k_a$ dashed arrows; write $s_a$ for its number
of solid arrows.  If $\mu_a$ is the coset type of $\mathfrak m_a$, define
\[
 d_a:=|\mathfrak m_a|=k_a-\ell(\mu_a)
      =k_a-\#(p_a\vee q_a),
 \qquad
 g_a:=s_a-d_a\ge0,
 \qquad
 g_{\rm Wg}:=\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}g_a.
\]
Thus $g_{\rm Wg}$ is the total number of solid arrows beyond shortest
orthogonal-Weingarten paths; unlike the unitary excess, it need not be
even.

Let $w_\Gamma$ be the scalar coefficient of this chosen product path,
including the bounded local wedge and direct/cross coefficients.  Write
$\operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}$ for the typed raw
contraction determined by the record and its circuit state, and put
\[
 F_\Gamma=\#(p\vee r),\qquad
 \ell_\Gamma=\#(p\vee q)
      =\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}\#(p_a\vee q_a),\qquad
 \omega_\Gamma=n^{F_\Gamma}w_\Gamma,\qquad
 \mathcal A_\Gamma=w_\Gamma
       \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}.
\]
Thus $w_\Gamma$ is a scalar coefficient, not the value or norm of an
open contraction; $\omega_\Gamma$ merely expresses the same coefficient
in once-normalized original-circuit units.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A square over a field (R or C in the numerical statements)","unit lower triangular L fixes the normalisation; L D U variants move the diagonal into D"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479562+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_9b87fdf50aa592bb2dcee21b2e13402fec32970a0b5820f287442e30505c9e85","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an n x n matrix over a field. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. Partial pivoting is backward stable in practice (the growth factor is bounded by 2^{n-1} in the worst case, attained by Wilkinson's example, but is small on almost all matrices), whereas elimination without pivoting can be unstable on matrices with small pivots even when A is well conditioned. Symmetric positive definite matrices need no pivoting (Cholesky); diagonally dominant matrices need none either.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measurable","invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437948+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, foundations","id":"claim_9ba1defc34ee3afb4584a993f111afbfc82e7640f9230052afb1810248d72dbf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \\to X$ is measure-preserving if $\\mu(T^{-1} A) = \\mu(A)$ for every $A \\in \\mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\\mu(TA) = \\mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\\mu$ if $\\mu(T^{-1}A \\,\\triangle\\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \\circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \\subset A$ mod $\\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \\supset A$ mod $\\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{I} = \\{A : T^{-1}A = A\\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:49.285452+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9c471a05d7eb45b29fb21187337f223cade51337b11a9ddc12d3434167122209","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 10 (Broadcasting process) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the tree growth model above. Each vertex carries one of two colours, which we identify with the values \(-1\) and \(1\). The root vertex \(1\) is assigned a random bit \(B_1\in\{-1,1\}\), chosen uniformly at random. For each \(n\geq 1\), once the new vertex \(n+1\) has chosen its parent \(p_{n+1}\), it inherits the bit of its parent with probability \(1-q\) and flips it with probability \(q\), independently of the tree growth and all previous broadcasting steps. Equivalently,
	\[
	B_{n+1}=B_{p_{n+1}}Z_{n+1},
	\]
	where \((Z_n)_{n\geq 2}\) are independent \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables satisfying
	\[
	\mathbb P(Z_n=-1)=q,
	\qquad
	\mathbb P(Z_n=1)=1-q.
	\]
	The parameter \(q\in[0,1]\) is called the bit-flip probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure","statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach","the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553548+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_9c99a22f279aba04c24062eeaa629c6222d83b8f4cd18106908536d318f9894e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. (3) For 0 < p < 1 and mu nonatomic (e.g. Lebesgue on [0,1]) the dual is trivial: (L^p[0,1])* = {0}, so no duality/Hahn-Banach argument survives below p = 1. Only the range 1 < p < infinity is safe for an arbitrary measure space: there L^p is reflexive and (L^p)* = L^{p'} for every measure, whereas L^1 and L^infinity are reflexive only in degenerate finite-dimensional cases.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ca68baa0660aa59223fcaebbdec10b169d0c2892b9d78d08095d1f75675fc1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The matching bound away from 1 needs the same input for the dual model (at criticality on a self-dual lattice it follows by duality); a lower bound for the primal model alone does not give it, since in the supercritical phase both crossing probabilities tend to 1. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.330086+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cbcd78b7765e37629a4e4c04458e9267e4d0fa65711078f1ccbdb64fb956a06","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Hydrodynamic limit) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(\{\mu^n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be a sequence of probability measures on \(\Omega_n\) associated with \(\bm\rho_0\). 
	Then, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), every \(\delta>0\), every \(k\in\{1,2\}\), and every \(f_k\in C^\infty([0,1];\mathbb R) \),
	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty}
	\mathbb P_{\mu^n}^n
	\left(
	\left|
	X_k^{n,t}(f_k)
	-
	\int_0^1 f_k(u)\rho_k(t,u)\,du
	\right|>\delta
	\right)
	=0,
	\]
	where $ \bm\rho(t,u)
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		\rho_1(t,u)\\
		\rho_2(t,u)
	\end{pmatrix} $
    is the unique weak solution of the reaction-diffusion system with Robin boundary conditions
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{cases}
			\partial_t\bm\rho(t,u)
			=
			\Delta\bm\rho(t,u)+M\bm\rho(t,u),
			& t>0,\ u\in(0,1),\\[0.2cm]
			\partial_u\bm\rho(t,0)
			=
			K_L\bm\rho(t,0)-\bm\alpha,
			& t>0,\\[0.2cm]
			\partial_u\bm\rho(t,1)
			=
			\bm\beta-K_R\bm\rho(t,1),
			& t>0,\\[0.2cm]
			\bm\rho(0,u)=\bm\rho_0(u),
			& u\in[0,1].
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Here $ \bm \alpha = \left( \alpha_1,\alpha_2 \right)^{\top} $, $ \bm \beta = \left( \beta_1,\beta_2 \right)^{\top} $, and
	\[
	M=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		-\gamma_1 & \gamma_2\\
		\gamma_1 & -\gamma_2
	\end{pmatrix},
	\qquad
	K_L=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1-\alpha_2 & \alpha_1\\
		\alpha_2 & 1-\alpha_1
	\end{pmatrix},
	\qquad
	K_R=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1-\beta_2 & \beta_1\\
		\beta_2 & 1-\beta_1
	\end{pmatrix}.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is densely defined (automatic in reflexive X under the range condition)","A is dissipative","a range condition: Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) for some λ_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771500+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, evolution equations","id":"claim_9cc7074f8de110e84e704f7481a4bebc14d6b3c2eb606e5b71dc671682f7125e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space and A: D(A) ⊂ X → X linear and densely defined. (1) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0, and A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (2) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) is merely dense for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closable, its closure Ā is dissipative with Ran(λ − Ā) = X for all λ > 0, and Ā generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (3) Conversely, if A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup, then A is densely defined, closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for all λ > 0, and A is dissipative in the strong sense that Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ D(A) and every x* ∈ J(x). (4) If X is reflexive, a dissipative A with Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0 is automatically densely defined. (5) Hilbert space corollary: if A is densely defined and closed and both A and A* are dissipative, then A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup; and a densely defined symmetric operator S with S ≤ 0 that is self-adjoint generates the contraction semigroup e^{tS}. Quasi-contractive version: if A − ω is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > ω, then A generates a C_0-semigroup with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a Banach space","K compact and linear","the statement is about I - K; for lambda I - K with lambda not zero divide by lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476530+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_9cd24333d102074cf31fdaac1e3b28d41b51bfe803503d2d5cfac25fbe524fc7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space, K : X -> X a compact linear operator, and T = I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional and the range of T is closed; (ii) T is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case T has a bounded inverse; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T* where T* = I - K* is the adjoint on the dual X*, and the equation T x = y is solvable exactly when y annihilates ker T* (the closed-range theorem). So either T x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation T x = 0 has a nontrivial finite-dimensional solution space and T x = y is solvable exactly for y orthogonal (in the duality sense) to the finitely many solutions of the adjoint homogeneous equation. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199499+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cdd95b748fea298de1a2af88b5ce1ac2dba3e772343b6d54cc9e46d419d944e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 132 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $u,v$ be real numbers such that $v\geq u^2 - \bar{\lambda}$, and let $P_1,P_2>0$.
Set
\beq
    \sigma 
    \equiv
    \bigg(
    \frac{P_1v + 2
    (P_1P_2)^{1/2}
    u+P_2}{P_1+P_2}
    \bigg)^{1/2}
\eeq
Then we have the bound
\beq
  u^2 + \Big((v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda})^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
  \ge \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,.
\eeq
Given any $\sigma\ge0$, if we let $(u,v)$ be defined by the equations
	\[
	u^2 = \frac{P_2}{P_1}(\sigma-1)^2 
	= v-\sigma^2 + 2\bar{\lambda}\,,
	\]
then $(u,v)$ achieves equality in both \eqref{e:sigma.of.u.v} and \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound}. 

\begin{proof}
Denote $\tilde{v}\equiv v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda} \ge0$. The above definition of $\sigma$ can then be rewritten as
	\beq    
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	= P_1 \tilde{v}  +
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Consider optimizing the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} subject to the constraint 
\eqref{eq:LM-constraint}: the Lagrangian is
	\[
	\mathscr{L}
	= u^2 + \Big(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
	+ \lambda
	\bigg\{
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	- P_1 \tilde{v}  -
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The Lagrangian stationarity conditions are
	\begin{align*}
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial u}
	= 2u - 2\lambda (P_1)^{1/2}
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)\,\\
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial\tilde{v}}
	= 1-\frac{1}{\tilde{v}^{1/2}}
	- \lambda P_1\,.
	\end{align*}
Simplifying the above equations gives
	\[
	u
	= \bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	 \frac{\lambda P_1}{1-\lambda P_1}
	=
	\bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)
	\,.
	\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:LM-constraint} gives $\sigma^2=\tilde{v}$. Substituting this back into the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} gives
	\[
	u^2 + (\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\]
so \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} holds with equality in the case of an interior stationary point. It remains to check the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. In this case we have
	\[
	\sigma
	=\bigg|\bigg( \frac{P_1}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2} u
	+\bigg( \frac{P_2}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg|
	\equiv
	\Big| (A_1)^{1/2} u + (A_2)^{1/2}
	\Big|\,,
	\]
with $A_1+A_2=1$. The desired bound \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} then simplifies to
	\begin{align*}
	u^2 + 1
	&= \bigg(\frac{-(A_2)^{1/2}\pm\sigma}{(A_1)^{1/2}}\bigg)^2+1
	= \frac{A_2 + \sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
		+1
	= \frac{1+\sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
	\\
	&\ge
	\frac{1 + \sigma^2-2\sigma}{A_1}
	= \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\end{align*}
which gives the bound for the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.563701+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cfd534613ed55caea4ac885b202cccb4eadb1a59a50f8583f7ea1019ebdde36","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Granularity) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] A scale may be shared \\emph{per-tensor} (one $s$), \\emph{per-row} (one $s$ per output row of $W$, the \\emph{per-output-channel} weight scale, which the weight-only literature usually just calls \\emph{per-channel}, or one $s$ per token row of $X$, the \\emph{per-token} activation scale that is the deployed default), \\emph{per-column} (one $s$ per input channel, the axis a \\emph{per-channel activation} scale shares), or \\emph{per-group/block} (contiguous groups of $G$ entries, e.g.\\ $G\\in\\{32,128\\}$). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.671591+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cfda76ffe77e4015412dad65a5f0da489e5612fa48cd38580b5203349577f8e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 32 (Diameter and circle convergence on a persistent large-diameter tail) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be \(\TT^3\), a compact \(\Nil\) torus bundle with nontrivial
unipotent monodromy, or a compact \(\Sol\) torus bundle with hyperbolic

Fix a particular application of
Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-fixed-threshold}, with cutoff \(c_0\) and tail

        \diam(M,g(t))\geq c_0\sqrt t

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.199426+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cfe0ebeca0342ec2e95769900db90cd9b07740f4ca08a3dc4c7102a0fcfbe80","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 (Regular polygonal \(N\)-gaskets) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(N\ge3\) with \(4\nmid N\).  Identify \(\R^2\) with \(\mathbb C\), and put
\[
  q_j=\exp(2\pi\mathrm i j/N),
  \qquad
  V_0^{(N)}=\{q_j:j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\}.
\]
Let \(F_0^{(N)}\) be the cycle on \(V_0^{(N)}\).  Write
\[
  k_N=\lfloor N/4\rfloor,
  \qquad
  \ell_N=N-4k_N,
  \qquad
  s_N=k_N+1,
\]
and define
\[
  \rho_N
  =
  \frac{\sin(\pi/N)}
       {\sin(\pi/N)+\sin((2s_N-1)\pi/N)},
  \qquad
  \Psi_j^{(N)}(x)=q_j+\rho_N(x-q_j).
\]
The attractor of the \(N\) homotheties
\(\{\Psi_j^{(N)}:j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\}\) is the
\emph{regular polygonal \(N\)-gasket}.  Its finite graphs and its one-sided graph
are denoted by \(F_m^{(N)}\) and \(F_\infty^{(N)}\).  In the construction
\eqref{eq:finite-graphs}, the
indices are relabeled by \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\), the root is
\(O=q_0\), and \(\Psi_0^{(N)}\) is the map fixing \(O\).  The number
\(\rho_N\) is the \emph{first-contact
ratio}~\cite[Section~7]{TysonWu2006}.
When \(4\mid N\), two consecutive first-level fractal cells in the
first-contact construction share a non-degenerate line segment.  Since
\(V_0^{(N)}\) is finite, this intersection cannot equal the intersection
of their boundary vertex sets.  Thus \textup{(NF4)} fails, so this
construction is not a nested fractal and is excluded from the definition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.031700+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d1c1095e08d3c20c6ca94e1e94576e0368bf2489f037cbbcab0213f291e98b9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Conjecture 6 ({Global orientation principle, Paper~III}) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Under \textup{(S1)--(S4)},
\[
\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\partial_\gamma C(\pi,\gamma)\bigr)
=\operatorname{sgn}\,L_\gamma(\pi)
\qquad\text{for all }\pi\in\Delta_{m-1}^\circ,\
\gamma\in(0,1).
\]
By \eqref{eq:C-minus-Cstar}, $\operatorname{sgn}L_\gamma(\pi)
=\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(C(\pi,\gamma)-C^\ast\bigr)$ identically,
so the conjectured identity reads
$\operatorname{sgn}\partial_\gamma C
=\operatorname{sgn}(C-C^\ast)$ whence, wherever $C(\pi,\gamma)\neq C^\ast$,
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma}\bigl|C(\pi,\gamma)-C^\ast\bigr|
=\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(C(\pi,\gamma)-C^\ast\bigr)\,
\partial_\gamma C(\pi,\gamma)>0 .
\]
Thus $|C(\pi,\cdot)-C^\ast|$ is non-decreasing on $(0,1)$ and
strictly increasing on any interval on which it does not vanish.
\textup{(}The qualification matters: $\pi\notin\Sigma$ only says
that $C(\pi,\cdot)$ is non-constant, and $L_\gamma(\pi)$ may still
vanish at isolated rates.\textup{)} The response would then be
monotone in $\gamma$ for every interior $\pi$. The geometric reading as a two-sided
boundary, however, requires care, because three distinct objects
are in play. The instantaneous zero set at a given $\gamma$ is the
hyperplane
$\ker\bigl(\psi(\gamma)|_{T_{\pi^\ast}\Delta_{m-1}}\bigr)$, of
codimension one, which moves with $\gamma$. Its intersection over
all $\gamma$ is the local separatrix $\Sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=V^\perp$,
of codimension $r$ in the tangent space. And $\Sigma$ itself is the
global object, with
$\dim(\Sigma^\circ)=n_{\mathrm{pair}}+n_0-1$, so
that it too has codimension $r$. The three coincide only when
$r=1$; and only then does a single hyperplane, fixed as $\gamma$
varies, separate the simplex into two sides. For $r\ge2$ each
instantaneous hyperplane strictly contains $\Sigma$, no one of them
is $\Sigma$, and a set of codimension $r\ge2$ does not separate at
all. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d,p>=1,n>=0,s>0,B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0","zero-mean GP k(x,xprime)=z(x)^T z(xprime), ||z||<=R, |z_j(x)-z_j(xprime)|<=K||x-xprime||_1","independent N(0,s) observation noise and a new noisy predictive observation","raw coordinate inputs plus fixed context/query flags, zero padding, arbitrary real weights","residual normalized ReLU attention with tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs; no layer normalization or softmax"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:45:13.521203+00:00","domain":"Gaussian-process prediction; transformer approximation","id":"claim_9d334e1823168adc9513ce779a2ecd295afb9bd7b665e440dcd4079a0b666dba","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C004 v1; urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 ac56184efa730025dd3c81b11d4fced2712fb1d3290a9bc2a089ca9a9af705a5. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

For raw inputs in [0,1]^d, every bounded rank-at-most-p GP with coordinatewise K-Lipschitz feature map has an explicit residual ReLU-attention transformer attaining uniform noisy predictive forward KL <= eps over contexts of length <=n and labels bounded by B. Unlike C002, feature computation is counted. The constants, grid size, width, heads, hidden width, and depth are explicit in C004 Sections 1-5. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C004 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 with raw inputs and an explicit Lipschitz feature encoder

Claim T336-w727-C004 v1. Rung: proof (unaudited), subject to recorded checks and dependent on unaudited C002 v1. No Lean certification or independent audit is claimed. This gives a quantitative raw-input subclass of Target 1, rather than assuming exact feature computation outside the size count.

The hardest steps are the explicit residual-MLP encoder and the perturbation budget linking its feature errors to the original GP predictive distribution. The proof does not use a triangle inequality for KL.

## 1. Assumptions and explicit size

Fix integers d,p>=1,n>=0, real s>0, B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0. The raw domain is X=[0,1]^d. The fixed zero-mean GP prior has kernel k(x,x')=z(x)^T z(x'), where z:X->R^p satisfies ||z(x)||_2<=R and, for each coordinate j,

    |z_j(x)-z_j(x')|<=K ||x-x'||_1.

The observation noise is independent N(0,s). Context labels satisfy |y_i|<=B, and contexts have length t<=n. The target is the predictive law of a new noisy observation. The input encoding supplies only raw coordinates, labels, two binary role flags (context and query), and fixed constants. Zero padding fixes N=n+1 tokens. A padding token has raw coordinates zero and both flags zero; the query has only its query flag set; actual context tokens have only their context flag set. No label is supplied for the query.

Define the following fixed constants:

    S=R+1,
    C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s + S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s > 0,
    eta=min(1, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)), s sqrt(eps)/(2 C_v), s/(4 C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16),
    m=max(1,ceil(K d sqrt(p)/eta)), J=(m+1)^d, E=3+ceil(log_2 J).

For the solver set

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a residual normalized ReLU-attention transformer (Bai et al. Definition 1 and Definition 2) with

    token width D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    depth L_total=E+T+2=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    tokenwise MLP hidden width at most H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,

whose Gaussian output satisfies forward KL<=eps uniformly over all these raw-input contexts and queries. A dense parameter upper bound is

    L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

Fixed affine input placement is not counted; all nonlinear feature computation is counted. Every weight is specified below or in C002 v1 and depends only on the fixed prior feature map (through finitely many grid samples) and the displayed bounds, never on observed contexts, query labels, or future data. This is a real-weight size theorem, not a finite-bit complexity theorem or training guarantee.

## 2. Posterior perturbation caused by an approximate feature map

First suppose a map ztilde satisfies sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=eta<=1. Then ||ztilde||<=R+eta<=S. For any fixed admissible context and query, put

    A=sI+sum_i z_i z_i^T, b=sum_i z_i y_i, q=z(x_*),
    Atilde=sI+sum_i ztilde_i ztilde_i^T, btilde=sum_i ztilde_i y_i, qtilde=ztilde(x_*).

Both matrices are symmetric positive definite with inverse operator norm <=1/s. For vectors u,v,

    ||uu^T-vv^T||_op
      =||(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T||_op
      <=||u-v|| (||u||+||v||).

Thus

    ||A-Atilde||<=n(2R+eta)eta<=C_A eta,
    ||b-btilde||<=nB eta, ||b||<=nRB,
    ||A^{-1}-Atilde^{-1}||
      =||A^{-1}(Atilde-A)Atilde^{-1}||<=C_A eta/s^2.

The true and perturbed noisy predictive parameters are

    mu=q^T A^{-1}b, v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q,
    mutilde=qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}btilde,
    vtilde=s+s qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}qtilde.

Both variances are >=s. Add and subtract qtilde^T A^{-1}b and qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}b. Cauchy-Schwarz and the preceding bounds give

    |mu-mutilde|
      <=eta nRB/s + S C_A eta nRB/s^2 + S nB eta/s
      =C_m eta.

For the variance, first replace both q factors while retaining A^{-1}, and then replace the inverse. This gives

    |v-vtilde|
      <=s[eta(R+S)/s+S^2 C_A eta/s^2]=C_v eta.

The definition of eta ensures

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

No probabilistic context distribution or independence between observed features is needed here.

## 3. A finite-grid cone encoder

Let G={0,1/m,...,1}^d, so |G|=J. For each feature coordinate define

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[z_j(a)+K sum_{r=1}^d |x_r-a_r|].

The Lipschitz assumption shows every term in this minimum is >=z_j(x). Choose a nearest grid point coordinate by coordinate; its L1 distance is <=d/(2m). The same Lipschitz bound then gives

    0<=ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)<=Kd/m.

Consequently ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)Kd/m<=eta. This also holds for K=0, when the error is zero and m=1. In particular |ztilde_j(x)|<=||ztilde(x)||<=S on the whole input cube.

The encoder is exact as an implementation of this finite minimum, including all absolute values. It is not a numerical approximation to the finite minimum.

## 4. Exact tokenwise residual-MLP construction

Use the 7p+4 core registers of C002. Add d registers for raw x, Jd zero-initialized absolute-value registers, pJ zero-initialized cone registers, and two role flags. This is D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ. Initially the feature registers z_c,z_q are zero. The core constant is one=1; the variance-output register starts at s, and the query/padding label register is zero. Encoder MLP layers preserve raw x, the flags, and all core constants.

Each MLP has the residual form h^+=h+W2 ReLU(W1 h), with a constant register implementing affine biases. All unspecified matrix entries are zero. The attention block in each encoder layer is the identity (all value matrices zero).

Layer 1 uses 2Jd hidden units for ReLU(x_r-a_r) and ReLU(a_r-x_r), for all a in G,r. Their sums are written into the initially zero absolute-value registers, yielding |x_r-a_r| exactly.

Layer 2 uses Jd identity-ReLU units on the nonnegative absolute registers and one unit on the constant one. Its output matrix writes

    F_{j,a}=z_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|

into each initially zero cone register. Negative fixed grid values cause no difficulty: they occur in the output matrix applied to the constant unit.

Next compute the minimum independently for each coordinate j by a balanced binary tournament on the J cone registers. A pair of current registers u,v is replaced in the first slot by

    u-ReLU(u-v)=min(u,v),

leaving the other slot unused thereafter. This is one residual MLP unit: W1 reads u-v and W2 subtracts its ReLU from the u register. Distinct pairs at the same level use disjoint output slots. An unpaired register passes unchanged. After ceil(log_2 J) levels one designated cone slot contains ztilde_j(x). Each level uses at most p floor(J/2) units, bounded by pJ. This works for signed cone values and for every J, not only powers of two.

One final gating layer writes the feature registers. For any |f|<=S and binary flag r define

    g(f,r)=ReLU(f+S(r-1))-ReLU(-f+S(r-1)).

If r=1, this equals f; if r=0, both arguments are <=0 and it equals zero. Apply g to every computed feature with the context flag to populate z_c, and with the query flag to populate z_q. The registers start at zero, so the residual connection adds precisely the desired values. This uses 4p units. Query, padding, and context feature routing now matches C002 exactly. Both flags and the raw x registers are preserved throughout.

There are E=3+ceil(log_2 J) MLP encoder layers. The stated H bounds every hidden width. Biases are realized through the constant register, rather than being omitted from the construction. All grid feature values are fixed weights of the known prior; no context-dependent parameter is selected.

## 5. Solver composition and KL budget

Apply C002 v1 to ztilde with feature bound S and accuracy eps0. Its core 7p+4 registers embed in the larger width D; all additional registers are preserved by zero extension of its matrices. The solver uses its one-head broadcast layer, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout layer. All solver MLPs are identities. The resulting parameters muhat,vhat obey

    vhat>=s,
    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps0)<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=s sqrt(eps0)<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Combine these with Section 2 using ordinary triangle inequalities for scalar errors, not for KL:

    |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)).

Since v,vhat>=s, put h=(v-vhat)/vhat in [-1/2,1/2]. As proved directly in C002 Section 5,

    KL(N(mu,v)||N(muhat,vhat))
      <=(mu-muhat)^2/(2s)+(v-vhat)^2/(2s^2)<=eps.

The depth is E+T+2. There are at most five heads, each with three D-by-D matrices. Counting two D-by-H/H-by-D MLP matrices at every layer, even when they are zero, and a two-coordinate linear readout, gives the stated dense parameter bound.

## 6. What this does and does not settle

This is a quantitative raw-input theorem for every bounded finite-rank GP feature map satisfying the displayed Lipschitz assumption, in every fixed input dimension. It counts the encoder rather than treating it as a free feature oracle. The bound is deliberately explicit and can be very large because J=(m+1)^d.

C003 shows that dropping all raw-feature regularity makes the literal bounded-kernel statement false for continuous Gaussian-output transformers. C004 therefore supplies a precise constructive assumption, while C002 remains the smaller theorem when features are supplied directly.

The finite-grid envelope and ReLU min/max identities are classical elementary constructions, not claims of new approximation theory. The claimed target contribution is their fully costed composition with the accelerated posterior solver and a uniform original-posterior forward-KL budget. C004 remains a proof candidate dependent on C002 until independent review passes both exact versions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9940d5d71c04317ee6bf6c7af44330e25833e47c30d0a08c189418c3460668","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 161 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1 \leq \ell\leq \ubl$ we have:
  \begin{align}
  
  \bbE[\hat U^{\ell}-\hat U^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat V^{\ell}-\hat V^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat M,\tilde M}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0
  \,.
  \end{align}

\begin{proof}
  We will show inductively that
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} with $\ell+1$ in place of $\ell$.
We therefore proceed with the inductive argument: 

\begin{itemize}
\item \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}: 
for this we use
the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}. Note that $w^{\ell-1}(\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1})$ is measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-field $\cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)$, which in turn is contained in the $\sigma$-field 
$\cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)$. Therefore
  \[
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
    ~|~
    \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  = \frac{w^{\ell-1}(\hat{R}^\eta\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1}) }
    {\hat{\gamma}(\ell,\delta,\eta)}
  \E[\hat{U}^\ell-\hat{U}^{\ell-1}
  ~|~ \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)
  ]=0\,,
  \]
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}. This implies
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}:
it follows from the state evolution definition that the random variables $\hat{V}^{\ell,k}$ and $\tilde{V}^{\ell,k}$ are jointly gaussian. Using the covariance formula \eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}, for $0\le k\le s \le \ell-1$ we have
  \begin{align*}
  \E[(\hat{V}^{\ell,k}-\hat{V}^{\ell-1,k})
  \tilde{V}^{s,k}]
  &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}}{=} \E\bigg[
   \Big(h_{\chaos,\ell,k}(\hat{U}[[\ell]])-
  h_{\chaos,\ell-1,k}
  (\hat{U}[[\ell-1]])
  \Big)
    h_{\chaos,s,k}
    (\tilde{U}[[s]])
    \bigg]\\
  &\stackrel{
  \eqref{e:f.h.l.k.explicit.CHAOTIC}
  }{=} (a_k)^2
  \E[(\hat{Y}^\ell-\hat{Y}^{\ell-1})
    \tilde{Y}^s]
  = 0\,,
  \end{align*}
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}. A similar calculation gives the same identity but with $\hat{V}^{s,k}$ in place of $\tilde{V}^{s,k}$. Since the $V$ are jointly gaussian, this implies \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}: this follows from the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}, by the same reasoning as for \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} above.

\item
\eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}:
this follows by similar reasoning as for
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} above.
\end{itemize}
The above steps give one complete round of the induction, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:01:15.321162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9ae8a1780512450e7be376ea0339c654dfea0a9a749db538cea12dc5781d95","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 15 (A sufficient deletion-chord curvature bound) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] \label[corollary]{cor:cpp-bound}
Fix $\kappa\in[0,\infty)$.
For every $i\in[n]$, $0\leq\alpha_0\leq(n-1)^{-1}$, and
$P=P_n+\alpha_0 h_i\in\mathfrak P_S$ with $h_i\ne0$, define the
sample-dependent realized normalized deletion direction
$\widetilde h_i:=h_i/\|h_i\|_{\TV}\in\mathcal M_0$.  For every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and
$t\in[0,T]$, suppose there is an interval containing zero on which the flows
trained under $P+\alpha\widetilde h_i$ exist, the map
$\alpha\mapsto\theta_t^{P+\alpha\widetilde h_i,\lambda}$ is twice
continuously differentiable, and the first and second $\alpha$-derivatives of
$\theta_t^{P+\alpha\widetilde h_i,\lambda}$ commute with the time derivative
and may be passed through the training and population-risk integrals.  Suppose
there are
$G_h,H_h,J_3,G_0,H_0\in[0,\infty)$, possibly depending on the realized sample
$S$, such that, uniformly over
$i\in[n]$ with $h_i\ne0$, $\alpha_0\in[0,(n-1)^{-1}]$, $\lambda\in\Lambda$, and
$t\in[0,T]$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \left\|\int\nabla\ell^{\rm tr}_{\lambda,z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})
          \,\dd\widetilde h_i(z)\right\|\leq G_h,\quad
 \left\|\int\nabla^2\ell^{\rm tr}_{\lambda,z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})
          \,\dd\widetilde h_i(z)\right\|_{\op}\leq H_h,\\
 \|\nabla_\theta^3F_{P,\lambda}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|_{\op}\leq J_3,
 \quad \nabla^2F_{P,\lambda}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\succeq-\kappa I,\\
 \|P_0\nabla\ell^{\rm ev}_{\lambda,Z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|
 \leq G_0,\quad
 \|P_0\nabla^2\ell^{\rm ev}_{\lambda,Z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|_{\op}
 \leq H_0.
\end{gathered}
\]
The averaged first-order cancellation condition
\eqref{eq:average-first-order-cancellation} holds, and the curvature condition
\eqref{eq:measure-curvature-bound} holds with
\begin{equation}
 C_{PP}=H_0G_h^2\phi_\kappa(T)^2
 +G_0\{2H_hG_h\chi_\kappa(T)+J_3G_h^2\mathcal J_\kappa(T)\}.
\end{equation}
If $h_i=0$, then $P_n+\alpha_0 h_i=P_n$ for every
$0\leq\alpha_0\leq(n-1)^{-1}$.  Consequently, the scalar chord map
$\alpha_0\mapsto\psi_{i,t,\lambda}(\alpha_0)$ in

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:31.956840+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9b0b9fca3fd9626f8242630d713c23a815ac23022fe8fe06de411303fb4066","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2512.01483, 'Scaling Limits of Line Models in Degenerate Environment'] Let $(\xi(t))_{t \geq 0}$ be a one-dimensional, simple random walk with generator given by

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:09:15.296305+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9dfcfd9148212b171023e88a4dc0d3d75d9def20ca67805badfbb98a4db01324","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm.fIForParablic of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let
\begin{align} 
    b^{j k}=b^{k j} \in L_{\mathbb{F}}^2\left(\Omega ; C^1\left([0, T] ; W^{2, \infty}(G)\right)\right), \quad j, k=1,2, \cdots, n,
\end{align}
$\ell \in C^{1,3}((0,T)\times G)$ and $\Psi \in C^{1,2}((0,T)\times G)$.
Let $ u $ be an $H^2(G)$-valued continuous Itô process.
Set  $\theta=e^{\ell}$ and $w=\theta u$. Then, for any $t \in[0, T]$ and a.e. $(x, \omega) \in G \times \Omega$,
\begin{align}\notag
    & 2 \theta \Big [\!-\!\sum_{j, k=1}^n \big(b^{j k} w_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w \Big ]\Big[d u\!-\!\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} u_{x_j}\big)_{x_k} d t\Big]
    \!+\! 2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} w_{x_j} d w\big)_{x_k}
    \\\notag
    &
     \quad+2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n\Big[\sum_{j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}=1}^n\big(2 b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}} w_{x_j} w_{x_{k^{\prime}}}-b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_j} w_{x_{j^{\prime}}} w_{x_{k^{\prime}}}\big)
    \\
    &
     \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad  ~ +\Psi b^{j k} w_{x_j} w-b^{j k}\Big(\mathcal{A} \ell_{x_j}+\frac{\Psi_{x_j}}{2}\Big) w^2\Big]_{x_k} d t
    \\\notag
    &
     =2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n c^{j k} w_{x_j} w_{x_k} d t+\mathcal{B} w^2 d t+d\Big(\sum_{j, k=1}^n b^{j k} w_{x_j} w_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w^2\Big)
     -\theta^2 \mathcal{A}(d u)^2,
    \\ \notag
    &
     +2\Big[-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} w_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w\Big]^2 d t
      -\theta^2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n b^{j k}\big(d u_{x_j}+\ell_{x_j} d u\big)\big(d u_{x_k}+\ell_{x_k} d u\big)
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
    
    \left\{\begin{aligned}
        & \mathcal{A} \triangleq-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} \ell_{x_j} \ell_{x_k}-b_{x_k}^{j k} \ell_{x_j}-b^{j k} \ell_{x_j x_k}\big)-\Psi-\ell_t, \\
        & \mathcal{B} \triangleq 2\Big[\mathcal{A} \Psi-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(\mathcal{A} b^{j k} \ell_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}\Big]-\mathcal{A}_t-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} \Psi_{x_k}\big)_{x_j}, \\
        & c^{j k} \triangleq \sum_{j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}=1}^n\Big[2 b^{j k^{\prime}}\big(b^{j^{\prime} k} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}}\big)_{x_{k^{\prime}}}-\big(b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}}\big)_{x_{k^{\prime}}}\Big]-\frac{b_t^{j k}}{2}+\Psi b^{j k}.
        \end{aligned}\right.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_\ell^\circ}
\sum_{\substack{J\in\mathcal D_{\ell+1}^\circ\\J\subset I}}
D_{J,n},
\]
and
\[
D^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,n,L}
=
\sum_{\ell=m_{\xi,d}}^{L-1}
\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_\ell^\circ}
\sum_{\substack{J\in\mathcal D_{\ell+1}^\circ\\J\subset I}}

+
D^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d,n},
\]
and, for every \(L>m_{\xi,d}\),
\[

=
F^{\mathrm{post,cap}}_{\xi,d,n,L}
+

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.730004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e422d4608cc0dee24fad17871092c60bbee41500f0d3abcf32ac100adefa6fc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:blocks of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Fix integers \(d\ge2 , r\), and a positive real number $\beta>0$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198131+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_9e45874fad796149c5ac8f2b58760157b9ee22954ae7f56d86aa7e03bdd65509","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a subset A of a topological space X: the interior int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A (the largest open set inside A); the closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A - which is closed, being an arbitrary intersection of closed sets, contains A, and lies inside every closed superset of A, hence is the smallest closed set containing A; the boundary is cl(A) minus int(A), equivalently cl(A) intersect cl(X\\A). Then A is open iff A = int(A) and closed iff A = cl(A). Point characterization: x is in cl(A) iff every open neighborhood of x meets A (if not, X\\cl(A) is an open neighborhood of x missing A; conversely a neighborhood U of x missing A makes X\\U a closed superset of A avoiding x). The closure operator satisfies the Kuratowski axioms - cl(empty)=empty, A subset of cl(A), cl(cl(A))=cl(A), cl(A union B)=cl(A) union cl(B) - and these four axioms on a set determine a unique topology whose closed sets are exactly the closure-fixed subsets.","status":"unverified"}

The error covariance in the per-sample relative metric is the same average with each case weighted by the inverse squared norm of its target, $$\\Sigma_E^{\\mathrm{rel},(d)} = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\frac{(e_i^{(d)} - \\bar e^{(d)}_{w})(e_i^{(d)} - \\bar e^{(d)}_{w})^T}{\\|y_i\\|^2}, \\qquad \\bar e^{(d)}_w = \\frac{\\sum_i e_i^{(d)}/\\|y_i\\|^2}{\\sum_i 1/\\|y_i\\|^2}.$$ It is the covariance whose minimum-variance portfolio $w = \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1}/(\\mathbf{1}^T\\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ minimises the calibration value of the objective $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|^2/\\|y_i\\|^2$ restricted to that coordinate, i.e. the squared version of the mean per-sample relative $L^2$ error that emulator benchmarks report, rather than the unweighted squared error that ordinary least squares minimises. Its spectrum is typically far more heavy-tailed than the ordinary one, because the cases with the smallest $\\|y_i\\|$ carry weights orders of magnitude larger than the rest.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.826168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e921c133639f91577ad1e61903f1b2c770594171ef59a29710ffce4f1dafedf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $\fh = \fh_1 + \fh_2$ be a graded Heisenberg algebra.  Let $U(\fh) = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)$ be its  universal enveloping algebra with the grading induced by the grading of $\fh$ and let $U(\fh)^* = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)^*$ be its graded dual.
We can identify $U(\fh)^*$ with the space of polynomial functions on the Heisenberg group $\sH$ of $\fh$ by regarding $U(\fh)$ as the space of left-invariant differential operators on $\sH$ (see Remark \ref{r.jet}). Let $\iota:\fh_2\hookrightarrow U_2(\fh)$ be the natural inclusion and let $\rho_2:=\iota^*:U_2(\fh)^*\to\fh_2^*$ be the restriction map.  
 A finite-dimensional graded subspace $$S = \oplus_{k \geq 0} S^k \subset U(\fh)^*, S^k \subset U_k(\fh)^*,$$ is called a {\em contact symbol system} on $\fh$,
if $S^0 = \C, S^1 = \fh_1^*$, $\rho_2(S^2)=\fh_2^*$, and $S$ is preserved under the operation of right-invariant vector fields on $\sH$.  The {\em rank} of a contact symbol system $S$ is ${\rm rk}(S):=\max\{k\mid S^k\ne0\}.$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.236857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e981c1c18c2fda3836a68827750c2394a5d2147a40b20d18736d1d354ae694f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:velocity-conjugacy of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $\rho_H=H_\#\widetilde\rho$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164817+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e9fc1f22fbbd6aed0546c786bb0cc9eb865e002d311d3614d9fe68ef5df37cd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 36 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The following functions are $C_6$-Lipschitz, with $C_6 = 2/\iota$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  $z \mapsto m^{-1}(1/z)$, on $(0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto \beta_\star(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
    A routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} implies
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz} m^{-1}(1/z) = \frac{1/z^2}{m_2(m^{-1}(1/z))}
        \le \frac{1/z^2}{\iota / z^2} = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-m-inv-lipschitz}.
    Since $m$ is strictly decreasing, and $\beta_\star \ge \beta_{
    \min}$, we also have, for $\gamma > 0$,
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} g(\gamma^2) 
        = 2\gamma m(\beta_\star(\gamma^2))
        \le 2\gamma m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma^2))
        = 2\gamma m(s_2(1/\gamma^2))
        \le \frac{2}{\iota^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
where the final inequality is by Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion}.
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$ is $2/\iota^{1/2}$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since $g$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (see the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-g-sq-lipschitz}. For part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}, it suffices to prove that the function
    \[
        \gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)
        = s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
    \]
    is $O(1)$-Lipschitz on $[0,+\infty)$. Similarly as above, a routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} shows that at any $\gamma > 0$, 
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} 
        s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
        = \frac{1/\gamma^3}
            {m_3(s_2(1/\gamma^2))}
        \le \frac{1/\gamma^3}{\iota / \gamma^3}
        = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)$ is $1/\iota$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since the function $\beta_{\min}$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (again we refer to the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n","A measurable and uniformly elliptic; b, c in L^infinity(Omega)","u in H^1_loc(Omega)","f in L^2_loc(Omega), or more generally in H^{-1}"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.146784+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations","id":"claim_9ea2ee1ebfc2341ed6666c0de202fa3fcddc26d6ef74a9f9346e7802ea76d630","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open, L = -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + c u uniformly elliptic with A measurable and b, c in L^infinity(Omega), and f in L^2_loc(Omega). A function u in H^1_loc(Omega) = W^{1,2}_loc(Omega) is a weak solution of Lu = f in Omega if B[u,phi] = integral_Omega f phi dx for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); a weak subsolution (Lu <= f) if B[u,phi] <= integral f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega) with phi >= 0; a weak supersolution (Lu >= f) if B[u,phi] >= integral f phi for every such phi >= 0. By density the test class extends to phi in H^1(Omega) with compact support in Omega (phi >= 0 for the one-sided notions), and, when u in H^1(Omega) and f in L^2(Omega), to all phi in H^1_0(Omega) (nonnegative ones for the one-sided notions). If a^{ij} in C^1 and u in C^2, u is a weak solution iff it is a classical solution (integrate by parts). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.371335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9edab7a4b69da7064491fee98243307eeedc86c96af59570444be65b938df1b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Any Hilbert space $H$ has an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, which is by definition a set of vectors whose span is dense in $H$, and which satisfy
$$<e_i,e_j>=\delta_{ij}$$

$$H\simeq l^2(I)$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.985539+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f1c64c712eae10a20f6b2e05f07c1cff9f14a011e6a4e76aa8bf2e7b57643c0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:two-stream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$,
a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, and a non-negative integer~$\tau$.
A \emph{two-stream process} 
with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$\tau$ 
is a pair $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ of generalised backoff processes with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, 
birth distribution
 $\mathcal{D} =  \mathsf{Po}(\lambda/2)$
and some initial populations $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^A}(\tau)$ and $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^B}(\tau)$. 
We refer to $Z^A$ and $Z^B$ as the \emph{streams} of~$Z$. 
The streams
evolve independently  
except 
that $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)$ are defined as follows for $t> \tau$. 
\begin{itemize}
    \item  
If there are distinct $C$ and $D$ in $\{A,B\}$ such that
$s^{Z^C}(t) = 0$ and $s^{Z^{D}}(t)>0$ then for all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^C}(t)=\emptyset$. In this case, a bin~$J^D$ is chosen with probability proportional to $s^{Z^{D}}_{J^D}(t)/s^{Z^{D}}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_{J^D}^{Z^D}(t)$
contains a single uniformly-chosen ball from 
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_{J^D}$.
Also, 
for all $j\neq J^D$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^D}(t)=\emptyset$. 
\item Otherwise, for   all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)= \mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)=\emptyset$.
\end{itemize}
There are no end-of-step arrivals after step~$\tau$. That is, for all $D\in \{A,B\}$, all $t> \tau$, and all positive integers~$j$, $\mathbf{arr}_j^{Z^D} = \emptyset$.","status":"unverified"}
