{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.404623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f2d587caff488ee4b6cbc40da3bc5a5222c2231869c7d00bbf014685b39182a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of solutions to the approximated penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold.
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exists a solution $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ of \eqref{eq:appro penalized eq}, defined on the original probability space $\Omega$, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:Weak solution approximating penalized}.
Furthermore, let $\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ be the kinetic function of $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$.
Then, $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ satisfies that, almost surely for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
  & \quad-\alpha\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\nabla_{x}u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_{x}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}+\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma_n^{2}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k},\nonumber
\end{align}
where the kinetic measure $m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ is
\begin{align}\notag
m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}&:=\delta_{0}(\xi-u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\Big(\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}+\alpha|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}\Big).
\end{align}
It follows from  (\ref{eq:priori}) that the $\{m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ are finite kinetic measures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.495747+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f3ececc00a879053077142270413ad4b0e1fd5e09a1033a4ccfb05de13e5204","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 38 of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{thm:main}
Let \(w,w'>0\) and \(u,u'\geq 0\), and assume
\[
\frac{u}{w^2}=\frac{u'}{(w')^2}.
\]
Set
\[
a^2=w^2+u^2,\qquad b^2=(w')^2+(u')^2,
\qquad \delta=u+u'.
\]
Suppose 
\(c_{**}\) is the positive solution of
\[
\delta^2
=
\frac{
2c_{**}^4(c_{**}^2-a^2-b^2)
}{
(c_{**}^2-a^2+b^2)(c_{**}^2+a^2-b^2)
}.
\]

Let \(h_n\) be the hive obtained from the two deformed GUE minor processes by
applying the octahedron recurrence, and write
\[
q_n:=\operatorname{Density}(h_n).
\]
Then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(
q_n\,
\middle\|\,
\operatorname{Density}\bigl(\mathcal H_n(a\sqrt n,b\sqrt n,c_{**}\sqrt n)\bigr)
\right)
=
O(n\log n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:57.303096+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f590952359f5d25106964bae057c1e4fa8f95fdb7e4b3fdbe79e26b70ae1fda","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def: DP of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let $n, m\geq 1$ and 
    let $M$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with non-negative entries. 
    Given $S\subset [m], T \subset [n]$, define the edge count as  
    \[
    e_{M}(S,T):=\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in T} M_{ij}.
    \]
    Furthermore, we say that the matrix $M$ has the discrepancy property $DP(\delta,\kappa_1, \kappa_2)$ with parameters 
    $\delta \in (0,1)$, $\kappa_1>0$, $\kappa_2 \geq 0$ 
    if for all nonempty $S \subset [m]$ and $T \subset [n]$  either 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(1)] $\frac{e_{M}(S,T)}{\delta|S||T|} \leq \kappa_1$, or 
        \item[(2)] $e_{M}(S,T) \log \frac{e_{M}(S,T)}{\delta|S||T|} \leq \kappa_2 (|S| \vee |T|) \log \frac{en}{|S| \vee |T|}$.
    \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651277+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f5a771b1ffe3a4acbf98295922ef93fd51f56c64993cc38d5117c6b2577103d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:decay} holds for $W$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$  $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $W$. Define the likelihood ratios by
\beq
	 \caL(\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right]
\eeq
and
\beq
	\ol \caL (\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Define
\[
	F_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p'(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x, \quad F_d:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p_d'(x))^2}{p_d(x)} \dd x, \quad G_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x.
\]
Then, for any $\SNR \in (0, 1/F_p)$,
\[
	\log \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L), \quad \log \ol \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $\log \caL(\SNR)$ and $\log \ol\caL(\SNR)$ converge in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $-\rho_L$ and the variance $2\rho_L$ as $N \to \infty$, where
\[
	\rho_L:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\SNR F_p) + \SNR(F_p- 2F_d) + \frac{\SNR^2}{4} (2F_p^2 - G_p) \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:24:20.607015+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f66bc33a933b1c40540b68971336387825ab00823afa9ede69b81b9ffe94daf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a Hilbert space $H$, consider the linear operators $T:H\to H$, and for each such operator define its norm by the following formula:
$$||T||=\sup_{||x||=1}||Tx||$$
The operators which are bounded, $||T||<\infty$, form then a complex algebra $B(H)$, which is complete with respect to $||.||$. When $H$ comes with a basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, we have
$$B(H)\subset M_I(\mathbb C)$$
with the correspondence $T\to M$ coming via the usual linear algebra formulae, namely:
$$T(x)=Mx\quad,\quad M_{ij}=<Te_j,e_i>$$
In infinite dimensions, the inclusion $B(H)\subset M_I(\mathbb C)$ is not an equality.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349925+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f7133cf76bbe3c22618d5a11bf099dc0e39c448a3983850dae3d03d23b8a44c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 174 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\Ising}$, $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$, and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The bound of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}
also holds with $X^{\Ising}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$: for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,
	{i(q_{d+1})})
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds with 
$X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall from \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising} that
	\[
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	= \sqrt{\delta_d}
	({\boldsymbol e}_i,\by(q_{d+1}))
	\]
where ${\boldsymbol e}_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector in $\R^N$.
The claim then follows essentially by the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}, replacing $\bar{\bg}(q_d)/N^{1/2}$ with
${\boldsymbol e}_i$. (Moreover, since clearly $\|{\boldsymbol e}_i\|=1$, we can skip the step of restricting to the event that
$\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|$ is not atypically large.) It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure","rho in [-1, 1]"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:12:41.903179+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_9f78cfe62e16aba75338f7bcf920192f2e0618d0cde23dec79b5b0c791f58125","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.660595+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f7df1a1fa73f988dc2ff406193c4f0c5ae111bbfa57cfd482a55d0d9f027179","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 29 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every $1 \le i \le m \le 2^N - 1$, let $\mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset}$ denote the number of operations required to compute
\[
\sum_{|\omega| = 1}^{\kappa} \sum_{m=i+1}^{j+1} K^{(\omega)}(i,m) \, \mathbf{X}^{(\omega)}_{m-1, m}.
\]

Then, for $d > 1$, there exists $\alpha^* \in [0,1/2]$ that maximizes the expression on the left, such that
\[
c\left(d^{1 - \alpha^*} \frac{2^{H(\alpha^*)}}{\sqrt{\kappa + \zeta}}\right)^{\kappa + \zeta}
\;\leq\; \mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset} \;\leq\; C(d+1)^{\kappa+\zeta},
\]
where $H(\alpha) = -\alpha \log_2 \alpha - (1-\alpha) \log_2 (1-\alpha)$ is the binary entropy function and some constants $C,c \geq 0$ independent from $\kappa, \zeta$ and $d$.

In the special case $d=1$, we have
\[
\frac{2^{\kappa + \zeta}}{\kappa + \zeta + 1}  \leq \mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset} \leq C\left(2^{\kappa + \zeta}\right).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.335662+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9fafb24fdba01f6b4ab24c9875f68b6b72edc92350586ce3f01464fa1d072cd9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The following three estimates will be used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainwholeline}.

\textup{(i)} Assume $\lambda<\Lp(\R)$. Suppose that there exist $W\in C^1(\R)$, $W\ge1$, $W(x)\to+\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, a compact interval $K$, and $\delta>0$ such that
\[
\cA_\R W+\lambda W\le-\delta W\;\hbox{in }\R\setminus K.
\]
Then $\cA_\R+\lambda$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle.

\textup{(ii)} Let $\lambda<\Lp(\R)$ and assume $\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}(a(x)+\lambda)<0$.
Then $\cA_\R+\lambda$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle. In particular, if $\Lp(\R)>0$ and $\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}a(x)<0$, then $\cA_\R$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle.

\textup{(iii)} For every $\mu\in\R$,
\[
\Lp(\cA_\R+\mu)\ge \mathfrak G(\mu).
\]
In particular, $\Lp(\cA_\R+\mu)\ge H_d(q_0)-\sup_\R(a+\mu)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.342419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9fbd7d9be9908aedf937e9455b4532f61cc4bf1e15963c5e6f0d01ba8ebb5f39","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 33 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] For later perturbation arguments we also record the adjoint critical limit and the resulting first-variation limit.

\textup{(i)} Let $\phi_\sigma^*>0$ be the positive adjoint eigenfunction of $\cA_{\sigma,2,L}$. Normalize it by $\|\phi_\sigma^*\|_{L^2(-L,L)}=1$. Then
\[
\phi_\sigma^*\longrightarrow\phi_0^*\quad \hbox{strongly in }L^2(-L,L),
\]
where $\phi_0^*>0$ is the normalized Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of
\[
d_Jv''-(qv)'+av+\lambda_0v=0\quad \hbox{in }(-L,L),\qquad v(-L)=v(L)=0.
\]
The zero-extension energies satisfy
\[
E_\sigma(\phi_\sigma^*)\longrightarrow d_J\int_{-L}^{L}|(\phi_0^*)'|^2\,dx,
\]
and $\phi_\sigma^*(L)\to0$.

\textup{(ii)} Let $h\in C([-L,L])$ and, for $|\tau|$ small, replace $a$ by $a+\tau h$. Denote the corresponding principal eigenvalue by $\lambda_\sigma(\tau)$. Then
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)=-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
After normalizing the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions in $L^2$,
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)\longrightarrow-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
The right-hand side is the first variation of the local Dirichlet principal eigenvalue.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010","Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero","Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e","Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:45.041953+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_9ffa636677134a5540e6a704a86f6f5fe37015b52ad2241f167a16f3bc581359","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.481789+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ffaf82fc3ee8484462ec0f4b23141b14e93c763064333c37a470c703675f4c6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 52 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a BCM-regular pair.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The BCM-regular threshold $\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $0\neq r\in\m$ is defined as
\begin{align*}
\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)
&:=\sup\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is BCM-regular} \} \\
&=\inf\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is not BCM-regular} \}.
\end{align*}
\item
The local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta) := \inf_{0\neq r\in\m} \bcmt(R,\Delta;r)\cdot\nord_{\m}(r), \]
where $\nord_{\m}(r)$ denotes the normalized order of $r$.
\end{enumerate}
When $R$ is of characteristic $p>0$,
the BCM-regular threshold coincides with the $F$-pure threshold, and
the local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ coincides with the local $F$-alpha invariant $\alpha_{F}(R,\Delta)$ recently introduced by Takagi and Yamaguchi \cite[Definition~3.3]{TY}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.403908+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a05a99961fccd76be10f8880990fae2a96c0e5a9c99ef183629288be063edf33","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 11 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a stochastic kinetic

 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u_\varepsilon)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.542748+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a066ca5a723bc272ac6d47762feb4e1ceb7b51afdba3eef74716a5638a577e0e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 (Factor of i.i.d.) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider a locally finite transitive graph $G=(V,E)$
    (with respect to some group $\Theta\subset\operatorname{Aut}(G)$).
    Let $S$ denote a measurable space,

    Let $(T,\lambda)$ denote a probability space, and consider $\P:=\lambda^V$.
    A \emph{factor of i.i.d.}\ (FIID) is a map $\phi:T^V\to S^V$
    with the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebras on $T^V$ and $S^V$,

For a long virtual knot $K$, take its long virtual knot diagram $D$. 
Let $-D$ denote the long virtual knot diagram obtained by reversing the orientation of $D$. 
Let $D^{\#}$ denote the long virtual knot diagram obtained by replacing each classical crossing of $D$ by a crossing of the opposite sign.

Set $-K$, $K^{\#}$ and $K^{*}$  to be long virtual knots represented by $-D$, $D^{\#}$ and $D^{*}$, respectively, and call them {\it the reverse of} $K$, {\it the vertical mirror} of $K$ and {\it the horizontal mirror} of $K$, respectively.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.097477+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a0cb3164ea0cf119256002924e4811662e1a676ff41b26058db40ae80db66742","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:universal-root of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $X,Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$ be arbitrary, let $a_1,\ldots,a_N$ be the Kac
orthonormal basis of $W=\mathfrak{so}(n)$, and put $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(X,Z)&=\{X,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(X,Z)&=\{X,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(X,Z)&=\{[A_i,X],Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(X,Z)&=\frac1N\sum_iE_i(X,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10a}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$.  Then, with no projection onto curvature
summands,
\[
 \mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)-\bar E,
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H(X,Z),\qquad V_j=XZa_j,
\tag{3.2.10b}
\]
where
\[
 H(X,Z)=\frac1N\{-X\Psi(Z)+Z\Psi(X)\}.
\tag{3.2.10b$'$}
\]
Moreover, writing $\|\cdot\|_2$ for Hilbert--Schmidt norm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac4N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac1N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{16(n-2)}N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10c}
\]
The residue satisfies
\[
 \|H(X,Z)\|
 \le\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}N
 \bigl(\|X\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2+\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}\|X\|_2\bigr).
\tag{3.2.10e}
\]
If $X$ and $Z$ are symmetric, then $\Psi(X)=\Psi(Z)=0$, so $H=0$.
The identities and estimates remain valid when all maps are tensored by
an ancillary identity and the Hilbert--Schmidt norm is taken on the
amplified space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["g a norm on R^2, even in the transversal coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T03:39:47.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_a12c2b183a67ea70d9e183fc859334195570a83942c6e5d103a55a95913d7a60","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 that is even in the first coordinate (g(-h, m) = g(h, m)), as every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm is. For fixed m, the map h -> g((h, m)) is even and convex, hence minimized at h = 0, so g((h, m)) >= g((0, m)) = |m| g(e_2). Consequently, for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) with j = r + m, m > 0 (longitudinal overshoot past the far endpoint): g(v) + g((0,r) - v) - g((0,r)) >= (r + m) g(e_2) + m g(e_2) - r g(e_2) = 2 m g(e_2), and symmetrically for j = -m < 0. The dogleg excess grows at least LINEARLY in the overshoot, with the explicit constant 2 g(e_2), using convexity and symmetry alone - no curvature hypothesis of any kind. The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. Numerical attack: 0 violations in 300,000 trials on an anisotropic convex norm, worst ratio 1.000019.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.851747+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a12c8fdab6d24cecaac83ff606867d678a437527fc4d04be1c54b26ebb9aa0dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Inverse Riffle Shuffle with Concentrated Pile-Size Law) of arXiv:2605.19084, 'Limit Profiles for Separation Distance'] Let $f_n$ be a probability distribution on $[n]$, and consider the inverse riffle-type shuffle which chooses $K_n$ with law $f_n$, then moves a uniformly chosen set of $K_n$ cards to the top. $\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=o\left(\frac1{\log n}\right).$
Define
$$q_{2,n}:=\sum_{k=1}^n f_n(k)\frac{\binom{k}{2}+\binom{n-k}{2}}{\binom{n}{2}}.$$
If $t_n$ is any sequence of integer times such that
$$t_n=\frac{2\log n+c+o(1)}{-\log q_{2,n}},$$
then
$$s_n(t_n)\to 1-\exp\left(-\frac12e^{-c}\right).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

 \begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.866139+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1666659cde4c8dd8f37c476cd3c618c7d1faff23f0aec462c6b13d9a65b70bc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Quadratic local objective under scalar CFG) of arXiv:2608.29107, 'PathGuide: Dynamic Classifier-Free Guidance via On-Policy Transport Alignment'] Assume scalar CFG:
\begin{equation}
    v_t^\theta(x\mid y;\omega)
    =
    v_t^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    +
    \omega
    \Bigl(
        v_t^\theta(x\mid y)-v_t^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr).
\end{equation}
For fixed \(y,\vec\omega_i,\psi\), define
\begin{equation}
    A_i(\psi)
    :=
    \int_{\R^d}
    \Bigl(
        u_{t_i}(x\mid y)
        -
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr)\cdot
    \grad\psi(x)\,
    \hat p_{t_i}(x\mid y;\vec\omega_i)\,\dd x
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
    B_i(\psi)
    :=
    \int_{\R^d}
    \Bigl(
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid y)
        -
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr)\cdot
    \grad\psi(x)\,
    \hat p_{t_i}(x\mid y;\vec\omega_i)\,\dd x .
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal L_i(\omega_i\mid y;\vec\omega_i,\psi)
    =
    \bigl|A_i(\psi)-\omega_i B_i(\psi)\bigr|^2 .
\end{equation}
In particular, the exact local objective is quadratic in \(\omega_i\).","status":"unverified"}

This identification is induced by coordinate-wise projection.

\[

{"assumptions":["Allen-Cahn on the 1-d torus with 1-d quadratic noise, critical gamma^2 = 2","deterministic constant initial data u_0 = a > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.448302+00:00","domain":"stochastic partial differential equations, critical spaces","id":"claim_a215289259f9cccbe1cb7c19d537e22e0c0239f3b17a21caf7771d147f98140b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Agresti and Veraar, Nonlinear parabolic stochastic evolution equations in critical spaces (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 4 asks whether in the variational setting of their Theorem 6.4 there is a constant C_T with E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 <= C_T (1 + E ||u_0||_H^2) for all u_0 in L^2(Omega; H). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815831+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2166a98ab376a45c0d5df2ab5b5538d1c7067d53f83ae87c0936aa4c267691f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:iterated-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and put $A^{(0)}=A$.  For each $1\leq i\leq t$, choose an

 \mathcal H_{A^{(t)}}(z)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:14:37.637414+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a25823976a543d1fca0644ecf9d3ac21a700a7c4601c780733023929ac92ca65","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (Stopped physical-state stability) of arXiv:2608.19151, 'Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions'] Suppose that Assumption~\ref{ass:standing}(S1) holds. Fix
$K\geq1$ and $a\in\mathcal A$. Let
\[
    (X^a,N^a,\lambda^a)
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    (X^{K,a},N^{K,a},\lambda^{K,a})
\]
be constructed with the same Brownian motion, the same Poisson random
measures, the same initial condition, and the same admissible control
process $a$. For $R\geq1$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_R^{K,a}
:=
\inf\Bigl\{
t\in[0,T]:\;&
\norm{N_t^{K,a}}_1+\norm{N_t^a}_1>R

\]
Set
\[

        X_{u\wedge\tau_R^{K,a}}^{K,a}
        -
        X_{u\wedge\tau_R^{K,a}}^a
    }
\right],
\]
and
\[
D_{\lambda,R}^{K,a}(t)
:=
\E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_R^{K,a}}

+

0\leq t\leq T.

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(H_n) predictable: H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable","boundedness of H_n, or integrability of each H_n (X_n - X_{n-1})","for the supermartingale/submartingale versions: H_n >= 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627067+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a26f5d17686c1e295dc0e7eed296742f44e2d3fbf07ead7842c7484b505a8f62","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n) be a martingale for (F_n) and let (H_n)_{n >= 1} be PREDICTABLE, meaning H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable. Define the transform (H . X)_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} H_k (X_k - X_{k-1}), with (H . X)_0 = 0. If each H_n is bounded (or, more generally, if H_n (X_n - X_{n-1}) is integrable for every n), then (H . X) is a martingale. If (X_n) is a SUPERMARTINGALE and in addition H_n >= 0 for every n, then (H . X) is a supermartingale; the same with submartingale. Predictability is the load-bearing hypothesis: H_n may depend on everything known strictly before time n but not on the outcome at time n. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.364175+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a28565dbf9879768ac55633f60c138429f4821f0af08b9e821dc7abfb8db04a7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:shiftable-kernel of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $K$ denote the NURS transition kernel induced by a shiftable direction law
$q$, and let $K^t$ denote its $t$-step iterate.
Given a current state $\sigma \in S_n$, one step of $K$ is constructed as
follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample an index pair $(I,J)$ uniformly from
  $\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n\}$, and then sample a direction
  $\eta \in \Omega_{IJ}$ according to a fixed, state-independent law.
  \item Let $2m := \ord(\eta)$ and set $W := \{0,1,\dots,2m-1\}$.
  Sample an index $r \in W$ with probability proportional to
  $w(\sigma \eta^{r})$, and update the state to $\sigma' = \sigma \eta^{r}$.
\end{enumerate}
For the coupling across an edge $(\sigma,\sigma\circ\tau_{ij})$ we use the same
random choices $((I,J),\eta)$ for both chains.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.318165+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2a0a49c4b2f8417ae837c75976b2291342732fc1d238860a6fcc3f6e736ddb1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:from-r-to-l of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let the graph $G$ be finite and take $0\le l\le r$. We endow the subdivided graph $G_r$
  with i.i.d.\ edge weights $W_e>0$, $e\in E_r$. Consider the family $W^{(l)}$ of
  corresponding random weights
from Theorem (thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of the paper), all realized on the same probability space
with expectation operator ${\mathbb E}$. We abbreviate
$C_\alpha:=2^{-\alpha}\Gamma(\tfrac12-\alpha)/\sqrt{\pi}$
for $0\le\alpha<\frac12$ and ${c_2}:=\gamma+\log 2=1.27036\ldots$, where 
\begin{align}
  
  \gamma=-\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\log t\, dt=0.57721\ldots
\end{align}
denotes the Euler Mascheroni constant. 
For all $\bar e\in E_l$ and $e'\in E_r$, one has
  \begin{align}
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
    &\le (2^{-\alpha})^{r-l}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]
    &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
     &\le \frac{1}{C_\alpha}\min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}\left(C_\alpha 
       (2^{-\alpha})^{r-m}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]\right)^{2^{m-l}}
     &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),
    \\
      
    {\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{\bar e}]
    &\le \min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}
      2^{m-l}\left({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]-(r-m)\log 2+{c_2}\right)-{c_2}.
  \end{align}
  Set $m_0:=r-2-\lfloor\alpha^{-1}\log_2(C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha])\rfloor$
  and $m_1:=r-2-\lfloor(\log 2)^{-1}({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]+{c_2})\rfloor$.
  If $m_0\in\{l,\ldots,r\}$, a minimizer in (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper)
  is given by $m=m_0$. If $m_0<l$ or $m_0>r$, it is given by
  $m=l$ or $m=r$, respectively. The analogous statement holds for $m_1$
  with (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper) replaced by (equation eq:combined-log of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:40:21.313356+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2f89434fe7373fa5b4b466df429d0df189d2373db29ee2bebd3acde20d12721","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 39 ({\cite[Theorem~B) of arXiv:2604.08127, 'Asymptotics of Brownian occupation measures \\ with unusually large intersections'] {Weinstein1982/83}}]

    For any $d$ and $q > 1$ such that $d(q-1) < 2q$, there exists a constant $\kappa_{d, q}$ such that
    \[  
    \| \psi \|_{2q} \le \kappa_{d, q} \| \nabla \psi \|_2^{\frac{d(q-1)}{2q}} \| \psi \|_2^{1 - \frac{d(q-1)}{2q}} \quad \text{for all } \psi \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d).

    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

 distribution function $F$.

 then we have

{"assumptions":["phi is continuous on the unit circle (for merely bounded measurable symbols the criterion is different)","T_phi acts on the Hardy space H^2 of the circle","the winding number is that of the curve phi about 0, defined because phi is nonvanishing"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573131+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Toeplitz operators, index theory","id":"claim_a336e41f1363f4a04acdf30204d079af81761e9aab33543cfff3898ac6f7532f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H^2 be the Hardy space of the unit circle T, realised as the closed subspace of L^2(T) spanned by the exponentials z^n with n >= 0, and let P: L^2(T) -> H^2 be the orthogonal projection. For a continuous symbol phi in C(T) define the Toeplitz operator T_phi on H^2 by T_phi f = P(phi f); the bound ||T_phi|| <= ||phi||_infinity is immediate from ||P|| = 1, and in fact ||T_phi|| = ||phi||_infinity. Then T_phi is Fredholm if and only if phi has no zero on T, and in that case ind T_phi = - wind(phi), the negative of the winding number of the closed curve phi about the origin. In particular T_phi is invertible if and only if phi is nonvanishing with winding number 0, and a Fredholm Toeplitz operator with continuous symbol is never invertible when its winding number is nonzero, even though it may be injective or surjective.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.331543+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a3382a831f68ec8c5f8a538c70dafc8f73dc7392704e49e1eb2a2f556cb73a42","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] For $n\in\mathbb N$, let
\[
\cA_nu=d(J_n*u-u)+q_n(x)u'+a_n(x)u,
\qquad
\cA u=d(J*u-u)+q(x)u'+a(x)u.
\]
Assume that the kernels satisfy common support, normalization and nondegeneracy hypotheses and that $q_n,q\ge q_0>0$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{(i) Semicontinuity under local convergence.}
Suppose that $J_n\to J$ in $C_c^1(\R)$ with a common compact support, and that $q_n\to q$, $a_n\to a$ locally uniformly in $\R$, with common local bounds. Then $\Lp(\cA)\ge \limsup_{n\to\infty}\Lp(\cA_n)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{(ii) Quantitative global stability.}
Let $\cA_1,\cA_2$ satisfy common global structural bounds, including a common bound for the supports and $C^1$ norms of their kernels, the bounds for $q_i,a_i$, and the positive lower bound for $q_i$. There exists $C>0$, depending only on these structural data, such that
\[
\big|\Lp(\cA_1)-\Lp(\cA_2)\big|
\le C\Big(
\|J_1-J_2\|_{L^1(\R)}
+\|q_1-q_2\|_{L^\infty(\R)}
+\|a_1-a_2\|_{L^\infty(\R)}
\Big).
\]
Consequently, under uniform convergence of the coefficients and $C_c^1$ convergence of the kernels with common structural bounds, $\Lp(\cA_n)\to\Lp(\cA)$. If $\phi_n>0$ is a principal eigenfunction normalized by $\phi_n(0)=1$, then every subsequence contains a further subsequence converging in $C^1_{\rm loc}(\R)$ to a positive eigenfunction associated with $\Lp(\cA)$. If $\Lp(\cA)$ is simple in the positive cone, the whole sequence converges to the normalized principal eigenfunction. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:06.328985+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a342a90688739159df3d8effea5d04efec052692d18ea6c6205816bc2f816e80","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2607.06428, 'Impact of spinning on the early-warning signs in non-Markovian stochastic systems'] Let $(W^H_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a scalar fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index in $H(0,1)$. Then:
\begin{description}
    \item[{\bf(Long-range dependence)}] If $H>1/2$ then 
    \[ \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty \E [W^H_1(W^{H}_{n+1}-W^H_n)]=\infty. \]
    \item[{\bf(Short-range dependence)}] If $H<1/2$ then
    \[ \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty \E [W^H_1(W^{H}_{n+1}-W^H_n)]<\infty. \]
 \item [(Self-similarity)] Let $a>0$. Then 
 \[ (a^H W^H_t)_{t\geq 0} \stackrel{\text{law}}{=}(W^{H}_{at})_{t\geq 0}. \]
 \item [(Time-inversion)] It holds
 \[ (t^{2H}W^H_{1/t})_{t>0}\stackrel{\text{law}}{=}(W^H_t)_{t> 0}.  \]
\item [(Stationarity of the increments)] For all $h>0$ we have 
\[ (W^{H}_{t+h} -W^H_t )_{t\geq 0} \stackrel{\text{law}}{=} W^H_h. \]
\item [(Regularity of the increments)] The scalar fractional Brownian motion has a version which is $\alpha$-H\"older continuous with $\alpha<H$. 
\end{description} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:40:59.378418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a36cd0c90090bc8ce342d5236e0e5fe393d264a36d8d728bb8f128f0799e946a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2609.03962, '$L^p$ isomorphisms for the fractional Laplacian on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their application'] Let $n\ge2$, $s\in(0,2)$, and $p\in(1,\infty)$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[\textup{(i)}] Suppose $f\in L^p(\R^n)^n$ and $g\in V_{s,p}$.
        Then \eqref{intro_stokes} has a solution
        $(u,P)\in\Lambda^{s,p}(\R^n)^n\times W_0^{1,p}(\R^n)$, and the
        solutions in this class are exactly the pairs $(u+\lambda,P+c)$
        with $(\lambda,c)$ in
        \[
          \mathcal N_{s,p}
          :=\big\{(\lambda,c)\in(\mathcal P_{[s-n/p]})^n\times
          \mathcal P_{[1-n/p]}:\ \mathrm{div}\,\lambda=0\big\}.
        \]
        Moreover every solution satisfies
        \[
          \inf_{(\lambda,c)\in\mathcal N_{s,p}}
          \big(\|u-\lambda\|_{\Lambda^{s,p}}+\|P-c\|_{W_0^{1,p}}\big)
          \le C\big(\|f\|_{L^p}+\|g\|_{L^p}+\|\flap g\|_{W_0^{-1,p}}\big).
        \]
  \item[\textup{(ii)}] Suppose $f\in\Lambda^{-1,p}(\R^n)^n$ and
        $g\in\Lambda^{s-2,p}(\R^n)$. Then
        \eqref{intro_stokes}---its two equations holding in
        $\Lambda^{-1,p}(\R^n)^n$ and $\Lambda^{s-2,p}(\R^n)$ respectively,
        with the operators extended along the scale as in
        Section~\ref{sec:appstokes}---has a solution
        $(u,P)\in V_{s,p}^n\times L^p(\R^n)$ if and only if
        \[
          f\perp\mathcal P_{[1-n/p']}\quad\text{and}\quad
          g\perp\mathcal P_{[2-s-n/p']}.
        \]
        In that case the pressure $P$ is unique and the solutions are
        exactly the pairs $(u+\lambda,P)$ with
        $\lambda\in(\mathcal P_{[s-1-n/p]})^n$; thus the solution is
        unique whenever $s-1<n/p$, in particular for all $0<s\le1$, and
        unique up to an additive constant vector when $s-1\ge n/p$.
        Moreover every solution satisfies
        \[
          \|P\|_{L^p}
          +\inf_{\lambda\in(\mathcal P_{[s-1-n/p]})^n}
           \|u-\lambda\|_{\Lambda^{s-1,p}}
          \le C\big(\|f\|_{\Lambda^{-1,p}}+\|g\|_{\Lambda^{s-2,p}}\big).
        \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a38bfef1213fcf21c8e687ba500fc7e018cc939949e65c6c1d21ca8ae2d1ac36","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 92 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
\MSRheader\\
\hline
\BOGPdefn{sy}\\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, it suffices to show $\sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0)) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$, where $\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0)$ is defined in \eqref{e:sM.Lip.0.chaos}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ (recall \eqref{e:cM.Lip.0.chaos}), where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,\epsilon$.
    There exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \[
    \WERR((\cA_{N_j})^\circ,\mu)
    =
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,,
    \]
    and the correlation functions $\chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}$ satisfy $\lim_{j\to\infty} \chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}(0) = 0$ and
    \beq
        
        \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon) \le \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
    That is, we have the same information about the algorithms $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Lip.in.BOGP} (instantiated with $q_0 = 0$), and in addition the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos}.
    For $\cA_{N_j}$ the perturbation of $(\cA_{N_j})^\circ$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable},  the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos} implies
    \[
        \chi_{\cA_{N_j}}(1-\epsilon)
        = \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon)
        + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \epsilon + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le 2\epsilon\,,
    \]
where the last inequality holds for $L$ sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,\epsilon$. By passing to a subsequence of the $j$'s, we may assume that $\chi_{\cA_{N_j}}$ converges both pointwise and in $L^1$ to a limiting function $\chi$, which must then satisfy 
    \[
        \chi(1-2\epsilon) \le \chi(1-\epsilon) \le 2\epsilon\,.
    \]
Therefore $p \equiv \chi^{-1}$ satisfies $p(2\epsilon) \ge 1-2\epsilon$, as required by condition~\ref{it:3.6} (with $2\epsilon$ in place of $\epsilon$).
Arguing identically to the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Lip.in.BOGP} shows that for some $\hat\epsilon(\epsilon) \ge 2\epsilon$ tending to $0$ as $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$, we have 
    \[
        \cM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
        \subseteq \cB_{\hat\epsilon}\Big(
            \cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;\tilde C(L),\hat\epsilon)
        \Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union in $L$ and intersection in $\epsilon$, and applying $\sym$ to both sides, shows
    \begin{align*}
       & \sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0))
        \subseteq \sym\bigg(
        \adjustlimits
            \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
                \cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
            \Big)
        \bigg)\\
       &\qquad \subseteq 
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
            \sym(\cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon))
        \Big)\\
        &\qquad\stackrel{\eqref{e:BOGP.sym.relation}}{=} \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
        \cM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
        \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.sym.cM}}{=} \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.
    \end{align*}
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.258771+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a3bcbd10bdd0776cb380f08155d69bf095c00bf8dca0c4910ec8d32f32b4e09d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 10 (Composition of pseudo-differential operators) of arXiv:2609.01105, 'Obstruction to quasi-invariance of Gaussian measures under transport flows on Riemannian M'] \cite[Théorème 10.13]{Alazard2023}
Let $m,n \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a \in S^m$ and $b\in S^n$. Then there exists $a\#b \in S^{m+n}$ satisfying
\[
    \Op(a) \circ \Op(b)=\Op(a\#b). 
\]
Moreover, $a\#b$ admits the following asymptotic expansion: 
\[
    a\#b (x,\xi) \sim \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^d} \frac{1}{i^{|\alpha|}\alpha !}\partial_{\xi}^\alpha a(x,\xi) \partial_x^{\alpha}b(x,\xi),
\]

=q(x)u'(x)+\varepsilon\int_{-L}^{L}u(y)\,dy-\delta u(x)+a(x)u(x).
\]
Its principal eigenvalue $\lambda_{\varepsilon,\delta}$ is the unique real number satisfying
\[
1=\varepsilon\int_{-L}^{L}\int_x^L\frac1{q(t)}
\exp\left(\int_x^t\frac{a(r)+\lambda_{\varepsilon,\delta}-\delta}{q(r)}\,dr\right)dt\,dx.
\]
Up to multiplication by a positive constant, the corresponding eigenfunction is
\[
\phi_{\varepsilon,\delta}(x)
=\int_x^L\frac1{q(t)}
\exp\left(\int_x^t\frac{a(r)+\lambda_{\varepsilon,\delta}-\delta}{q(r)}\,dr\right)dt.
\]
Put
\[
T_q=\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{dx}{q(x)},\qquad
A_q=\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{a(x)}{q(x)}\,dx.
\]
Then, as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$,
\[
\lambda_{\varepsilon,\delta}
=\delta+\frac1{T_q}\left[
\log\frac1\varepsilon+2\log\log\frac1\varepsilon
-2\log T_q-\log q(-L)-A_q
\right]+o(1).
\]
The remainder is independent of $\delta$; in particular it is uniform when $\delta$ ranges in arbitrary subsets of $[0,\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:05:57.774716+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a3dac5678c79304c314a00b76246f3c2bf821743299e85aa08747d083f4022f5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] The weights of a neural network are a tuple of the form
  \[
    \CalW = \bigl( (A_1, b_1), \dots, (A_L, b_L)\bigr)
  \]
  of matrices $A_\ell \in \R^{N_\ell \times N_{\ell-1}}$ and bias vectors $b_\ell \in \R^{N_\ell}$,
  where $N_\ell \in \N$ specifies the width of the $\ell$-th layer of the network.
  We define the \emph{input- and output dimensions} of $\CalW$ as
  $d_{\mathrm{in}}(\CalW) := N_0$ and $d_{\mathrm{out}}(\CalW) := N_L$.

  The associated \emph{neural network function} using the ReLU activation function
  $\varrho : \R \to \R$, $\varrho(x) = \max \{ 0, x \}$ is given by
  \[
    R_\varrho (\CalW) : \quad \R^{d_{\mathrm{in}}(\CalW)} \to \R^{d_{\mathrm{out}} (\CalW)},
    \quad
    R_\varrho (\CalW)
    := T_L \circ (\varrho \circ T_{L-1}) \circ \cdots \circ (\varrho \circ T_1)
    ,
  \]
  where $T_\ell \, x = A_\ell \, x + b_\ell$, and where $\varrho$ acts componentwise on vectors,
  i.e.,
  \[
    \varrho \bigl( (x_1,\dots,x_m)\bigr)
    = \bigl(\varrho(x_1), \dots, \varrho(x_m)\bigr)
    .
  \]
  In this paper, we measure the ``complexity'' of
  $\CalW$ in terms of the \emph{number of non-zero weights}
  \[
      \norm{\CalW}_{\ell^0}
    := \sum_{j=1}^{L} \bigl(\| A_j \|_{\ell^0} + \| b_j \|_{\ell^0}\bigr)
    ,
  \]
  in terms of the \emph{network depth} $L(\CalW) := L$,
  and in terms of the \emph{weight magnitude}
  \[
      \| \CalW \|_{\ell^{\infty}}
    := \max_{1 \leq j \leq L} \bigl(\| A_j \|_{\ell^\infty} + \| b_j \|_{\ell^\infty}\bigr)
    .
  \]
  Here, for a matrix (or vector) $A$, the quantity $\| A \|_{\ell^0}$
  counts the total number of non-zero entries of $A$,
  and $\| A \|_{\ell^\infty} := \max_{i,j} |A_{i,j}|$.

  Now, given $d,g \in \N$, we define for $n \in \N$ the set of ReLU networks $\R^d \to \R$
  with at most $n$ non-zero weights, weight magnitude "of moderate growth",
  and number of layers growing at most poly-logarithmically with $n$ as
  \[
    \CalNN_n (g, \R^d)
    := \Bigl\{
         R_\varrho (\CalW)
         \,\,:\,\,
         \begin{array}{l}
           \CalW \text{ neural network weights with }
           d_{\mathrm{in}}(\CalW) = d,
           d_{\mathrm{out}}(\CalW) = 1, \\
           \norm{\CalW}_{\ell^0} \leq n, \,\,
           \norm{\CalW}_{\ell^{\infty}} \leq g \cdot n^{g},
           \text{ and }
           L(\CalW) \leq (\ln(e n))^g
         \end{array}
       \Bigr\}
    .
  \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.653385+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a41107f6a57007ed017cfd4d6c9f4aba5abda5be913d82580b83487e992b3bc6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:softlocal of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $J$ be an at most countable index set and let $(Z_j)_{j\in J}$ be independent random points
of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with densities $g_j$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\in J}$ be i.i.d.\ exponential random variables
of mean $1$ and define the soft local time
\[
  H_J(y)=\sum_{j\in J}\xi_j\,g_j(y),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^d .
\]
Let $\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable and deterministic. Then there is a coupling
$\mathbb Q$ of $(Z_j)_{j\in J}$ with a Poisson point process $\psi$ of intensity $\rho$

\item $\mathbb Q\big(\psi\cap A\subseteq\{Z_j\}_{j\in J}\big)\ \ge\

{"assumptions":["case weights depend on the row only (the per-sample relative L2 has w_i = 1/||y_i||^2; unit weights give the RMSE case); the predictor's outputs are scored by a sum of per-output squared errors","the bootstrap variance is the coordinate-wise variance over resamples, summed over outputs; the empirical sentence refers to the 2026-09-05 measurement (RMT_ENSEMBLE_THEORY.md 6aj, P34)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T14:55:30.513781+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment / transductive selection","id":"claim_a43a57adcd7e79c75b2fa7755a022cf05983f02a1411a8bebe7c1e6164bbabc0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let a multi-output predictor f_t(x) in R^D be a family indexed by t (for instance a blend f_t = (1 - t) f_0 + t f_1 of two fitted bases), scored by a case-weighted squared error L(t) = mean_i w_i ||y_i - f_t(x_i)||^2 with weights w_i that depend on the row only. Then L(t) = sum_d L_d(t) with L_d(t) = mean_i w_i (y_id - f_td(x_i))^2, and likewise the case-weighted bootstrap variance of the predictor at a set of rows, V(t) = mean_i w_i sum_d Var_b f_td^(b)(x_i), equals sum_d V_d(t). Hence the transductive covariance penalty R(t) = CV_cal(t) + [V_ev(t) - V_cal(t)] is a sum of per-output criteria R_d(t), and if the family is allowed a separate index t_d per output, the joint minimiser is the vector of per-output minimisers: min over (t_1..t_D) of sum_d R_d(t_d) = sum_d min_t R_d(t) <= min_t R(t). The per-output choice therefore never increases the criterion. It does not follow that it lowers the risk: each R_d is an estimate whose noise is not reduced by the averaging that makes R usable, and D separate argmins select on that noise. Measured on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (D = 285 and 40 outputs, 70 cells, two calibration/evaluation splits): the per-output blend gives up 0.41 and 0.53 percent of the score against the per-cell blend on EMIT (winning 14 and 12 of 40 cells) and 0.02 and 0.08 on OCO-2, with the identity sum_d R_d = R verified to 4e-16 in the driver's selftest. The information of the criterion is in the sum, not in its summands.","status":"unverified"}

Gaussian observations","M/n -> q in (0, 1)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911589+00:00","domain":"statistics of portfolio optimization","id":"claim_a453bab6cdb57297886d2f46c3cf9c2a4103d60d6717b3495d848c2573b78ab5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\Sigma$ be a positive definite $M \\times M$ covariance matrix. The minimum-variance weights subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ are $w^* = \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ with risk $R^* = w^{*T}\\Sigma w^* = 1/(\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$. Let $S$ be the sample covariance of $n > M + 1$ i.i.d. Gaussian observations with covariance $\\Sigma$ and let $\\hat w = S^{-1}\\mathbf{1}/(\\mathbf{1}^T S^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ be the plug-in weights. THEOREM (Pafka and Kondor, 2003; the finite-$n$ moments are those of the inverse Wishart law). In the limit $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = M/n \\in (0, 1)$: (i) the true (out-of-sample) risk of the plug-in portfolio satisfies $\\hat w^T \\Sigma \\hat w / R^* \\to \\frac{1}{1 - q}$; (ii) the in-sample risk $\\hat w^T S \\hat w / R^* \\to 1 - q$; so the realized risk exceeds the optimum by the factor $1/(1-q)$ while the naive in-sample estimate understates the optimum by the factor $1 - q$, the two differing by $1/(1-q)^2$. {"assumptions":["A Hermitian (symmetric in the real case)","positive definite for existence with a strictly positive diagonal and for uniqueness"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479375+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_a456a3e325bc76743808041802880a3b7d0b3e39a7260821e678465f0bff4aaf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A Hermitian matrix A in C^{n x n} is positive definite if and only if it can be written as A = L L^* with L lower triangular having strictly positive real diagonal entries; when it exists this factorisation is unique. For real symmetric positive definite A the factor L is real, A = L L^T. Equivalently A = R^* R with R = L^* upper triangular. The factor is computed by the Cholesky algorithm in n^3 / 3 flops (half the cost of LU, no pivoting needed): for j = 1..n, l_jj = sqrt(a_jj - sum_{k<j} |l_jk|^2) and l_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k<j} l_ik conj(l_jk)) / l_jj for i > j; the algorithm is backward stable (Wilkinson), and it fails - a nonpositive quantity under the square root - exactly when A is not positive definite, which makes it the standard numerical test of positive definiteness. For positive semidefinite A a factorisation A = L L^* with nonnegative diagonal still exists but is no longer unique. Uses: solving A x = b by two triangular solves, sampling Gaussian vectors with covariance A (x = mu + L z), least squares via the normal equations, and the Kalman filter.","status":"unverified"}

For each $n\ge1$, let $X^{(n)}$ be a c\`adl\`ag adapted solution, driven by the same pair $(W,Z)$, such that the pair $(X,X^{(n)})$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}. Suppose that $X^{(n)}$ solves
\[
X_t^{(n)}=x_0^{(n)}+\int_0^t b_n(X_s^{(n)})\dd s
+\int_0^t a_n(X_s^{(n)})\dd W_s
+\int_0^t \sigma_n(X_{s-}^{(n)})\dd Z_s.
\]
Assume that there exist common constants $L_b,L_a,L_\sigma$ and exponents $\eta_n\in[\wt\eta,1]$, with $\wt\eta\in[1/\alpha,1]$, such that for all $n$ and all $x,y\in\R$,
\[

\qquad

\]
and

Then the family satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:perturbed} uniformly with exponent $\wt\eta$. Define
\begin{align*}
B_n&:=\int_0^T\E |b(s,X_s)-b_n(X_s)|\dd s,\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.825004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a4987029613af4c85414a33cb50cc1c363c0c183d05b66bd473dae5d5cfd0b82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:fourpoint-relation-ball of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let
\[
 A=\{0,a,b,D\},\qquad 0<a<b<D,\qquad \gcd(a,b,D)=1,
\]
and suppose that every nonzero homogeneous relation of $A$ has relation
degree at least $H$, where $H\in\mathbb R$ and $H\geq2$.  Then
\[
 D\geq \binom{H+1}{2}.
\]
If equality holds, then, for the gaps
\[
 g_1=a,\qquad g_2=b-a,\qquad g_3=D-b,
\]
one has

 g_1+g_3=H,\qquad
 \gcd(g_1,g_3)=1,\qquad
 g_2=\frac{H(H-1)}2.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.022614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a4a66c5ef2226c51ee2d48c031c804bf32596f1676b64aa001aab18fe4e7a945","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(U\subset Y^{\rm rv}\) be a Zariski-open product region.  Suppose
\[
 q_i\longrightarrow q_\infty\in U,
 \qquad x_i\in F_{q_i},
 \qquad t_i\nearrow T.
\]
Set \(\tau_i=T-t_i\) and assume that
\begin{equation}
             \tau_i|\Rm(g(t_i))|_{g(t_i)}(x_i)\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{equation}
Choose nested coordinate sets
\[
 q_\infty\in V_0\Subset V_a\Subset V_b\Subset V\Subset U
\]
and holomorphic coordinates \(w=(w^1,\ldots,w^m)\) on \(V\).  After
discarding finitely many terms, assume that \(q_i\in V_0\).

Then there are \(\sigma_j\searrow0\) and a subsequence
\(i(j)\nearrow\infty\) such that the pointed flows
\begin{equation}
 \widehat g_j(t)
 =\frac{1}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}
   g\bigl(t_{i(j)}+\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}t\bigr),
 \qquad
 -\frac{t_{i(j)}}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}\le t\le0,
\end{equation}
have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Equipped with the point conjugate heat kernels based at
$(x_{i(j)},0)$, the flows converge in $\mathbb F$, and smoothly on the
full regular spacetime, to a connected noncollapsed K\"ahler shrinking
soliton \(\mathcal Z\).  Write \((Z,g_Z)=\mathcal Z_{-1}\) and
\[
 d\nu_{Z,-1}=(4\pi)^{-(m+1)}e^{-f_Z}\,dV_{g_Z}
\]
for its distinguished shrinker probability measure.  Its normalized
Nash entropy satisfies
\[
 \mathcal N(Z):=
 \int_{\Reg Z}f_Z\,d\nu_{Z,-1}-(m+1)<0.
\]

\item On the localized convergence charts, the maps
\begin{equation}
 \widehat H_j
 =\frac{(w-w(q_{i(j)}))\circ\pi}
        {\sqrt{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}}
\end{equation}
converge smoothly on compact subsets of the regular spacetime to a map
$H_Z$.  Its time-$-1$ restriction extends uniquely to a globally
Lipschitz holomorphic map $H_Z:Z\to\C^m$ satisfying on $\Reg Z$
\begin{equation}
 \nabla^{g_Z}dH_Z=0,
 \qquad
 c|a|^2\le |d(a\cdot H_Z)|_{g_Z}^2\le C|a|^2
 \quad(a\in\C^m).
\end{equation}

\item The time-$-1$ space is smooth.  More precisely, there exists
\(L\in\mathrm{GL}(m,\C)\), with no target translation, such that
\begin{equation}
 Z\cong\C^m\times\PP^1,
 \qquad LH_Z=\operatorname{pr}_{\C^m},
\end{equation}
where $\PP^1$ carries the round metric normalized by
$\Rc(g_{S^2})=\frac12g_{S^2}$.

\item The convergence is realized on a regular exhaustion by embeddings
$\Psi_j$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j^*\widehat g_j(-1)\longrightarrow g_Z,
 \qquad
 \widehat H_j\circ\Psi_j\longrightarrow H_Z
\end{equation}
smoothly on compact subsets of \(Z=\Reg Z\).  For every \(U'\Subset Z\)
and all sufficiently large \(j\),
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j(U')\cap\widehat H_j^{-1}(0)
 =\Psi_j(U')\cap F_{q_{i(j)}}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663321+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a521a73f68a79e41c548a6f2c09f0df35b059c9076a37cf796292e3ae0fdd109","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be iid real random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n. Then, $\Theta_{post}$ is a CRSM with three parts.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.054254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a568f2e0c8c9940af6e4c22153847bfcd7fd98fefbf71c1f6aad27ef2c326443","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 53 (Path space and shift) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\XX^{\Nz}$ be the set of all sequences $\omega = (\omega_{0},\omega_{1},\dots)$
with $\omega_{n} \in \XX$, let
\[
  X_{n} : \XX^{\Nz} \longrightarrow \XX, \qquad X_{n}(\omega) := \omega_{n}
  \qquad (n \in \Nz),
\]
be the coordinate maps, and let $\XXA^{\otimes\Nz}$ be the smallest $\sigma$-algebra
on $\XX^{\Nz}$ making every $X_{n}$ measurable. Sets of the form
$\{X_{0} \in A_{0},\dots,X_{m} \in A_{m}\}$ with $m \in \Nz$ and
$A_{0},\dots,A_{m} \in \XXA$ are called \emph{rectangles}. They form a $\pi$-system
--- the intersection of two of them is again one --- and they generate
$\XXA^{\otimes\Nz}$; this is what is used to identify a measure on
$\XXA^{\otimes\Nz}$ by its values on them. They do \emph{not} form an algebra: the
complement of $\{X_{0}\in A_{0}, X_{1}\in A_{1}\}$ is in general not a rectangle. The
family
\[
  \mathcal{A} := \bigcup_{m \in \Nz} \sigma(X_{0},\dots,X_{m})
  \;\subseteq\; \XXA^{\otimes\Nz}
\]
\emph{is} an algebra --- it is an increasing union of $\sigma$-algebras --- and it
generates $\XXA^{\otimes\Nz}$, since it contains every rectangle. It is $\mathcal{A}$
that is used in the approximation step of Proposition \ref{prop:ergodic}.
The \emph{shift} is the map
\[
  \vartheta : \XX^{\Nz} \longrightarrow \XX^{\Nz}, \qquad
  (\vartheta\omega)_{n} := \omega_{n+1} ,
\]
which is measurable and satisfies $X_{n} \circ \vartheta^{k} = X_{n+k}$.","status":"unverified"}

Probab. 2006) makes the free MSF a single tree when there is no percolation at criticality and the infinite cluster is unique above criticality; for the Poisson-Boolean (Gilbert) model uniqueness above criticality is classical and absence of percolation at the critical radius in high dimensions follows from the lace expansion for the random connection model (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad-Last-Matzke 2019). If the LPS criterion transfers verbatim to Poisson point processes, the MSF IS a single tree for d large, the reverse of the source's suspicion. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.746840+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5abe4b7b2f1bbaf1c1f7056fab6f5392aea2c743002878883712dc250b6d979","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ converges
  in law to an exponential distribution
  with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $t < 0$ and recall definition \eqref{eq:extra term}.
    The reciprocal of the
    moment-generating function of
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ is
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{1}{I_{m,p}(p\,(1-p)^m\,t)}
      &=
      (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t))-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx \\
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx + o(1)
    \intertext{where we have used the binomial approximation
      $(1-x)^\alpha = 1 - \alpha \, x + O(\alpha^2)$, uniform in $x$,
      and a first-order expansion
      $m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m \, (-t)) - m = p\,m\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)
      + O(p^2\,m\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      Together these give
      $(1-x)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)) - m}
      = 1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m + O(p^2\,m^2\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      This error suffices because, upon distribution to form another integral,
      we are left with a trivial term
      $O(p^3\,m^3\,(1-p)^m) \int_0^1 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx =
      O((p\,m)^3 \, e^{-2pm}) = o(1)$, which we have written above.
      The remaining steps involve the dominated convergence theorem:
      }
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^{pm}
      \left(1 + x\,t\,(1-p)^m\right)
      (1-x/m)^{m-1}\, dx + o(1)\\
      &= (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \underbrace{\int_0^{pm} 
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{1-(1-p)^m}\\
      &\quad\, -
        {\underbrace{\int_0^{pm}
          x\,t
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{t+o(1)}} + o(1) \\
      &= 1 - t + o(1).
    \end{align*}
    The \textsc{mgf} of a rate $1$ exponential is
    $(1-t)^{-1}$, so we are done by Theorem \ref{thm:convergence}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.561430+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5ccff55c3ae9cd79f5eecd8fb93ddf1c696d6f6e33af9f6efdfe65708ab4622","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:cost}, problem~\eqref{eq:WOT}
admits a unique minimizer $\pi^*\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)$, and there exists a pair of
potentials $(\phi,\psi)\in L^1(\mu)\times L^1(\nu)$ such that
\begin{align*}
c(x,\rho)+\varepsilon H(\rho\,\|\,\nu)
&\;\geq\;\phi(x)+\rho(\psi),
&&\forall\,(x,\rho)\in\Xc\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\\
c(x,\pi^*_x)+\varepsilon H(\pi^*_x\,\|\,\nu)
&\;=\;\phi(x)+\pi^*_x(\psi),
&&\mu\text{-a.e.\ }x.
\end{align*}
In particular, $\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)} J(\pi) = \mu(\phi)+\nu(\psi)$.

Moreover, the optimal coupling is given explicitly in
terms of the dual potential $\psi$ and the cost gradient $\hat{c}$
of~\eqref{eq:def-chat} by
\begin{equation}
\frac{d\pi^*}{d(\mu\otimes \nu)}(x,y)
\;=\;
\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\big(\phi(x)+\psi(y)
-\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)\big)\right).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the disintegration of the optimal coupling is 
\begin{equation}
\pi^*_x(dy)
\;=\;
\frac{1}{Z(x)}\,
\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
\;+\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy),
\qquad \mu\text{-a.e.\ }x,
\end{equation}
where $Z(x)$ is the normalizing constant
\[
Z(x)\;=\;\int\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
+\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy)
\;=\;\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\phi(x)\big).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E X^2 < infinity (finite variance); with only a finite mean use Markov on |X - mu|","t > 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_a5eaf1118b8ba6fc5c186263978f4e647cf0b4a4166fb927bf4a20b143d4268f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with finite mean mu = E X and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X. Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; when sigma > 0 this is equivalent to P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0 (for sigma = 0 the standardized form fails: X = mu almost surely and the left side is 1). The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

    A family $\mathcal{E}\subset \mathcal{P}(S\times S)$ is called a \emph{coarse structure} on $S$ if it satisfies the following five conditions (see Section \ref{subsection:notation} for notation):
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\diag(S) \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1 \cup E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1\circ E_2\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E' \in \mathcal{E}$ for each $E' \subset E$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The pair $(S, \mathcal{E})$ is called a \emph{coarse space} and 
    each element of $\mathcal{E}$ is referred to as an \emph{coarse entourage} or simply an \emph{entourage}.
    An entourage $E\in \mathcal{E}$ is called \emph{symmetric} if the equality $E=E^\dagger$ holds.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.167259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a63777394c2ea4625a6dcc05aaf5845678eb8d5bd84c7635c800e4167c5c6aaa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_gen_perm_model of arXiv:2412.07258, 'Permuton limit of a generalization of the Mallows and $k$-card-minimum models'] Assume given a strictly decreasing $C^1[0,1]$ function $g$ satisfying $g(0)=1$ and $g(1)=0$.

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}
We say that a random element $\sigma_n$ of $S_n$ is a $g$-random permutation, or briefly write $\sigma_n \sim \mathrm{PERM}(g,n)$, if it can be generated as follows. We write the number $i$ on the $i$'th card of the original deck (counted from the bottom up).
$\sigma_n(i)$ will denote the number written on the card that is at position  $i$  in the new deck (counted from the bottom up). We build the new deck by picking a card from the remaining old deck  in each step and placing it at the top of the new deck.
\begin{itemize} \item  Let $C^{(n),i}, \, i \in [n]$ denote independent random variables with distribution \begin{equation*} C^{(n),i} \sim \nu^{(n),i}_{g}.\end{equation*}
\item For any $i \in [n]$ we will denote by $D^{(n)}_i$ the set of cards remaining in the old deck before the $i$'th step. Note that $|D^{(n)}_i|=n-(i-1)$.
\item
Let us define $D^{(n)}_i$   and $\sigma_n(i)$ for $i \in [n]$  recursively. Let $D^{(n)}_1 = [n]$.
\item If $D^{(n)}_i$ is already defined,  we pick the $C^{(n),i}$-th card of $D^{(n)}_i$ (counted from the bottom of $D^{(n)}_i$) and let $\sigma_n(i)$ be the number written on this card. We remove this card from the old deck, i.e., we let $D^{(n)}_{i+1} = D^{(n)}_i \setminus \{\sigma_n(i)\}$, and we place it on the top of the new deck.
\item We continue this procedure until there are no cards left in the old deck.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.475247+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a66546df5d6e9d57f4c98b8d050ab0f062f2e05e8740353ba4f22bf3cf98da14","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:dyadic-maximal of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Let $N\ge2$, and let $Z_{N+1},\ldots,Z_{2N}$ be centered square-integrable random variables.
For an interval $I\subset\{N+1,\ldots,2N\}$ write
\(
    Z(I):=\sum_{t\in I}Z_t .
\)
Assume that there exist constants $B_N>0$ and $\gamma\ge1$ such that, for every interval
$I\subset\{N+1,\ldots,2N\}$,
\[
    \mathbb E|Z(I)|^2
    \le
    B_N^2\left(\frac{|I|}{N}\right)^\gamma .
\]
Then there exists a universal constant $C<\infty$ such that
\[
    \mathbb E
    \max_{N\le n\le2N}
    \left|
        \sum_{t=N+1}^{n}Z_t
    \right|^2
    \le
    C(\log N)^2B_N^2 .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:44.799493+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_a69b4271c80fa20aa2fea9d95ad80807bc72e1765e618476cb1e679b00be37b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the mathematical field of graph theory, the Erdős–Rényi models are two closely related models for generating random graphs and the evolution of a random network. These models are named after Hungarian mathematicians Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, who introduced one of the models in 1959. Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. In the model of Erdős and Rényi, all graphs on a fixed vertex set with a fixed number of edges are equally likely. In the model introduced by Gilbert, also called the Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model, each edge has a fixed probability of being present or absent, independently of the other edges. These models can be used in the probabilistic method to prove the existence of graphs satisfying various properties, or to provide a rigorous definition of what it means for a property to hold for almost all graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.230089+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6daeea6a634ba135f17653f65a2f4b1bc0272ae1e7a068528c16331ba36eb5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 20 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] A \textbf{partial positive semidefinite} matrix with \textbf{block sizes} $k$, $\ell$ and $m$ is a $5$-tuple
