{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.774583+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b1fcdbf5e423a491c5c66fbee6023c3bd7d71bb383190f85b60655b82350babb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:wn of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] The set $\mathcal{W}_N$ consists of all collections $\mathbf{W}$ of $n$ random walk trajectories $\mathbf{W} = (W^i : i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\})$,
where each $W^i$ is a function $[\ell,r]_N \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mathbb{Z}$, such that $\mathbf{W}$ satisfies the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ and all $t_1, t_2 \in [\ell,r]_N$ with $|t_1 - t_2| = \frac{1}{N}$, we have
    $\mleft| W^i(t_1) - W^i(t_2) \mright| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$, so that $W^i$ is a diffusively rescaled random walk trajectory.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$, we have the nonintersection constraint $W^1(t) > \dotsb > W^n(t)$.
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$, the trajectory $W^i$ has appropriate boundary conditions, which we now explain.
    We would like to have $W^i(\ell_N) = x^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$ and $W^i(r_N) = y^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$,
    but some care is needed here.
    First, if $x^i$ and $x^{i+1}$ are very close (or equal), then choosing arbitrary discrete approximations of the boundary conditions
    may violate the strict ordering of the random walk trajectories.
    Furthermore, since the parity of the two boundary conditions must be compatible in order for $W^i$ satisfying the above conditions to exist,
    we will need to correct this issue if it arises.
    So we will impose the boundary conditions
    \begin{equation}
        W^i(\ell_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} x^i \mright\rfloor + 2 (n-i) \mright)
        \qquad \text{ and } \qquad
        W^i(r_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} y^i \mright\rfloor + 2(n-i) + \epsilon^i \mright),
    \end{equation}
    where $\epsilon^i \in \{0,1\}$ is chosen (depending on $x^i, y^i$, and $N$) to mitigate the parity issue,
    and the term $2(n-i)$ is added to ensure strict ordering of the boundary conditions.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$ and each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ we have the floor and ceiling constraints.
    To state these constraints, we introduce the linear interpolation $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = (\widetilde{W}^i)_{i=1}^n$ of $\mathbf{W}$, which is a continuous function
    $[\ell,r] \to \mathbb{A}_+^n$ obtained by interpolating $\mathbf{W}$ linearly between points of $[\ell,r]_N$, and extending by a constant
    in $[\ell,r] \setminus [\ell,r]_N$ (i.e.\ at the edges).
    The floor and ceiling constraint is then that $\widetilde{W}^i(t) \in (f^i(t), g^i(t))$ for all $t \in [\ell,r]$. 
\end{enumerate}
This completes the definition of our set of possible states $\mathcal{W}_N$ in the
discrete model of a line ensemble. Note that due to our choices of boundary
conditions,
$\mathcal{W}_N$ is nonempty as long as $N$ is large enough and the
boundary conditions are compatible with the floors and ceilings.

For example,
to construct one element $\mathbf{W} \in \mathcal{W}_N$, we may first let $W^n_\ell$ take
downwards steps away from the left boundary, only taking upwards steps when a
downwards step would intersect $f^n$.  Similarly, we may let $W^n_r$ take
downwards steps away from the right boundary, and set $W^n =
\max\{W^n_\ell,W^n_r\}$.  Then we may inductively construct $W^i$ in the same
way, ensuring that it also does not intersect $f^i$ or $W^{i+1}$.  As long as
$N$ is large enough, the ceiling constraint will also be satisfied since there
is some constant minimum amount of room between $f^i$ and $g^i$ as $\mathbf{f} \prec
\mathbf{g}$ and these functions are continuous on a compact interval.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.817816+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b2012cdac154439a003d3316b6b2a692644d15b4a8e23f06b080508d86ce2746","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (Uniform Pigato-type inverse covariance estimate) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Fix $\eps>0$.  For the cutoff regularized family of
Lemma~\ref{lem:chain-compatible-cutoffs}, use the block order
\[
    X^1=r,\qquad X^2=p,\qquad X^3=\theta .
\]
Let $J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}$ be the Jacobian flow from time $s$ to time
$t$ along the full cutoff regularized process.  The three constant noise
matrices in the block order $(r,p,\theta)$ are
\begin{equation}
    \Sigma_r=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \sqrt{2\gamma\eps/L}\,I_d\\ 0\\ 0
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_p^\delta=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\ \sqrt{2\eps\delta}\,I_d\\ 0
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_\theta^\delta=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\ 0\\ \sqrt{2\eps\delta}\,I_d
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Each matrix in \eqref{eq:regularized-noise-blocks} belongs to
$\R^{3d\times d}$.  Define the Malliavin covariance contribution generated
only by the $r$-Brownian motion by
\[
    \mathcal M_{t,r}^{\delta,\mathsf O}
    =
    \int_0^t
    J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}
    \Sigma_r\Sigma_r^\top
    \left(J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}\right)^\top\,ds.
\]
Set
\[
    T_t=\operatorname{diag}\left(t^{1/2}I_d,t^{3/2}I_d,t^{5/2}I_d\right).
\]
Then, for every $q\ge1$, every $M<\infty$, and every compact
$K_0\subset\mathsf O$,
\[
    \sup_{\substack{
        0\le\delta\le1\\
        z\in K_0\\
        0<t\le M}}
    \mathbb E_z\left[
        \lambda_{\min}\left(
            T_t^{-1}\mathcal M_{t,r}^{\delta,\mathsf O}T_t^{-1}
        \right)^{-q}
    \right]
    <\infty .
\]
The same estimate holds for the adjoint cutoff family.  All constants are for
fixed $\eps$ and may depend on $\eps$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.590641+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b241f781a6295e908ccae5b2f358a1c89adc646634ecfb315ed7765c128c7e4c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.03819, 'Stochastic damped wave and Euler-Bernoulli equations with singular locally H\\\"older...'] Let $U$ and $H$ be two separable Hilbert spaces and $T>0$. We consider a stochastic differential equation which evolves in the Hilbert space $H$ of the form \\begin{align} dX(t)=AX(t)dt+B(t,X(t))dt+GdW(t), \\quad t\\in[0,T], \\quad X(0)=x \\in H, \\end{align} where $A:D(A)\\subseteq H\\to H$ is the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous semigroup $(e^{tA})_{t\\geq0}$, $W=(W(t))_{t\\geq0}$ is a $U$-cylindrical Wiener process defined on a normal filtered probability space $(\\Omega,\\mathcal{F},\\{\\mathcal{F}_t\\}_{t\\in [0,T]},\\mathbb{P})$, $G:U\\to H$ is a linear bounded operator and $B:[0,T]\\times H\\to H_\\beta$ is a locally $\\theta$-H\\\"older continuous function with respect to the second variable, uniformly with respect to the first one, for some suitable $\\theta\\in(0,1)$. Here, $H_\\beta$ is a Hilbert space which contains $H$ with continuous embedding, so that the drift term is singular: it is not well-defined from the ambient space $H$ into itself. The coefficient $\\beta\\geq0$ measures the order of such a singularity and the case $\\beta=0$ corresponds to a drift term with values in $H$. We prove that, under suitable assumptions on the coefficients, weak and pathwise uniqueness hold true for equation \\eqref{SDEa}. In particular, the conditions assumed on the coefficients cover the stochastic damped wave equation in dimension $1$ and the stochastic damped Euler--Bernoulli beam equation up to dimension $3$, even in the hyperbolic case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b246d11cd7903d8c6088cf77c46e0bfd50f8b07422a32d6f33af4b4d07225324","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 238 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\delta>0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,L,\delta) > 0$ such that the following holds for all $\fq\in [1,2]$ and all sufficiently large $N$.
Recall $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}. For any fixed $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ and $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, abbreviate $\bx\equiv\bx_N\equiv \cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ as before, and define the random variables
	\begin{align*}
	X&\equiv X_N
	\equiv X(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\bx_N),\mu\Big)\,,\\
	J&\equiv J_N
	\equiv J(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv 
	\bbW_\fq\Big(
	\EmpDist(\bx_N),\cP(\{\pm1\})
	\Big)\,.
	\end{align*}
 We then have the bounds
\begin{align}
		\bbP\Big(
			|X_N - \E X_N|
			\le \delta
		\Big)
		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,\\	
		\bbE\Big[
			(X_N - \E X_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,,\\
		
		\bbP\Big(
			|J_N - \E J_N|
			\le \delta
		\Big)
		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\\

		\bbE\Big[
			( J_N - \E J_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.
	Analogous inequalities to \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.tail} and  \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var} hold with $\mu_{\bG,\sym}(\bx_N)$ in place of $\mu_\bG(\bx_N)$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R_{\ge 0})$.
\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof, $c$ denotes a constant that depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$, which can change line by line.
	Let $C = C(\alpha)$ be given by Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, let
	\[\bar{\bx}
	\equiv\bar\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
		\equiv \bx \min \bigg\{
			1, \frac{2N^{1/2}}{\|\bx\|}\bigg\}\,.\] 
However, in contrast with the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, we now let $\bar{\bg}^a$ denote the $a$-th row of 
	\[\bar\bG = \bG \min\bigg(1,\frac{CN^{1/2}}{\|\bG\|_{\op}}\bigg)\,.\]
 We then define the measure
	\[
		\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux) = \EmpDist\bigg(\frac{\bar\bG \bar{\bx}}{N^{1/2}}\bigg)
		\equiv \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M \delta\bigg\{
		\frac{(\bar\bg^a, \bar{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\}\,,
	\]
	By  the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the event
	\[
		\cE = \bigg\{
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \le C \textup{ and }
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
occurs with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$. We abbreviate
	\[Y \equiv Y_N
	\equiv Y(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
	\equiv \bbW_\fq\Big(\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)\]
We will first show that
	\beq
		\max_{\fp \in \{1,2\}}
		\Big|\E[X^\fp] - \E[Y^\fp]
		\Big| \le e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
		Note the trivial bound $\bbW_2(\nu,\mu) \le \|\nu\|_{L^2} + \|\mu\|_{L^2}$. Thus, for $\fp \in \{1,2\}$,
	\[
		\bbW_2(\nu,\mu)^\fp \le 2\Big\{
		(\|\nu\|_{L^2})^\fp + 
		(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Note also that on event $\cE$, $X=Y$. Thus, for each $\fp \in \{1,2\}$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		&|\E[X^\fp] - \E[Y^\fp]|
		\le \E\Big[
		(X^\fp + Y^\fp);\cE^c\Big] 
		\le \E\bigg[
			\Big\{
			\bbW_2\Big(\mu_\bG(\bx),\mu\Big)^\fp + \bbW_2\Big(\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)^\fp
		\Big\}
		;\cE^c\bigg]\\
		&\qquad\le 2\E\bigg[
		\Big\{
		(\|\mu_\bG(\bx)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
		+ (\|\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
		+ 2(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
		\Big\}
		;\cE^c
		\bigg] \\
		&\qquad\stackrel{*}{\le} 4\E\bigg[ \Big\{
			(\|\mu_\bG(\bx)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
			+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp\Big\}
		;\cE^c
		\bigg] 
		= 4\E\bigg[
		\bigg(
				\frac{\|\bG \bx\|^\fp}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
				+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
			\bigg)
			;\cE^c
		\bigg] \\
		&\qquad\le 4\E\bigg[
			\ind\{\cE^c\}\bigg(
				\frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op})^\fp \|\bx\|^\fp}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
				+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
			\bigg)
		\bigg]\,.
	\end{align*}
	The  inequality marked $*$ uses that $\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}$ stochastically dominates $\|\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux)\|_{L^2}$. Using H\"older's inequality, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{4\P(\cE^c)^{1/2}
		\E[\|(\bG\|_{\op})^{4\fp}]^{1/4}
		\E[\|\bx\|^{4\fp}]^{1/4}}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
		+ 4\P(\cE^c) 
		(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp\,.
	\]
Recalling Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgauss","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.301734+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b316277e278c85b6e6775ef62781d73eb2ca6b44dc5ffbdd79a717e7c1cd569b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma le:strongly-convex-anti-concentration of arXiv:2608.30382, 'Convergence rates for the RMSprop optimizer with full control of the hyperparameters'] Let $\mu,B,R\in(0,\infty)$, and suppose that $U$ has a Lebesgue density $g$

\bas{
\|g\|_{L^\infty}\le B
\qquad

\qquad
{\mathbb P}\bigl( | U | < R \bigr)=1.
}
Let $\varphi:{\mathbb R}^m\to{\mathbb R}$ be $\mu$-strongly convex. Let $\omega_m$ denote
the Lebesgue volume of the
Euclidean unit ball in ${\mathbb R}^m$. For every $\varepsilon\in(0,\infty)$, set
\bas{

  \delta_\varepsilon
  =
  2 \sqrt{ \tfrac{ \varepsilon }{ \mu } } .
}

\begin{align}\begin{split} 
  {\mathbb P}\bigl(
    | \varphi(U) - a |

    - ( R + \delta_\varepsilon )^m
  \bigr)
  .
 \end{split}\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.829547+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b318b16a07df2db464fb352d710b07837a5af9196fc8651ffa3b797328d0965e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 34 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $\fn_-=\fn_{-1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\fn_{-d}$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.493980+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b31e705d22c61c67d0f6be38d0bd38a0aef6b3178f37fba3b3334c5033d12e8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 18 (Maximum entropy quadruply augmented double hive) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-maxent}
Let \(\bar a,\bar b,\bar d>0\).  Assume either
\[
\bar f \geq 0,
\]
or
\[
\bar f^2<0,
\qquad
T:=\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2<0.
\]
Let \(\mathbb D^4\) be the cone of double hives
augmented on the four exterior boundary components:
\[
\mathbb D^4
=
\bigcup_{\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi,\nu}
GT(\alpha)\times GT(\beta)\times GT(\eta)\times GT(\phi)
\times H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu)
\times H_n(\eta,\phi^\vee;\nu^\vee),
\]
where
\[
\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi\in \Spec_n+\mathbb R\one,
\qquad
\sum_i\alpha_i+\sum_i\beta_i+\sum_i\eta_i-\sum_i\phi_i=0,
\]
and
\[
\nu^\vee=(-\nu_n,\ldots,-\nu_1),\qquad
\phi^\vee=(-\phi_n,\ldots,-\phi_1).
\]
Thus the fiber volume over
\((\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi,\nu)\) contains the exterior factor
\[
\frac{V_n(\alpha)V_n(\beta)V_n(\eta)V_n(\phi)}
     {V_n(\tau_n)^4}
|H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu)|\,|H_n(\eta,\phi^\vee;\nu^\vee)|
\]

Define a density \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) on \(\mathbb D^4\), with respect to
Lebesgue measure on this cone, by
\[
p_{\mathrm{dbl}}(x)
=
Z_{\mathrm{dbl}}^{-1}
\exp\left[
-\frac12
\left(
\frac{|\alpha(x)|^2}{\bar a^2}
+
\frac{|\beta(x)|^2}{\bar b^2}
+
\frac{|\eta(x)|^2}{\bar d^2}
+
\frac{|\phi(x)|^2}{\bar f^2}
\right)
\right].
\]
Then \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) is the unique probability density on
\(\mathbb D^4\) maximizing differential entropy among all densities \(q\)
such that
\[
\mathbb E_q|\alpha|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\alpha|^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q|\beta|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\beta|^2,
\]
\[
\mathbb E_q|\eta|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\eta|^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q|\phi|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\phi|^2.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["L is a vector lattice of real-valued (finite everywhere) functions on a set X","Stone's condition: f in L implies min(f,1) in L","I : L -> R is linear","I is positive: f >= 0 implies I(f) >= 0","Daniell continuity: f_n in L with f_n decreasing pointwise to 0 implies I(f_n) -> 0","for the uniqueness clause only: there are f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant 1","no topology on X is assumed, and no regularity of the resulting measure is claimed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090141+00:00","domain":"measure theory, integration, representation of positive functionals","id":"claim_b330fea79f8371289214536b62fd4e02f8348d302f06b862ea12c798689edb94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a nonempty set and let L be a vector lattice of real-valued functions on X: L is a real vector space of functions X -> R, and f, g in L implies max(f,g) and min(f,g) are in L. Assume STONE'S CONDITION: f in L implies min(f, 1) in L. Let I : L -> R satisfy (i) linearity; (ii) positivity: f >= 0 pointwise implies I(f) >= 0 (equivalently f <= g implies I(f) <= I(g)); (iii) the DANIELL CONTINUITY CONDITION: whenever f_n in L decrease pointwise to 0 at every point of X, I(f_n) -> 0. Granted (i) and (ii), condition (iii) is equivalent to: f_n in L increasing pointwise to f with f in L implies I(f_n) -> I(f). CONCLUSION (Daniell-Stone): there is a measure mu on sigma(L), the smallest sigma-algebra on X making every member of L measurable, such that every f in L is mu-integrable and I(f) equals the integral of f with respect to mu. If moreover there exist f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant function 1 (an exhaustion, i.e. sigma-finiteness along L), then mu is unique on sigma(L). WHERE IT FAILS: (a) condition (iii) is the whole content and cannot be dropped. On X = (0,1] take L to be the set of restrictions to (0,1] of the continuous functions on the closed interval [0,1] - a vector lattice satisfying Stone's condition - and let I(f) be the limit of f(x) as x decreases to 0, which exists for every member of L. This I is linear and positive, but f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n x) lies in L and decreases pointwise to 0 on (0,1] while I(f_n) = 1 for every n, and I is not integration against any Borel measure on (0,1]: the 'missing' representing measure is a unit mass at the point 0, which does not lie in the space. A positive linear functional on a lattice always yields a finitely additive set function; (iii) is exactly what upgrades finite additivity to countable additivity. (b) Stone's condition is what manufactures indicator functions: for f in L and c > 0 the functions min(n (f - c)^+, 1) lie in L and increase pointwise to the indicator of {f > c}, which is how the measure of a generating set is defined. Without it one still gets a representation, but on a lattice of sets rather than on a sigma-algebra. (c) Without the exhaustion hypothesis uniqueness can fail: sets that no member of L 'sees' are unconstrained. Example: X = {p} union (0,1] with L the continuous compactly supported functions on (0,1] extended by the value 0 at p; then {p} lies in sigma(L) but its measure may be chosen freely without changing any I(f). (d) The theorem produces a measure on sigma(L) only; regularity (inner or outer) of mu is NOT part of the conclusion and needs topological hypotheses, which is where Riesz-Markov-Kakutani differs from Daniell-Stone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measurable with respect to Σ","invariance is defined through preimages T⁻¹(E), not images T(E)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110366+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, measure-preserving dynamics","id":"claim_b37bfdbafedccacf12edc1ee9bd940c9966158655c818a0c9f8f9b11bdc70a19","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Σ) be a measurable space and T: X → X a measurable map (T⁻¹(E) ∈ Σ for every E ∈ Σ). A measure μ on Σ is T-invariant (equivalently: T preserves μ, or T is a measure-preserving transformation of (X, Σ, μ)) if μ(T⁻¹(E)) = μ(E) for every E ∈ Σ, i.e. the push-forward T_*μ := μ∘T⁻¹ equals μ. Equivalent formulation for a finite measure: ∫ f∘T dμ = ∫ f dμ for every bounded measurable f; when X is a compact metrizable space with its Borel σ-algebra and T is continuous, it suffices to test f ∈ C(X), because finite Borel measures on such a space are determined by their integrals against continuous functions. Note the direction: invariance is stated with the PREIMAGE T⁻¹(E), not the image T(E); for non-injective T the image condition μ(T(E)) = μ(E) is a different (and generally false) statement, e.g. the doubling map x ↦ 2x mod 1 preserves Lebesgue measure but doubles the length of short intervals. For a flow (φ_t)_{t∈ℝ} invariance means φ_t*μ = μ for every t.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.051330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b3903b89a7eaa60ceeeff7cede0f154048d81e0924f3173b5e0a1e46026d2709","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm aronsson-package of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant $p$-harmonic function in a planar domain $\Omega$.
\begin{enumerate}[\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The critical set
$$
  \operatorname{Crit}(u):=\{x\in\Omega:D u(x)=0\}
$$
is discrete.  In particular, if $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then there exists $\rho>0$ such that $D u\ne0$ in $B_\rho(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$.

\item If $x_0\notin\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then $u$ is real analytic in a neighborhood of $x_0$.

\item Let $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$.  Then there are an integer $N\ge1$, a number $\delta>0$, and a nonzero homogeneous $p$-harmonic function $P$ in $\mathbb R^2$ such that, after subtracting the constant $u(x_0)$,
$$
  P(r\theta)=r^{\lambda_N(p)}\Phi(\theta),
  \qquad \theta\in\mathbb S^1,
$$
and, uniformly for $\theta\in\mathbb S^1$ as $r\to0$,
$$
  u(x_0+r\theta)-u(x_0)=P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)+\delta}),
$$
$$
  D u(x_0+r\theta)=D P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)-1+\delta}).
$$
Moreover $|D P(\theta)|>0$ on $\mathbb S^1$, and the hodograph representation gives the logarithmic-gradient expansion
$$
  \partial_r\log |D u(x_0+r\theta)|
  =
  \frac{\lambda_N(p)-1}{r}+O(r^{-1+\delta})
$$
uniformly in $\theta$.
\end{enumerate}
Here
$$
  \lambda_N(p)=\frac{\beta_{N+1}(p)}{\beta_{N+1}(p)-1},
$$
with
$$
  \beta_{N+1}(p)
  =
  \frac{\sqrt{(p-2)^2+4(p-1)((N+1)/N)^2}-(p-2)}{2}.
$$
For $p=2$, the same statement is understood in the classical harmonic sense and gives $\lambda_N(2)=N+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["γ is a continuous closed curve in ℂ","z₀ does not lie on the image of γ"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110598+00:00","domain":"algebraic topology, complex analysis","id":"claim_b3a02e8f0726857a802fa42855fcd7acf8b442a81228e97aa6f877a727c5c99f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let γ: [a,b] → ℂ be a continuous closed curve (γ(a) = γ(b)) and let z₀ ∈ ℂ be a point NOT on the curve, z₀ ∉ γ([a,b]). Because γ(t) − z₀ never vanishes, there is a continuous function θ: [a,b] → ℝ (a continuous choice of argument) with γ(t) − z₀ = |γ(t) − z₀| e^{iθ(t)}; θ is unique up to adding a constant integer multiple of 2π. The winding number of γ about z₀ is n(γ, z₀) := (θ(b) − θ(a)) / (2π). It is an integer (since γ(b) = γ(a) forces θ(b) − θ(a) ∈ 2πℤ) and does not depend on the choice of θ. For piecewise C¹ curves it equals the contour integral (1/2πi) ∮_γ dz/(z − z₀). Basic properties: z₀ ↦ n(γ, z₀) is constant on each connected component of ℂ \\ γ([a,b]) and equals 0 on the unbounded component; it is additive under concatenation of closed curves at a common point and changes sign when the orientation of γ is reversed; it is invariant under homotopies of closed curves that avoid z₀ (see the classification theorem). The circle t ↦ z₀ + r e^{2πikt}, t ∈ [0,1], k ∈ ℤ, has winding number k about z₀ and winding number 0 about any point with |z − z₀| > r. The winding number is NOT defined when z₀ lies on the curve, and it is not a homotopy invariant for homotopies that are allowed to cross z₀ (the circle about z₀ is null-homotopic in ℂ but has winding number 1).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.284317+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b3ac63ce4a76d00d7bb1ebdbe6c6e3414c1af0a6779375592a8365b56d4dabef","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:smc-prime of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y'_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov jump
process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When
$Y'_{\ell}=y$, recombination events occur at rate $y$. Given
that a recombination occurs at time
$r\in(0,y)$, the detached lineage recoalesces with either of the
two existing lineages at rate $1$ each (total rate $2$). If recoalescence
occurs with its own ancestral lineage before time $y$, then the recombination
is \emph{silent} and the state does not change. Otherwise---either
if recoalescence occurs with the other lineage, or if no recoalescence
occurs before time $y$---the recombination is \emph{visible}, and
the process jumps to a new TMRCA determined by the time of this coalescence
event.
The probability of a visible recombination at current TMRCA $s$ is
\begin{equation}
p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s)=\frac{2s+1-e^{-2s}}{4s},\qquad
p_{\mathrm{sil}}(s)=1-p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s).

\end{equation}

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y'_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X'_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain, and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$
random variables, independent of the chain. Given $X'_{n}$, define
the holding time 
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X'_{n} p_{\mathrm{vis}}(X_{n}')}
\]
and the jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\[
Y'_{\ell}:=X'_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),
\]
and $X'_{n+1}\sim q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}( \cdot \mid X_{n}'),$ where
\[
q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2t})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}}, & 0<t<s,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2s})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}} e^{-(t-s)}, & t\ge s.
\end{cases}
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.206439+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b3ac82c8f4519447657225ed7258f168d1dc93c341fd6fc530927d56e2d2be0c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:Weighted-Polyhedron of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] A weighted space $(X,\lambda)$ is called a

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:19.983494+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b42794b871cf7558b2c2b2f656d8f405a7f5361111125499bd6a2a43fd1e4978","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Introthm 1 (Convergence via asymptotic equivalence with the target) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\XX,\XXA)$ be a measurable space and  $T$ be a Markov kernel with invariant probability measure $\pi$ on

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.970316+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4994d402199f87c7c1741cafc93dc729175174f2d87ced3fc217417783f0df2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Stochastic approximation) of arXiv:2607.22438, 'A deterministic scalar reduction for the phase transition in two interacting urns'] Let \(\alpha>1\) and \(p\in[0,1]\). Let \(\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) be the equilibrium set of
\[
 \dot z=F_p^{(\alpha)}(z)
\]
on \([0,1]^2\). The vector field is a gradient field: $F_p^{(\alpha)}=\nabla L_p^{(\alpha)}$,
where
\begin{equation}
 L_p^{(\alpha)}(x,y)
 =(1-p)\{G(x)+G(y)\}+2pG\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)
 -\frac{x^2+y^2}{2},
 \qquad
 G(t)=\int_0^t h(u)\dd u .
\end{equation}
Stability is understood relative to the invariant square \([0,1]^2\). An equilibrium
\(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is called stable if it is a strict local maximum of
\(L_p^{(\alpha)}\) relative to \([0,1]^2\). We call \(z_*\) unstable if the top
eigenvalue \(\lambda_+(z_*)\) of \(DF_p^{(\alpha)}(z_*)\) is positive.

Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=*]
    \item for \(p>0\), the equilibrium set \(\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is finite;

    \item every equilibrium other than
    \[
      (0,0),\qquad \left(\frac12,\frac12\right),\qquad (1,1)
    \]
    lies in one of the two off-diagonal rectangles
    \[
      \left(0,\frac12\right)\times\left(\frac12,1\right),
      \qquad
      \left(\frac12,1\right)\times\left(0,\frac12\right);
    \]

    \item the urn process \((x_n,y_n)\) converges almost surely to an equilibrium of the ODE;

    \item if \(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is stable, then
    \[
      \PP_p^{(\alpha)}
      \left(\lim_{n\to\infty}(x_n,y_n)=z_*\right)>0;
    \]

    \item if \(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is unstable, then
    \[
      \PP_p^{(\alpha)}
      \left(\lim_{n\to\infty}(x_n,y_n)=z_*\right)=0 .
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:01:15.318933+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4acf615d67589583fa4dc7d50cea5e049ef8733aac45c59b7cc2266f3cf4201","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 12 (Finite-sample population-risk curve recovery) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] Let $\tau_n\in[0,1)$ be deterministic, and let
\(

\)
be deterministic nonnegative scalars.  Suppose a measurable event
$\mathcal E_n^{\rm reg}$ satisfies
$\Pp(\mathcal E_n^{\rm reg})\geq1-\tau_n$.  On
$\mathcal E_n^{\rm reg}$, suppose \cref{ass:tube} and
\eqref{eq:evaluation-gradient-bound} hold.  On
$\mathcal E_n^{\rm reg}$, suppose also that

 M\leq\overline M_n,\quad
 L_3\leq\overline L_{3,n},\quad

 C_{PP}\leq\overline C_{PP,n}.

Assume globally one of the two enumerated sets of concentration hypotheses.

deterministic interval $I_{n-1}$ of finite length

$\beta_{n-1}<\infty$ for the quantity in \eqref{eq:uniform-stability}, the
deterministic nondecreasing modulus $\omega_{n-1}$ satisfies
$\lim_{v\downarrow0}\omega_{n-1}(v)=0$ and
\eqref{eq:hyper-modulus}, and \eqref{eq:loo-joint-measurability} holds.
Fix $r>0$ with $\mathcal N(\cH,d_{\cH},r)<\infty$.
\item[\emph{Chained.}] The quantities in
\cref{eq:hyper-lipschitz-constant,eq:mixed-stability} satisfy
$L_{n-1}^{\rm hyp},\beta_{n-1}^{\rm mix}<\infty$, the entropy integral in
\eqref{eq:entropy-integral} satisfies

\eqref{eq:loo-joint-measurability} holds with $\mathcal U=\cH$ and
$u=(t,\lambda)$.  A deterministic anchor $(t_0,\lambda_0)\in\cH$ satisfies

$\mathfrak r_n:(0,1-\tau_n)\to[0,\infty)$ by
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak r_n(\delta)
 =\frac{\overline G_{{\rm out},n}\overline L_{3,n}
              \overline M_n^2}{2(n-1)^2}
       \mathcal J_{\overline\kappa_n}(T)
  +s_n^\star(\delta)

Then there is a measurable event $\mathcal O_{n,\delta}$ with
$\Pp(\mathcal O_{n,\delta})\geq1-\delta-\tau_n$ such that, on

\begin{equation}

{"assumptions":["both processes centred and Gaussian","Sudakov-Fernique: increment variances compared; conclusion only for expected suprema","Slepian: additionally equal pointwise variances; conclusion is distributional"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628762+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4b2e0be77f5756917d65ef45275366760a72b9a8c024ebef3f9c4928a398295","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t) and (Y_t) be CENTRED Gaussian processes indexed by a finite set T. SUDAKOV-FERNIQUE: if E[(X_s - X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s - Y_t)^2] for all s, t in T, then E[ sup_t X_t ] <= E[ sup_t Y_t ]. Note that only the increment variances are compared and the individual variances may differ; the conclusion is about EXPECTED suprema only. SLEPIAN: if in addition E[X_t^2] = E[Y_t^2] for every t - so that the increment comparison is equivalent to E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s, t - then the stronger distributional conclusion P( sup_t X_t >= u ) <= P( sup_t Y_t >= u ) holds for every u, and indeed the whole joint law is stochastically ordered coordinatewise. Slepian's extra hypothesis of equal variances is not decorative: without it the distributional conclusion is false, while the Sudakov-Fernique conclusion about expectations survives. Both require CENTRED and GAUSSIAN; there is no comparable general statement for non-Gaussian processes. The finite index set is a convenience; both extend to separable processes by approximation. [Slepian (1962), Sudakov (1971), Fernique (1975); see Adler and Taylor, Random Fields and Geometry, Chapter 2, or Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d >= 3, G connected and d-regular (bipartite graphs have lambda_n = -d, which is excluded from the Ramanujan condition together with +d)","the Alon-Boppana bound is asymptotic in n for fixed d","existence results are cited, not proved"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:17:03.041240+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_b4cff0d243e113602094a9e01462d26887e25896b93bb86c6b28ac1795f048d4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a connected d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n >= -d. G is Ramanujan if every eigenvalue other than +-d satisfies |lambda| <= 2 sqrt(d - 1); the number 2 sqrt(d-1) is the spectral radius of the infinite d-regular tree. Alon-Boppana theorem: for every fixed d >= 3 and every epsilon > 0, every d-regular graph with sufficiently many vertices has lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d - 1) - epsilon; more precisely lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d-1) (1 - O(1/ log^2 n)) (Friedman; Nilli). So Ramanujan graphs are the best possible spectral expanders. Existence: Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (1988) and independently Margulis constructed explicit infinite families of (p+1)-regular Ramanujan graphs for every prime p congruent to 1 mod 4 (Cayley graphs of PSL(2, Z/qZ) or PGL(2, Z/qZ) according to the Legendre symbol of p modulo q, the eigenvalue bound coming from the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for modular forms proved by Deligne), later extended to all prime powers (Morgenstern 1994); Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved by the method of interlacing families, non-constructively, that infinite families of bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree d >= 3 exist (Ann. Math. 2015, via 2-lifts) and then that bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist on every even number of vertices (interlacing families IV, 2018); Friedman (2008) proved Alon's conjecture that a random d-regular graph is nearly Ramanujan, lambda_2 <= 2 sqrt(d-1) + epsilon with high probability, and Bordenave (2020) gave a shorter proof. Ramanujan graphs give the optimal expander mixing lemma constant and near-optimal derandomisation gadgets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.857233+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4e7bdb1c707f4857c18b1df1d9d42d590fb2b7ab1d6fcb95e8f7291e7ab4bf1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let Assumption~\ref{Hypo-Q} hold, and let $\delta_{\mathcal Q}$ be defined

		\[

		\]

		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf (\arabic*)},leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}

			$\mathcal Q_n\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^{-\infty}$.

			$\{\mathcal Q_n\}_{n\ge1}$ is bounded in $\mathbb A^\alpha$.
			If the selected description is

			\item For every $r\ge0$,

			\item Let $r,\theta\ge0$ and

			\[
			\|\mathcal Q_n-\mathcal Q_m\|_{
				\mathscr L(H^r;H^\theta)}
			\lesssim

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.654103+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4ec36f6fa1a64461c5ae68df118339a198ef6beb4e44c1dfd4354b02b6c007b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:surface of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] A \emph{two-sided Lipschitz surface} $F$ is a set of base-height cells $(b,h)\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1}$ such
that for every $b\in\mathbb{Z}^d$ there are exactly two, possibly equal, integers $F_+(b)\ge0$ and
$F_-(b)\le0$ with $(b,F_+(b)),(b,F_-(b))\in F$, and such that $F_+$ and $F_-$ are Lipschitz
functions. We say that $F$ \emph{exists} if $F_+(b)<\infty$ and $F_-(b)>-\infty$ for every $b$.
For $D\in\mathbb{N}$ we say that $F$ \emph{surrounds} a cell $(b',h')$ at distance $D$ if every path
$(b',h')=(b_0,h_0),(b_1,h_1),\dots,(b_n,h_n)$ with $\|(b_k,h_k)-(b_{k-1},h_{k-1})\|_1=1$ for all
$k$ and $\|(b_n,h_n)-(b_0,h_0)\|_1>D$ intersects $F$. We say that a space-time cell belongs to
$F$ if its base-height index does.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.567230+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4f25deea9780b6bdb90adecee88856eb26387cc9e629b62d09a06f15e34c6df","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] As $n\to\infty$, the process $R^{(n)}$ has a distributional limit $R^{\mathsf{DL}}=\{R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, under the uniform-on-compact topology. 
    We can describe the process $R^{\mathsf{DL}}$ explicitly as follows.
	
Let $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{2k})$ be $2k$ independent Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ of diffusivity $2$, drift $\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_i, i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$ and $-\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_{2k+1-i}$. Next, let $\{X(-i, j) : i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket, j \in \llbracketi +1, 2k +1 - i \rrbracket\}$ be an array of exponential random variables, independent of each other and $\mathcal B$, satisfying 
\[
X(-i, j) \sim \begin{cases}
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \lambda_j/2), \qquad &j \in \llbracketi + 1, k \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 + \lambda_{2k + 1 -j}/2), \qquad &j\in\llbracketk + 1, 2k - i \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \rho), \qquad &j=2k + 1- i.
\end{cases}
\]
We turn this array into a 
sequence of cadlag functions $X = (X_1, \dots, X_{2k})$ on $(-\infty, 0]$ by the rule that $X_j(0) = 0$ for all $j$, and the measure $dX$ has atoms of size $X(-i, j)$ at each coordinate $(-i, j)$ where $X(-i, j)$ is defined (and is supported on these points). Equivalently, the path $X_j$ has a jump of size $X(-i, j)$ at location $-i$.

Let $X \mathcal{B}$ be the concatenation of $X$ and $\mathcal{B}$. (See Figure (fig:hfsh of the paper) for an illustration.) Then:
$$
R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i(x) = \begin{cases}
X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; x, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \ge 0, \\
X\mathcal{B}^{\Delta_{2k+1}}(-i, i; |x|, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \le 0.
\end{cases}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627864+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4f8bc22f460f25f8d49dffc484368ee58c01fdabcf876f2f9b6345b6ceebd5f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.828010+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b53b0a23500cb6be305f31581dcfc273c83e174f8830ff85d12eb075a9c4f4bc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:label-configuration-reversal of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For fixed $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$, as $q\to\infty$ a uniformly random
$A\in\binom{[q]}k$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb P(A\text{ is not }B_h)
 =\frac{k!K_{h,k}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),
 \qquad K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}.
\]
For each $2\leq r\leq h$,
\[
 \mathbb P(|hA|=M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k})
 =\frac{k!\kappa_{k,r}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(|hA|)\leq1\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),\\
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_h(A)=1\mid A\text{ is not }B_h\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By contrast, if $k\geq4$ is fixed and $N_{h,k}$ is uniform in the finite set
$\mathcal R(h,k)$, then, as $h\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(N_{h,k})\leq1\bigr)
 =\frac{h}{|\mathcal R(h,k)|}
 =h^{-(k-2)+o_k(1)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Thus principal labels are asymptotically negligible among attainable
cardinalities, although their realizations account for asymptotically almost
every fixed-order configuration in a growing interval.
Here $h$ is fixed before $q\to\infty$;
no joint $(h,q)$ assertion is made.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H: R^n → R is finite everywhere and convex (hence continuous)","H is superlinear: H(p)/|p| → ∞ as |p| → ∞","for part (iv): H ∈ C^2 and D^2H ≥ θI with θ > 0 (which already implies superlinearity)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415976+00:00","domain":"convex analysis for Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b547a366acd0d9caa05bd0fd6c74e4b7c9b6d81ddd9e55157d9fc2c6927f0355","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, i.e. H(p)/|p| → +∞ as |p| → ∞. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.368344+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b55041acf7ac818829dcc62a0c2d128b6a81bc82746cba91e931f44eceb6f4e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The chi laws in small dimensions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item At $n=1$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{1t}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{t\pi}}\,e^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=\sqrt{\frac{(2t)^k}{\pi}}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k+1}{2}\right)$$

\item At $n=2$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{2t}=\frac{1}{t}\,xe^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=\sqrt{(2t)^k}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k}{2}+1\right)$$

\item At $n=3$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{3t}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{t^3\pi}}\,x^2e^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=2\sqrt{\frac{(2t)^k}{\pi}}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k+3}{2}\right)$$
\end{enumerate}
The law $\chi_{2t}$ is called Rayleigh law, and the law $\chi_{3t}$ is called Maxwell-Boltzmann law.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.428658+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b56fdc10aa73df40b6aa6c0ad331dc029ab643f3264dc005cb857f6a717f5f6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem pre:gamblersRuin of arXiv:2605.19835, 'Reemergence of the Epidemic Threshold in SIRS Infections on Connected Stars'] {feller1957introduction}}]
    In the gambler's ruin game, a player starts with some amount of money $P_0 \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 1}$ and then repeatedly throws a coin that shows head with probability $p \in (0,1)$, independent of all other outcomes. If it shows heads, the player's money increases by~$1$, otherwise, it decreases by~$1$. The game ends at time~$T$ when the player either reaches the lower bound $\ell \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{< P_0}$ or the upper bound $u \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{> P_0}$ of money.
    Let $(P_t)_{t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}}$ be the amount of money that a player has in a gambler's ruin game that has a probability of $p \in (0,1)\setminus\{1/2\}$ for them to win in each step. Let $q=1-p$.  Then
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Pr{P_T = \ell} = \frac{1-(p/q)^{u-P_0}}{1-(p/q)^{u-\ell}}$ and
        \item $\Pr{P_T = u} = \frac{1-(q/p)^{P_0-l}}{1-(q/p)^{u-\ell}}$.\qedhere
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:26:52.673800+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b586c936717730e5a59ad7f47cb6c8974d61395c55c5c31d515e7bc5df892843","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03750, '\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D Stochas'] For every $v, \widetilde{v}, \widehat{v}\in V$, the trilinear form $b$ is continuous on $V\times V\times V$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that

&\left| \langle B(\widetilde{v}, \widetilde{v}) - B(\widehat{v}, \widehat{v}), \widetilde{v} - \widehat{v} \rangle \right|

{"assumptions":["H convex and superlinear; L = H*","g Lipschitz (plus, in (i), semiconcave with constant C)","in (ii): H ∈ C^2 with D^2H ≥ θI, θ > 0","t > 0 (the bound in (ii) degenerates as t ↓ 0)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.416852+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b5973a35bd060d224baea5579490f1724a84640f8bbf24fa4699085d03bb0478","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, L = H*, g: R^n → R Lipschitz, and let u(x,t) = min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) be the Hopf-Lax function. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.461095+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5aca9b87a0a53a376c1614a4e342956b8df7107e354946f0c5c2d4ce94de36a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] We consider a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$, its lower jumps $l_1<\cdots <l_s$, and its upper jumps $u_1<\cdots<u_s$. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The lower and upper jumps determine uniquely each other by the recursive identities $l_1:=u_1$ and $l_i:=l_{i-1}+p^{i-1}(u_i-u_{i-1})$ for each $i\in\llbracket2,s\rrbracket$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket $ we have $l_j=u_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} p^i(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have identities 
$$\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{l_i}{p^i}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^j p^{i-1}u_i}{p^j}$$
and
$$p^{j-1}u_j:=l_j+(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}l_ip^{j-i-1}.$$

{\bf (4)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, write
\[
b=\delta_{1,b}+\delta_{2,b}p+\cdots+\delta_{s,b}p^{s-1}
\]
with $\delta_{i,b}\in\llbracket0,p-1\rrbracket$ for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and define
\[
N_{s,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}\bigl[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i\bigr].
\] Then for each $b\in \llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, if $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ is the largest such that $p^j\mid b$, then we have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}&=p^{s-j-1}\Big[l_{j+1}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j p^{j+1-i}l_i\Big]\\
&=p^{s-j-1}[l_1+\sum_{i=1}^j p^i(u_{i+1}-pu_i)].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}\ge p^{s-j-1}l_1\ge l_1>0$ and therefore we have $\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\ge\frac{l_1}{p^{j+1}}>0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5e3fa35e1a6d931ebdc3e155642b0dc3bd61f17553d02dc415ed8ee523ff71e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.030867+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5f7b31b3eb5e4eb8f36aaec33631fb202c78baa9143519a46382173c2d87edb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:reduced-same-shell-increment of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Fix a regular \(f\in(f_{\mathrm{eq}},f_1)\), write
		\(\theta=\theta_f\) and \(\zeta=\zeta_f\), and let \(q\) be the first
		positive contact point of \(\zeta\). Let \(X\) be the
		Auffinger--Chen process associated with \(\zeta\). For
		\(\varepsilon>0\), fix \(\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N\), and define \(b_i\) by
		\[
		m_i=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i).
		\]
		Write \(\mathbf{b}=(b_i)_{i\le N}\).
		Assume that
		\[
		|q_\mathbf{m}-q|\le\varepsilon,
		\qquad
		W_2\left(
		\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{b_i},
		\mathrm{Law}(X_q)
		\right)\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		For \(f'\in[f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon]\), condition on
		\[
		F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf',
		\qquad
		\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0.
		\]
		Assume also that
		\[
		\left|
		f'
		+\frac1N\left(
		F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{m})-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
		\right)
		-f
		\right|
		\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		Denote the corresponding conditional expectation by
		\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\).
		There is a centered Gaussian field \(G_\mathbf{m}\), independent of the
		conditioned value and gradient, such that, for every fixed
		\(r\in(-q,q)\),
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}')-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
				&=G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}')
				+\sum_{i=1}^N\left[
				\frac{\xi'(r)}{\xi'(q)}m'_i b_i
				+\Phi_\zeta^*(q,m'_i)-\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)
				\right]\\
				&\quad+N\theta\bigl[\xi(r)-r\xi'(r)-\xi(q)+q\xi'(q)\bigr]
				+N o_\varepsilon(1)+N o_\delta(1)+o_N(N),
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		uniformly when \(\lvert q_{\mathbf{m}'}-q\rvert\le\delta\) and
		\(\lvert R(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}')-r\rvert\le\delta\). Here
		\(o_N(N)/N\to0\) for fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta\), while
		\(o_\varepsilon(1)\to0\) and \(o_\delta(1)\to0\) as their respective
		parameters tend to zero. All errors are uniform over the displayed
		\(\varepsilon\)-window conditions. For two points
		\(\mathbf{m}'^1,\mathbf{m}'^2\) in this slice,
		\[
		\frac1N\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\left[
		G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^1)G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^2)
		\right]
		=
		\xi(R_{12})-
		\frac{\xi'(r)^2}{\xi'(q)}R_{12}+C_r
		+o_\varepsilon(1)+o_\delta(1)+o_N(1),
		\]
		where \(R_{12}=N^{-1}\langle\mathbf{m}'^1,\mathbf{m}'^2\rangle\) and \(C_r\) depends
		only on \(q\) and \(r\).","status":"unverified"}

 \varphi(x)
 =\varphi(\kappa_1)+m_0(x-\kappa_1)

Consequently, $\varphi$ is realized by an architecture in

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6037c8c8459122d7c3759452aab6b463cb95829c2fce94e8bb116ffceef2ba7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\chi'(1) \le L^2$.

\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof we abbreviate $\bg\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$.  Consider small positive $\delta$, and define
    \[\begin{aligned}
    \bx&=\cA( (1-\delta)^{1/2}\bg+\delta^{1/2}\bg')\,,\\
    \by &= \E(\bx\,|\, \bg)\,,\\
    \bz &= \bx-\by\,.
    \end{aligned}\]
By iterated expectations, we have
    \[
    \frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\by)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta)\,, 
    \]
as well as $\E(\by,\bz)=0$. It follows that
    \beq
    \chi(1)
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\bx)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}+\frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta) + \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}\,.\eeq
Let us treat $\bz$ as a function of $\bg'$ for fixed $\bg$. Note that $\E(\bz\,|\,\bg)=0$. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, we see that $\bz$ is $(L\delta^{1/2})$-Lipschitz as a function of $\bg'$. It follows (using e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
    \[
    \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N} \le O(L^2\delta)\,.
    \]
Recalling \eqref{eq:bz}, we see that $\chi(1-\delta) \ge \chi(1)-O(L^2\delta)$, which implies $\chi'(1) \le L^2$ as claimed. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.228500+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b611e1c92b803b450068416aa660dcb674500a40f671d6832b57bd068ca4c54b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 13 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] If $S$ is any set (not necessarily finite), $Q$ is a positive semidefinite $S$-by-$S$ matrix, and $E,F$ are disjoint finite subsets of $S$, then we write
\[Q[F\mid E] := Q[F] - Q[F,E]Q[E]^\dag Q[E,F],\]
the generalized Schur complement of $Q[E]$ in $Q[E\cup F]$.  Now we define the \textbf{conditional log-determinant entropy of $F$ given $E$ in $Q$} by
\[\rmH_Q(F\mid E) := \log \det Q[F\mid E],\]
and the \textbf{log-determinant mutual information between $E$ and $F$ in $Q$} by
\[\rmI_Q(E\,;\,F) := -\log \det \big(I_{|F|} - (Q[F]^\dag)^{1/2}Q[F,E]Q[E]^\dag Q[E,F](Q[F]^\dag)^{1/2}\big).\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2","the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:18:07.915757+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_b65e4f03214b2aa782f369b54d75f83a80e5af182457d205fd6bc537075ff3c0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (23 and 18 members; 285 and 40 outputs; 932 and 800 calibration rows; the per-sample relative metric; 70 cells, paired). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\\lambda_{\\max}/\\lambda_{\\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\\,\\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result, paired gains against the $0.05$-floor RIE: the raw covariance, the eta-RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie at full calibration (median paired gain 0.00 on both corpora; means +0.05, +0.04, +0.09, -0.86 on 40 EMIT cells, the last from one cell at -16; +0.16, +0.01, +0.15, +0.09 on 30 OCO-2 cells), while at $n = 60$ the eta-RIE itself is the worst of them: on OCO-2 raw +6.4, LW2020 +6.0, NERCOME +4.9 percent over it on 30 of 30 cells (on EMIT +0.6, +1.3, +1.0 with 20-28 of 40 wins), and at $n = 240$ on OCO-2 +1.1, +1.0, +0.8 on 30 of 30 at full calibration and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose 1.2 and 6.5 percent on EMIT at full calibration (0.2 and 1.1 on OCO-2), 4.5 percent for the heavy floor at $n = 60$ on EMIT; linear shrinkage loses 6.3 percent on EMIT at full calibration and 15 percent at $n = 60$ (a wash on OCO-2, where the members are fewer and the shrinkage target closer); and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose 2 to 7 percent at full calibration on EMIT and 13 to 105 percent at $n = 60$; on OCO-2 the raw sum-to-one form is off by factors of 30 to 3,000 (an 18-member rank-deficient covariance inverted). Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\\times10^{2}$-$3\\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$); the floors and the linear shrinkage keep MORE members active (EMIT: raw 7.2, RIE 7.6, RIE with the 0.05 floor 8.3, floor 0.2 9.4, floor 1.0 12.2, linear shrinkage 13.9, LW2020 7.3, NERCOME 9.6 of 23; OCO-2: 6.9, 7.5, 8.0, 9.1, 11.3, 8.9, 7.1, 7.2 of 18), which is how they lose - a lifted small eigenvalue makes a duplicate look independent. By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; by the entrywise risk bound all of them obey the same $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ excess-risk guarantee while a floor is a bias that does not vanish with $n$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.340592+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6703bad009d889652cc64f04abead235202be056bb91938fe6e010ea70e1bed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Pointwise macroscopic-loop bounds for integer loop weights) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(d\ge 3\), let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, and let \(p_{d,n}\) denote its law. Assume
    \[
    d>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(d)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). Assume
    \[
    \lambda>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\lambda)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and
    \[
    \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
    \]
    If
    \[
    \rho>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
    \]
    then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.022007+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b68d956a8150dd4b2d3657fe3a9647aaca24dfe2b14c95585403e9b970d21acc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 29 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] Let $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ be a random population vector with $p_1 < p_2 < p_3$, and define $x = \frac{p_2}{p_1}$, $y = \frac{p_3}{p_1}$. Assume that the induced ratios satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{tau_ratio_uniform}; namely, that
$u = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{p_2}{p_3}$ is asymptotically uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$ and $y \to \infty$ in density.

Let $A$ be a divisor method that guarantees nonzero allocations, and let $\tau$ be as in Definition \ref{tau_def}. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\tau \sim \mathrm{Unif}\!\left(-\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}\right)$ asymptotically.
    \item The probability that $A(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ exhibits a lower quota violation caused by nonzero allocations satisfies
    \[
    P(\text{quota violation}) =P(\text{quota violation caused by nonzero allocation})   = P(\tau \text{ is ultimately violatory}).
    \]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, this probability coincides with that obtained under the asymptotic uniform distribution on reduced population vectors $(1,x,y)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:57:16.069187+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b69ad0796f255bad8d3ead8ceb4c3b8c3e9f14a677957f93095fbb04d96de909","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:contact-process of arXiv:2507.00329, 'Oriented bond-site percolation in random environment and contact processes with periodic r'] Let $G=(V',E')$ be a graph with vertex set $V'$ and edge set $E'$. Let $\mathbb{X},\mathbb{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}$ be random closed sets. We associate to vertices $v\in V'$ i.i.d.\ recovery times $\mathbb{Y}_v$ distributed like $\mathbb{Y}$ as well as to edges $e\in E'$ i.i.d.\ infection times $\mathbb{X}_e$ distributed like $\mathbb{X}$. Given an initial configuration of infected vertices $J_0\subset V'$, we define the set $J_t$ of infected vertices at time $t\geq0$ as follows:
    $v\in J_t$ if and only if there exists $v_0\in J_0$ and a finite path $\gamma=(v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k=v)$ together with contact times $0=t_{-1}\leq t_0\leq t_1,\dots,t_{k-1}\leq t_k=t$ such that,
    $$t_i\in \mathbb{X}_{(v_i,v_{i+1})}\quad \text{ for every } 0\leq i\leq k-1
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    [t_{i-1},t_i]\cap \mathbb{Y}_{v_i}=\emptyset \quad\text{ for every } 0\leq i \leq k.$$
    We say the contact process dies out if $J_t=\emptyset$ for some $t\geq0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:01:01.831134+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6af90830cb80ac2e4c7d425d881a2e6d5844369a2cda6eb604afc0c9725148a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:logarithmic-pairing of arXiv:2609.00556, 'Higgs--Demailly System and Positivity of Higgs Bundles'] Define
\begin{align}

 B,\partial^{h_{\rm ref}}u
 \right\rangle_{h_{\rm ref},\omega},

 \mathscr Q_\theta(u)

 \sqrt{-1}\Lambda_\omega
 [\theta,g^{-1}\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*g
          -\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*],
 u
 \right\rangle_{h_{\rm ref}}.
 
\end{align}
Then
\begin{align}
&\left\langle
 \sqrt{-1}\Lambda_\omega
 \left(
   \bar\partial B
   +[\theta,g^{-1}\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*g
                 -\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*]
 \right),u
\right\rangle_{h_{\rm ref}}
\notag\\

=

\[

 \qquad
 \mathscr Q_\theta(u)\geq0.
\]
If \(\|u\|_{C^0}\leq L\), then there exists a constant \(c_L>0\),

There exists a Skorohod coupling of the disorder matrices $\bG^N$ for which, with probability one over $(\bG^N)_{N\ge1}$, 
we have as $N\to\infty$ the following weak convergence, restricted to the time interval $[q_*,1]$:
\[
(\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N},\rho_{\vY,N},\rho_{D,N},\rho_{V,N},\rho_{U,N},\rho_{\rrr,N},\rho_{\www,N})
\Longrightarrow
(\mu,\rho_{\vY},\rho_D,\rho_V,\rho_U,\rho_\rrr,\rho_\www).
\]
Here the former measures are as in Definition~\ref{d:discrete.occ}, and the latter are as in Definition~\ref{d:cts.occ}.

\begin{proof} 
It follows from Definition~\ref{d:discrete.occ} that for all bounded continuous $f$, we have
	\[
	\int_{\R^4}
	f(t,y) \rho_{\vY,N,t}(d\vy)
	= \bE_{\bG^N} 
	\Big[f(t, \vY^{\frozen,\bullet,N}(t))
	\Big]
	\]
where $\bE_{\bG^N}$ is expectation with respect to $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$, and $Y^{\frozen,\bullet,N}$ is the piecewise constant variant of $Y^{\frozen,N}$.  By Theorem~\ref{t:tightness}, we have a Skorohod coupling along which $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}\Rightarrow\mu$. This implies, for each fixed $t$,
	\begin{align*}
	&\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_{\R^4}
		f(t,y) \rho_{\vY,N,t}(d\vy)
	=\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\bE_{\bG^N} f(t,
		\vY^{\frozen,\bullet,N}(t))
	= \bE f(t,\vY^\frozen(t))
	=
	\int_{\R^4}f(t,y) \rho_{Y,t}(d\vy)
	\end{align*}
almost surely, which implies 
$\rho_{\vY,N,t}\Rightarrow\rho_{Y,t}$ for each $t$. This can be integrated over $0\le t\le 1$ using the dominated convergence theorem, so 
	\begin{align*}
	&\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\int_{[0,1]\times\R^4}f(t,\vy) \rho_{\vY,N}(dt\,d\vy)
	-\int_{[0,1]\times\R^4}f(t,\vy) \rho_{\vY}(dt\,d\vy) \\
	&\qquad=
	\lim_{N\to\infty} \int_0^1\bE_{\bG^N} f(t,
		\vY^{^\frozen,\bullet,N}(t))
	-\int_0^1 \bE f(t,\vY^\frozen(t))

	\end{align*}

	= \bE_{\bG^N} \int_0^1
	f(t,\vY^{\frozen,\bullet,N}(t))
	\,\nu_{D,N}(dt)\,.
	\]
It follows that, for any bounded continuous function $f$, we have

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","Ω = R^n, or Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary (an extension domain); for W^{1,p}_0 any open Ω","compactness statements require Ω bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492521+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, embedding theorems, compactness","id":"claim_b6b2ca78bf6d58de47692329336d31951c68502f00143a7631b268179675e75b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 1, 1 ≤ p < ∞, and let Ω ⊂ R^n be either all of R^n or a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary (more generally a bounded W^{1,p}-extension domain). For p < n write p* = np/(n − p) (Sobolev conjugate, 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n).

(i) Subcritical case p < n (Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) continuously. On R^n one has the scale-invariant form ||u||_{L^{p*}(R^n)} ≤ C(n,p) ||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(R^n). For bounded Ω, W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every 1 ≤ q ≤ p*, and the embedding is COMPACT for every q < p* (Rellich–Kondrachov), but not for q = p*.

(ii) Critical case p = n ≥ 2. W^{1,n}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every q ∈ [1, ∞), compactly when Ω is bounded, but W^{1,n}(Ω) is NOT contained in L^∞(Ω): in the unit disc of R^2, u(x) = log log(1 + 1/|x|) belongs to W^{1,2} and is unbounded. (For n = 1, W^{1,1} on an interval consists of absolutely continuous functions and does embed into the continuous functions.)

(iii) Supercritical case p > n (Morrey). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{0,γ}(Ω̄) with γ = 1 − n/p: every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) has a representative that is Hölder continuous with exponent γ, and ||u||_{C^{0,γ}(Ω̄)} ≤ C ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}. For bounded Ω the embedding into C^{0,β}(Ω̄) is compact for every β < γ, in particular into C(Ω̄).

(iv) Higher order, Ω bounded Lipschitz, k ≥ 1. If kp < n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) with 1/q = 1/p − k/n, compactly into L^r for r < q. If kp > n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{k − ⌊n/p⌋ − 1, γ}(Ω̄), where γ = ⌊n/p⌋ + 1 − n/p when n/p is not an integer, and γ is any number in (0,1) when n/p is an integer.

(v) Zero boundary values. Every statement holds for W^{1,p}_0(Ω) (resp. W^{k,p}_0) on an ARBITRARY open set Ω, bounded for the compactness claims, with no regularity of ∂Ω, because such functions extend by zero to W^{1,p}(R^n).

Where it fails. Without an extension property (Lipschitz or comparable boundary) the embedding W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) can fail for bounded Ω: there are bounded domains with a sufficiently sharp outward cusp on which it is false. Compactness fails at the critical exponent q = p* (the rescaled bubbles u_λ(x) = λ^{(n−p)/p} u(λx) keep constant L^{p*} norm and W^{1,p} seminorm but converge weakly to 0) and fails on unbounded domains such as R^n (translates of one bump). The inequality ||u||_{L^q(R^n)} ≤ C||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} is FALSE for every q ≠ p*: dilation invariance forces q = p*. W^{1,n} ↪ L^∞ fails for n ≥ 2 as shown. The Hölder exponent in (iii) cannot be improved beyond 1 − n/p in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) probability measure on the input coordinates","f is a bounded, typically boolean, function of finitely many coordinates","existence of a randomized decision tree computing f exactly, with well-defined per-coordinate revealments","revealments computed under the same measure used for Var(f) and Inf_i(f)"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972746+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b71abce6cf84475d6e6984b0c6a4d7ee2a29f331d669301354889ab502d006c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} be evaluated exactly by a randomized decision-tree algorithm T that, over its internal randomness, queries coordinate i with probability delta_i(T) (its revealment), and let Var(f) denote the variance of f under a product probability measure on the input. The OSSS inequality states Var(f) <= sum_{i=1}^n delta_i(T) Inf_i(f), where Inf_i(f) is the influence of coordinate i under the same measure. Consequently, exhibiting an algorithm with small maximal revealment forces the sum of influences to be large, giving lower bounds on total influence and noise sensitivity via algorithmic constructions; for critical planar percolation, an exploration-path algorithm gives revealments comparable to arm-event probabilities, and combined with quasi-multiplicativity this yields sharp bounds on noise sensitivity and, via the Duminil-Copin-Raoufi-Tassion route, on sharpness of the phase transition in all dimensions without reflection positivity or duality. The inequality does not directly compute Inf_i itself, does not apply to non-product (dependent-coordinate) measures without a separate generalization, and it is an inequality rather than an identity, so it can be loose or even vacuous if the algorithm chosen is not well matched to f's structure. Typical failure: Plugging in a naive, non-adaptive algorithm (e.g. querying coordinates in a fixed deterministic order) and expecting a sharp bound; the inequality is only informative when the algorithm is cleverly matched to the function's geometric structure, such as an exploration process for a crossing event, and a poorly chosen algorithm produces a valid but essentially vacuous bound that is easy to mistake for a genuine obstruction to sharper influence or sensitivity estimates. Canonical reference: O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm and Servedio, 2005, Proceedings of the 46th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science; Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion, 2019, Annals of Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.584221+00:00","domain":"combinatorics","id":"claim_b77b87e08d73f761ed5ff25ec04b1c15efb7d1bd8d686854a4b8fb7376cb33b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider finite rooted trees with vertices labeled from a fixed well-quasi-ordered set. One tree topologically embeds in another if there is an injective, ancestor-order-preserving map of vertices to vertices sending labels to weakly larger labels and sending each edge to a path, these paths being internally vertex-disjoint. Kruskal's tree theorem states that finite labeled trees, ordered by topological embeddability, form a well-quasi-order: in any infinite sequence of such trees, some tree embeds into a later one. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:16.152996+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b77f7def15b8beed58d0a2a6f104076a097150a5d2a84ba2160773e9755c1f2f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Arizmendi and Perales {\cite[Proposition 3.3) of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] {arizmendi2018cumulants-joctsa}}]
Given $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$, the finite free cumulants $\kappa_{1}^{(d)}, \dots, \kappa_{d}^{(d)}$ are unique maps satisfying the following conditions. 
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f)$ is a polynomial in $p_{1}(f), \dots, p_{i}(f)$ with leading term $\frac{d^{i-1}}{(d)_{\underline{i}}} p_{i}(f)$. 
That is, there exists a polynomial $F_{i}$ in $i-1$ variables such that 
$$
\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f) = \frac{d^{i-1}}{(d)_{\underline{i}}}p_{i}(f) + F_{i}(p_{1}(f), \dots, p_{i-1}(f)).
$$ 
\item Homogeneity: $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(D_{r}f) = r^{i}\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f)$ for any $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and $i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$.
\item Additivity: $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f \boxplus_{d} g) = \kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f) + \kappa_{i}^{(d)}(g)$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:29:00.269210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7911cc88f0c4e9cbcd38f7c8f3a5c04","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality in the replace-one bound (in either form) holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates; equality in the bound with arbitrary Z_i holds if and only if, in addition, Z_i = E[Z | X_j, j != i] almost surely for every i. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Nonzero feasible rank-at-most-r target; full-row-rank design and noiseless labels","B0=0; nondegenerate Gaussian A0","Step schedule fixed conditional on design independently of A0","Isotropic population prediction risk"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:54:30.733548+00:00","domain":"LoRA gradient dynamics and excess risk","id":"claim_b794a3607b41a0b1d035b802d142402b820e6cfccddde42c0fd0b798721070a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; T419-C006 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claim. Let Delta be any nonzero m-by-p matrix of rank at most r and X a fixed full-row-rank p-by-n design. For noiseless Y=Delta X, the global rank-r empirical least-squares estimate equals Delta, so its isotropic population parameter risk is zero. Simultaneous factor GD from B0=0 and nondegenerate Gaussian A0, with any step schedule fixed conditional on X independently of A0, almost surely has B_t A_t != Delta at every finite t. Each finite-iterate entry is a polynomial in A0; at A0=0 both factors remain zero, so a residual entry corresponding to nonzero Delta_ij has a nonzero constant term. Its zero set is Lebesgue-null, and a countable union over t remains null. This also excludes exact recovery at an almost-surely finite integer stopping time selecting these iterates. Consequently a finite-time constant-factor comparison to the noiseless zero-risk benchmark needs a limit, an additive optimization tolerance or other qualification. This does not cover arbitrary initialization-dependent adaptive step rules and does not refute the intended infinite-time or noise-dependent-stopping target.","status":"unverified"}
