{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents and multiplicities are measurable and f-invariant, constant a.e. when mu is ergodic; the subspaces are measurable and Df-equivariant","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_bf769101c6fe8505c33df1958690eca784e10a921c4b8007d731b67c59e25eca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x) and the multiplicities dim E_i(x) are measurable and f-invariant, and if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere; the subspaces E_i(x) are measurable and Df-equivariant, Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(fx). The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^1_loc(R^d), Lebesgue measure","averaging sets shrink nicely to x (bounded eccentricity); unbounded eccentricity breaks the theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751496+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_bf8b9a4334173b1b42ad155604b5dabb90ceb6c0b2b33e20cc69bf001127fc26","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be in L^1_loc(R^d). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy -> 0 as r -> 0; such an x is called a Lebesgue point of f. In particular the averages of f over shrinking balls converge to f(x) for a.e. x. The result persists if balls are replaced by any family of sets U_r shrinking NICELY to x, meaning U_r is contained in B(x,r) and |U_r| >= c |B(x,r)| for a fixed c > 0 (cubes centred at x, for instance). It FAILS for families of arbitrary eccentricity: in R^2 there is an integrable f whose averages over rectangles centred at x with sides parallel to the axes and both side lengths tending to 0 fail to converge at almost every x, because the strong maximal function is not of weak type (1,1). The a.e. exceptional set genuinely depends on f and cannot be taken empty. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Chapter 3, Corollary 1.5 and Section 1.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.969953+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bfaf6c758aebeb9ade6830f3d3db0a0f0ff9ce1c2b2b960272aa4c5c4020aac9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (\textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $\mathsf{S}\in\{{ \mathsf{P}},{\mathsf{R}}\}$, $r\in\N$, and
$\lambda\in(0,\infty)$.  For each $n\in\N$, let\footnote{The sum $\sum_{j=1}^0$ is understood to be empty.}

\noi
\begin{align*}
 F_n\in\cC_{r}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP),
 \quad
 B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_{n,j},
\AND
 B_{n,j}\in\cC_{j}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP).
\end{align*} 

\noi
Suppose that $F_n+B_n$ satisfies the lattice condition
\eqref{cond_La} with shift $\theta_n>0$, and define
$X_n:=\theta_n+F_n+B_n$.  Put
$\eps_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\norm{B_{n,j}}_4$.
For every $n$ such that $\theta_n>0$, with
$c_{\theta_n}:=(1-e^{-\theta_n})/\theta_n$, define

\noi
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak{R}_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n)
 :=
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[ 2 \|F_n\|_4\eps_n+\eps_n^2+\frac{\eps_n}{2}
 + 14\bigl(1+ \|F_n\|_4+\eps_n\bigr)^3\eps_n  \bigg]
 +\left(1+\frac{c_{\theta_n}}2\right)\eps_n.
 
\end{align}
Then,

\noi
\begin{align} 
\begin{aligned}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n,  P_{\theta_n}\bigr)  
   & \leq
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[  | m_2(F_n)-\theta_n|  + \frac{2r-1}{2r}\sqrt{\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)} \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad  + \frac23\sqrt{m_2(F_n)\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)}
 +b_{\mathsf{S}}\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)  \bigg]  
   +\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n).
\end{aligned}
\end{align}

\noi
In particular, $\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,0)=0$.  Hence, when
$\eps_n=0$, one has $B_n=0$ and \eqref{pert_main_bdd} reduces exactly
to Corollary~\ref{cor_P_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={ \mathsf{P}}$ and to
Corollary~\ref{cor_R_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={\mathsf{R}}$.

If, in addition,
$
 \big(\theta_n,  m_2(F_n), \mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)\big)
 \xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}(\lambda, \lambda, 0)$
and
 $\eps_n\to0$,
then
$\dTV(X_n, P_\lambda)\to0$,
the first four moments of $X_n$ converge to those of
$P_\lambda$, and $(X_n^4)_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable.
In the Rademacher case, under $m_2(F_n)\to\lambda$, the condition
$\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{R}}(F_n)\to0$ is equivalent to
$\cR(F_n)\to0$ and $\cM(F_n)\to0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.551427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bfd6ea94967816b09342b71cb9d9f8638fb720adab7c3deb916c0b1890d5b6b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 8 (Fourier transforms of radial homogeneous distributions) of arXiv:2609.01403, '2609.01403'] Under the normalization \eqref{eq:fourier-normalization}, the following
statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item For \(0<\alpha<n\),
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal F^{-1}(|\xi|^{-\alpha})(x)
    =

\end{equation}
The family \(|\xi|^{-\alpha}\), initially defined as a tempered
distribution for \(\Re\alpha<n\), admits a meromorphic continuation
to \(\alpha\in\mathbb C\), with possible poles at
$\alpha=n,n+2,n+4,\cdots$.
The identity \eqref{eq:riesz-kernel-formula} extends accordingly by
meromorphic continuation. Away from the origin, this continuation is
represented by
$\kappa_{n,\alpha}|x|^{\alpha-n}$.
In particular, if \(\alpha=-2k\), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), then

Then

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.817132+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bfe34b4620b759b26ab1274ad07ca3b34dc6edf94c99aebfc801f306734a9364","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:shift-stable-chart of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix an integer $d\geq1$ and $0<\gamma<1$.  A \emph{shift-stable $d$-chart
of depth $\gamma h$} is a family
$(B_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta_h}$, indexed by all sufficiently large integers
$h$ with $\Theta_h\ne\varnothing$, of primitive
$(d+1)$-subsets of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ containing zero for which there are
fixed integers $s\geq1$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_s$, and integer residuals
$x_\nu(\theta,h)$, such that, uniformly for $\theta\in\Theta_h$ and
$J\in\mathbb Z$ with $0\leq J\leq\gamma h$,
\begin{equation}
 |(h-J)B_\theta|
 =\sum_{\nu=1}^{s}c_\nu
  \binom{x_\nu(\theta,h)-J+d}{d},
 \qquad x_\nu(\theta,h)-J\geq0.
\end{equation}
Terms for which $x_\nu(\theta,h)-J<0$ throughout the shift window are
omitted.  This condition is satisfied, in particular, when the family
remains in one finite Hilbert-numerator chamber throughout the window.
Here $d=|B_\theta|-1$ is the dimension of the ambient simplex and the degree
of the binomial coefficient as a polynomial in its upper index; it is not
the dimension of the associated projective curve.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.498381+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0026b7000ee4cc3be8d71c6dfe6267809a0564af1a38fde5f0375e3ca531374","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal invariance of Coulomb gas integral of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i \cdot z_i + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_j \cdot \xi_j$ be a divisor on the Riemann sphere $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$, where each screening charge $\tau_j \in \{-2a,\, 2(a + b)\}$ is chosen so that its conformal dimension satisfies $\lambda_b(\tau_j) = 1$. Let $h: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \to \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a Möbius transformation, and define
\[
\zeta_j := h(\xi_j), \quad h(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) := \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i \cdot h(z_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_j \cdot \zeta_j.
\]

Then the Coulomb gas integral transforms covariantly under $h$ as
\begin{equation} 
\left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} h'(z_i)^{\lambda_b(\sigma_i)} \right) 
\oint_{h(\Gamma)} C_{(b)}[h(\boldsymbol{\sigma})] \, d\zeta_1 \cdots d\zeta_m
=
\oint_{\Gamma} C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] \, d\xi_1 \cdots d\xi_m,
\end{equation}
where $h(\Gamma)$ denotes the image of the integration contour $\Gamma$ under $h$.

Each differential $d\zeta_j$ transforms as $d\zeta_j = h'(\xi_j) \, d\xi_j$, and since $\lambda_b(\tau_j) = 1$, the integrand $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]\, d\xi_1 \cdots d\xi_m$ is invariant under pullback by $h$, up to the multiplicative factor $\prod_{i} h'(z_i)^{\lambda_b(\sigma_i)}$ determined by the insertion points.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fixed finite d,n,T and step gamma>0; bounded nonzero training inputs and bounded nonzero-input population independent of initialization","m=2N independent Gaussian hidden pairs with opposite fixed heads +/-nu,0<nu<=1; all parameters subsequently trained without tying","Squared empirical loss normalized by n; bounded labels; zero ReLU derivative at zero","Width tends to infinity before any time, sample-size or input-law limit; mathematical and literature review pending"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:15:10.683358+00:00","domain":"two-layer ReLU learning; population neural tangent kernel limits","id":"claim_c05778d0768f5d9377765bf96953205bc672897c685dd1f7ce32845f258f62b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical review pending; novelty unestablished. This is a finite-horizon supporting method, not full Target1 closure.

## 1. Finite-horizon transfer statement
Fix finite d,n,T, gamma>0, 0<nu<=1, Y<infinity, nonzero training inputs
x_1,...,x_n with norms <=M, and a probability law P supported on nonzero
inputs of norm <=M. Inputs and P are independent of initialization.
The loss is (1/(2n)) sum_i (f(x_i)-y_i)^2, with |y_i|<=Y.
Use m=2N neurons, f(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x).
For each independent W_l~N(0,I_d), initialize one pair at (nu,W_l),
(-nu,W_l); update every parameter by ordinary simultaneous GD of step gamma,
with derivative 1{w.x>0}. The pairing is only at initialization, not enforced.
Let H be the deterministic full initial kernel from C014 Section2:
H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z].
Let f^H_k be zero-start kernel GD with this H, the same sample and labels.
Then, as N tends to infinity,

 max_{k<=T} ||f_k-f^H_k||_{L2(P)} -> 0 in probability.       (1)

The event bounds proving this hold uniformly for every y in [-Y,Y]^n.
No positive training eigenvalue or nonzero gate margin is assumed. T is
fixed before this width limit; constants below can grow rapidly with T.

## 2. Width-independent finite-horizon bounds
Write u_j=1+||w_j(0)||. The empirical mean S_m=m^(-1)sum u_j^2 is a pair
average and tends almost surely to E(1+||W||)^2. Fix S above that expectation
and work on S_m<=S, an event eventually true almost surely.
Define H_0=D_0=0, R_0=Y. Given H_k,D_k,R_k, set
 A_k=1+H_k, B_k=1+D_k, c_k=gamma M R_k,
 H_{k+1}=H_k+c_k B_k, D_{k+1}=D_k+c_k A_k,
 R_{k+1}=R_k+M c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
Induction gives, uniformly over the label cube,
 |a_j(k)-a_j(0)|<=H_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||w_j(k)-w_j(0)||<=D_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 |a_j(k)|<=A_k u_j, ||w_j(k)||<=B_k u_j,
 ||r_k||/sqrt(n)<=R_k, where r_i=f_k(x_i)-y_i.
Indeed Cauchy-Schwarz in the exact parameter updates gives
 |Delta a_j|<=c_k B_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||Delta w_j||<=c_k A_k u_j/sqrt(m).
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz and homogeneous, so at every ||x||<=M,
 |Delta f_k(x)|<=||x|| c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
This proves the induction and a finite uniform output bound through T.
Let H,D,A,B,c denote maxima of these constants through the required steps.

## 3. Population gate bands shrink in L2, not just on the sample
Put L_m(x)=m^(-1)sum_j u_j^2 1{|w_j(0).x|<=D u_j||x||/sqrt(m)}.
For each training x_i, L_m(x_i)->0 almost surely. Also

 ||L_m||_{L2(P)} -> 0 almost surely.                         (2)

Proof: for fixed q>0, the pair-averaged integrable function
 Z_q(W)=(1+||W||)^2 P_x{|W.x|<=q(1+||W||)||x||}
has its empirical average tending to E Z_q by the ordinary scalar SLLN.
For m large with D/sqrt(m)<=q, integral L_m dP is bounded by that average.
For every fixed nonzero x, Gaussian W.x has no atom at zero; Fubini and
dominated convergence imply E Z_q->0 as q decreases to zero. Apply SLLN
simultaneously on countably many q=1,1/2,1/3,..., then let q decrease.
Thus integral L_m->0 almost surely. Since 0<=L_m<=S_m, its squared L2 norm
is at most S_m integral L_m. The finite training-point assertion follows
by the same fixed-q argument without integration over P.
This is uniform over trajectories obeying Section2; no independence between
trained gates and initialization is asserted or needed.

## 4. Both train and cross kernels remain close
Let H^m_k be the empirical full tangent kernel at step k. Product expansion
and the movement bounds give, for every training point x_i,

 |H^m_k(x,x_i)-H^m_0(x,x_i)|
 <= ||x||||x_i|| [C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(L_m(x)+L_m(x_i))],       (3)

where C=D(B+1)+H(A+1) is finite. The RF-product part is bounded by
D(B+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). The readout-square change is bounded by
H(A+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). A changed gate at x forces the initial weight into
the band defining L_m(x); likewise at x_i. These inequalities remain valid
when a trained preactivation equals zero, using the stated derivative.
Equations (2),(3) imply uniform-in-k convergence of the training normalized
Gram matrices and of the population cross rows, relative to their INITIAL
empirical kernels. In particular define K^m_k=(H^m_k(x_i,x_l)/n),
b^m_k(x)=(H^m_k(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i. Their respective operator and L2(row)
differences from step0 tend to zero; the latter is bounded by
M^2[C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(||L_m||_2+max_i L_m(x_i))].

At initialization, each independent pair contributes the same feature
kernel F_W(x,z)=ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z.
It satisfies |F_W(x,z)|<=M^2(||W||^2+1). Its squared envelope is integrable.
Thus the empirical initial training kernel tends to K=(H(x_i,x_l)/n).
For the population cross row b(x)=(H(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i, independence of pairs
and Fubini give E||b^m_0-b||_2^2<=M^4 E(||W||^2+1)^2/N.
Hence this difference tends to zero in probability too. This explicitly
controls the missing test-to-training kernel; it is not inferred from K.

## 5. Discrete-step gate remainder off the sample
The exact prediction update is
 f_{k+1}(x)=f_k(x)-gamma b^m_k(x).v_k+Z_k(x), v_k=r_k/sqrt(n),
where, writing h=ReLU(w.x), h'=ReLU((w+Delta w).x),
 Z_k(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j[Delta a_j(h'-h)
             +a_j(h'-h-1{w.x>0}Delta w_j.x)].
If the second summand is nonzero, the segment from w to w+Delta w crosses
its gate at x. Because both endpoints are within the Section2 cumulative
radius of w(0), the initial preactivation lies in the D-band above.
The Lipschitz inequality therefore gives

 |Z_k(x)|<=||x||[c^2 A B S/sqrt(m)+c A^2 L_m(x)].           (4)

It follows that max_{k<T}||Z_k||_{L2(P)}->0 and max_{k<T,i}|Z_k(x_i)|->0.
No approximation replaces discrete GD by flow.

## 6. Close the training and population prediction recurrences
Let v^H_{k+1}=(I-gamma K)v^H_k, v^H_0=-y/sqrt(n).
The true normalized residual update is
 v_{k+1}=(I-gamma K^m_k)v_k+z_k,
where ||z_k||<=max_i |Z_k(x_i)|. Sections2,4,5 imply by finite induction
max_{k<=T}||v_k-v^H_k||->0 in probability, uniformly over bounded labels.
For example each error is bounded by ||I-gamma K|| times the previous
error plus gamma ||K^m_k-K|| R_k+||z_k||. The multiplier is finite; neither
a contraction nor a spectral gap is required at this finite horizon.
Both output initializations are exactly zero. Sum the prediction updates:
 f_k-f^H_k=-gamma sum_{j<k}[(b^m_j-b).v_j+b.(v_j-v^H_j)]
                         +sum_{j<k}Z_j.
The population L2 norm is bounded by the sum of cross-kernel errors times
R_j, deterministic ||b||_2 times training residual errors, and remainder
norms. Every term tends to zero by the preceding sections, proving (1).
The same controlling random bounds work for all bounded label vectors.
For any bounded teacher, clean risks averaged over the bounded independent
label noises consequently converge uniformly through T in probability,
by Cauchy-Schwarz and the finite uniform output bound from Section2.


Here zero-start kernel GD means f^H_{k+1}(x)=f^H_k(x)-(gamma/n)sum_i H(x,x_i)(f^H_k(x_i)-y_i), with f^H_0=0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:32:34.746300+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c059a854a6d0f3983951de7ed37203b1b4c502b645c83e7873b05ceef5fa6a29","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma mart_bound_dim_free of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{Y}_i$, $\mathbf{V}_i$ and $\mathbf{Z}_k$ be as in Proposition~(prop:mart_bound of the paper), i.e., $(\mathbf{Y}_i)_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{H}(d)$ is a matrix-valued stochastic process adapted to filtration $(\mathscr{F}_i)_{i=1}^n$,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.755110+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c05ff4c09ef60b1f7cf58fab071a24827d69eb7c5fde2e3587fd82d0cfe9bd78","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:abstract-kato-slice of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $t_0\in\mathbb R^N$, there exists a complex neighborhood
$\mathcal U\subset\mathbb C^N$ of $t_0$ such that the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The family of sesquilinear forms $(a_z)_{z\in\mathcal U}$, defined by
\begin{equation}
 a_z(u,v):=\mathcal E(m_zu,m_{\bar z}v),
 \qquad \operatorname{Dom} a_z=V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C},
 
\end{equation}
is a holomorphic family of closed sectorial forms with common domain; in Kato's
terminology, it is a family of type~\textnormal{(a)}.  Let $\widehat A_z$
denote the associated $m$-sectorial operator.  For real $t\in\mathcal U\cap\mathbb R^N$,
this agrees with the previously defined $\widehat A_t$.
\item For every $z\in\mathcal U$, the operator $\widehat A_z$ has compact
resolvent, and the map
$z\mapsto(\widehat A_z+1)^{-1}$ from $\mathcal U$ into
$\mathcal L(L^2(\mu_0))$ is holomorphic in the operator norm.
\item Suppose that a positively oriented contour $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ lies
in the resolvent set of $\widehat A_{t_0}$ and encloses a finite cluster of its
eigenvalues.  After shrinking $\mathcal U$ if necessary, $\Gamma$ remains in
the resolvent set of $\widehat A_t$ for every real
$t\in\mathcal U\cap\mathbb R^N$, and
\begin{equation}
 R_{\Gamma}(t)
 =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma}
   (\zeta-\widehat A_t)^{-1}\,d\zeta
 
\end{equation}
is a real-analytic family of finite-rank projections satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 \rankR_{\Gamma}(t)=\rankR_{\Gamma}(t_0).
\end{equation*}
The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of
$\widehat A_t|_{\operatorname{Ran}R_{\Gamma}(t)}$, and hence its
discriminant, depend real-analytically on $t$.
\end{enumerate}
If $t\mapsto(\lambda(t),\Phi(t))$ is a local real-analytic eigenpair branch of
$\widehat A_t$, normalized by
$\left\|\Phi(t)\right\|_{L^2(\mu_0)}=1$, then $\Phi$ is real analytic as a map with
values in $V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C}$ and
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{t_k}\lambda(t)
 =(\partial_{t_k}a_t)(\Phi(t),\Phi(t)),
 \qquad 1\le k\le N.
 
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.474167+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c075c73823754600d1d2ed37cce52c5b8c12db74ea7ef124c59660be6b85772a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Let
  $Z \sim \mathcal{F}(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha > 0$,
  and let 
  $W$ be a random variable whose distribution function $F_W$
  is absolutely continuous on $[K, +\infty)$ for some $K>0$, with 
  density function~$f_W$.
\begin{enumerate}[i)] 
\item Kolmogorov bound. For any $\alpha >0$, we have
\begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
\mathrm{d}_{K} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) ) \leq (\alpha + 1)F_{W}(K) + \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}
\item Wasserstein bound.
  Let $\alpha > 1$ and
  $p \in (1,\alpha)$ such that $\esp[\vert W \vert^{p}] < \infty$.
  We have
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
      \mathrm{d}_{W} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) ) \leq \esp [\vert W \vert^{p} ]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}} & + \Big(
      \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - 1}\Big)
      F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  rF_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r,\numberthis
\end{align*}
  where $q = p/(p-1)$ denotes the conjugate of $p$. 
\item Moment bound.
  Let $\alpha > 0$ and
  $b \in (0, \alpha)$,
  assume that $W$ is a.s. nonnegative and that there exists $p \in (1, \alpha / b)$ such that $\esp[W^{pb}] < \infty$, with $q = p/(p-1)$. Then, we have  
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
\vert \esp [W^{b} ] - \esp [Z^{b}]\vert \leq \esp [ W^{pb}]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}} & + \Big( \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{b}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - b}\Big) F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  r^{b}F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}

\item Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $b \in (0, \alpha)$.
  Suppose that there exists $p \in (1, \alpha / b)$ such that $\esp[\vert W \vert^{p}]< \infty$, with $q = p/(p-1)$. Then, we have 
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
      \mathrm{d}_{W_b} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) )
      \leq \esp [ W^{pb}]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}}
      &
      + \Big(
      \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{b}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{2\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - b}\Big)
       F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  r^{b}F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:57:16.077138+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c07e826dd6517e2ca595ad72af5006a8f4392f1a2668b60a9c569a6486363fa6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo genen of arXiv:2507.00737, 'Dispersion models on a circle: universal properties and asymptotic results'] Consider a sequence of DDM\xspace (or ${\sf CDM}\xspace$) such that, for some sequence of times $(t_n,n\geq 0)$,   
	\[
	\left(\alpha_n S^{(n)}(t_n,x),x\in [0,1]\right)\xrightarrow[n]{(d)} \left(S^{\infty}(x),x \in [0,1]\right) 
	\]
	where $\alpha_n/n \to 0$ and $\alpha_n\to+\infty$, with $S^\infty(1)<0$, and where the convergence holds in $C[0,1]$ (or in $D[0,1]$).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.823508+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0a6f28c660c1e769b888b2c1bd6c56a80bcea8d52b84044883a319733a1ef80","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:critical-window-saturation of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq3$.  For each $h\geq2$, put
\[
 H_{h,k}=(k-1)h^{k-2},\qquad
 \mathcal M_{h,k}
 =\{A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,H_{h,k}\}:0\in A,\ |A|=k\}.
\]
The maps from $\mathcal M_{h,k}$ onto the realized weak types and onto the
realized ordered $h$-addition-table types are surjective.  Moreover, as
$h\to\infty$,
\[
 |\mathcal M_{h,k}|=\binom{H_{h,k}}{k-1}
 =\Theta_k\!\left(h^{(k-1)(k-2)}\right),
\]
and both target sets have the same order of magnitude.  Consequently, the
average fibre of either type map has order $\Theta_k(1)$, and choosing one
representative from each fibre gives a positive-proportion subfamily on which
the map is injective.  For either type map, such a full-order subfamily may
be chosen entirely among representatives of maximal-rank weak types, and
hence inside the exact core $[0,h^{k-2}]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.953522+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0f6569fe40b75e82233252e0aa32767f8b51829c2c878837afe78f36ffb1f4e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 6 (Gaussian-noise bulk and full-trace LSS) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let $f$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Gaussian-f-assumptions-main}, let $\lambda\ge0$ be

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0fc8f01bf0470a4e19c40cfcbd48f63ad3e9919d3e37b9d46aff505e0204a9c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 187 (approximate quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, define $\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq

Denote also $E^{\sigma,\tau}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\tau}-\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$. We define likewise $\Delta\tilde{Q}^\frozen$ using increments of $X^\frozen$. Then,

A similar relation holds between $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}$ and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\Ising}$, and likewise between

{"assumptions":["the per-sample relative L2 loss as used by the EMIT/OCO-2 stacking pools; independent errors across rows","the multiplicative-versus-additive question is empirical and is measured by ens_rmt_elast.py (P21 of the RMT program)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T11:47:28.061008+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / weighted regression","id":"claim_c109e1a78941f0a6a45f877d2453aa489942de8d28e336dd0f0d21122d68470e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a stack (or any linear predictor) under the per-sample relative L2 loss, mean over rows of ||y_i - yhat_i||^2 / ||y_i||^2, is weighted least squares with case weights s_i = 1 / ||y_i||^2. By the two-regimes corollary those are Aitken's variance-stabilising weights exactly when the error scale is proportional to the target norm (multiplicative error, elasticity of log ||e_i|| on log ||y_i|| equal to one); then the relative-metric fit is the efficient one and its optimism is 2m/n relative to its own noise level, regardless of how concentrated 1/||y_i||^2 is. If the error carries an additive floor, the rows with the smallest targets - exactly the rows the relative weights concentrate on - have the largest floor relative to their target, the concentration re-enters, and Kish's n_eff of the relative weights measures how far the fit is from balanced. The discriminating measurement is the elasticity of the out-of-fold residual norm to the target norm and the nonnegative fit ||e_i||^2 = a + b ||y_i||^2 (the floor share a / (a + b median ||y||^2)) on the calibration rows; on a pool whose targets vary by orders of magnitude (the EMIT radiance outputs) the question is live, on one whose targets are homogeneous (the OCO-2 retrievals, n_eff within a few percent of n) the two metrics coincide and it is moot.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.594873+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c11c93a31630fef9ceceed0d5860dd7b8408b9f813e6ced1defab956704fd454","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398, '\\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Recent work has shown that sub-Gaussian random variables are dominated in convex order by a sharp multiple of a Gaussian. We study the analogous question for the sub-Gamma class underlying Bernstein's inequality, with the Laplace law as the majorant. Here the moment generating function is controlled by a Bernstein-type bound over a finite range of frequencies, rather than by a purely quadratic bound. We derive a variational formula for the optimal multiple, show that it is strictly larger than the natural scale $σ\\vee α$, and prove that this value is sharp, being attained by an asymmetric two-point distribution. We then turn to the sub-exponential class, which has a quadratic bound as in the sub-Gaussian case, but only over a bounded range as in the sub-Gamma case. Interestingly, the sub-exponential class displays a different behavior: the optimal multiple is exactly $σ\\vee α$, but is attained only when $α\\leq σ$; when $α> σ$, the constant remains sharp, but equality cannot hold for any non-affine convex function. Both results rely on a sharp finite-range variant of the Kearns-Saul inequality, which is of independent interest. (abstract text taken from the arXiv listing metadata; the TeX carried no abstract environment)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.016157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c12bf9d3c3a8abb63308ee247eecf7accaa4b1b45fcd8237561c328d3a969ba9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \begin{enumerate}
\item A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Kato class measure} if it satisfies \( \lim_{\alpha \to \infty}\|U_\alpha \mu\|_{\infty, q} =0.\) Denote by \(\mathcal{K}\) the set of all Kato class measures.
\item  A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Dynkin class measure} if it satisfies \(\|U_1 \mu\|_{\infty, q} < \infty \). Denote by \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of all Dynkin class measures.
\item A Kato class measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Green-tight measure} for \(R_1\) if, for any \(\varepsilon >0\), there exists a compact set \(K\) such that \(\|R_1(1_{K^c}\mu)\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon\). Denote by \(\mathcal{K}_\infty= \mathcal{K}_\infty(R_1)\) the set of all Green-tight measures.

\item A Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_1(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0\) the set of all Radon measures of finite energy integrals.

\item When $(\form,\dom)$ is transient, a Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it \(0\)-order finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0^{(0)}\) the set of all Radon measures of finite \(0\)-order energy integrals.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

For $c \\ge 1$ let $\\mathcal{W}_c = \\{w : \\mathbf{1}^T w = 1,\\ \\|w\\|_1 \\le c\\}$, let $\\hat w \\in \\arg\\min_{w \\in \\mathcal{W}_c} w^T \\hat\\Sigma w$ and $w^* \\in \\arg\\min_{w \\in \\mathcal{W}_c} w^T \\Sigma w$. Then (i) $|w^T(\\hat\\Sigma - \\Sigma)w| \\le \\varepsilon\\, c^2$ for every $w \\in \\mathcal{W}_c$, and (ii) $0 \\le \\hat w^T \\Sigma \\hat w - w^{*T}\\Sigma w^* \\le 2\\varepsilon c^2$. The long-only simplex is the case $c = 1$: the out-of-sample risk of the long-only plug-in exceeds the long-only oracle's by at most $2\\varepsilon$, whatever the conditioning of $\\Sigma$ or $\\hat\\Sigma$ and whatever the ratio $M/n$. {"assumptions":["Omega is bounded and open in R^n with C^1 (or piecewise C^1) boundary, so the divergence theorem applies","u is in C^2 up to the closure of Omega","for the Pohozaev form: u = 0 on the boundary, f is continuous, F(t) = integral_0^t f and F(0) = 0","for the nonexistence corollary: n >= 3, Omega star-shaped about the origin, f(u) = |u|^(p-1)u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2), and strict star-shapedness plus Hopf or unique continuation in the critical case"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396148+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, variational identities and nonexistence","id":"claim_c1db80201085a9bde5ef4703381e7acf672f7231bfba2a288812bae9f615e2b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with boundary of class C^1 and outward unit normal nu. RELLICH IDENTITY: for every u in C^2(closure of Omega) one has integral_Omega (x . grad u) Laplacian(u) dx = ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx - (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |grad u|^2 dS + integral_{boundary} (x . grad u)(du/dnu) dS. POHOZAEV IDENTITY: if in addition u = 0 on the boundary of Omega and -Laplacian(u) = f(u) in Omega with f continuous and F(t) = integral_0^t f(s) ds, then, since on the boundary grad u = (du/dnu) nu, the two boundary terms collapse and one gets ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx + (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |du/dnu|^2 dS = n integral_Omega F(u) dx. CONSEQUENCE (nonexistence): let n >= 3, let Omega be star-shaped with respect to the origin (x . nu >= 0 on the boundary) with C^1 boundary, and let f(u) = |u|^(p-1) u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2). Multiplying the equation by u gives integral |grad u|^2 = integral |u|^(p+1), while Pohozaev gives ((n-2)/2) integral |u|^(p+1) + (1/2) integral_{boundary}(x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = (n/(p+1)) integral |u|^(p+1). Since p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is exactly n/(p+1) <= (n-2)/2, the boundary term is <= 0 while star-shapedness makes it >= 0; hence it vanishes and integral |u|^(p+1) = 0 for p > (n+2)/(n-2). In the critical case p = (n+2)/(n-2) the two bulk terms cancel identically and one concludes only that (x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = 0 on the boundary; if Omega is strictly star-shaped (x . nu > 0) this forces du/dnu = 0 on the whole boundary and then u = 0 by the Hopf lemma or unique continuation. WHERE IT FAILS: star-shapedness is essential, not technical - on an annulus {a < |x| < b} in R^n there exist positive radial solutions of -Laplacian(u) = u^p vanishing on both boundary spheres for EVERY p > 1, including supercritical p (Kazdan-Warner). Regularity is also essential: the identity is proved for u in C^2 up to the boundary (it is valid for H^1_0 weak solutions only after elliptic regularity has upgraded them, which requires growth conditions on f), and the boundary must be regular enough for the divergence theorem. The origin matters: star-shapedness is with respect to the point used in the multiplier x . grad u.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726188+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_c1ffc6c7824bf7e532852028244a4f3f17e1d97b6a2fce726d3b11f59a0d7c16","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(R×R^n)} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²} the exponents must satisfy 2/q + n/r = n/2 exactly, and q ≥ 2 (and r ≥ 2). None of these can be relaxed, so an argument that 'interpolates' to a pair off the scaling line, or that uses a short-time-looking pair with q < 2, is wrong. Scaling: for f_λ(x) = f(λx) one has (e^{itΔ}f_λ)(x) = (e^{iλ²tΔ}f)(λx), hence ‖e^{itΔ}f_λ‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} = λ^{−2/q − n/r}‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} while ‖f_λ‖_{L²} = λ^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L²}. If 2/q + n/r ≠ n/2 the ratio of the two sides is λ^{n/2 − 2/q − n/r}, which is unbounded as λ → 0 or λ → ∞ for any fixed f ≠ 0. So an estimate off the scaling line fails for every nonzero f. Necessity of q ≥ 2 (the case r > 2; on the scaling line r = 2 forces q = ∞, so there is nothing to prove there): take φ ∈ S(R^n) and f_N = Σ_{k=1}^N e^{−i t_k Δ}φ with t_1 ≪ t_2 ≪ ... ≪ t_N separated enough that Σ_{j≠k}|t_k − t_j|^{−n(1/2−1/r)} is small for every k. Since |⟨e^{isΔ}φ, φ⟩| ≤ (4π|s|)^{−n/2}‖φ‖_{L¹}² → 0, the summands are almost orthogonal in L² and ‖f_N‖_{L²}² ≈ N‖φ‖²_{L²}; and for t within O(1) of t_k the dispersive estimate makes every term but the k-th small in L^r_x, so ‖e^{itΔ}f_N‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} ≳ N^{1/q}‖e^{itΔ}φ‖_{L^q_t([−1,1]) L^r_x}. The ratio is ≳ N^{1/q − 1/2}, unbounded when q < 2. Known excluded endpoints, where the pair is on the scaling line and q = 2 but the estimate is still false: (q,r) = (2,∞) for Schrödinger in n = 2 (Montgomery-Smith), and (q,r) = (2,∞) for the wave equation in n = 3 (Klainerman–Machedon). Also for the wave equation the Lebesgue-space estimate is stated with r < ∞; at r = ∞ one must pass to Besov spaces.","status":"unverified"}

\[

and the stopping time

\]
with the convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$.
For every $N\ge1$, after decreasing $t_0$ if necessary,
\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:32:58.363785+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c226a2c7f1b05f071ff1d7d3b07885611556c5fba25a89c94df53037ad91759a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition H-reduced graph of arXiv:2506.06559, 'Bi-infinite incipient cluster in high dimensions'] Let $G$ be a multigraph, we say that an edge $\{x,y\}$ is \emph{H-reducible} if $x$ and $y$ both have an edge degree at least 3 in $G$ and $x$, $y$ are only connected by one edge. 

We define a multigraph $\tilde{G}$, called \emph{H-reduction of $G$ by $\{x,y\}$}, in the following manner:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $x$ and $y$ have degree 3, then $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)\setminus \{x,y\}$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G) \setminus (\{\{x,z\}; x\sim_G z\} \cup \{\{y,z\}; y\sim_G z\}) \cup \{e_{x\setminus y}, e_{y \setminus x}\}$ with $e_{x\setminus y}=\{z_1, z_2\}$ where $z_1,z_2$ are the neighbours of $x$ which are not $y$ (and a symmetrical definition of $e_{y\setminus x}$)
\item if $x$ has degree 3, $y$ has degree at least 4, then then $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)\setminus \{x\}$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G) \setminus (\{\{x,z\}; z\sim_G z\} ) \cup \{e_{x\setminus y}\}$.
\item if $x$ and $y$ both have degree at least 4, then  $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G)\setminus \{x,y\}$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.351843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c24518fdc9bb8c7d0548e84810d71223fe8017f26734138f246472f2715b9fe5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 ($\AS$) of arXiv:2511.07350, 'Decoupling of clusters in independent sets in a percolated hypercube'] Define the random independent set $\hat{I}$ in $\Qp$ via the following procedure.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $\cH$ be $\cE$ or $\cO$, with probabilities proportional to $e^{\Psi^\cE}$ and $e^{\Psi^\cO}$ respectively.
		\item Let $\tilde{S}$ denote a subset of $\cH$ which includes each $v \in \cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{2^{-\N(v)}}{1 + 2^{-\N(v)}}$.
		\item If $\tilde{S}$ contains any triple of vertices which is \emph{2-linked},
        terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, remove all dimers from $\tilde{S}$ and let $S_1$ denote the resulting set of well-separated singletons (which share no neighbors).
		\item Let $S_2$ denote a collection of dimers constructed by including each $\{u,v\} \in \Dim^\cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{2^{-\N(\{u,v\})}}{1 + 2^{-\N(\{u,v\})}}$.
		\item If any neighbor of a dimer in $S_2$ also neighbors a vertex in $S_1$, {or if any pair of dimers in $S_2$ overlap or share a neighbor,}
        terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, let $\hat{S} = S_1 \cup S_2$.
		\item Let $\hat{I}$ denote the independent set with $\hat{I} \cap \cH = \hat{S}$ and with every vertex in $\Q \setminus \cH$
		which does not neighbor $\hat{S}$ included independently with probability $\fr{1}{2}$ each.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.524718+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2471f025e9ff4fdd0876a25b1c49abacb37c9c87a63abcb440a4c96f18cf150","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-thin-disk of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W\in(0, \frac{\gamma^2}{2})$. 
	    Sample $(\mathcal{W}, T) \sim \mathcal{M}^\mathrm{wed}(W) \times (1-\frac{2}{\gamma^2}W)^{-2}\textup{Leb}_{\mathbb{R}_+}$, and write $\mathcal{W} = \{(u, \mathcal{D}_u)\}$. The \emph{weight $W$ quantum disk} is the concatenation of the quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u \: : \: u \leq T\}$ according to the ordering induced by $u$. Its left (resp.\ right) boundary length is the sum of the left (resp.\ right) boundary lengths of its constituent $\mathcal{D}_u$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:45:32.074836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c250ebe165fef6567b4cc6693b2f130eee07803853c8239ccc8d8163db983e46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm sharp of arXiv:2411.14236, 'Size of chaos for Gibbs measures\\of mean field interacting diffusions'] Suppose that the following three conditions hold true.
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Log-Sobolev inequalities)
There exists $\rho > 0$ such that the non-linear and linear
log-Sobolev inequalities hold:
\[
\forall m \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X),
\qquad
2\rho H(m|m_*)
\leqslant
\begin{cases}
I(m|\Pi[m]),~\text{and} \\
I(m|m_*).
\end{cases}
\]
\item
(Transport inequalities)
There exists $\gamma \geqslant 0$ such that
for both $\mu = m^{N,k|[k-1]}_{*,\bm{x}^{[k-1]}}$ and $\mu = m_*$,
the probability measure $\mu$ satisfies the transport inequality
\[
\forall \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X),\qquad
\lvert \langle \nabla_1 W(x^k, \cdot),
\nu - \mu \rangle\rvert^2
\leqslant \gamma
H(\nu | \mu )
\]
uniformly in $k \in [N]$, $\bm{x}^{[k]} \in \mathcal X^{k}$.
\item
(Square integrability)
There exists $M \geqslant 0$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_{\mathcal X^2} \lvert \nabla_1 W(x,y)
- \langle \nabla_1 W(x,\cdot), m_*\rangle\rvert^2
m^{N,2}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} y) &\leqslant M, \\
\int_{\mathcal X} \lvert \nabla_1 W(x,x)
- \langle \nabla_1 W(x,\cdot), m_*\rangle\rvert^2
m^{N,1}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x) &\leqslant M.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
Then for all $k \in [N]$,
\[
\int_{\mathcal X^{k-1}} H(m^{N,k|[k-1]}_{*,\bm{x}^{[k-1]}} | m_*)
m^{N,k-1}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bm{x}^{[k-1]})
\leqslant
\frac{36\bigl(1+\frac\gamma\rho\bigr)^3M}{\rho N^2}
\biggl( k + \frac{3\gamma}{\rho}\biggr),
\]
and consequently,
\[
H(m^{N,k}_* | m_*^{\otimes k}) \leqslant
\frac{18\bigl(1+\frac\gamma\rho\bigr)^3M}{\rho N^2}
\biggl( k^2+ \Bigl(1+\frac{6\gamma}{\rho}\Bigr)k\biggr).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c26dbe1967eabd9968a58da43f41afdfaebe56d66241b6d5ae45dbc5bb37aa7a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Localized regime of the bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms (Proposition 4). Let X_1..X_n be independent with densities <=1 and Q(x)=x^T A x with A symmetric. (a) If some 2x2 PRINCIPAL submatrix B of A (two original coordinates i, j) is definite, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/sqrt(det B). Proof: condition on the other n-2 ORIGINAL coordinates (independent, so Fubini is genuine); given them Q is a quadratic-plus-linear form in (X_i, X_j); complete the square (B invertible), which shifts (X_i, X_j) and keeps their joint density <=1; for definite B each set {s <= y^T B y <= s+h} is an elliptic annulus of area at most pi h/sqrt(det B), so the conditional density is at most pi/sqrt(det B); average. (b) Hence if A has a 3x3 PRINCIPAL submatrix A_[S] all of whose eigenvalues have modulus >= c>0, and A_[S] is definite or diagonal, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/c: for definite A_[S], Cauchy interlacing puts both eigenvalues of every 2x2 principal block of A_[S] at modulus >= c with one sign, so det >= c^2; for diagonal A_[S], two of the three diagonal entries share a sign and form a definite diagonal block with det >= c^2. This contains the separable case. (c) For other well-conditioned blocks the bound K/c is not proved. A block may have no definite 2x2 principal block at all, e.g. [[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0]] (eigenvalues 2, -1, -1), and the rank-3 coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K||rho||_inf^{2/3} is false for general bounded densities on R^3: a density rho <= B placed on a thin shell around {S = s} gives p_S of order B s^{1/2}/sqrt(l1 l2 l3) for a definite form, unbounded in s. So the localized regime is settled for forms with a definite 2x2 principal block of determinant >= c^2, in particular when a well-conditioned 3x3 principal block is definite or diagonal; the other localized forms stay open, together with the DELOCALIZED forms (every 3x3 principal block near-singular), which is the CLT regime.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu and nu are measures on a common measurable space (X, Sigma); nu may be signed or complex","the epsilon-delta characterisation requires nu finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251367+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_c2889b5313a76c0af8fa3f49c365322c4a2e27291177d6ab0a182d09f34f8d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ be measures on the same measurable space $(X, \\Sigma)$, with $\\nu$ possibly signed or complex. $\\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\\mu$, written $\\nu \\ll \\mu$, if $\\nu(A) = 0$ for every $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ (for signed $\\nu$, equivalently $|\\nu|(A) = 0$, where $|\\nu|$ is the total variation). If $\\nu$ is FINITE (or finite signed/complex), this is equivalent to the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition: for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\\delta > 0$ with $|\\nu(A)| < \\varepsilon$ whenever $\\mu(A) < \\delta$; for infinite $\\nu$ the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition is strictly stronger (e.g. $\\nu(A) = \\int_A |x|^{-1}dx$ on $(0,1)$ has $\\nu \\ll$ Lebesgue but fails $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$). Any measure of the form $\\nu(A) = \\int_A f\\,d\\mu$ with $f \\geq 0$ measurable (or $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ for signed $\\nu$) satisfies $\\nu \\ll \\mu$; the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the converse under $\\sigma$-finiteness. $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ are mutually singular, $\\mu \\perp \\nu$, if there is $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ and $\\nu(X\\setminus A) = 0$. Lebesgue decomposition: for $\\sigma$-finite $\\mu, \\nu$ there is a unique splitting $\\nu = \\nu_{ac} + \\nu_s$ with $\\nu_{ac} \\ll \\mu$ and $\\nu_s \\perp \\mu$. Related but different: a FUNCTION $F: [a,b]\\to\\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous iff its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure iff $F(x) = F(a) + \\int_a^x F'$ with $F' \\in L^1$; the Cantor function is continuous, increasing, but not absolutely continuous (its measure is singular). Sharp edge: $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ is not symmetric, and $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ with $\\mu \\ll \\nu$ (equivalence) does not make the density bounded or bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356302+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c28ac3ae4d8e7ea64f8166fb4e0c699b29ccee4086b9570d919c226f9391a1e9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 232 (truncated Lipschitz algorithm) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Consider an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with input $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$. Denote its output $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. For $a\in [M]$, define the random variable
	\[\fm_a\equiv
		\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)
		\equiv
		\frac{(\bg^a,\bx)}{N^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we recall that $\bg^a$ is the $a$-th row of $\bG$.
	For $K > 0$, define
	\[
		S_K(\cA_N) = \bigg\{
			a \in [M] : 
			\Big|\E\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)\Big|
			\ge K
		\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Let $\hbG \in \R^{M\times N}$ be a matrix of i.i.d. gaussians independent of $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$.
	Then define the \textbf{truncated algorithm} $\cA_{N[K]}$ as the function
	\[\cA_{N[K]}\Big(\bG, 
	\bg^{\aux+}
	\equiv(\bg^\aux, \hbG)\Big)
	\equiv
	\cA_N\Big(\tbG(\bG,\hbG;S_K(\cA_N)), \bg^\aux\Big)\,,
	\]
where $\tbG$ is the row-splicing operation from Definition~\ref{d:row.splice}. In words, if $|\E\fm_a| \ge K$, then $\cA_{N[K]}$ ignores the $a$-th row $\bg^a$ of $\bG$ and replaces this input with the independent gaussian vector $\hat\bg$. 	Clearly $\cA_{N[K]}$ is also an $L$-Lipschitz function, with output
	\[\tilde{\bx} \equiv 
		\cA_{N[K]}(\bG, (\bg^\aux, \hbG)) \stackrel{\textit{d}}{=}

{"assumptions":["the transversal obstruction is for the cyclic square (Cayley table of Z_n) with n even; it does not transfer to arbitrary Latin squares of even order","Tarry's result is specific to order 6; orthogonal mates exist for every order other than 2 and 6","a transversal is a set of n cells, one per row, column and symbol"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048970+00:00","domain":"combinatorial designs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_c2a935feb9d5a1be9d3032095348234a9a1e5cc7691477012e8f97b64cdb76ec","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tarry (1900) showed by exhaustion that no Latin square of order 6 has an orthogonal mate, so Euler's thirty-six officers problem has no solution; a pair of orthogonal Latin squares exists for every order n except n = 2 and n = 6 (Bose, Shrikhande, Parker 1960, refuting Euler's conjecture for all n congruent to 2 mod 4 beyond 6). A Latin square has an orthogonal mate if and only if it can be decomposed into n disjoint transversals. For the cyclic Latin square of order n (the Cayley table of the integers mod n): when n is odd the diagonals give n disjoint transversals, so it has an orthogonal mate; when n is even it has no transversal at all, because a transversal would be a complete mapping of Z_n and the sum of all elements of Z_n, n/2, is not zero (a parity obstruction), so in particular it has no orthogonal mate. The even-order cyclic result is a statement about the cyclic square only; other Latin squares of the same even order (n = 4, 8, 10, ...) can have transversals and mates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.154577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2eb21a5cc39c0c3fffe3fb5b1b7a2350df0572a37ca7f08d6204162f254e734","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 (Product-shell bookkeeping) of arXiv:2609.01570, 'A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture'] For distinct \(a,b\in A\), write
\[
 d_{ab}=\normQ{ab^{-1}},\qquad P_{ab}=bd_{ab}.
\]
Then
\[
 P_{ab}\in\{a,Q-a,Q+a,2Q-a,2Q+a,\ldots\},
 \qquad \frac1{d_{ab}}=\frac b{P_{ab}}.
\]
For every \(a\in A\), every subset \(B\subseteq A\setminus\{a\}\),
and all real numbers \(L\ge0\) and \(T>0\), if
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}b\le L
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 P_{ab}\ge T\quad(b\in B),
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}\frac1{d_{ab}}\le\frac LT.
\]
Also, \(P_{ab}=a\) implies \(b\mid a\).

In the special case \(s=1\), call \(b\) good when
\(b\mid Q-1\) or \(b\mid Q+1\).  If such a good \(b\) satisfies
\(P_{ab}\in\{Q-a,Q+a\}\), then \(b\mid a-1\) or \(b\mid a+1\).
If moreover \(a>1\) and \(b>a\), this forces \(b=a+1\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3092bf5adfd353dc1b6027a3f20a6ae44e2f31050c739a2a2102928d191e63b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (weak pullback calculus) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X$ be an orientation-preserving global bi-Lipschitz map as above.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $E_i$ is skew-adjoint on $L^2(\mu)$. In particular
  \[
   \int_{\Real_y^n}(E_if)\phi d\mu=-\int_{\Real_y^n}f(E_i\phi)d\mu
  \]
  whenever $f,\phi,E_if,E_i\phi\in L^2(\mu)$.
\item[(ii)] Let $F=F^i\eframe_i$ be a vector field along $X$ whose Cartesian components belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\Real^n_y;\Rn)$. If
  $q,c^{ij}\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$, then
  \[
   \Div_{\gmetric}F=q,
   \qquad
   (\curl_{\gmetric}F)^{ij}=c^{ij}
  \]
  in the conjugated distributional sense if and only if
  \[
   \partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aF^i)=Jq,
   \qquad
   \partial_a\!\left(J\Kmat_i^aF^j-J\Kmat_j^aF^i\right)=Jc^{ij}
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real^n_y).
  \]
  Equivalently, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Real^n_y)$,
  \begin{equation}
   \int q\varphi d\mu=-\int F^i\Kmat_i^a\partial_a\varphi d\mu,\qquad
   \int c^{ij}\varphi d\mu=-\int\bigl(F^j\Kmat_i^a-F^i\Kmat_j^a\bigr)
          \partial_a\varphi d\mu.
  \end{equation}
  With the convention in \eqref{eq:metric-tensor-divergence}, the same
  calculation gives, whenever
  $H:=\Div_{\gmetric}T\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$,
  \begin{equation}
   JH^j
   =\partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aT^{ji})
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_y^n)
  \end{equation}
  for every locally integrable tensor $T$.
\item[(iii)] If $\mathcal C_X^{-1}F\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ for some
  $1\le p\le\infty$, then 
  \begin{equation}
      \partial_aF^i=A_a^jE_jF^i,
  \end{equation}
  and the conjugated divergence and curl in
  (ii) agree almost everywhere with the pointwise formulas $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^i$ and
  $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^j-\Kmat^a_j\partial_aF^i$.
\item[(iv)] The conjugated derivatives commute on their common
distributional domain:
  \[
   E_iE_j=E_jE_i.
  \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

	\(X=(X(\cdot,\xi))_{\xi \in [0,1]}\) is called a \emph{strong solution} to (equation eq:fibered-McKean-Vlasov-SDE of the paper) if
	the following conditions hold: 
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item For almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\), \(\mu^{\xi}=\mathrm{Law}(X(\cdot,\xi))\).  
		\item For almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\), the process \(X(\cdot,\xi)\) has continuous paths, is adapted to the filtration generated by the Wiener process \(W(\cdot,\xi)\) and the initial condition \(X_0(\xi)\), and satisfies the following integral equation \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.:
		\[
			X(t,\xi) = X_0(\xi) + \int_{0}^{t} b_{\xi}(s,X(\cdot,\xi),\mu) \,ds + \int_{0}^{t} \sigma_{\xi}(s,X(\cdot,\xi),\mu) \,dW(s,\xi), \quad t \in [0,T].
		\]  
	\end{enumerate}
	We say that \emph{strong uniqueness} holds if any two strong solutions \(X\) and \(X'\), defined on the same probability space, driven by the same family of Wiener processes, and starting from the same initial conditions, satisfy \(X(\cdot,\xi)=X'(\cdot,\xi)\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.\ for almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\).

	We say that \emph{uniqueness in law} holds if for any two strong solutions \(X\) and \(X'\), possibly defined on different probability spaces and driven by different Wiener processes but sharing the same fibered law for their initial conditions, one has that \(\mathrm{Law}(X(\cdot,\xi))=\mathrm{Law}(X'(\cdot,\xi))\) for almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is dissipative","the range condition Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) is the hypothesis at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772454+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, boundary value problems","id":"claim_c354d651b0d3d4c7e46b9aa4b5480a1f39abee205e5d85399db455e11dffea4d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: A is densely defined, dissipative, AND Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or at least dense) for some λ_0 > 0. What fails without the range condition: a dissipative operator can be closed and densely defined and still generate nothing. Counterexample: X = L²(0, 1), A f = f' with D(A) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. Then A is densely defined and closed, and Re⟨f', f⟩ = (|f(1)|² − |f(0)|²)/2 = 0, so A is dissipative (indeed both A and −A are). But solving λf − f' = g with f(0) = 0 gives f(x) = −∫_0^x e^{λ(x−s)}g(s) ds, and the second boundary condition f(1) = 0 forces the constraint ∫_0^1 e^{−λs} g(s) ds = 0: Ran(λ − A) is a closed subspace of codimension 1, not dense, for every λ > 0. Hence A is not a generator, although dropping one boundary condition (D = {f ∈ H¹ : f(1) = 0}) gives exactly the generator of the left shift semigroup. The range condition is what encodes 'the right number of boundary conditions'. What fails without density: X = C[0,1] with the sup norm, A f = f' on D(A) = {f ∈ C¹[0,1] : f(1) = 0}. Solving λ f − f' = g with f(1) = 0 gives f(x) = ∫_x^1 e^{λ(x−s)}g(s)ds, so ‖f‖ ≤ ‖g‖/λ: A is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0. Yet the closure of D(A) is {f ∈ C[0,1] : f(1) = 0}, a proper closed subspace, so A generates no C_0-semigroup on C[0,1] (generators are densely defined); it generates one on the smaller space. Density is automatic only when X is reflexive, which C[0,1] is not. Related trap: for the norm inequality version, dissipativity means ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 - checking it for a single λ, or checking Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 only on a core without knowing the operator is closed or closable there, proves nothing about the closure being a generator unless the range condition is verified on that same core.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:06:42.683852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3b7e779e62c432a68ec0191123230a19ac04e5aa7494f32c23cf10738870265","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thmq of arXiv:2411.03942, 'Asymptotic expansions relating to the distribution of the product of correlated normal ran'] Let $\mu_X,\mu_Y\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0$, $-1<\rho<1$ and $n\geq1$. 

Let $q=1-p$. 

\vspace{2mm}

\noindent 1. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/q))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X+r_Y)^2}{1+\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X+r_Y|}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/q))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 2. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/q))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/q)}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 3. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/p))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X+r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X-r_Y)^2}{1-\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X-r_Y|}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/p))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 4. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/p))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/p)}\bigg). 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:10.890411+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3b87282f3e0b8e11cb4453730629ed5800bb8522d9913c57ef6d6ee38800baf","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a connected semisimple real Lie group, $X$ be its symmetric space  and $\Gamma\subseteq G$ be a discrete subgroup.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:31:47.862564+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_c3c80143d15ab676baf153d5122491674bbe827b1df26eaa2282025c9331125e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the Cartan–Hadamard theorem is a statement in Riemannian geometry concerning the structure of complete Riemannian manifolds of non-positive sectional curvature. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:19.991176+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3ccd1bf9fdf996f58aff1fbbbb9cb3cb4655e8e5fa0081e12bb7b1dfa0df511","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 (Action on measures) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] For a finite signed measure $h \in \Sign$ and a number $n \in \Nz$ we define
the finite signed measure $T^{n} \circ h \in \Sign$ by
\[
  (T^{n} \circ h)(A) := \int_{\XX} T^{n}(A \mid x)\, h(\dd x)
  \qquad (A \in \XXA),
\]
the integral of a bounded measurable map against $h$ being defined, as usual, as its
integral against $h^{+}$ minus its integral against $h^{-}$.
The map $h \mapsto T^{n}\circ h$ is a linear map $\Sign \to \Sign$ which
maps $\Prob$ into $\Prob$, and it satisfies
\[
  T \circ (T^{n} \circ h) = T^{n+1} \circ h \qquad (n \in \Nz),
\]
because for every bounded measurable map $g : \XX \to \R$ one has
$\int g \dd(T^{n}\circ h) = \int \bigl( \int g(z)\,T^{n}(\dd z \mid x) \bigr)
h(\dd x)$. That identity holds for indicator maps by the displayed formula, hence for
nonnegative simple maps by linearity, hence for every measurable
$g : \XX \to [0,\infty]$ by monotone convergence, applied to $h^{+}$ and to $h^{-}$
separately; a bounded measurable $g : \XX \to \R$ is then treated by writing
$g = g^{+}-g^{-}$.","status":"unverified"}

\[

\]
for every \(x\in D\).

\[

\]

\[

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:01:56.372007+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c409b06dbbfd938e7ecb6038a179a5e4bfb533513a5da17631bf453aa4e996d5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop_omega_rk1 of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Suppose that $E$ is a complex of ``rank 1'' representations of $Q$, i.e.\ $\dim E_i^n\leq 1$ for all $i\in Q_0,n\in\bZ$.
Then the component of $\Omega$ on $E_i^n$ (complex scalar) is given by
\begin{align*}
\Omega_i^n= \,&(-1)^n  e^{-\beta_i^n-\beta_i^{n+1}}\Bigg(z_i \\
&+\sum_{a\colon i\to j}\left(\alpha_a^n +(\alpha_a^n-\alpha_a^{n-1})(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n)\varphi_2(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n+\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_j^{n-1})\right) \\
&+\sum_{a\colon k\to i}\left(-\alpha_a^n+(\alpha_a^{n+1}-\alpha_a^{n})(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1})\varphi_2(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1}+\beta_i^{n}-\beta_k^{n+2})\right)\Bigg)    
\end{align*}
where
\[
\alpha_a^n\coloneqq\rho^n(a)\rho^n(a)^\dagger,\qquad \beta_i^n\coloneqq d^n_i(d^n_i)^\dagger,\qquad \varphi_2(s)\coloneqq\frac{e^s-s-1}{s^2}.
\]
Here, $d_i^n\colon E_i^{n-1}\to E_i^n$ and $\rho^n(a)\colon E_i^n\to E_j^n$ for $a\colon i\to j$ and $\alpha_a^n$, $\beta_i^n$ are considered as non-negative real scalars.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space","mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]","the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets","convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only","no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732492+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_c423ff08a284a7ccfc7dc1d8f089019abb153806f7c00355fd50d003464125fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.027627+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4410c896141666b1e31538b30d1b5b28bfab0e4a4b61c4c2a9b702f426e6814","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ with the following property. Let $Q$ be an $\So{n}$-valued random matrix whose law is $(d_{\mathrm{ph}},L)$-pseudo-Haar in the sense of \eqref{EqJLPseudoHaarDef}. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil C\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil.
\ee
Assume
\be 
4r\leq d_{\mathrm{ph}},\qquad
\ell\geq C\varepsilon^{-2}r,
\qquad
L\log n\geq \log\frac{2\binom{N}{2}}{\delta}+2r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon\ell}.
\ee
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $Q$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_Q(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.388242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c48365866ce534c77114704d0db89b51cd9ee0418e1cdad2bbed722719835d1f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem homo multilinear recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Homogeneous Multilinear Recursion]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.671542+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_c489fd51aa6e454aa668829db6d73ad3a6b78daefea3d31570d5f2f408f5ad38","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350409+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c49ed582047c4cb6f5e89c53325b0de3d7f6b9478d7f83ec9740f9f1a7410e51","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 179 (annealed second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ 
be defined by \eqref{e:barD} and \eqref{e:barD.plus} (see also \eqref{e:drift.error.II}). We have 
the second moment bound 
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}
		{p(q_d)}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS \delta}{N}\,,
	\]
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.
\begin{proof}
Recalling the notation from
\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.g} and \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y},
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}
		{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$. 
It follows by applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} that 
	\[
	\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	=\frac{1}{M}\E\bigg[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)^2
		\bigg]
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}}{M}
	\E\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|^2}{N}\,.
	\]
We then note that if $\ind_B\in\R^M$ is the indicator of the coordinates in $B$, then
	\[
	\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|
	=\bigg\| \bar{\bG}(q_d) \frac{\ind_B}{|B|^{1/2}}\bigg\|
	\le \|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	\le
	\frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS 
		\E[\|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|^2]}{MN}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS}{N}\,,
	\]
where the last bound follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}.
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.507698+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a29a9821f86641b73c9a2bd61db74a52d87562589038f7e6c1d25cbde5925f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (From scalar wavelets to vector-valued wavelets) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $(\phi,\psi)$ be an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ associated with an MRA.
Fix $m\ge 2$ and set $D=2^m$. Define $\Phi,\Psi$ by \eqref{eq:Phi-def}--\eqref{eq:Psi-def}.
For $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $j\ge 0$ set
\[
\widetilde\Phi_k=\Phi(\cdot-k),
\qquad
\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}=D^{j/2}\Psi(D^j\cdot-k).
\]

Then the family
\[
\{\widetilde\Phi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\ \cup\ \{\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\}_{j\ge 0,\ k\in\mathbb Z}
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] is an orthogonal wavelet basis of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m)$ (for the usual scalar $L^2$ inner product); moreover $\|\widetilde\Phi_k\|_{L^2}^2=\|\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\|_{L^2}^2=m$,
\item[(b)] is an $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--orthonormal system in the Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module
$\big(L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)$, i.e.
\[
\big\langle \widetilde U_\alpha,\widetilde U_\beta\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,I_m
\quad(\alpha,\beta\in\{(0,k)\}\cup\{(j,k):j\ge 0\}),
\]
and it is a Parseval $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module frame with the canonical reconstruction
\[
f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Phi_k\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Phi_k
+\sum_{j\ge 0}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k},
\qquad f\in L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),
\]
with convergence in the module norm.
Moreover, each component inherits compact support, regularity and vanishing moments from $\phi$ and $\psi$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.562017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a7efd4ffd532c6e9f1d326b2cbedbb130db89d3f3815a1d60f3704ee973b3b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:cond-Fokker-planck-a} is a measurable map
\[
    \tilde \P:\R_+\times\Xc\longrightarrow \Pc(\R^d),
    \qquad
    (t,x)\longmapsto \tilde\P_{t,x},
\]
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\), the map
    \(t\mapsto \tilde \P_{t,x}\) is weak continuous.

    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_\Xc
    \int_{\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,\tilde\P_{t,x}\bigr)

    \[
    \E^{\tilde\P_{t,x}}[h]
    =
    \E^{\tilde\P_{0,x}}[h]
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\tilde\P_{s,x}}\!\left[
    \nabla h(Y)\cdot
    \left(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,x,Y,\tilde\P_{s,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \right)
    +
    \Delta h(Y)
    \right]ds .
    \]

    \item

    $
    \P_t(dx,dy)
    :=
    \mu(dx)\,\tilde\P_{t,x}(dy),
$
    then, for a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.336865+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4b0b3c78d60a8233c772b75e1763993f89eda62c0d6d97c1f53fbebf289d552","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] We collect the adjoint and interval-size differentiability statements in one proposition.

\textup{(i)} The formal adjoint is
\[
\cA_L^*v=d\int_{-L}^{L}J(x-y)v(y)\,dy-(qv)'(x)+b(x)v(x).
\]
It possesses a positive principal eigenfunction $\phi_L^*$ satisfying
\[
\cA_L^*\phi_L^*+\lambda_p(L)\phi_L^*=0\ \hbox{in }(-L,L),\quad \phi_L^*(-L)=0,
\]
and this eigenfunction is unique up to multiplication. For all $u,v\in C^1([-L,L])$ satisfying $u(L)=0$ and $v(-L)=0$,
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}v\cA_Lu\,dx=\int_{-L}^{L}u\cA_L^*v\,dx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\phi_L'(L)<0,\quad \phi_L^*(L)>0,\quad \phi_L(-L)>0.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Let $\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}=(\alpha,\beta)$ and let $\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\Lp(\cA_{\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}})$. Assume the coefficients are $C^2$ and normalize the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions by
\[
\int_\alpha^\beta\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx=1.
\]
Then $\lambda$ is $C^1$ in $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
\[
\partial_\beta\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}'(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(\beta)<0,
\]
while
\[
\partial_\alpha\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=d\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\alpha)\int_\alpha^\beta J(x-\alpha)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx>0.
\]
Thus moving the outflow endpoint to the right and moving the inflow endpoint to the left both strictly decrease the principal eigenvalue, but the two shape derivatives have different structures.

\textup{(iii)} The maps $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ and, after pull-back to $(-1,1)$ and the above normalization, $L\mapsto\phi_L$, $L\mapsto\phi_L^*$ are continuous. On every compact interval $[L_0,L_1]\Subset(0,\infty)$ the convergence is uniform in $C^1$ for the eigenfunctions.

\textup{(iv)} The map $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is of class $C^1$ on $(0,\infty)$. With the normalization above,
\[
\partial_L\lambda_p(L)=q(L)\phi_L'(L)\phi_L^*(L)-d\phi_L(-L)\int_{-L}^{L}J(x+L)\phi_L^*(x)\,dx.
\]
In particular, $\partial_L\lambda_p(L)<0\quad L>0$.
Thus $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is strictly decreasing.","status":"unverified"}
