{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164177+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8dd5d6dbd908dc76ffcd01c3c853b2848ddab7bef6bfcc98f9f6c9096bc819d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 32 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If case \eqref{i:fp-case1} of Remark~\ref{r:fp.cases} does not hold, then in any local
   maximizer $(\vvvv,\xxxx,\vwww)$ of the function $F_\diamond$ defined by \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}, the vector $\vwww$ must be entrywise positive.
\begin{proof}
    If case \eqref{i:fp-case1} does not hold, we have $\hv_1 > 0$, $\hx > 0$, or $\mu_1 < \alpha$. We assume for contradiction that $\vwww$ is not entrywise positive, and divide the analysis into a few cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item     \emph{Case 1:} $\hv_1 > 0$ or $\hx > 0$. In this case, let  $\www_{j_1}$ be a positive entry of $\vwww$, which must exist due to the constraint $(\mu,\vwww) = 1$. Now suppose for contradiction that we have $\www_{j_2} = 0$. For small positive $\delta$, the replacement
\[(\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2})
\mapsto \bigg(\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta
    \bigg)\]
increases the value of the budget
    \[\frac1\alpha
    \bigg( \sum_{j=1}^s \mu_j (\www_j)^{1/2}\bigg)^2\]
by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$. It follows that we may replace $\vvv_1$ with $\vvv_1 + \Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, or $\xxxx$ with $\xxxx + \Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, while remaining inside the set $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$. Recalling
\eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}, we can do this in a way which increases the value of $F_\diamond$ by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, contradicting the assumption that we were at a local maximizer.

\item \emph{Case 2:} $\hv_1 < 0$, $\hx \le 0$, and $\mu_1 < \alpha$.
We divide further into two cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item     \emph{Case 2a:} $\vvvv$ is not identically zero.
    As above, let $\www_{j_1} > 0$ and $\www_{j_2} = 0$.
    Further let $\vvv_{j_3} > 0$, and note that $\hv_{j_3} \le \hv_1 < 0$.
    Therefore the replacement
    \[
        (\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2},\vvv_{j_3}) \mapsto
        \lt(\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta,
        \vvv_{j_3} - \Theta(\delta^{1/2})\rt)
    \]
    improves \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam} by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$ while remaining inside $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$.
    This gives a contradiction.

\item     \emph{Case 2b:} $\vvvv$ is identically zero. Then the constraints defining $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$ reduce to
 \beq
        
        1 + \xxxx \le \frac1\alpha \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^s \mu_j (\www_j)^{1/2}\bigg)^2\,, \quad
        (\mu,\vwww) = 1\,.\eeq
    Since $\mu_1 < \alpha$, we have $\vwww \neq (1/\mu_1, 0, \ldots, 0)$.
   Thus there must exist at least one index $j_1\ge2$ for which $\www_{j_1}$ is positive.
    If $\www_1 = 0$, then the replacement
    \[(\www_1,\www_{j_1}) \mapsto
        \bigg(\delta,\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_1}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta\bigg)\] improves the value of \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}
while remaining inside $S_\diamond$.
    Therefore we must have $\www_1 > 0$.
    Finally, if $\www_{j_2} = 0$ for any $j_2 \ge 2$, the replacement
    \[
        (\www_1,\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2}) \rightarrow
        \lt(\www_1 + \delta^{2/3}, \www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_1}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta^{2/3} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta \rt)
    \]
    improves the value of \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam} by $\Theta(\delta^{2/3})$ while remaining inside $S_\diamond$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-09T16:48:21.513714+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_c8df104912a240938197f2669f3805c8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be an inner product space with norm ||x|| = sqrt(<x,x>). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.374369+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8e8d5862c639944cb0487f49591d4f0ca638d936f88c94d80bb799ba8187029","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:exist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] {\rm[Jan-Ras-20-aop]} There exists a probability space $(\widehat\Omega,\widehat{\mathfrak{S}},\widehat\mathbb{P})$,  equipped with an additive group of continuous bijections $\widehat{T}=\{\widehat{T}_x:x\in\mathbb{Z}^2\}$ and satisfying the hypotheses of Section (sec:probsp of the paper), on which there exists a stochastic process

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.766306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8f269c00a0b2323cc27ad2722d492913ab2f66a9ea2c9b39e621b44966c2522","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Suppose that we have a family $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions}$ of resistance metrics coupled with $\Gamma$ where $\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}\colon (\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma) \times (\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma) \to [0,\infty)$.  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
  \item The metric $\rmetres{C}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}$ is continuous with respect to $\dpathY$.

  \item Let $U \subseteq \C$ be open, simply connected. The conditional law of the collection $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ given $\Gamma\setminus\Gamma_{U^*}$ and $(\rmetres{V'}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V' \in \metregions[\C\setminus\ol{U}]}$ is almost surely measurable with respect to~$U^*$.

  \item Let $U \subseteq \C$ be open, simply connected. There exists a probability kernel $\mu^{U^*}$ such that for each $z \in \C$, the conditional law of $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions[U+z]}$ given $(U+z)^*$ is $(T_z)_* \mu^{U^*}(\cdot -z)$ where $T_z \FR(x,y) = \FR(x-z,y-z)$ denotes translation by $z$.

  \item Let $V,V' \in \metregions$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $x,y \in \ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$ such that for every $u \in V' \setminus V$ there is a point $z \in \ol{V}$ that separates $u$ from $x,y$ in $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$. Then
  \[ \rmetres{V}{x}{y}{\Gamma} = \rmetres{V'}{x}{y}{\Gamma} . \]

  \item Suppose that $V_1,V_2 \in \metregions$ with $\ol{V_1} \cap \ol{V_2} = \{z\}$ (where the closure is taken with respect to $d_{\ol{V}}$, see Section~\ref{subsec:main_results}). If $x \in \ol{V_1} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$, $y \in \ol{V_2} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$, then
  \[ \rmetres{V_1 \cup V_2}{x}{y}{\Gamma} = \rmetres{V_1}{x}{z}{\Gamma} + \rmetres{V_2}{z}{y}{\Gamma} . \]

  \item There exists a countable set $\{z_m\}_{m \in \N} \subseteq \Upsilon_\Gamma$ that is dense with respect to $\dpathY$ and such that the following holds. Suppose that $V \in \metregions$ consists of a single connected component and let $\CL \in \Gamma$ be a loop contained in $\ol{V}$ and intersecting $\partial V$. Then there exist two distinct points $a,b \in \CL \cap \partial V$ such that the following holds for sufficiently large $m \in \N$. Then
  \[
   w(x,y) =
   \begin{cases}

    w_{a,b}(x,y) ,& x,y \in A_{a,b} ,\, \{x,y\} \neq \{a,b\} ,\\

Consequently, for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) with j = r + m, m > 0 (longitudinal overshoot past the far endpoint): g(v) + g((0,r) - v) - g((0,r)) >= (r + m) g(e_2) + m g(e_2) - r g(e_2) = 2 m g(e_2), and symmetrically for j = -m < 0. The dogleg excess grows at least LINEARLY in the overshoot, with the explicit constant 2 g(e_2), using convexity and symmetry alone - no curvature hypothesis of any kind. The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:14:46.370162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8fb536f65f3707a16689c9a1cd71714b1acf74252d2fd40a6d9f030c1183972","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a space $X$ with a sum operation $+$, we can define the convolution of any two discrete probability measures on it,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.691651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c91bb9984ea148e40ded2a45ac845506a68bfcb1c39e0f6c9edc1af271c4cc7f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 30 (Finite-frequency prefix factorisation) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Choose $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Let $\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, so that
$\Lambda=-\Lambda$. Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm, let $W_{\C}$
be its complexification, and define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum. Define the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_\Lambda\in[0,T]$ such that
\begin{equation}
r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda\bigr).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with
\[
a_\Lambda=r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236802+00:00","domain":"game theory","id":"claim_c9565091907e96d8504914374b1b2370362648e70aac2f39f97cdfa7046dceb0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Solving a finite two-player zero-sum game with m x n payoff matrix A (row player maximizing, column player minimizing the same quantity) is equivalent to solving a pair of dual linear programs. The row player's LP is: maximize v subject to sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i * A_{ij} >= v for all j=1,...,n, x_i >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1. The column player's LP, minimize w subject to sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} * y_j <= w for all i=1,...,m, y_j >= 0, sum_j y_j = 1, is exactly the LP dual of the row player's program. Because both programs are feasible and bounded, strong LP duality guarantees their optimal values agree (v* = w*), recovering von Neumann's minimax theorem as a consequence of linear programming duality; standard LP algorithms, such as the simplex method or interior-point methods, applied to either program simultaneously compute the game's value and both players' optimal mixed strategies.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.332050+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c95bedaa89d59dce96801447751c1a5efc29276a50e44011b95e888115a332fe","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lm:pointwise-par-colimit of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] For any object $(f\colon Y\to X)\in \Spc_{S\triangleright T/X}$, we have an equivalence
\[ T_i(f)\simeq\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{Y}(i\circ f)\]
in ${\mathcal{C}}(1)$, where $\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{Y}\colon \ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{Y}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},\mathcal C)\to {\mathcal C}$ denotes the parametrized colimit-functor (left adjoint to the inclusion of constant diagrams).
\begin{proof}
    As $Y\in\Spc_{S\triangleright T}$ and $T_i$ is an $S$-cocontinuous extension of $i$, it suffices to show that $f\in\Spc_{S\triangleright T/X}$ is the parametrized colimit of the composite $y\circ f\colon{\mathpalette\ulhelper{Y}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{X}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}\to\ul\Spc_{T/X}$.

    If we write $f_!\colon\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T/Y}\to\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T/X}$ for the unique $S$-cocontinuous extension of $yf$ as in the previous example, then we have seen in said example that $f_!(\textup{id}_Y)\simeq f$. On the other hand, $yf=f_!y$ by construction. As $f_!$ is $S$-cocontinuous, this reduces us to considering the case $f=\textup{id}_Y$, i.e.~we want to show that the colimit of $y\colon {\mathpalette\ulhelper{Y}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}\to\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T/Y}$ is the terminal object $\textup{id}_Y$. By [martiniwolf2021limits]*{Proposition 6.1.3}, this holds in $\ul\Spc_{T/Y}$. As $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T/Y}\subset\ul\Spc_{T/Y}$ is a full subcategory containing the terminal object, this then also holds in $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T/Y}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

    Then there exists a kernel $H$ such that the Fourier multiplier operator $T_hf(x):=\sF^{-1}(h\widehat{f})(x)$ admits the integral representation

{"assumptions":["The dyadic-burst tree defined in this bundle","Ray measures are on infinite simple rays of the graph in question","Independent critical percolation and independent thinning"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T10:10:00.547865+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c97d33a12205f83623a01e4dfc812d0d41e162ae92b39440f42849bc97110ec0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Independent review pending. The proposed implication 'finite common-edge ray energy on a host graph implies that a surviving critical component inherits finite ray energy at some thinning retention r<1' is false without an additional structural premise. For two independent rays from a Borel ray measure mu write I_r(mu)=E[r^(-K)], where K counts common undirected edges. On the dyadic-burst tree, the uniform-child host measure has I_(1/2)=5/4 and critical root survival probability is at least 4/5.  $,   and $t> \tau^{\Psi}$ is an integer.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.161096+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c9aa5873b85cdbbd4ed8e7a37c9f057c8e92e26f99e25b0f8929f249102cf7dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma quotient-pb of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a map of free $G$-spaces, such that $X$ is Hausdorff. Then
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
            X\arrow[r,"\textup{proj}"]\arrow[d,"f"'] & X/G\arrow[d,"f/G"]\\
            Y\arrow[r,"\textup{proj}"'] & Y/G
        \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    is a pullback square.
    \begin{proof}
        By [schwede2018global]*{Proposition~B.13(i)}, the quotients $X/G$ and $Y/G$ are preserved by the forgetful functor to sets. Thus, to show that the comparison map $c\colon X\to X/G\times_{Y/G}Y$ is bijective, we may instead prove the analogous statement in the category of sets. This can be checked fiberwise over $X/G$; the fiber over some class $[x]$ is then given by the orbit $Gx$ (for some fixed representative), while the fiber of the projection $X/G\times_{Y/G}Y$ over the same $[x]$ is given by $\{[x]\}\times Gf(x)$. By assumption, both of these are free $G$-orbits, and any equivariant self-map of $G$ is bijective, proving the claim.
    
        It remains to show that the induced map 
        \[
            {\textup{Hom}}(K,c)\colon{\textup{Hom}}_{\textbf{\textup{Top}}}(K,X)\to{\textup{Hom}}_{\textbf{\textup{Top}}}(K,X/G\times_{Y/G}Y)
        \]
        is bijective for every compact space $K$. As we already know that $c$ is bijective, it will be enough to show surjectivity, for which we consider any $(\alpha,\beta)\colon K\to X/G\times_{Y/G}Y$. The space $X/G$ is again Hausdorff by [tom-Dieck-trafo]*{Proposition~3.1(v)}, so $\alpha(K)\subset X/G$ is compact, and Proposition~3.6(ii) of \emph{op.\ cit.} shows that also the preimage $X'$ of $\alpha(K)$ under $X\to X/G$ is compact.         
        By [schwede2018global]*{Proposition B.13(iii)}, the map $X'/G\times_{Y/G}Y\to X/G\times_{Y/G}Y$ induced by the inclusion $X'\hookrightarrow X$ is an embedding, so $(\alpha,\beta)$ factors through a continuous map $K\to X'/G\times_{Y/G}Y$, and it will be enough to show that this admits a lift to $X'$. Replacing $X$ by $X'$, we may therefore assume without loss of generality that $X$ is compact. But then $X\to X/G\times_{Y/G}Y$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a weak Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K compact","each f_n continuous","for each x the sequence f_n(x) is monotone in n, in the same direction for every x","the pointwise limit f is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751214+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_c9b13faaa47bc5e4c48eaac0e195f673c255de2096f3e248b1dfd899c8f459b1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact topological space and f_n : K -> R continuous. Suppose the sequence is monotone in n at every point (f_n(x) <= f_{n+1}(x) for all n and all x, or the reverse for all n and all x), that f_n -> f pointwise, and that the limit f is continuous. Then f_n -> f UNIFORMLY on K. All four hypotheses carry weight: (a) compactness - on the non-compact [0,1) the sequence f_n(x) = x^n decreases continuously to the continuous limit 0 but not uniformly; (b) continuity of the limit - on the compact [0,1] the same f_n(x) = x^n is monotone and continuous with a discontinuous limit and the convergence is not uniform; (c) monotonicity - the moving bump f_n which is the piecewise-linear tent of height 1 on [1/(n+1), 1/n] and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 with all data continuous and compact, but sup |f_n| = 1; (d) continuity of each f_n - on [0,1] the indicators of the OPEN intervals, f_n = 1_{(0, 1/n)}, decrease pointwise to the identically zero function, which is continuous, on a compact space, so every hypothesis except the continuity of the f_n holds, yet sup |f_n| = 1 for every n. Monotonicity is required POINTWISE IN THE SAME DIRECTION for all x, not merely that each f_n is a monotone function of x. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.13]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:00:45.292926+00:00","domain":"QA-corrected (round 3, audit-driven)","id":"claim_c9b6d95c44e30bbf0aba5f38e4fd929fea5c1f7eb1dd7adbd897cf92e839250a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Implicit function theorem (planar case): Let F be a real-valued function that is continuously differentiable on an open subset of R^2 containing a point (a, b), with F(a, b) = 0 and F_y(a, b) = (partial F / partial y)(a, b) nonzero. Then there are open intervals I containing a and J containing b and a unique continuously differentiable function g : I -> J such that g(a) = b and, within the rectangle I x J, the solution set of F(x, y) = 0 is exactly the graph {(x, g(x)) : x in I}; moreover g'(x) = -F_x(x, g(x)) / F_y(x, g(x)). Example: for F(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 (the unit circle) at (a, b) = (0, 1) one gets g(x) = sqrt(1 - x^2), the upper semicircle; no such g exists near (1, 0), where F_y = 0. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580085+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c9d342de5d2740b126d2418ad05e8c8a337104c8b8bb0b44fac37cd61368b81c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Simplicity, positivity, monotonicity, analyticity) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $M(\theta)$ have entries $M_{d,d'}(\theta)=m_*q(d')p_{d,d'}(\theta)$, with $\theta\mapsto p_{d,d'}(\theta)$ real-analytic (it is a ratio of analytic Wald integrals \eqref{eq:wald}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Krein--Rutman is unnecessary.) $\rho(M)$ is a simple, isolated eigenvalue with a strictly positive right eigenvector $\psi$ and left eigenvector $\phi$, by the Perron--Frobenius theorem for irreducible nonnegative matrices.
\item (Monotonicity.) $\rho(M)$ is nondecreasing in each entry of $M$, strictly so under irreducibility, since $\rho(M)=\lim_n\|M^n\|^{1/n}$ and $M^n$ is entrywise monotone.
\item (Analyticity and the gradient.) $\theta\mapsto\rho(M(\theta))$ is real-analytic on the region where $M$ is irreducible (a simple eigenvalue of an analytic matrix family is analytic, Kato \cite{Kato66}, finite-dimensional case, with no eigenvalue crossing at the top because the Perron root is simple and isolated), and
\[
\partial_{\theta_i}\rho(M)=\frac{\phi^\top(\partial_{\theta_i}M)\psi}{\phi^\top\psi}\qquad(\ne0\text{ generically, since }\partial_{\theta_i}M\ge0\text{ with a positive entry}).
\]
\item (Operator van den Driessche--Watmough lift is unnecessary.) Writing $M=FV^{-1}$ with $V=\diag(\alpha_d)$ and $F$ the $m\times m$ fertility block, the finite-dimensional next-generation theorem \cite{vdDW02} gives directly: $s(J)<0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)<1$ and $s(J)>0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)>1$, where $J=F-V$ is the linearised drift and $s(\cdot)$ its spectral abscissa.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.954998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ca0d7ebacf2e9376009eb20f6df8f422c6b2ba7331c4a878f5ae0a04951f9ed2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:explicit_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (by Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t(V)]=\E^\mu[V]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t \frac{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}{c_\rho^2} h\left(\frac{c_\rho a}{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}\right)  \right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1 + 2u}$ and we define 
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_\rho^2 \equiv \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(V)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}},
  \qquad
  c_\rho \equiv \frac{\|V - \E^\mu[V]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

Let $K_1,K_2,K_3>0$ be constants, and let $\mathcal F$ be a sigma-field independent of the Gaussian family $((g_j)_{j\le N},\xi)$. Assume the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item For each $N\in\N$ and $\beta\in J$, the random variables $\{X^N_{j,\beta}:1\le j\le N\}$ are $\mathcal F$-measurable and satisfy
\[
  |X^N_{j,\beta}|\le K_1\qquad\text{for all }1\le j\le N,\ \beta\in J.
\]
\item The measurable functions $f_1,f_2:\N\times I\times J\to\R$ satisfy, for all $(N,t,\beta)\in\N\times I\times J$,
\[
  |f_1(N,t,\beta)|\le \frac{K_2}{\sqrt N},
  \qquad
  |f_2(N,t,\beta)|\le K_3.
\]
\item The continuous function $U:\R\to\R$ satisfies, for some $A>0$ and
\[
  0<a<\min\left\{\frac1{8K_1^2K_2^2},\frac1{4vK_3^2}\right\},
\]
that
\[
  |U(x)|\le A e^{a x^2}\qquad\text{for all }x\in\R.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists a constant $K>0$, depending only on $(A,a,K_1,K_2,K_3,v,I,J)$, such that
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{N\in\N}\sup_{\beta\in J}
  \E_0\left[\sup_{t\in I}\left|U\left(f_1(N,t,\beta)\sum_{j=1}^Ng_jX^N_{j,\beta}+f_2(N,t,\beta)\xi\right)\right|\right]\le K,
\end{equation}
where $\E_0$ denotes conditional expectation with respect to the Gaussian randomness $((g_j)_{j\le N},\xi)$, with $\mathcal F$ fixed. In particular, the bound is uniform in the realization of the additional randomness. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Dirichlet case: U bounded in at least one direction gives lambda_1 > 0","Neumann case: U bounded, connected, Lipschitz, and the datum must be measured against its mean","Reaction terms shift the rate by sup c"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107251+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ca75748799e3142c7793ceaf79dab6a7fc33eb9daceaf19a3c9b6049728cbd2e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The estimate $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\|u(0)\\|_{L^2}$ comes from the Poincare inequality $\\|\\nabla v\\|^2\\ge\\lambda_1\\|v\\|^2$ on $H^1_0(U)$, i.e. from a positive spectral gap; it is not a property of the heat equation as such. (1) Unbounded domains: on $U=\\mathbb R^n$ the Dirichlet spectrum is $[0,\\infty)$, $\\lambda_1=0$, and $\\|e^{t\\Delta}\\|_{L^2\\to L^2}=1$ for every $t$, so no rate is uniform over the unit ball of $L^2$; individual solutions do decay, but only algebraically in general -- for $g=\\Phi(\\cdot,1)$ one has $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}=(8\\pi(t+1))^{-n/4}$. Half-spaces and cones behave the same way. (2) Neumann boundary conditions: constants solve the Neumann heat equation, $u\\equiv1$ does not decay at all. The correct statement is decay to the mean: for $U$ bounded, connected and Lipschitz (so that $H^1(U)\\hookrightarrow L^2(U)$ is compact and the Neumann spectrum is discrete), $\\|u(t)-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\mu_2t}\\|g-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}$, where $\\bar g$ is the mean of $g$ and $\\mu_2>0$ is the first nonzero Neumann eigenvalue. (3) Zeroth-order terms: for $u_t=\\Delta u+cu$ the decay rate becomes $\\lambda_1-\\sup c$, which is a growth rate as soon as $\\sup c>\\lambda_1$. Auditor's check: whenever an exponential-decay claim appears, identify the eigenvalue being used, verify it is positive on the stated function space, and verify that the domain's geometry (boundedness in at least one direction for Dirichlet, connectedness and mean-zero for Neumann) actually supplies the gap.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287033+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_caaf82ba26dd526b12d4960d0679adfbfe0cf5e77618ccf990d13e89716944b2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma xxphi of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$ and fix $q\in[0,1]$.
		Let $(X_t)_{t\in[q,1]}$ solve the Auffinger--Chen SDE 
		\[
		\mathrm{d} X_t=\xi''(t)\,\zeta([0,t])\,\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,X_t)\mathrm{d} t+\sqrt{\xi''(t)}\,\mathrm{d} B_t.
		\]
		Write $u(t,y):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,y)$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
		\begin{equation}
			\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,x)
			=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,u(q,x)^2
			-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[u(t,X_t)^2\,\middle|\,X_q=x\right]\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Consequently,
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}\big[u(q,X_q)^2\big]
		-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\big[u(t,X_t)^2\big]\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\]
		Moreover, if $\mathbb{E}[u(t,X_t)^2]=t$ for $\zeta$-a.e.\ $t\in[q,1]$
		and also $\mathbb{E}[u(q,X_q)^2]=q$,
		then
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,q-\int_{[q,1]}t\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t)
		=\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\mathrm{d} t.
		\]","status":"unverified"}

Y. Shmalo, Degree fluctuations in bilateral preference random graphs (October 2026). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.741389+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cacc7b69b610a23a1e0040aa6e604bfb5a9801c5189b2cdd44d542ddd54935d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main_result of arXiv:2603.24803, 'Critical Spectral Invariants in Random Walks with Geometric Resetting'] Consider a random walk on $\{0,1,\ldots,a\}$ with absorbing boundaries at $0$ and $a$,
transition probabilities $p,q \in (0,1)$ ($p+q=1$), and geometric resetting with
parameter $\gamma \in (0,1]$. Let $q_z(\gamma)$ denote the probability of absorption
at $0$ starting from position $z \in \{1, 2, \ldots, a-1\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Existence and uniqueness of sign-change point:}
For fixed $\gamma \in (0,1]$, define
$h_z(\gamma) := \partial q_z(\gamma)/\partial\gamma$ for
$z \in \{1, 2, \ldots, a-1\}$.
There exists a unique pair of consecutive integers $(z_0, z_0+1)$ such that
$h_{z_{0}}(\gamma) \cdot h_{z_{0}+1}(\gamma) < 0$. This defines a \emph{sign-change point}
$z^{\dagger}$ satisfying:
\[
h_z(\gamma) > 0 \ \text{for } z < z^{\dagger}, \quad
h_z(\gamma) < 0 \ \text{for } z > z^{\dagger}.
\]

\item \textbf{Midpoint invariance (even $a$):}
If $a$ is even, then $z^{\dagger} = a/2$ for all $p \in (0,1)$, $\gamma \in (0,1]$.
Moreover, the absorption probability at the midpoint is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{a/2}(\gamma)& = \frac{(q/p)^{a/2}}{1 + (q/p)^{a/2}} \quad\\
& \text{for all } \gamma \in (0,1], \; p \in (0,1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and consequently $\partial q_{a/2}(\gamma)/\partial\gamma \equiv 0$.

\item \textbf{Location for odd $a$:}
If $a$ is odd, $z^{\dagger}$ lies between $(a-1)/2$ and $(a+1)/2$, with the
precise location depending on $p$ according to the asymptotic expansion,
valid for $|p-q| \ll 1$:
\[
z^{\dagger}(\gamma,p) = \frac{a}{2} - \frac{C(\gamma,a)}{2}(p-q) + O(|p-q|^2),
\]
where $C(\gamma,a) > 0$ for all $\gamma \in (0,1]$ and satisfies $C(\gamma,a) = \Theta(a)$.

\item \textbf{Approximate invariance for odd $a$:}
When $a$ is odd, no exact invariance exists at integer sites. However, for the
two central positions $z \in \{(a-1)/2, (a+1)/2\}$,
\[
\left|\frac{\partial q_z(\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}\right|
\le \frac{K(\gamma)}{a},
\]
where $K(\gamma) > 0$ is independent of $p$ and may grow moderately with $\gamma$.
Consequently, the sensitivity to resetting at these sites is significantly
reduced compared to bulk positions.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.740044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cad48e1173243dc7f8b71f18d8aca5cf18221840afadb34f88c430fb297f373f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Bilateral words, relative height, shifts})
$(\textbf{a})$ A \emph{bilateral word} is a sequence 
$u\! =\!  (a_k)_{k_1 <k\leq k_2}$ where $k_1\ino \bbZZ$, $k_2 \ino \bbZ$ and $a_k \ino \bbN^*$, $k_1 \leko k \leqo k_2$.   
If $k_1\! \geq \! k_2$, then $u\! = \! \varnothing$. We denote by $\overline{\bbU}$ the set of bilateral words. 

\smallskip

\noi
$(\textbf{b})$ Let $u\eqo (a_{k})_{k_1 < k\leq k_2 } \ino \obbU$, as above. Then 
\begin{equation}  

\bbn u\bbn_-\! =\!  k_1 , \quad \textrm{and} \quad \bbn u \bbn\! = \! k_2 .
\end{equation}
Here $\bbn u \bbn$ is called the \textit{relative height} 
of $u$ and $\bbn u \bbn_-$  its \emph{depth}. 

\smallskip

\noi
$(\textbf{c})$  Let $u\eqo (a_{k})_{k_1 < k\leq k_2 } \ino \obbU$ as above. 
Let $l \ino \bbZ$. We denote by $\varphi_l (u)$ the \emph{$l$-shifted word $u$}. Namely, 
\begin{equation}  

\varphi_{l} (u) = (a_{k+l})_{k_1 -l < k\leq k_2 -l }, 
\end{equation}
Therefore, $\bbn \varphi_{l} (u) \bbn_- \! = \! \bbn  u\bbn _- \! -\! l$,  $\bbn  \varphi_{l} (u) \bbn \! = \! \bbn  u \bbn \! -\! l$.  We adopt the convention $\varphi_l (\varnothing)\! = \! \varnothing$. Observe that the $\varphi_l\! : \! \obbU \! \to \! \obbU$ are bijections such that $\varphi_l \! \circ \! \varphi_{l^\prime} \! = \! \varphi_{l+ l^\prime}$, $l,l'\ino \bbZ$. For all $k \ino \bbZ$, we then set

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.190810+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb0d9ad222facc8d59b1559d22cc9305191285dcd3ed707c0b3ada8b0bc9e12c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \rm

 \item[\rm (iv)]  We say that the transition density lower bound estimate for the Dirichlet transition density, ${\rm NDL}(\phi)$ for short, holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$   has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist  $\e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \in (0, 1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:2.15}} > 0$ so that for every $x_0 \in \sX$, $r > 0$, $t\in (0, \phi (\e_{\ref{e:2.15}}r))$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb10364dace7dba743898e874e7664b4dd7421f41ae9cdd370defd519baac0d2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 184 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.Ising.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0\le d\le\dmax-1
	\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\]
where $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX^N(\Ising) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le \exp
	\bigg(
	-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}
	\bigg)
	\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.Ising} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)}{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}
	=\frac{1}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\sum_{i\in B}
	\frac{\be_i}{|B|^{1/2}},
	\by\bigg)
	\equiv \frac{(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))}{|B|^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we abbreviate $B\equiv B^\Ising$.
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\Ising)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\Big|( \be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1, B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE[\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2]
	= \frac{\delta_d}{N}
	\sum_{B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)}
	(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))^2
	\le  \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\,.
	\]
The bound on $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ follows by a similar argument as the bound for $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}, with the simplification that $\|\be_B\|=1$ is trivially bounded. 
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

\[

\]
denote the usual Shannon entropy, and define the complementary entropy functional
\[
  H_{\mr c}(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d(1-q_i)\log(1-q_i).
\]
We call the difference
\[
  S(\bs{q}):=H(\bs{q})-H_{\mr c}(\bs{q})
\]
the local Bethe entropy functional.
If $\mu$ is a
probability distribution on a finite set, we write $H(\mu)$ for the
entropy of its probability vector; for a finite random variable $U$, we write $\mc{L}(U)$ for its law and set $H(U):=H(\mc{L}(U))$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:42:57.183102+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb46b0f84139a0238bf1fbc72025695b844fab752763a68a43e5a1be3354746b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem {\cite[Theorems~1.1.4 and 1.1.5 of arXiv:2609.04140, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ III:\\ uniqueness'] {LevelLineGFFI}}]
	Let $h$ be a GFF on $\BH$ with piecewise constant boundary conditions that change only finitely many times. For all $u \in \BR$ and $x \in \partial \BH$, we denote by $\gamma_u^x$ the level line of $h$ with height $u$ starting from $x$ and ending at $\infty$. Fix $x_2 \leq x_1$ and $u_1, u_2 \in \BR$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $u_2 < u_1$, then $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ a.s.\ stays to the left of $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$.
		\item If $u_2 = u_1$, then $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ may intersect $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$ and, upon intersecting, the two curves merge and never separate.
		\item If $u_1 - u_2 \geq 2 \lambda$, then $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$ and $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ do not intersect each other a.s.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Then the L^p(mu) norm of the y-average dominates in the direction: || integral_Y f(., y) dnu(y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} <= integral_Y || f(., y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} dnu(y). For signed or complex f the same holds provided the right-hand side is finite, and then the inner integral converges absolutely for mu-a.e. x. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:09.912563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb747603c79d77aa79718c00a9de7c40d84202044ece436d07d35762ab744718","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 of arXiv:2603.26936, 'Sharp Riemannian heat kernel estimates on the cut locus and the Parabolic Anderson model'] Let $\alpha>0$ and consider the following Hilbert space of space-time functions,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.473363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb79141dcb1fc490b9d4b16fe109e95273ae65cd23a5e2b93b438fb424cfff0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma eq:mixture-remainder-X of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:product-mixture-path}
Let \(\mu_i\) and \(\gamma_i\), \(1\le i\le M\), be probability laws whose
moments agree through order \(m\), and put
\[
 \mu_{i,t}=(1-t)\mu_i+t\gamma_i,
 \qquad \lambda_t=\bigotimes_{i=1}^M\mu_{i,t},
 \qquad A(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^M}F(z)\,\lambda_t(\,\mathrm d z),
\]
where \(F:\mathbb R^M\to(0,\infty)\) is \(C^{m+1}\).  Let
\(Z\sim\lambda_t\), \(X_i\sim\mu_i\), and \(Y_i\sim\gamma_i\) be
independent.  Assume \(0<A(t)<\infty\) on \([0,1]\), that the
expressions below are absolutely integrable, and that differentiation
under the finite product measure is justified.  Set
\(\Delta_i^X=X_i-Z_i\) and \(\Delta_i^Y=Y_i-Z_i\).  If, uniformly in
\(t\in[0,1]\),
\begin{align}
 &\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbb E\left[
  \left\lvert\Delta_i^X\right\rvert^{m+1}
  \int_0^1(1-s)^m
  \abs{\partial_i^{m+1}F(Z+s\Delta_i^Xe_i)}\,\mathrm d s\right]
 \le R A(t),\\
 &\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbb E\left[
  \left\lvert\Delta_i^Y\right\rvert^{m+1}
  \int_0^1(1-s)^m
  \abs{\partial_i^{m+1}F(Z+s\Delta_i^Ye_i)}\,\mathrm d s\right]
 \le R A(t),
\end{align}
then
\begin{equation}
 \left\lvert\log A(1)-\log A(0)\right\rvert\le \frac{2R}{m!}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.589301+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb7cc8fd1114c41bfc16383467dd69f2f04c77f37babab12ced15ff799e959af","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:SaS-measure of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Let $(E,\mathcal{E})$ be a measurable space with $\sigma$-finite measure $m$.
Set $\mathcal{E}_0 := \{A \in \mathcal{E} : m(A) < \infty\}$.
A mapping $M_\alpha : \mathcal{E}_0 \to L^0(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$
is a \emph{S$\alpha$S random measure with control measure $m$} if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For every $A \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha(A) \sim \mathrm{S}\alpha\mathrm{S}(m(A)^{1/\alpha})$, i.e.,
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{i\theta M_\alpha(A)}\bigr]
  = e^{-|\theta|^\alpha m(A)},
  \quad \theta \in \mathbb{R}.
  \end{equation}
\item For pairwise disjoint $A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{E}_0$,
  the variables $M_\alpha(A_1), M_\alpha(A_2), \ldots$ are independent.
\item For pairwise disjoint $\{A_j\} \subset \mathcal{E}_0$ with
  $\bigcup_j A_j \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha\!\left(\bigcup_j A_j\right) = \sum_j M_\alpha(A_j)$
  almost surely.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.644464+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb857d1dad3494a3cf99dabc2cda5ddc7e0cc4e2b95cf9ad1e32505945ce3e4d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 (Wasserstein-1 distance) of arXiv:2605.24445, 'Matrix concentration inequalities for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains'] Let $(\Omega, d)$ be a Polish metric space and let $\mu,\nu$ be two probability measures on $\Omega$ with finite first moment.
The \emph{Wasserstein-1 distance} between $\mu$ and $\nu$ is
\[
    W_1(\mu,\nu)
    \;:=\;
    \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)}
    \int_{\Omega\times \Omega} d(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x,y),
\]
where $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is the set of all couplings of $\mu$ and $\nu$,
i.e., all probability measures $\pi$ on $\Omega\times\Omega$
with marginals $\mu$ and $\nu$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.062061+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb874539e13deba5947fe6e95375e80c8e031e1c5d52cdef72f24b040655a49e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Consider the birth-death process with immigration introduced above and let
    $A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, X_s$.
For $0<\theta<a/(c-b)$, define $r_\theta=\sqrt{\frac{c\theta}{a+b\theta}}$ and $\beta_\theta
      =br_\theta+\frac{c}{r_\theta}-b-c$.
Moreover, let
\[
    v_\theta
      =\frac{2ac r_\theta^3}{(c-br_\theta^2)^3},
    \qquad
    I_{\mathrm{BDI}}(\theta)
      =\left(
          \sqrt{a+b\theta}-\sqrt{c\theta}
       \right)^2.
\]
Then, for every fixed $n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
    \bbP_n(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim
    \frac{
      \psi_{\beta_\theta}(n)
      \langle\psi_{\beta_\theta},\mathbf 1\rangle_{\ell^2(\pi)}
    }{
      \beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}
    }
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_{\mathrm{BDI}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\]
On every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges in total
variation to the birth-death process with rates
\[
    q^{(\theta)}(n,n+1)=r_\theta(a+bn),
    \qquad
    q^{(\theta)}(n,n-1)=\frac{c}{r_\theta}n.
\]
Its invariant law is negative binomial with shape parameter $a/b$ and
mean $\theta$.","status":"unverified"}

Let $\{X(t)\}_{t\in S}$ be a mean-zero continuous Gaussian process.
Denote $\sigma^2 := \sup_{t\in S} \|X(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. Suppose that  there exist constants $M > \sigma$, $p > 0$, and $0 < \varepsilon_0 \leqslant \sigma$ such that
\[
N(S, d_X, \varepsilon) \leq (M/\varepsilon)^p \quad \text{for all } \varepsilon < \varepsilon_0.
\]
Then, for any $u > \sigma^2[(1 + \sqrt{p})/\varepsilon_0]$, the following holds:
\[
\mathbb{P}\left\{ \sup_{t\in S} X(t) \geq u \right\} \leq \left(\frac{KMu}{\sqrt{p}\,\sigma^2} \right)^p \Phi\left(\frac{u}{\sigma} \right),
\]
where $\Phi(x) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} \int_x^\infty e^{-y^2/2}\,dy$ and $K$ is a universal constant. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911677+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_cb9f0a5bfb69e6d801c7f9b4c969831d7a650fa1a7cd92d88cc350fba9aa3034","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $M$ predictors $f_1, \\dots, f_M$ of a target $y$ have errors $e_m = f_m - y$ with error covariance $\\Sigma_E$ (the $M \\times M$ covariance of the vector $(e_1, \\dots, e_M)$ over the population of inputs). An affine stack $\\sum_m w_m f_m + b$ with $\\sum_m w_m = 1$ has error $\\sum_m w_m e_m + b$, so after the intercept removes the mean error its risk is $w^T \\Sigma_E w$, and the optimal weights are the minimum-variance portfolio $w^* = \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$; without the sum constraint the least-squares stack is the ordinary regression of $y$ on $(f_1, \\dots, f_M, 1)$. Consequently every random-matrix result about the noisy-covariance portfolio problem transfers to ensemble weighting with $q = M / n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$, $n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ the number of calibration cases the weights are fitted on: the plug-in (least-squares) stack's out-of-sample risk is inflated by the factor $1/(1 - q)$ relative to the optimum, its in-sample risk understates the optimum by $1 - q$, and any cleaning of the covariance must be applied to $\\Sigma_E$. The covariance of the predictions themselves, $\\operatorname{Cov}(f_1, \\dots, f_M)$, is NOT the object to clean: writing $f_m = y + e_m$ it equals $\\operatorname{Var}(y)\\mathbf{1}\\mathbf{1}^T + (\\text{cross terms}) + \\Sigma_E$, a rank-one spike of the size of the signal variance over the error covariance. The stacking weight's departure from equal weights, $w - \\mathbf{1}/M$, is orthogonal to $\\mathbf{1}$, so it lives entirely in the small-eigenvalue subspace of the prediction covariance; a bulk-versus-spike cleaner applied to that matrix (Marchenko-Pastur truncation, shrinkage toward $\\operatorname{tr}/p \\cdot I$, a rotationally invariant estimator floored relative to the top eigenvalue) keeps the signal spike and destroys exactly the directions stacking needs. At $q = 0.025$ (23 members, 932 calibration rows) the whole prize from cleaning $\\Sigma_E$ is bounded by about $2.5$ percent; the prize grows like $q/(1-q)$ as the calibration set shrinks.","status":"unverified"}

Consider the weight operator
$ W_{\mathbf{X}, \varepsilon} : \R^{d_1 \times d_2} \to \R^{d_1 \times d_2} $

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.443181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cbe1d106d31bbfccb55cb83bd63076c04f8b9acb51cde99d137a30200c0b3de4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $n,d$ be any parameters for the Rook's Walk. Then for $\epsilon\in(0,1)$,
   \[t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) \leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n} \log d + c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}\]
   where $c_u(\epsilon)$ is a constant dependent only on $\epsilon$.
   \begin{proof}
      Let $u=4\epsilon^2+1$. Then,
      \[u^{1/d} =e^{\log(u^{1/d})}=e^{\frac{1}{d}\log(u)}\]
      Now, $e^x$ is concave up so the first order Taylor approximation is a lower bound; That is, $e^x \geq 1+x$. Therefore,
      \[e^{\frac{1}{d}\log (u)} \geq 1+ \frac{1}{d}\log( u)\]
      or equivalently,
      \[u^{1/d} -1 \geq \frac{\log u}{d}\]
      Now, recall our upper bound from Theorem \ref{main1} and substitute,
      \begin{align*}
          t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) &\leq -\frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left((4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 \right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{1}{(4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 }\right)\\
          &\leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{d}{\log (4\epsilon^2 +1)}\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\left(\log(d) -\log\log(4\epsilon^2+1)\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log(d) +c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}
      \end{align*}
      as required.
      
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

	\[

	\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.494629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc0dddb7760abf212a455a84f79978f7553eac177655077c985b40a08031c6d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 25 (Eigenvalue rigidity) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:rigidity}
Let \(A\) be a matrix such that \(A/\sqrt n\) has the distribution of GUE.
Let
\[

\]
denote its eigenvalues, and let \(\gamma_i\) be the corresponding classical
location for the semicircle law, defined by
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\gamma_i}
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{(4-x^2)_+}\,dx
=

\]
Then for every \(1\leq i\leq n\),
\[

n^{O(1)}\exp(-cT^c)
\]
for all \(T>0\), where \(c>0\) is an absolute constant.

In particular, with overwhelming probability,
\[
\lambda_i
=
\sqrt n\,\gamma_i
+
O\!\left(
n^{1/3}\min(i,n-i+1)^{-1/3}\log^{O(1)} n

\]
and the same estimate holds with \(\lambda_i\) replaced by

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc1b2d0e0e60b2fab206e1bb831beb4f89e5103ec099debaccf925d39496b78b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 30 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that $z_{\min}$ is the unique minimizer of $V$ on the interval $[z_0,\infty)$.
    We have $z_{\min} = z_0$ if and only if
    \beq
        
        \alpha \le \mu_1 \textup{ and } \hv_1 < 0\,.
    \eeq
    If \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0} does not hold, $z_{\min}$ is the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that if $\hv_1 > 0$, then $V(z)\uparrow\infty$ as $z\downarrow z_0$, so in this case clearly $z_{\min} > z_0$.
If instead $\hv_1 < 0$, then $z_0 = \hw_1$, so we have $z_{\min}=z_0$ if and only if the derivative $V'$ stays nonnegative as $z\downarrow \hw_1$. To this end, recall that as $z\downarrow \hw_1$ we have $m(z)\uparrow\infty$, so
    \[\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg(
        \frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2
        \longrightarrow \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j = 1\,.\]
We also have $m_2(z)/m(z)^2 \to 1/\mu_1$, and substituting into
\eqref{e:fp-V-pr} gives
    \[
        V'(z)
        \longrightarrow 1 - \frac{\alpha}{\mu_1}
    \]
   as $z\downarrow\hw_1$. This is nonnegative if and only if $\alpha \le \mu_1$, which yields the condition \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0}. Otherwise, we must have $z_{\min} > z_0$; in this case, since $V$ is strictly convex and twice differentiable, the value $z_{\min}$ must be the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

For every such strongly convergent subsequence, with limit $u$, one also has the sharp lower-semicontinuity estimate

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.168228+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccc0df09822bfa3a5d90fb1bef1737321977369413bb52b928df8763118ba57f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 62 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP}(\alpha,q_0)$.
\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$, where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$. Recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, this means there exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_j)^\circ$ (acting in $N_j$ dimensions) such that
    \begin{align} \nonumber

    \end{align}
    Let $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be the perturbations of the $( (\cA_j)^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}, which are also $L$-Lipschitz.
    Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} further yields
    \[
        \frac{1}{N} \bbE \Big[\| (\cA_j)^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) 
        	- \cA_j(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2\Big]
        \le \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2}\,.
    \]
Thus Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx} implies that for $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$ and $C_2(\alpha,L)$ given therein,
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_j,(\cA_j)^\circ)
	\le 
	\bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) \cdot \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2} + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j}

    where the last inequality holds if $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$ (consistent with our assumptions), and $j$ sufficiently large depending on $q_0,\epsilon,L$. Hence, by omitting finitely many $j$, we can assume it holds for all $j$ that

         \max\bigg\{

    By passing to a further subsequence, we can assume (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}) that $\chi_{\cA_j}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, both pointwise and in $L^1$.

We assume without loss that $\tilde{\epsilon}\le1$. 
    We will now verify that for $C(L)$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main},
    \beq
        
         (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) 
         \in \Adm^{\BOGP}\Big(
         \alpha,q_0;
         \tilde C = \max\{C(L),L^2\}, \tilde\epsilon 
         \Big)\,.
    \eeq
    Indeed, we verify each of the conditions from Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} specifying the $\Adm^{\BOGP}$ class:
    \begin{itemize}
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-Lip}
    implies condition~\ref{it:1.1bogp};

\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-diffusivity}
    implies condition~\ref{it:2.1}; 

\item We have $p(q_0) = 0$ because we defined $\chi(0) = q_0$. 
        Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} asserts $p(q_*) \le \tilde\epsilo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.775784+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cceb8926ad8613162a17b69260373e15646c727032d01959ed3b249d6320261b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def: Berger_good_box_definition of arXiv:2608.00399, 'The Heavy-tailed Frog Model'] Let $Q$ be a $k$-block

    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2pt]
    \item A $0$-block $Q$ is \textbf{good} if there is no directed edge $(u,w)$ with
    $u,w\in Q$ and $|u-w|>A_0/100$.

    \item For $k\ge1$, a $k$-block $Q$ is \textbf{good} if the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}, leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2pt]
    \item there is no directed edge $(u,w)$ with
    $u,w\in Q$ and $|u-w|>A_{k-1}/100$;
    \item among the $(k{-}1)$-blocks (children) of $Q$,
    all but at most one are good;
    \item for every
    $v\in\{0,\pm A_{k-1}/2\}^d$, the shifted inner block $Q^{\mathrm{int}}+v$
    also satisfies \textup{(b)} (i.e., among its $(k{-}1)$-subblocks, all but at most
    one are good).
    \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352896+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccec066ffa0ec9499357e450b8a09d076a5e7a35b2314061cdccc3fc37f950af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, and let $\bx(q_d)$ be as defined by
\eqref{e:x.q.mean}. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\bigg|
    \frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}-q_{\min\{d,\ell\}}
    \bigg|\ge
    \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\bigg) 
    \le \exp(-N^{0.1})\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
This follows easily from gaussian Lipschitz concentration (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}).
Indeed note that $\|\cA(\bG,  \bg^\aux)\|_2\leq N^{1/2}$ almost surely, while by definition $\bx(q_d)$
is an $L$-Lipschitz function of the gaussian vector $(\bG(q_d),\bg^\aux(q_d))$. It follows that for $\ell \le d$, the normalized inner product
    \[\frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}\]
is an 
 $O(LN^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function of 
    \[\Big(\bG(q_\ell),
    \bg^\aux(q_\ell),
    \bG(q_d) - \bG(q_\ell),\bg^\aux(q_d) - \bg^\aux(q_\ell)\Big)\,.\]
 Therefore it concentrates around its mean by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}, which gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.552657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccecdb2b3a682f61a22c6f6e603f65d48bccf2f7c9c088a4551638b51f29d639","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (Absolute Fourier estimate) of arXiv:2609.01413, 'Sharp Threshold for Universality of Rational Canonical Forms over a Finite Field'] Fix a positive integer $m$ and a constant $c>1$, and put
    $$
    \beta_n:=\frac{c\log n}{n}.
    $$
    Let $V$ be an $m$-dimensional $\F_p$-vector space, and let
    $\mu_{ij}$, $1\leq i,j\leq n$, be arbitrary
    $\beta_n$-balanced probability measures on $\F_p$. Fix a nontrivial
    additive character
    $$
    \psi:\F_p\longrightarrow\C^\times,
    $$
    and write
    $$
    \widehat{\mu}_{ij}(u)
    :=
    \sum_{a\in\F_p}\mu_{ij}(a)\psi(ua),
    \qquad
    u\in\F_p.
    $$
    Then
    \begin{align}
        
        &p^{-mn}
        \sum_{\substack{g_1,\ldots,g_n\in V\\
        \Span_{\F_p}\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}=V}}
        \ \sum_{\substack{h_1,\ldots,h_n\in V^\vee\\
        (h_1,\ldots,h_n)\neq(0,\ldots,0)}}
        \prod_{i,j=1}^n
        \left|
        \widehat{\mu}_{ij}\bigl(h_j(g_i)\bigr)
        \right|
        =
        o(1),
    \end{align}
    where the estimate is uniform over the choices of
    $\mu_{ij}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0","Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter","Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418709+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_cd2c0cd0a6c998918c8d20dec220a3380322e8bf670c19046ddde117aec30ea3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Two equations with identical classical solutions can have different weak solutions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190407+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_cd8b3fd8a8f4ae722c7b30ce5ede1b8d61ec46e770d6d666a20852c38aba2023","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle. The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group which can be computed as isomorphic to the group where corresponds to an even number of twists, and to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.097667+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdd5f54e5bdf05094dcfb32b770057456e8982935a922cb313566d05d62f9dba","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Uniform local bound for zero-truncated Poisson sums) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(N\ge2\), \(m\ge N+1\), and let \(\tau=\tau_{N,m}>0\) be the unique
solution of
\[
        \frac{\tau}{1-e^{-\tau}}=\frac{m}{N}.
\]
Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\) be iid zero-truncated Poisson variables with parameter
\(\tau\):
\[
        \Pbb(D_i=k)=\frac{\tau^k}{k!(e^\tau-1)},\qquad k\ge1.
\]
Write
\[
        \mu_\tau=\Ebb D_i=\frac{\tau}{1-e^{-\tau}},
        \qquad
        \sigma_\tau^2=\Var(D_i),
        \qquad
        B=N\sigma_\tau^2.
\]
Assume \(0<\tau\le C_0\log N\). If \(B\to\infty\), then
\[
        \Pbb(D_1+\cdots+D_N=m)
        =
        \frac{1+o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi B}},
\]
uniformly in this range. Consequently, for some constants \(c,C>0\),
depending only on \(C_0\),
\[
        \Pbb(D_1+\cdots+D_N=m)\ge c\,m^{-C}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(N\). If \(B\) is bounded, the same polynomial
lower bound still holds.","status":"unverified"}

In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). Assuming those two theorems, a Gaussian limit for the box counts in regimes (c) and (d) does not hold without a further regularity condition on the tail. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.037616+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cddf33c08cd90b9aef303fb27df6681c9ebd7af642b83aea8a737b6be7011ba1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 23 (Vertex condition) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The structure satisfies the \emph{vertex condition}
\textup{(V)} if there is $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ such that for
every active orbit $O$ and both of its sites $z\in O$,
\[
\varepsilon\,\mathcal W\bigl[\varphi_O,\,s(z;\cdot)\bigr](\gamma)>0
\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in(0,1).
\]
Equivalently, since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma}
\left(\frac{\varphi_O}{s_z}\right)
=\frac{\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s_z]}{s_z^{2}},
\qquad s_z>0,
\]
each ratio $\varphi_O(\gamma)/s(z;\gamma)$, $z\in O$, is strictly
monotone in $\gamma$, in the same direction for all orbits and both
orbit sites. Only these $2r$ scalar ratios
enter the theorem below, and the condition involves only scalar
functions of $\gamma$.

Two remarks on the shape of \textup{(V)}. First, it is stated
relative to the orbit representatives fixed once and for all in
Section~\ref{subsec:inherited-structure}: reversing the
representative of an orbit replaces $\mathbf d_O$ by
$-\mathbf d_O$, hence $\varphi_O$ by $-\varphi_O$ and both of that
orbit's Wronskians by their negatives. The genuinely invariant
content of \textup{(V)} is therefore the \emph{intra-orbit}
requirement that the two Wronskians of a given orbit share a sign;
the common value of $\varepsilon$ across orbits is a normalisation.
That it is always achievable is worth stating precisely: the choice
of representative is made \emph{independently in each orbit}, and
reversing it in a single orbit $O$ sends
$\mathbf d_O\mapsto-\mathbf d_O$,
$\varphi_O\mapsto-\varphi_O$, hence
$\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]\mapsto
-\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]$ at both $z\in O$ and leaves every
other orbit untouched. So if each orbit separately has a constant
Wronskian sign, the $r$ signs can be aligned one orbit at a time.
The substantive hypothesis is thus the intra-orbit one; the global
$\varepsilon$ follows. Second, and
consequently, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex-sign} is
orientation-independent, since only the product
$\varepsilon\cdot\operatorname{sgn}[\mathbf d_O]_z$ appears there,
and that product is unchanged by a reversal.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is consistent","T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)","T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378582+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_cde8bcbf7d8ce7708f2314743185825fb5c4235f909300f46e471371d1a885c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A increasing and depending on finitely many coordinates","product measure with a common density p","for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce028eff08f7ef08cc636b492788f905d03b4c3fa8e4ee1b14f0bc0ea2dcd3a1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Then p -> P_p(A) is a polynomial in p, hence smooth, and d/dp P_p(A) = sum_{e in E} P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p[ N(A) ], where N(A) is the number of pivotal edges. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). [Russo (1981), Margulis (1974); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.25]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.285568+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce2854bc46715b64a84e17e7e82c740cce538870a762eb52c14617533264e705","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551, '\bf Sparse Separable Factor Analysis in the Complex Domain with an Application to Local Fi'] For $j=1,\ldots,d$, let $\Lambdab_j\in\CC^{p_j\times k_j}$ denote the true loading matrix and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ denote its estimate. Define the orthogonal projectors onto their column spaces by
\begin{align*}
  \Pb_j
  &=
  \Lambdab_j
  \left(
    \Lambdab_j^\star\Lambdab_j
  \right)^+
  \Lambdab_j^\star,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\Pb}_j
  =
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \left(
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \right)^+
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star,
\end{align*}
where $+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. The null-space projection error is
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  \left\|
    \left(
      \Ib_{p_j}-\widehat{\Pb}_j
    \right)
    \Pb_j
  \right\|_F^2.
  
\end{align}
Let
\begin{align*}
  r_j
  &=
  \operatorname{rank}(\Lambdab_j),
  \qquad
  \widehat{r}_j
  =
  \operatorname{rank}(\widehat{\Lambdab}_j),
  \qquad
  r_{\min,j}
  =
  \min(r_j,\widehat{r}_j).
\end{align*}
Denote the principal angles between the column spaces of $\Lambdab_j$ and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ by
\begin{align*}
    0
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)1}
  \leq
  \cdots
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)r_{\min,j}}
  \leq
  \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  r_j-r_{\min,j}
  +
  \sum_{i=1}^{r_{\min,j}}
  \sin^2\left(\theta_{(j)i}\right),
  
\end{align}
where the sum \eqref{eq:appendix-null-err-proj-angle} is interpreted as zero when $r_{\min,j}=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Rather than propositions such as \"all humans are mortal\", in first-order logic one can have expressions in the form \"for all x, if x is a human, then x is mortal\", where \"for all x\" is a quantifier, x is a variable, and \"... is a human\" and \"... is mortal\" are predicates. {"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n","a^{ij} = a^{ji}, b^i, c real functions on Omega","lambda|xi|^2 <= a^{ij} xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for uniform ellipticity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.147082+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ce331292e9dfb7e46eae58cc677d147b6511a99448713cb6fd049abdfc239c02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open. A nondivergence-form operator is Lu = sum_{i,j} a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + sum_i b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} real (symmetry is no loss because D_{ij}u is symmetric) and b^i, c real. L is elliptic at x if the matrix (a^{ij}(x)) is positive definite; lambda(x) denotes its smallest eigenvalue. L is uniformly elliptic with constants 0 < lambda <= Lambda if lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for all x (a.e. x for measurable coefficients) and all xi in R^n. Sign convention: here L = +Laplacian when (a^{ij}) = I, b = 0, c = 0, so the maximum principle concerns Lu >= 0 and the favorable sign of the zeroth-order coefficient is c <= 0 (the opposite of the divergence-form convention -div(A grad u) + c u with c >= 0). A classical solution of Lu = f is u in C^2(Omega) with Lu = f pointwise; a strong solution is u in W^{2,p}_loc(Omega) for some 1 <= p <= infinity with Lu = f almost everywhere. If the a^{ij} are C^1 (or Lipschitz), a^{ij} D_{ij} u = D_i(a^{ij} D_j u) - (D_i a^{ij}) D_j u rewrites L in divergence form; for merely measurable a^{ij} the two forms are different theories (De Giorgi-Nash-Moser for divergence form, Krylov-Safonov for nondivergence form).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce670b13671e47792346799c4d9c36f0f335b9c93728f51c70d8c7f3484183c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:lipschitz of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty domain. We call $\Omega$ a (strongly) \textit{Lipschitz domain} if $n=1$ or if for every $x\in \partial\Omega$, there is an open neighborhood $U_x \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ around $x$, an orthogonal matrix $O_x \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and a Lipschitz function 
    $\phi_x: \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\to \mathbb{R}$ with 
    \begin{align*}
       O_x (U_x\cap \Omega) = \{(\xi,y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times \mathbb{R}~|~ y < \phi_x(\xi) \}\cap O_x(U_x).
    \end{align*}

    
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty, bounded Lipschitz domain, and let $\Omega_w,\Omega_h\subset \Omega$ be two disjoint, non-empty Lipschitz domains. If 
    $\overline{\Omega}=\overline{\Omega_w\cup \Omega_h}$, we call $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ a \textit{Lipschitz interface triple} with interface $\gamma.$ 
    In this case, we set
    $$\Gamma_w  \coloneq  \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_h, ~~\Gamma_h \coloneq \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_w,~~ \gamma \coloneq  \partial\Omega_w\backslash\overline{\Gamma_h} = \partial\Omega_h\backslash\overline{\Gamma_w}.$$
    Furthermore, we denote by $\nu_w,\nu_h$ the unit outer normal vectors on $\Gamma_w,\Gamma_h$, which exist almost everywhere due to Rademacher's Theorem for $n\geq 2,$ and trivially everywhere in the case $n=1.$

    
Our assumptions on $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ are weaker than the assumptions imposed in  [ines,zuazualongtime].

    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty Lipschitz domain, and let $\Gamma\subset \partial\Omega$ be a non-empty, relatively open subset of the boundary.
    We call $(\Omega,\Gamma)$ an \textit{admissible} Lipschitz pair, if there exists some domain $\Tilde{\Omega}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ such that 
    $$(\Omega\cup \Gamma\cup \Tilde{\Omega}, \Omega, \Tilde{\Omega})$$ is a Lipschitz interface triple with interface $\Gamma$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496825+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce8217e70fdb06c744eabae51c069fc0b750d8aec4ee06dee28df6c628b24330","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 (Conditional first-break law and moments) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level from
Lemma~\ref{lem:first-break}, and let
\[
        \mathcal B_d:=\{\text{the ultimate winner was never behind}\}.
\]
Then, conditional on $\mathcal E_A$,
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
The same convergence holds conditional on $\mathcal B_d$.

Moreover, for every fixed $p>0$,
\[
        \E\left[\left(\frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\right)^p\right]
        \longrightarrow
        \Gamma\left(1+\frac p2\right),
\]
and
\[
        \E\left[
        \left(\frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\right)^p

        \longrightarrow
        \Gamma\left(1+\frac p2\right).
\]
The same conditional moment convergence holds with $\mathcal E_A$ replaced by
$\mathcal B_d$.  In particular,
\[
        \E K_d\sim \frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\sqrt d,
        \qquad
        \operatorname{Var}(K_d)\sim
        \left(1-\frac\pi4\right)d,
\]
and the same expectation and variance asymptotics hold conditional on
$\mathcal E_A$ and conditional on $\mathcal B_d$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.513826+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cebac43e37aab5fd3a6ff3c520945d3e8cb4b923d1a12460d55a12c8c1761f6a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn H marginal of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] The locally commuting n chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ is a compatible family of measures $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}$ on $n$ tuples of continuous non-self-crossing curves $\left(\eta^{(1)}, \eta^{(2)},\ldots,\eta^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domain $\Omega$ with $\left(z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)$, and $\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)$ as above that satisfy additionally the conditions below. 

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \rightarrow \Omega^{\prime}$ is a conformal map fixing 0, then the pullback measure
$$
\varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^{\prime} ; \varphi\left(z_1\right), \varphi\left(z_2\right),\ldots,\varphi\left(z_n),\varphi(u)\right)\right)}^{\left(\varphi\left(U_1\right), \varphi\left(U_2\right),\right)}=\left(\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}\right) .
$$

Therefore, it suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)=\left(\mathbb{H}; z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,0\right)$.
We can extend our definition to arbitrary simply-connected domain $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $u$ by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\phi:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ sending $u$ to $0$.

\item
\textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_n\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots, U_n\right)}$ and we parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{H}$. Let $\mathbf{t}=\left(t_1, t_2,\ldots,t_n\right)$, such that $t_j$ is a stopping time for $\gamma^{(j)}$ and $\gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}$ is contained in the interior of $U_j$. Let
$$
\tilde{U}_j=U_j \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)}=\gamma^{(j)} \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad j=1,2,\ldots,n; \quad \tilde{\Omega}=\mathbb{H} \backslash\left(\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}\right) .
$$

Then conditionally on $\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup  \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}$, we have
$$
\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega} ; \gamma_{t_1}^{(1)}, \gamma_{t_2}^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma_{t_n}^{(n)}\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots,\tilde{U}_n\right)} .
$$

\item \textbf{Absolute continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}:
 In $\mathbb{H}$-uniformization, let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n)\right.}$. 

We assume that there exist smooth functions $b_j: \mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where the chamber: $$\mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u)=\left\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{H} \mid x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_n, u \in \mathbb{H} \right\}$$ 
such that the capacity parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_t^{(j)}$ of $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{~d} x_{j}(t)=\sqrt{\kappa} \mathrm{d} B_{j}(t)+b_j\left(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),u\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\mathrm{~d} x_{k}(t)=\frac{2}{x_{k}(t)-x_{j}(t)} \mathrm{d} t,  k\neq j
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $B_{j}$ is one-dimensional standard Brownian motion. 

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}
