{"assumptions":["All restricted four-point, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher and paired nonzero initialization assumptions of C010","Independent label noise amplitude sigma_e=c_e sqrt(kappa) eta_e^(1/4)~sqrt(kappa)e^(9/4)","Noise-averaged clean risk; simultaneous both-layer GD step 1/2; fixed nu in (0,1]","Even width limit precedes feature-scale limit; local windows only; eta_e is spectral ratio, not GD step size"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:50.829441+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_d89b9de19b9c660b1053843fd221195d71bd568e8a0d66ceffe03289fef81a6d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Joint low-noise central-window bifurcation

T267 / Target 2 / C012 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is a local, rescaled noise-onset result in C010's restricted model.
It is not an exact global two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Precise scaling and result

Use C010's four-point stratified design, centered unit-norm ReLU teacher,
paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite
support remain as in C010. Dependencies C009/C010 and this argument
await independent mathematical review; specialist novelty is unestablished.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:12:13.498213+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d8af25e7a543c3efb72534e729e40eba6c05e5db3fc5918d51e0827be2a590b8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2608.28410, 'Mean curvatures and symmetry\\of convex hypersurfaces'] Let $E\in Gr(n+1,\ol{m})$ with $\ol e:=P_Ee\ne0$. Then
$$
L^+_\xi(t)
=
\sup_{\substack{x\in\cl(\Omega)\\P_{\ol E}x=\xi}}
\left\{
\frac{\langle x,\ol e\rangle}{|\ol e|^2}+r(x)+tc(x)
\right\},
\quad
L^-_\xi(t)
=
\inf_{\substack{x\in\cl(\Omega)\\P_{\ol E}x=\xi}}
\left\{
\frac{\langle x,\ol e\rangle}{|\ol e|^2}-r(x)+tc(x)
\right\}.
$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.421240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d8b5cf3682c22bd5699ad777224252b9045437a827737f1d7ff7b7050f12b1cb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.31145, 'Gauge-compatible tensors on statistical manifolds: splitting and submanifold geometry'] Let $(M,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*},\Theta)$ be a Levi-Civita-parallel
$\Theta$-statistical manifold. Assume that the tangent bundle admits the orthogonal decomposition
\[
TM=\ker\Theta\oplus\operatorname{Im}\Theta.
\]
Then both distributions are preserved by
\[
\nabla^{g},\ \nabla,\ \nabla^{*},
\]
and
\begin{equation}
K_XY=0
\end{equation}
whenever one of $X,Y$ belongs to $\ker\Theta$ and the other belongs to
$\operatorname{Im}\Theta$.

Consequently, every point of $M$ admits a neighborhood $U$ for which
\[
(U,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*})
\cong
(U_0,g_0,\nabla^{0},(\nabla^{0})^{*})
\times
(U_1,g_1,\nabla^{1},(\nabla^{1})^{*}),
\]
where
\[
TU_0=\ker\Theta,
\qquad
TU_1=\operatorname{Im}\Theta.
\]
Thus the two local factors inherit statistical structures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726283+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / dispersive PDE","id":"claim_d948b0ea69eecd49bd6d6367620cfaf6003daf10d9fece613e380a2beca5623f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. {"assumptions":["for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory","for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied","independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation","non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998030+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d95edc3570f77641129fb8247438ed5ea704bbccb6be4cad5233917af61c0692","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.493241+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9619f115929734baab046145a93d1ace1842cc7f20f5d61cfb6bb39e4756f86","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 (Gelfand-Tsetlin facts, {\cite[Proposition 2) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] {NarSheffTao}}]
Let \(\lambda=(\lambda_1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n)\in\Spec_n\).  For
\(a\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) denote the real
Gelfand-Tsetlin polytope of triangular arrays
\[
        \Gamma=\{\lambda^{(k)}_i:1\leq i\leq k\leq n\}
\]
satisfying
\[
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_{i+1},
        \qquad
        1\leq i\leq k<n,
\]
with top row \(\lambda^{(n)}=\lambda\), and diagonal boundary condition
\[
        \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda^{(k)}_i
        =
        \sum_{i=1}^k a_i,
        \qquad 1\leq k\leq n.
\]
Let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}:=\bigcup_a\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\).
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), then the Schur--Horn relation
\(\diag(\lambda)\rel a\) holds if and only if
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) is nonempty.
\item[(ii)] The \(\binom n2\)-dimensional volume of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\) is \(V_n(\lambda)/V_n(\tau_n)\).
\item[(iii)] If \(A\) is Haar-uniform on the unitary orbit with spectrum
\(\lambda\), then the eigenvalues of the northwest principal minors of
\(A\) form a uniformly distributed point of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\). Its boundary vector \(a\) is the diagonal of
\(A\).
\item[(iv)] If \(\Lambda\in\Spec_n\) has large gaps,
\[
        \min_{1\leq i<n}(\Lambda_i-\Lambda_{i+1})
        >
        \lambda_1-\lambda_n,
\]
then for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) there is a volume-preserving linear
bijection
\[
        \GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}
        \longleftrightarrow
        H_n(\Lambda,\lambda;\Lambda+a).
\]
Under this bijection, a Gelfand-Tsetlin pattern
\((\lambda^{(k)}_i)_{1\leq i\leq k\leq n}\) is sent to the hive \(h:T_n\to
\mathbb R\) given by
\[
        h(i,j)
        =
        \Lambda_1+\cdots+\Lambda_j
        +
        \lambda^{(j)}_1+\cdots+\lambda^{(j)}_i .

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:20:55.630262+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d96947cd68bd5a5cba0c9976d9426dcee217294ab6bc482eb84c16efc072bdf6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:biregular of arXiv:2411.07809, 'Pirogov--Sinai Theory Beyond Lattices'] Suppose $G$ is bipartite, one-ended, vertex transitive within each
  parity class, and has polynomial volume growth. Suppose also that
  $G$ has a $D$-bounded cycle basis $\mathcal B$. There is a

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:37:20.359243+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d97463c8425c5edb42e765bd3f1c5bbad743dd782303dfb3731256ff50b17e30","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn de.2 of arXiv:2411.13099, 'Long time behavior of killed Feynman-Kac semigroups with singular Schr{ö}dinger potentials'] Let  $\mathbf F: \mathscr V\to [1,+\infty]$ be a measurable function. 
   We say that  $(Q^{\mathfrak X}_t,t\ge 0)$ is    $\mathbf F$ {\rm compact-ergodic} over $\mathscr V$   if:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[\textbf 1.] There exists a unique q.s.d.  $\rho$ for  $(P^{\mathfrak X}_t,t\ge 0)$ in   $  \mathcal P_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)$.  
 \item[\textbf 2.] 
  For all $t>0$, $Q^{\mathfrak X}_t:b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)\to b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)$ is compact and there exists $\lambda\ge  \inf_{\mathscr V} \mathbf V$   such that $\mathsf r_{sp}(Q^{\mathfrak X}_t|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)} ) =e^{-\lambda t}, \ \forall t>0$. 
  Furthermore,  $\rho    Q^{\mathfrak X}_t =e^{-\lambda t}\rho$, for all $t\ge 0$, and $\rho (O)>0$ for all nonempty open subsets $O$ of $ \mathscr V$. In addition,  there is a unique   function $\varphi \in \mathcal C_{b\mathbf F}( \mathscr V)$   such that  $\rho   (\varphi )=1$ and $
      Q^{\mathfrak X}_t \varphi= e^{-\lambda  t} \varphi  \text{ on } \mathscr V, \forall t\ge0$.  
 Moreover, $\varphi>0$   everywhere on $\mathscr V$.
\item[\textbf 3.] There exist   $\mathfrak m_1>0$, and   $\mathfrak m_2\ge 1$, s.t.  for all  $t>0$ and all   $\nu\in \mathcal P_{\mathbf F  }( \mathscr V)$:
$$
\sup_{\mathcal A\in\mathcal B(\mathscr V)}\big |  \nu P^{\mathfrak X}_t(\mathcal A)-\rho  (\mathcal A)\big |\le \mathfrak m_2 \, e^{-\mathfrak m_1 t} \frac{\nu(\mathbf F )}{\nu(\varphi)}.
$$
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.675639+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d97be235d01df4d78b67ce6366ce4d108aa22374e33abc12f3ab6cb220eb967c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:41:19.322996+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9879ec63d0dbd32ed7b5f45e477dbbdb43103b95918e0086cb6ce778da349f8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:conditional-bridge-functional-limit of arXiv:2609.03532, 'Airy limit for the Jack process and topological expansion'] [Xu]

Fix $x>0$ and $h_0,h_1\geq0$, and set
\[
  L_N=\lfloor xN^{2/3}\rfloor,
  \qquad
  H_{a,N}=\lfloor h_a\sigma N^{1/3}\rfloor,
  \quad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Normalize $\operatorname{wt}$ on
$\mathcal W(H_{0,N},H_{1,N},L_N)$ to a probability measure, and define
the right-continuous step process
\begin{equation*}
  \widehat W_N(u)
  :=\frac{W(\lfloor uN^{2/3}\rfloor)}{\sigma N^{1/3}},
  \qquad 0\leq u\leq x.
\end{equation*}
Then as $N\to\infty$, $\widehat W_N$ converges weakly in the Skorokhod space
$D([0,x])$, equipped with the $J_1$ topology, to the nonnegative
Brownian bridge of length $x$ from $h_0$ to $h_1$.

corresponding three-dimensional Bessel bridge, interpreted by time reversal

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.034516+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d98feba1bb71e6e4d6980179a25205901c9d83096617fcde4b9b35c89fed88d3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 (SDE for the second Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth},
and \ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform} hold. Fix
$ 0 \le r \le s \le t $, $ u \in [s,t] $,
$ i,j,k \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $, and
$ \alpha,\beta \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $.
Then, the process $\left(
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
\right)_{u \in [s,t]}$ solves the SDE
\begin{align}

D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
d\rho
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
dB_\rho^i ,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}$ denotes the initial
condition given by
\begin{align*}
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
&=
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{i,N}
e_\alpha
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{i,N}e_\beta
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}} \frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\alpha
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\beta ,
\end{align*}
with $ e_\alpha $ denoting the $ \alpha $-th vector of the canonical basis of $ \R^m $,
\begin{align}

G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N},
\end{align}
and $H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $, while
\begin{align}

R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\partial_{xx}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu\left[ \partial_x b \right]
\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_x\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( \cdot,\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{i,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_v\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1{N^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^N \sum_{q=1}^N
\partial_{\mu\mu}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N}, X_\rho^{q,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{q,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right],
\end{align}
and $ S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $. Finally, there exists a constant $ C > 0 $, independent of
$ r,s,t,\rho,N,i,j,k,\alpha,\beta $, such that, for every $ \rho \in [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

\norm{R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
+
\norm{S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
&\le
C \Bigg(
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
+
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}","status":"unverified"}

For example, of three gloves, at least two must be right-handed or at least two must be left-handed, because there are three objects but only two categories of handedness to put them into. This seemingly obvious statement, a type of counting argument, can be used to demonstrate possibly unexpected results. Then \(U(x,\cdot)\) satisfies smooth fit at the
    upper boundary:
    \[
        \lim_{y\uparrow b(x)} D_y U(x,y)

        =
        k'(x+b(x)).

    If \(a(x)>-x\), then \(U(x,\cdot)\) also satisfies smooth fit at the lower
    boundary:
    \[
        \lim_{y\uparrow a(x)} D_y U(x,y)
        =

        =

    \]

    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818757+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, central limit theorems","id":"claim_daa69de324d9215d86d9b0cc72766b88058053b14240299bf615129c670e3049","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 4.30 (p. 137) asks whether there is an explicit function psi(b,s) tending to 0 as s tends to infinity, not depending on the chain, with sup_x |P(S_t/(sigma sqrt t) <= x) - P(Z <= x)| <= psi(||g||_inf, t/tau2) for standardized g and continuous-time reversible chains. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.235220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dab15ba146eefad594bfb1127aa334a49aadee8418addb6be53fcfc3f5cb9226","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.
Let
\[
X^{(1)} \defeq X\times_{S,F_S}S
\]
be the relative Frobenius twist, and let
\[
F_{X/S}\colon X \to  X^{(1)}
\]
be the relative Frobenius.
  \begin{itemize}
      \item   The \emph{(absolute) de Rham stack} of \(X\) is defined as a functor
  \begin{equation*}
    X^{\dR} \colon \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p} \to \Ani; \  R \mapsto X(W(R)/^L p),
  \end{equation*}
  where \(W(R)\) is the ring of Witt vectors of \(R\), \(-/^L p\) is the derived quotient by \(p\), and \(X(W(R)/^L p)\) is the mapping space \(\Map_{\dSch_{\setF_p}}(\Spec(W(R)/^L p), X)\) in the \(\infty\)-category of derived schemes over \(\setF_p\).
  Since this is isomorphic to the relative Hodge--Tate stack \((X/\setZ_p)^{\HT}\) of \(X\) relative to the crystalline prism \((\setZ_p, (p))\) introduced in \cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Construction 7.1}, this is a stack on \(\CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\) (\cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Lemma 7.3}).

  This is equipped with natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X} \colon X \to X^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_X \colon X^{\dR} \to X
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks: For each \(R \in \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\), each morphism is given by precomposition of morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    R \xrightarrow{\Phi_R} W(R)/^L p \quad \text{and} \quad W(R)/^L p \xrightarrow{\res} R,
  \end{equation*}
  where \(\Phi_R\) is the animation of the morphism \(a \mapsto [a^p] \bmod p\) and \(\res\) is the restriction morphism.
  Note that the composition \(\nu_X \circ \pi_X\) is the absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_X \colon X \to X\) of \(X\).
\item The \emph{de Rham stack} of $X$ over $S$ is defined by
\[
(X/S)^{\dR} \defeq X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR},\pi_S} S.
\]
We define natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X/S} \colon X \to (X/S)^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks as follows:
The morphism $\pi_{X/S}$ is defined by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow[r,"\pi_{X/S}"'] \arrow[rd,bend right,"\iota"] \arrow[rr,bend left,"\pi_X"] & X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \\
& S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] & S^{\dR}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}$ is induced by the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \arrow[r,"\nu_X"] & X \arrow[d,"\iota"] \\
S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] \arrow[rr,bend right,"F"] & S^{\dR} \arrow[r,"\nu_S"] & S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item We assume that $\iota$ is smooth representable.
Then the cotangent complex \(L_{X/S}\) is a locally free \(\cO_X\)-module concentrated in degree \(0\).  
We set
\[
\Omega^1_{X/S} \defeq L_{X/S},
\qquad
\Omega^i_{X/S} \defeq 
\bigwedge_{\cO_X}^i\Omega^1_{X/S}.
\]
The universal \(S\)-derivation
\[
d_{X/S}\colon \cO_X \to  \Omega^1_{X/S}
\]
extends uniquely to the relative de Rham complex
\[
\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}
=
\left[
\cO_X
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^1_{X/S}
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^2_{X/S}
 \to \cdots
\right].
\]

We define a morphism of complexes of $\cO_{X^{(1)}}$-modules
\[
F^{\dR}_{X/S} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to F_{X/S,*}\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/S}
\]
as follows:
We have
\[
d_{X/S}\circ F_{X/S}^{\sharp}=0
\]
by checking smooth locally on \(X\).  
Therefore, the morphism
\[
F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}} \to  F_{X/S,*}\cO_X
\]
defines a morphism of complexes
\[
F_{X/S}^{\dR}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}}
 \to 
F_{X/S,*}\Omega^\bullet_{X/S},
\]
whose degree \(0\) component is \(F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\) and whose
positive-degree components are zero.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.258728+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dabd2d8a9c94c17b6e66ae3a98f56a0c89349c4f708e8d59a99c1a6e168d952a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:dg of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Let 
$G_1(x)\leq G_2(x)$
be two real continuous payoff functions.
Consider a L\'evy process $X$ and a discount factor $r>0$, 
such that conditions (equation eq:ic of the paper) and (equation eq:limit of the paper) above hold.
Given two stopping times $\sigma$ and $\tau$, define the expected payoff

$$
{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x\left(
e^{-r\tau}G_1(X_{\tau})\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq\sigma\}}
+
e^{-r\sigma}G_2(X_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma<\tau\}}
\right).
$$

The Dynkin game (DG) problem consists
in finding the value function $V(x)$ and two optimal stopping rules ${\sigma^*}$ and ${\tau^*}$ such that
\begin{align}
V(x)&=\inf_{\sigma}\sup_{\tau}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\sup_{\tau}\inf_{\sigma}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)={\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma^*,\tau^*).

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149110+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_db0bd50e4b1d3185e597734ebdf3437ca5f83b01bff6e16e23fd7c464aeb3f41","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Omega bounded. The proofs use boundedness twice - the auxiliary function exp(gamma x_1) must be bounded on Omega, and the maximum must be attained on a compact set. On unbounded domains the conclusion is false even for harmonic functions with zero boundary data. Unbounded counterexample: on the half-space {x_n > 0} the function u(x) = x_n is harmonic and vanishes on the whole boundary, yet u > 0 inside; sup u = infinity while sup over the boundary of u = 0. Bounded counterexample (so boundedness of u does not rescue the statement in general): for n >= 3 let Omega = {|x| > 1} and u(x) = 1 - |x|^{2-n}. Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous up to the boundary, bounded with 0 <= u < 1, u = 0 on the boundary sphere, and sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. In the plane, u(x) = log|x| on {|x| > 1} is an unbounded version of the same phenomenon. What restores the principle: treat infinity as a boundary point, i.e. assume limsup of u(x) as |x| tends to infinity is <= 0 (then the principle holds on any unbounded Omega, by exhausting with large balls), or impose a Phragmen-Lindeloef growth restriction adapted to the geometry. The admissible growth is set by the opening of the domain, and a thinner domain permits faster growth, not slower: in a plane sector of opening pi/a the threshold is exp(|x|^a), so a narrow sector allows faster growth than a half-plane, and in a strip of width d the threshold is exp(pi|x|/d), the extremal being exp(pi x_1/d) cos(pi x_2/d). The same caution applies to the H^1 weak maximum principle: its proof uses the Sobolev inequality together with the fact that the level sets have finite measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:35:10.797346+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db54afcbd5e689d1637dc49b9ae536d25e7ef2290533bc0230821f15e34d4c3c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defin 55 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\op{s}_{\rho}$ be the dilation with scale $\rho > 0$: $\op{s}_{\rho}(x)=\rho x$. Given $\mu \in \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$, its pushforward by $\op{s}_{\rho}$
is the unique probability measure $\op{s}_{\rho \#}\mu$  such that

$$\Int{\mathbb{R}}{} f(x) \, \mathrm{d}\op{s}_{\rho \#}\mu( x)  \, =  \, \Int{\mathbb{R}}{} f(\rho  x) \,  \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \, .$$

Note that $\mathrm{supp} \big[ \op{s}_{\rho \#} \mu \big] \,  =  \,  \rho \, \mathrm{supp} [ \mu ]$. For a probability measure $\mu$ and $\tau>0$, we denote by $\mu_\tau$
the probability measure obtained by the convolution

\begin{equation}

\mu_\tau=\frac{1}{2\tau} \mathbbm{1}_{[-\tau;\tau]} \ast \mu\,.

\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583768+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_db5eb654cfadf445fa059f8bceb44a8415837ad88ca812a4513a0ade0f74de10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, equivalently a compact Riemann surface, and let D be a divisor on X. Write l(D) for the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions on X whose poles are bounded by D and which have no other poles, and let K be a canonical divisor of X. The Riemann-Roch theorem states l(D) - l(K - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g, where deg(D) is the sum of the coefficients of D. Once deg(D) > 2g - 2 this gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - g exactly, since l(K-D) then vanishes. Proved by Riemann and Roch in the 1850s-60s; vastly generalized by Hirzebruch and Grothendieck.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:28:08.666103+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db5fde77b98da42fc66c429b065cbb835190a1758c4f92dfbc0e11369dcec23e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 28 of arXiv:2607.29495, 'Fast Mixing for Low-Temperature Potts Models via Poisson Trees'] Let $\Downg$  be the distribution of  $X\sim\Poisson(dp_\good)$.
Let $\Downgbig$ be the distribution of $X$ conditioned on $X\geq D$ and let $\Downgsmall$ be $\Downg$ conditioned on $X<D$. Let $\Downb$ be the distribution $\Poisson(dp_\bad)$.  The rooted random tree $\cT^{\down}$ is defined as follows.

\begin{itemize}
\item The root is set to be \emph{down-good} with probability $p_\good$ and \emph{down-bad} otherwise (with probability $p_\bad$).

\item From every down-good vertex, the number of down-good children is sampled independently from $\Downgbig$ and the number of down-bad children is sampled independently from $\Downb$.

\item From every down-bad vertex, the number of down-good children is sampled independently from $\Downgsmall$ and the number of down-bad children is sampled independently from $\Downb$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:53:00.814024+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db722a684036d88d3fed8ad5ff1061549c4e967a0edae2aee9aeb8f24e21e943","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Type forest, type rays and paths of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider the \\emph{Ulam-Harris forest} $\\mathscr{F}_S$ on the set of types $S$. For any fixed $s_0 \\in S$, the root of the tree $\\mathscr T(s_0)$ is $s_0$, and for any $v\\in \\mathscr T(s_0)$, it has $|S|$ many offspring $\\{vs:s\\in S\\}$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:04.961469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db75c2f89cf0c0e5614bf6efc2acc163da629893662959afc861c32c88072a49","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db9918fbc671f11eee90cd6406606fa76cc6077e21fc89d28df52ffb173bfd87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

\[
    \mathcal U(T,x)\coloneqq

    \bigl[Z(T,x)-Z(T-\tau,B_\tau)\bigr]\, ,
\]
where the supremum is over stopping times for Brownian motion. Then, for every $T>0$,
\[
    R^{-(2-d/2)}\,u^{(R)}_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}

\]
where the field on the left denotes the multilinear interpolation from $R^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^d$ of the values
$x/R\mapsto R^{-(2-d/2)}u_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}(x)$.

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.041687+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbecbcb9b13f161904a3293a0fba4ae24ea22a3e38c1603cc1251089b13c41ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 34 (Finite spectral reduction) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The reduction space, \emph{in symmetrised coordinates}, is exactly
the odd sector:
\begin{equation}
\widetilde V:=D^{-1}V = E_{\mathrm{odd}},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
V = D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}} .

\end{equation}
The distinction matters: $D$ does not commute with $S$ unless
$p=q$, so $D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}}\neq E_{\mathrm{odd}}$ for a biased
walk --- consistently with the fact, noted above, that it is
$\widetilde\psi$ and not $\psi$ that is antisymmetric. The space
admits the canonical decomposition
\begin{equation}
\psi(\gamma)=\sum_{k\ \mathrm{even}} f_k(\gamma)\,\mathbf m_k,
\qquad
\mathbf m_k := D\,P_k\,D^{-1}\xi = D\,P_k\,\widetilde\xi,
\qquad
f_k(\gamma)=\frac{t}{1-\lambda_k t},
\quad t=1-\gamma .

\end{equation}
The directions $\mathbf m_k$ are nonzero and linearly independent.
As for canonicity, the symmetrised directions $P_k\widetilde\xi$ are
determined by $(\widetilde P,S,\widetilde\xi)$; their
original-coordinate images are determined by $(P,S,\xi)$ alone. For
the present irreducible tridiagonal $P$ the positive diagonal
symmetriser is unique up to an overall scalar --- the ratios
$D_{z+1}/D_z$ being fixed by the neighbour relations --- and the
conjugation $D P_k D^{-1}$ is unchanged under $D\mapsto cD$; so no
normalisation of the symmetriser need be fixed. In particular $\dim V = r$, and all $\gamma$-dependence is
carried by the elementary scalars $f_k$.

The notation is deliberate: these $\mathbf m_k$ are \emph{not} the
normal directions $\mathbf n_\nu$ of Section~\ref{sec:finite-reduction}.
There are $N$ of the latter, one per spectral mode, spanning a space
of dimension $r$ and therefore dependent; there are exactly $r$ of the
former, indexed by the even $k$ alone, and they are independent. Both
families span $V$, which is all the two routes are claimed to share.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

\[

\[

\[
g^{\neq}_\delta(x,y)=\delta xy, \qquad g^{=}_\eta(x)=\eta x,

Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: A single idle-gap diagnostic is exact: for next-arrival gap G~Exp(Lambda), the chance the server becomes cold is exp(-Lambda*gamma), and expected on-idle duration is E[min(G,gamma)]=(1-exp(-Lambda*gamma))/Lambda. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.600084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc256567fe2e9178ffc3e664d5f0a3ae4ec6240edbfaa03b19b5239356ad256f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition proposition duality of arXiv:2412.05064, '\textbf{Sample path central limit theorem for the occupation time of the voter model on a '] For any integer $m\geq 1$, $y_1, y_2,\ldots, y_m\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $0\leq t_1\leq t_2\leq \ldots\leq t_m$, $\eta\in \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ and function $G$ from $\{0, 1\}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}$, we have

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845617+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc6b41a2e65e311eaddb446d8f516a18f90158f9f11f93d80d67fed31fc2a608","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 17 (Elliptical Brownian motions) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$ and let $\zeta\in\C$ with $0<|\zeta|\le\rho$.  Define
\begin{equation}
    
    \theta = \frac12\arg \zeta \qquad a = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho+|\zeta|)} \qquad b = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho-|\zeta|)}. 
\end{equation}
Then $a^2+b^2=\rho$ and $e^{2\i\theta}(a^2-b^2)=\zeta$, so that $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfy \eqref{eq.rho.zeta}.  This yields a bijective mapping
\begin{equation} \{(\rho,\zeta)\colon 0<|\zeta|\le\rho\}\mapsto\{(a,b,\theta)\colon a>b\ge 0, \theta\in[0,\pi)\}. \end{equation}
We may extend the definitions of $a,b$ to allow $\zeta=0$, in which case $a=b$; here $\theta$ is undefined.

Let $(X^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$, $(Y^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$. 
We define the general {\bf elliptical Brownian motion} $(W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$ by
	\[ W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(aX^N(t) + \i b Y^N(t)\right). \]
    Similarly, if $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(y(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are freely independent free semicircular Brownian motion, the {\bf free elliptical Brownian motion $(w_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$} is defined as
    \[ w_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(a x(t) + \i b y(t)\right). \]
In both cases, when $a=b$ (i.e.\ $\zeta=0$), all values of $\theta$ yield the same distribution for the right-hand-side, so we may take canonically $\theta=0$ in this case.

Note that the laws of $W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ and $w_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ are invariant under $a\mapsto-a$, $b\mapsto-b$, and $(a,b,\theta)\mapsto(b,a,\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})$.  It then follows from \eqref{eq.bijection} that $\rho>0$, $|\zeta|\le\rho$ paramaterize the laws of all possible elliptical Brownian motions.

To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\rho,\zeta$ if there can be no confusion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.478187+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc7f92a47f72e853d6ed6052ff3725a3345f24c23d06c222b2e1bdf27fc0359c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Parametric weighted lattice-corner expansion) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Let $U$ be a compact interval. For each $p\in U$, let $Z_p$ be a random vector supported by a fixed finite subset of $\Zz^d$, with masses that are positive and $C^{r+2}$ in $p$. Assume that the additive group generated by differences of support points is $\Zz^d$. Put
\[
 M_p(\lambda)=\Ee e^{\langle\lambda,Z_p\rangle}.
\]
Suppose there is a $C^{r+2}$ map $\lambda:U\to(0,\infty)^d$ satisfying
\[
 \nabla_\lambda\log M_p(\lambda(p))=0.
\]
Let
\[
 I(p)=-\log M_p(\lambda(p)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma(p)=\nabla_\lambda^2\log M_p(\lambda(p)).
\]
Let $w:\Zz_+^d\to\Rr$ be bounded and define
\[
 W(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}
 w(z)e^{-\langle\lambda(p),z\rangle}.
\]
For independent copies $Z_{p,1},\ldots,Z_{p,n}$, put $S_{n,p}=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{p,i}$ and
\[
 \mathcal T_n(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}w(z)\Pp(S_{n,p}=z).
\]
Then, for $\varepsilon_n=n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3r+6}$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n(p)
 =\frac{e^{-nI(p)}n^{-d/2}}
 {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p)}}
 \left[W(p)+O_{C^r(U)}(\varepsilon_n)\right].
 
\end{equation}
If $r\ge1$ and $I'(p_0)\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n'(p_0)
 =n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}
 \left\{-I'(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}+o(1)\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
If in addition $W(p_0)\ne0$, this may equivalently be written with a relative factor $\{1+o(1)\}$. If $r\ge2$, $I'(p_0)=0$, $I''(p_0)>0$, and $W(p_0)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n''(p_0)
 =-I''(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}
 n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}\{1+o(1)\}.
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.036644+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcb36ba39dd44d5895719498d4c735be156fcffb74b604526cb65b37c5bfa69f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 16 (The separatrix is the cone of square roots) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Suppose, as in Remark~\ref{rem:pi-mu}, that the underlying chain

the two pictures are of different kinds: in the $\pi$-coordinates

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Local existence for the characteristic IVP}}. 
Recall that the classical solution is $C^{\infty}$ on $\twoargMrough{[\timefunction_0,0],[- \rightu,\leftu]}{0}$
and therefore induces $C^{\infty}$ data on the characteristic surfaces
$\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\leftubar}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\moreinterestingu_1}{[\leftubar,0]}$; see Appendix~\ref{A:DATASSUMPTIONS}.
Then there exists a  
$\ubarlocal \in (\leftubar,0)$, depending on the data, such the characteristic data launch a unique $C^{\infty}$ solution
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$,
and the change of variables map $(u,\ubar,x^2,x^3) \rightarrow (t,x^1,x^2,x^3)$
is a diffeomorphism from $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$
onto its image in Cartesian coordinate space.

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Continuation criteria for the characteristic IVP}}.

Assume the following: 
\begin{itemize}
	\item The assumptions of Theorem\,\ref{T:EXISTENCEUPTOCAUCHYHORIZONBYCONTINUATIONCRITERIA} hold.
	\item $\ubarboot < 0$.
	\item The ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the wave variables $\wavearray$, and the acoustic geometry variables $u, \, \chi$, etc. are classical solutions on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$. 
	\item The bootstrap assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold for $(\ubar,u) \in [\leftubar,\ubarboot)\times[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$. 
\end{itemize}

Then there exists a $\Delta \in (0,|\ubarboot|)$ such that the ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the solution variables $\wavearray, \, u$, and all of the other geometric quantities defined throughout the article can be uniquely extended to a strictly larger region of the form $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot + \Delta)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$ on which all of the bootstrap
assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.627779+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2388135a2e2a8b9cbf66da57e0489396ea0b66e60989dbe12db6c40d0a2cb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:upper_lower_simple of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\alpha \in (0,2)\setminus\{1\}$, and suppose $\bm{Z}$ is $\alpha$-stable and $\bm{X}$ is in the domain of normal attraction of $\bm{Z}$.\\
{\normalfont{(a)}} Let Assumption~(\nameref{asm:T}) hold for $p\geqslant 1\vee 2(\alpha-1)$. Then, for any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$, as $t \downarrow 0$, 
\[
\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z}\big)
=\begin{dcases}
    \mathcal{O}\big(t^{1-q/\alpha}\big), 
   & \alpha<1,\\
   \mathcal{O}\big(t^{q(1-1/\alpha)}\big), 
   & \alpha>1.
\end{dcases}
\]
{\normalfont{(b)}} If $\bm{X}$ does not have the law of $\bm{Z}$, then for any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ there exists some $C_q>0$ satisfying 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})
    \geqslant\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}_1^t,\bm{Z}_1) 
    \geqslant C_q t^{1-q/\alpha},
\quad \text{for all sufficiently small }t>0. 
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2c5f1ca2ba7f115f24e4985d485e0ea81fbf2f9568b8bd5140a67410b7be1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["N >= 2 and 1 <= n <= N","the sample is uniform over n-subsets (or ordered n-tuples of distinct indices)","the population values are fixed real numbers"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T12:42:10.075440+00:00","domain":"finite populations, sampling without replacement","id":"claim_dcf317859569e07874d3f22a1c25d15cff649175055901dbb5087797cee46d75","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a uniformly random n-element subset of {1, ..., N}, with N >= 2 and 1 <= n <= N, and I_i = 1{i in A}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:53.443469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd038426f703dde2403154a36724715d1981820c0aa7f4d5dc7cdb10eb9bd4aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Multispecies mixed Ising model) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $N\geq 1$, $D\geq 1$ and $\Sigma_N=\{\pm 1\}^N$.
For all $\bmx\in\mathbb R^D$, define the covariance function
\[
    \xi(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \xi_k(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \sum_{\substack{\bm p\in\mathsf P_k}}
    \Delta_{\bmp}^2\prod_{d=1}^D x_d^{p_d}.
\]
where $\bmDelta=(\Delta_{\bmp}^2:\bmp\in\mathsf P_k,\, k\geq 1)$ is a family of nonnegative coefficients and
where
\[
    \mathsf P_k
    =
    \{\bmp=(p_1,\ldots,p_D)\in\mathbb Z_+^D:
      |\bmp|:=p_1+\cdots+p_D=k\}.
\]
We also assume that $\xi((1+\varepsilon)\bm{1})<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

For \(\sigma,\tau\in\SigN\), define the species overlap vector by
\[
    R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau)
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i\in I_{N,d}}\sigma_i\tau_i,
    \qquad
    \bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)=(R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau))_{d=1}^D,
\]
where \(\bmI_N=\{I_{N,1},\ldots,I_{N,D}\}\) is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The Hamiltonian of the \emph{multispecies mixed Ising model} is a centered Gaussian process
 \(H_N=(H_N(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\SigN}\)
with covariance
\[
    \mathbb E H_N(\sigma)H_N(\tau)
    =
    N\xi(\bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)),
    \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\SigN.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.314425+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd080d83fbf074c324e3efaa60fd751a80c059eea496c119736ac1502779a5f3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] For the two-parameter  Pitman-Yor model

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.323818+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd2bfae5c411e8b86196b40e82f444fb5fd2f6bb99e464bdf75e5ec77d0cfb6c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma appendix lemma proof of asymptotic variance formula of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] Consider a strongly continuous Markov semigroup $(P_t)_{t \geq 0}$ on 
a measurable space with an invariant probability measure $\mu$.
Let \(K\subset L_0^2(\mu)\) be a closed \(P_t\)-invariant subspace, and
let \(L_K\) denote the generator of the restricted semigroup
\((P_t \vert_K)_{t\ge0}\).
Fix \(g\in K\). Suppose there exists \(f\in \operatorname{Dom}(L_K)\) such
that
\[
        -L_K f=g.
\]
Then the asymptotic variance of \(g\) exists and is given by
\[
        \sigma_g^2
        :=
        \lim_{t\to\infty}
        t\,\operatorname{Var}_\mu(\mu_tg)
        =
        2\operatorname{Re}\langle g,f\rangle .
\]
In particular, if the local gap defined in (equation gap definition invariant subspace of the paper)
satisfies $\gamma_K > 0$, then
\[
        \sigma_g^2
        =
        2\operatorname{Re}\langle g,-L_K^{-1}g\rangle .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.381897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd546742303e39ccdfe4081945a75a3f4c296215f9a48e8614db95e698e17d77","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:local-direction of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Fix an integer $\ell\in\{2,\dots,n\}$.  
A random direction $\rho\in S_n$ with law $q_\ell$ is generated as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample a starting index $i$ uniformly from $[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}$.
  \item For $r=0,1,\dots,\ell-1$, define
  \[
    i_r \;:=\; 1 + \bigl((i-1+r)\bmod n\bigr)\ \in\ [n].
  \]
  \item Let $\rho$ be the $\ell$--cycle on these indices,
  \[
    \rho \;:=\; (i_0\ i_1\ \cdots\ i_{\ell-1}),
  \]
  i.e.\ $\rho(i_r)=i_{r+1}$ for $r=0,\dots,\ell-2$, $\rho(i_{\ell-1})=i_0$, and
  $\rho(k)=k$ for all $k\notin\{i_0,\dots,i_{\ell-1}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
We write $\rho\sim q_\ell$. The law $q_\ell$ is state independent (i.e.,
$q(\cdot\mid\sigma)\equiv q_\ell$ for all $\sigma\in S_n$) and is orbit--equivariant
in the sense of Definition~(def:direction-law of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

\[
Z_n^{[P_j]}

=

for all \(j\neq k\), where

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is a bounded linear operator X -> Y","compactness of I - ST and I - TS (not merely boundedness) is what makes the criterion work"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572195+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_dd902b48ae729c20df07599e1a8e793996632d7377d0e8bd78774bcd906c51d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y). Then T is Fredholm if and only if T is invertible modulo compact operators, i.e. there is S in B(Y,X) with I_X - S T in K(X) and I_Y - T S in K(Y). Moreover, if T is Fredholm one may choose S (a Fredholm regularizer, or parametrix) so that I_X - S T and I_Y - T S have finite rank, namely the projection onto ker T along a closed complement and the projection onto a finite-dimensional complement of ran T along ran T; any such S is itself Fredholm with ind S = -ind T. For X = Y this says: T is Fredholm if and only if its class in the Calkin algebra B(X)/K(X) is invertible.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.764803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd9208166dd05484a23daf9673b9aef5c8e7dea3fc0576c4ede0e2f0feef7150","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Consider the setup described just above where we let $\Gamma^\C$ be a nested whole-plane~\clekp{}. There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of resistance forms $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C}))_{k \in \N}$ that is measurable with respect to $\Gamma^\C$ and satisfies the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^\C} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^\C|_U$.
\item For each $z \in \C$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^\C+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that for each $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^\C} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statement holds for the \clekp{} Brownian motion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space over R or C","K: X -> X is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar (for lambda = 0 every assertion can fail)","in the Hilbert-space form, H is a Hilbert space and K* is the Hilbert adjoint, so the relevant homogeneous adjoint equation uses the complex conjugate of lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572093+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory, integral equations","id":"claim_ddaa1329528122fb80376912c0e3927070e563e1860806c39b21c8299d538814","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space over R or C, let K in K(X) be compact, let lambda be a nonzero scalar and set T = lambda I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional; (ii) ran T is closed; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T' = dim(X / ran T) < infinity, where T' = lambda I - K' on the dual X'; in particular T is Fredholm with ind T = 0; (iv) ran T = {y in X : f(y) = 0 for every f in ker T'}. Consequently exactly one of the following holds: either lambda x - K x = y has a unique solution for every y in X (and the solution depends continuously on y), or the homogeneous equation lambda x - K x = 0 has a nonzero solution, in which case the solution space is finite-dimensional of dimension d, the adjoint homogeneous equation lambda f - K' f = 0 also has a d-dimensional solution space, and lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly for those y annihilated by every solution f of the adjoint homogeneous equation (solutions then form an affine space of dimension d). In a Hilbert space H with K compact, the adjoint condition reads: lambda x - K x = y is solvable iff y is orthogonal to ker(conj(lambda) I - K*).","status":"unverified"}

\[
w_1(s)=\frac{1}{1+2^{-s}},
\qquad
w_2(s)=\frac{2^{-s}}{1+2^{-s}},
\qquad s\ge 0.
\]
Fix $\theta\in(1/2,1)$ and set
\[
s_\theta:=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\right).
\]
Then the expected quorum time has the explicit form
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{w_1(s)}+\dfrac{1}{w_2(s)}-1\right), & 0\le s\le s_\theta,\\[1.0em]
\dfrac{1}{\lambda\, w_1(s)}, & s>s_\theta.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover:
\begin{itemize}
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly increasing on $[0,s_\theta]$;
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly decreasing on $(s_\theta,\infty)$.
\end{itemize}
Hence global monotonicity in the aligned heterogeneity parameter is false.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Standard Borel covariate; strictly positive measurable score almost surely, finite mean score.","Fixed retention fraction strictly between zero and one.","Conditional unbiasedness and the mean positive-weight retention budget; no claim about estimator asymptotics."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:15.363712+00:00","domain":"Statistical data selection and inverse-probability weighting","id":"claim_ddd5fc36f48265162995ac3142dd2378fa412c120b9b084e148942e78dec54b7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon optimal unbiased selection, strictly positive-score specialization. Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). There is a unique c>0 such that E pi_star(X)=gamma. The minimum is E[Z(X)/pi_star(X)]=E[max(Z(X),sqrt(Z(X))/c)]<infinity. Every minimizer has this same retention probability almost surely and has constant weight 1/pi_star(X) on its retained observations, conditional on X. Uniform random retention has objective E Z/gamma; the optimal objective is strictly smaller unless Z is almost surely constant. This is the convex allocation problem in Proposition4.2 and AppendixB of Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon, with the strict-positive-score restriction stated explicitly to avoid zero-score conventions. On the nearest-neighbor ladder Z x {0,1} with iid Uniform[1,2] edge weights, almost surely a bigeodesic uses one of the two edges across the cut between columns 0 and 1. Every geodesic from (-n,0) to (n,0) crosses that finite cut; an infinite subsequence shares one cut edge, and anchored diagonal compactness yields a bigeodesic. {"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.746107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de12232140b00c54f654a321a766291084b9267f14677bea219692b0e6f96eed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P","Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha","Finite second moment of xi_0","Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k","Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:05:57.431397+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; Markov jump linear systems","id":"claim_de1b5940314d04a7ddcbc45caa566cc8e834b108f83b393e8aa92596fbff4e17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Fix real d-by-d matrices A_i, real d-vectors b_i and a constant alpha. Set H_i=I+alpha A_i and let xi_(k+1)=H_(z_k)xi_k+alpha b_(z_k). Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. For stacked q_k and v_k=(vec(Q_k^1),...,vec(Q_k^N)), columnwise vectorization gives q_(k+1)=H11 q_k+alpha(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_d)b and v_(k+1)=H22 v_k+H21 q_k+alpha^2(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_(d^2))b2, where b stacks b_i, b2 stacks b_i tensor b_i, H11_(j,i)=p_ij H_i, H22_(j,i)=p_ij(H_i tensor H_i), and H21_(j,i)=alpha p_ij[b_i tensor H_i+H_i tensor b_i]. In particular H22=(P^T tensor I_(d^2))diag_i(H_i tensor H_i); the update factor uses the departure state i. The raw second moment is sum_i Q_k^i and E||xi_k||^2=sum_i trace(Q_k^i); these Q_k^i are not centered conditional covariances. No irreducibility, stationarity, or zero stationary mean of b is needed for these finite-time identities.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}
