{"assumptions":["conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree with n vertices","N_d = number of vertices of outdegree d"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.318625+00:00","domain":"probability/random trees","id":"claim_e3850e9afeb448f99ec9561d012acf69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Janson's Problem 20.2 (Probability Surveys 2012, Section 20.2) asks whether the outdegree counts N_d of a conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree are asymptotically normal. (a) nu = 1 with finite variance: yes, jointly with the covariances (Janson, Random Structures Algorithms 48 (2016), Theorem 1.13 with Example 2.2 and Section 8). (b) nu = 1 with infinite variance and (c) nu < 1: yes when the offspring law is regularly varying (Thevenin, Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020), Theorems 6.2 and 6.7, variance pi_d(1 - pi_d)), but not in general. A subcritical law whose bulk sits on {0, 1}, with two rare atoms at (1 - q - c) n_r +/- A sqrt(n_r), each of probability n_r^{-4}, makes the conditioned tree carry exactly one of the two with probability tending to 1/2 each, so N_1 = n pi_1 -/+ A sqrt(n) up to smaller terms, a near two-point law (Theorem A, full proof); the critical infinite-variance case is the same construction with the pair straddling the missing mass of an absent rarer atom (Theorem B, a sketch that still needs a lattice local moderate-deviation expansion). Thevenin's conjecture that normality holds for every such law is therefore false. The regularly varying case survives because the giant's law is locally flat at scale sqrt(n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure on a FINITE index set","BK: both events increasing","Reimer: no monotonicity hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3854fb8e108d83f54f7a2c762956ced396b14b16573131eabefa9f8eab4f84b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E with E FINITE. For events A and B define the DISJOINT OCCURRENCE A box B as the set of configurations omega for which there exist DISJOINT sets of coordinates K and L such that every configuration agreeing with omega on K lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on L lies in B - informally, A and B occur for disjoint reasons. VAN DEN BERG-KESTEN: if A and B are both INCREASING then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B). REIMER: the same inequality holds for ARBITRARY events A and B, with no monotonicity hypothesis. The direction is opposite to Harris-FKG, which is the point: increasing events are positively correlated, but requiring them to occur on disjoint witnesses destroys that correlation and more. The finiteness of E is a genuine hypothesis of the standard statements; infinite index sets are handled by approximation, and the definition of disjoint occurrence itself needs care there. Typical use: bounding the probability of two disjoint open crossings, or of a self-avoiding open path of length n, by a product. [van den Berg and Kesten (1985); Reimer (2000), Combin. Probab. Comput. 9; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.12]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.487280+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3be3c9182f994af2806f0d42922ebf649a4ecf9e795918fbcd91230f3fe9f9f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Coulomb gas correlations for a divisor on the Riemann sphere of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let the divisor
$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum \sigma_j \cdot z_j,
$$
where $\left\{z_j\right\}_{j=1}^n$ is a finite set of distinct points on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$.
The Coulomb gas correlation $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is a differential of conformal dimension $\lambda_j$ at $z_j$, given by

\begin{equation}
\lambda_j=\lambda_b\left(\sigma_j\right) \equiv \frac{\sigma_j^2}{2}-\sigma_j b ,
\end{equation}

where $\lambda_b(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2}-\sigma b \quad(\sigma \in \mathbb{C})$
whose value is given by

\begin{equation}
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] =\prod_{j<k}\left(z_j-z_k\right)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k} ,
\end{equation}
where the product is taken over all finite $z_j$ and $z_k$. 

This defines a holomorphic function of $\boldsymbol{z}$ on the configuration space
\[

In general, the function is multivalued, and one must choose a single-valued branch for each factor $(z_j-z_k)^{\sigma_j\sigma_k}$, except in special cases where all $\sigma_j$ are integers. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.474714+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3dee286195256974c00320143178eec22488dc4238290cd51aec9f091188a29","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 37 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $p$ is odd, $\chi$ is injective, $m$ is even, and the morphism $X\rightarrow X/G$ is an HKG cover. Let $l_1<\cdots<l_s$ be the lower jumps and let $u_1<\cdots<u_s$ be the upper jumps of the wild cyclic subgroup $H=C_{p^s}$ acting on the completion of the local ring of $X$ at the ramified point. For each $j\in\llbracket0,s\rrbracket$ let $H_{s-j}$ and $Y_j$ be as in Corollary \ref{C4} and, if $j\ge 1$, let 
$$\l_j:=l_j-1.$$ Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We have $\textup{g}_{Y_0}=0$ and for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have
\[

{\bf (2)} For each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$, $p-1$ divides $\textup{g}_{Y_i}$.

$$\frac{\textup{g}_{Y_i}-\textup{g}_{Y_{i-1}}}{p^i-p^{i-1}}=\frac{\l_i+(p-1)\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\l_jp^{i-1-j}}{2p^{i-1}}=\frac{u_i-1}{2}$$
for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and hence a $B_0[H]$-linear isomorphism 
$$\mathcal R_X\cong\oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{\l_i+(p-1)\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\l_jp^{i-1-j}}{2p^{i-1}}\mathcal B_i= \oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{u_i-1}{2}\mathcal B_i.$$

$$H^0(\mathcal X,\Omega_{\mathcal X})\otimes_R B\cong H^1(\mathcal X,\mathcal O_{\mathcal X})\otimes_R B\cong\oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{u_i-1}{2}\mathcal B_i.$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:57:28.221127+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3e9050bed568a5832fc609ed28297c290eb9df777f984c24eb78ffc28b92d99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.17662, 'On the Strong Law of Large Numbers under Sublinear Expectations'] A \textit{sublinear expectation} $\mathbb{E}$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is a functional $\mathbb{E}\colon \mathcal{H} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}} := [-\infty, +\infty]$ satisfying the following properties for all $X, Y \in \mathcal{H}$:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item[(a)] \textit{Monotonicity.} If $X \geq Y$, then $\mathbb{E}[X] \geq \mathbb{E}[Y]$.
			\item[(b)] \textit{Constant preserving.} $\mathbb{E}[c] = c$, $\forall\, c \in \mathbb{R}$.
			\item[(c)] \textit{Positive homogeneity.} $\mathbb{E}[\lambda X] = \lambda\,\mathbb{E}[X]$, $\forall\, \lambda \geq 0$.
			\item[(d)] \textit{Subadditivity.} $\mathbb{E}[X + Y] \leq \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]$, provided that $\mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]$ does not take the form $\infty - \infty$ or $-\infty + \infty$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869358+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_e3fe93c1b93e4bf1bae09cdb537c1446b11a7eef12cc45dbf8842efaebdec015","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN you are about to prove a convex-order dominance for a Markov-modulated inter-event time by conditioning on the modulating state and calling the result a mixture of exponentials. THE ROUTE: conditionally on the chain's stationary sojourn structure the inter-event time is exponential with a state-dependent rate, and a MIXTURE of exponentials always dominates the matched exponential in the convex order by Jensen applied to t -> E[exp(-lambda t)]. CONDITION OF FAILURE: any modulating transition inside an inter-event interval. The route that worked instead was Palm inversion - see the E0078 result node.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.271306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e404df3cb2e235b58e9b1b2e17f50f5e1d2ec0e5026dbe3027870738508b3282","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 (Admissible analytic resolution) of arXiv:2609.01116, 'Vector-Carleson, Calder\'on, and Poisson--Atomic Criteria for\\ Generalized Hilbert Operat'] Let
\[
 I_k=\{n\in\mathbb N:2^k\le n<2^{k+1}\},\qquad k\ge0.
\]
A family of scalar sequences
$\sigma=(\sigma_j)_{j\ge0}$ on $\mathbb N$ is called
$(L,M,p)$-admissible if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
 \item $\sigma_j(n)=0$ for $n\in I_k$ whenever $|j-k|>L$;
 \item $\sum_{j\ge0}\sigma_j(n)=1$ for every $n\ge1$;
 \item for every $|\ell|\le L$, the patched sequence
 \[
  m_\ell(n)=\sigma_{k+\ell}(n)\qquad(n\in I_k),
  \tag{3.8}
 \]
 with $\sigma_j=0$ for $j<0$, is an $H^p$ coefficient multiplier of
 norm at most $M$.
\end{enumerate}
Put
\[
 W_j^\sigma\phi(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_j(n)\widehat\phi(n)z^n,
 \qquad
 \mathscr S_{\phi,p}^{\sigma}a
 =a_{-1}\phi(0)+
  \sum_{j\ge0}a_j2^{-j/p'}W_j^\sigma\phi.
 \tag{3.9}
\]
The hard resolution is $\sigma_j=\mathbf1_{I_j}$ and has $L=0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.227892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e40608a37e4de12076c5bc6e9e448876a6b9b555bdd13c5118d52fc6908afd03","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 5 (Large deviations principle) of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] The sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ obeys the \textbf{large deviations principle} (`\textbf{LDP}') with \textbf{rate function} $I$ if the following hold:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[i.] (Upper bound) If $x \in \X$ and $a < I(x)$, then there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ such that
		\[\mu_n U \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
		\item[ii.] (Lower bound) If $x \in \X$ and $I(x) < a < \infty$, then any neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ satisfies
		\[\mu_n U \ge e^{-a n - o(n)}.\]
		\item[iii.] (Exponential tightness) For every $a > 0$ there is a compact subset $K$ of $\X$ such that
		\[\mu_n (\X\setminus K) \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
	\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e444a01e4404c33f58e4f4f48ec3e8fbc8498651ff93b0fc01e5ff4adf5a47a1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 29 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The function $V$ defined by \eqref{e:freeprob.V} is strictly convex on the interval $(z_0,+\infty)$, with $V(z)\to\infty$ as $z\to\infty$.
As a consequence, $V$ has a unique minimizer on the interval $[z_0,+\infty)$, which we denote $z_{\min}$.

\begin{proof} For $z>z_0$, we calculate
    \beq
        
        V'(z)
        = 1 - \alpha \frac{m_2(z)}{m(z)^2} \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j
            \bigg(\frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2\,.
    \eeq
Recall that $m:(\hw_1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is strictly decreasing, and we have
$\alpha - \hv_j m(z) > 0$ for all $z>z_0$. It follows that, on  the interval
$(z_0,\infty)$, the function
    \[
    \frac{m(z)}{\alpha-\hv_j m(z)}
    = \frac{1}{\alpha/m(z)-\hv_j}
    \]
is strictly decreasing, \emph{regardless of the sign of $\hv_j$}. Consequently, in \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, each term
    \[      \bigg(\frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2\]
is strictly decreasing on $(z_0,\infty)$, again \emph{regardless of the sign of $\hv_j$}. In the special case $s=1$, we have $m_2(z)=m(z)^2$, so we conclude in this case that $V'$ is strictly increasing on the interval $(z_0,\infty)$. For $s\ge2$, we note that $m_2(z)/m(z)^2$ is positive, and
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz}\bigg[ \frac{m_2(z)}{m(z)^2}\bigg]
        = \frac{2}{m(z)^3} \Big(m_2(z)^2 - m(z)m_3(z)\Big)
        < 0
    \]
by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. It therefore follows in this case as well that $V'$ is strictly increasing, and so $V$ is strictly convex, on the interval $(z_0,\infty)$.
Finally, as $z\to\infty$, $m(z) \to 0$. Therefore the first term of $V(z)$ tends to $\infty$ while the second term remains bounded, and so $V(z) \to \infty$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y Banach (complete normed) spaces","T bounded, linear and surjective"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476341+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_e489e7b7acc66136446dc1661f51b080f4db00b5f31e3c0b7c1207dc83d347fd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T : X -> Y a bounded linear operator that is surjective. Then T is an open map: the image of every open subset of X is open in Y; equivalently there is c > 0 such that the image of the unit ball of X contains the ball of radius c in Y. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.424875+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e48d1c31ee50e160fa1e46d567717236adb315c63688f5abb4b567b9c82f86e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: Polish functor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Polish functor}] 
  We say that a functor $\tau$ is \textit{Polish} if there exist a functor $\tilde{\tau}$
  and, for each $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
  a sequence $(\tilde{\tau}_{k}(S))_{k=1}^{\infty}$ of open subsets in $\tilde{\tau}(S)$
  satisfying the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (P\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
      The functor $\tilde{\tau}$ is complete, separable and continuous. 
    \item 
      The functor $\tau$ is a topological subfunctor of $\tilde{\tau}$.
    \item 
      For every $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
      it holds that $\tau(S) = \bigcap_{k \geq 1} \tilde{\tau}_{k}(S)$.
    \item 
      Let $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$ be a root-and-distance-preserving map
      between $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}) \in \mathfrak{M},\, i=1,2$.
      Then, $\tilde{\tau}_{f}^{-1}(\tilde{\tau}_{k}(S_{2})) = \tilde{\tau}_{k}(S_{1})$
      for each $k \geq 1$. 
      In particular,
      $\tilde{\tau}_{f}^{-1}(\tau(S_{2})) = \tau(S_{1})$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We call $(\tilde{\tau}, (\tilde{\tau}_{k})_{k \geq 1})$ a \textit{Polish system} of $\tau$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.754498+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e4ee7b1b0c19bb8b82285bdfeda4e24623277fdb17afbb02be376dc92a798f9b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Df 34 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $E$ be a finite set.
    Let $E = E_0 \sqcup E_1 \sqcup E_2$ be a tripartition of $E$.
    Write $E_{01} = E_0 \cup E_1$ and $E_{12} = E_1 \cup E_2$.
    Suppose $M$ is a matroid on $E_{01}$ and $N$ is a matroid on $E_{12}$ such that
    $E_1$ is a modular flat of $M$ and
    $M|_{E_1} = N|_{E_1}$.
    
    One defines the \textbf{generalized parallel connection} of $M$ and $N$ along $E_1$---denoted $P_{E_1}(M, N)$---to be the unique matroid on $E$ whose flats are the subsets $F \subseteq E$ such that 
    $F \cap E_{01}$ is a flat of $M$ and 
    $F \cap E_{12}$ is a flat of $N$.
    The rank of this matroid is $\rk P_{E_1}(M, N) = \rk M + \rk N - \rk_M E_1$.
    When $E_1$ is modular in $N$ also, we say (following Ziegler) that $M$ is the \textbf{modular join} of $M$ and $N$ along $E_1$.
    In this case, $P_{E_1}(N, M)$ also exists and is equal to $P_{E_1}(M, N)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.693476+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e53b29e59e81738e45376b2c2bf7cd67a9e4cec7a398428857e3bc2fd0e42ba8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:two-vortex of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\boldsymbol\kappa=(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)$ satisfy
$\kappa_1>0>\kappa_2$, and let
$(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\in\Lambda_2(D)$ be a strict local
minimum point of $W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}$.  Choose $\rho>0$ such that
\[
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})
  \Subset\Lambda_2(D),
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  &>W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\\
  &\quad\text{for every }(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \overline{B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})}
  \setminus\{(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\}.
  \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Fix $M_i,R_i>0$ for $i=1,2$.  Then there exist positive constants
$C$, $\eta_0$, and $\varepsilon_0$, depending only on
$D,\rho$, and $\mathbf a_{*,i},\kappa_i,M_i,R_i$, $i=1,2$,
such that the following holds.

For every $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, let
$(\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon})
\in B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})$, and let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ be nonnegative and satisfy
\[
  \int_D\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=|\kappa_i|,
  \qquad
  \|\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty
  \leq M_i\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R_i\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_{i,\varepsilon}),
  \quad i=1,2.
\]
Set
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
:=\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,0}-\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,0}$.
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding Yudovich
solution of (equation eq:euler-intro of the paper), and let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t}$ denote the transport of
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}$ by the associated Euler flow map.
If
\begin{equation}
  \eta^{(2)}_{\varepsilon,0}
  :=\sum_{i=1}^2\mathcal D(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0})
  +\Bigl[W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon})
  -W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\Bigr]
  +\varepsilon
  \leq\eta_0,
\end{equation}
then, for every $t\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})
  \times\mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})
  \subset B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2}),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{align}
  &\sum_{i=1}^2\mathcal D(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t})
  +\sup_{(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})\times
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})}
  \Bigl[
  W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  -W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})
  \Bigr] \leq C\eta^{(2)}_{\varepsilon,0}.
  
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.352891+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e54419eb49572f4b1a442ecc64684351e4ef3ec96a2e3c53ebcaf1a66b6e10cb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 27 (Language relating to polymer models from \cite{ks}) of arXiv:2511.07350, 'Decoupling of clusters in independent sets in a percolated hypercube'] In these definitions, we use the notation $N(A)$ to denote the \emph{set of neighbors} of $A$ in $\Q$, rather than
the number of neighbors.
Additionally, $\cH$ denotes either $\cE$ or $\cO$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item
    A subset $A \sse \cH$ is said to be \emph{2-linked} if there is no decomposition $A = A_1 \cup A_2$ into
    nonempty sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ which satisfy $N(A_1) \cap N(A_2) = \emptyset$.

    \item 
    For a subset $A \sse \cH$, we denote by $[A]$ the \emph{closure} of $A$,
    defined to be the largest subset of $\cH$ with the same neighborhood set as $A$.
    In other words, $[A] = \{ v \in \cH : N(v) \sse N(A) \}$.

    \item
    A 2-linked set $\fp \sse \cH$ with $|[\fp]| \leq \fr{3}{4} 2^{d-1}$ is called a \emph{polymer}.

    \item
    Polymers $\fp_1$ and $\fp_2$ are said to be \emph{compatible} if $\fp_1 \cup \fp_2$ is not 2-linked.

    \item
		We denote by $\Sep[\cH]$ the set of pairwise compatible collections of polymers.
    
    \item
    The \emph{weight} of a polymer $\fp$ is $\omega(\fp) = \E[\phi_\fp]$, where $\phi_\fp = 2^{-\N(\fp)}$.
    We remind the reader that $\N(\fp)$ denotes the (random) number of vertices neighboring $\fp$
    in the percolated graph $\Qp$.

    \item
    We define \emph{clusters} and their weights as in the previous section, which is a general construction that
    works for all polymer models.
    The set of clusters will be denoted by $\cC^\cH$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["P is a set of partial computable functions","P is nontrivial: neither empty nor all partial computable functions"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378848+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e566adf01a15158b9f7ce6ec58f8cd9ca5acbd8ecb4145e42d80266d80928187","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Every nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Precisely: let P be any set of partial computable functions that is nontrivial, meaning some partial computable function belongs to P and some does not. Then the index set {encodings of Turing machines M : the partial function computed by M belongs to P} is undecidable. 'Semantic' is essential: the property must depend only on the function computed, not on the machine's text (syntactic properties such as 'has fewer than 100 states' are decidable). Only the two trivial semantic properties (satisfied by all machines, or by none) have decidable index sets. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.061688+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e5687ee2014797e01ddd176afbf0325910953c5ec57a43f11b7388e3882bb4e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let $X$ be the CIR process above, take
$A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, X_s$
and fix $0<\theta<\eta$.  With $r_{\beta_\theta}=\frac{\kappa\eta}{\theta}$ and $\beta_\theta
      =\frac{\kappa^2}{2\sigma^2}
        \left(\frac{\eta^2}{\theta^2}-1\right)$,
put
\[
    I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)
      =\frac{\kappa^2(\eta-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2\theta},
    \qquad
    v_\theta
      =\frac{\sigma^2\theta^3}{\kappa^2\eta^2}.
\]
Then, for every fixed $x>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\begin{split}
    \bbP_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim{}&
    \frac{1}{\beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}}
    \left(
       \frac{2r_{\beta_\theta}}
            {\kappa+r_{\beta_\theta}}
    \right)^\alpha
    \exp\!\left(
       -\frac{(r_{\beta_\theta}-\kappa)x}{\sigma^2}
    \right)
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\end{split}
\]
On every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges in total
variation to the CIR process
\[
    \de Y_t
      =r_{\beta_\theta}(\theta-Y_t)\,\de t
       +\sigma\sqrt{Y_t}\,\de B_t,
    \qquad Y_0=x.
\]
Its invariant law is Gamma with shape $\alpha$ and mean $\theta$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e5ace840b7a802a63627f4607d2573244712aad61251eef12fdf70c6287c7bb4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ribbon-majorant of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a ribbon record $\Gamma$, a circuit state $\tau$, and a designated
set $\mathcal E$ of factored endpoint or packet resources.  Expand every
remaining coefficient component in its circuit-anchored projective
presentation and insert every prescribed fixed gate before closing the
original circuit bases.  Define $\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\tau;\mathcal E}$
to be $|\omega_\Gamma|$ times the sum of the absolute scalar
coefficients multiplied by all remaining positive projective and
trace-class costs.  No endpoint weight or debit in $\mathcal E$ is
included.  In the monomer--dimer applications of (sec:moments of the paper), the
fixed recurrence scalar $(-\gamma)^a$ is also declared a factored
resource: it is not one of the ``scalar coefficients'' in this
definition and is restored exactly once by the resource ledger.
Local fold, transport, and projective-presentation coefficients do remain
inside the majorant.  When $\tau$ and $\mathcal E$ are clear we write
$\mathfrak a_\Gamma$; subscripts such as
$\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\mathcal C}$ name the part of the record left open.

This is a positive presentation cost, not the possibly cancelling value
of an open contraction.  Consequently it dominates every compatible
partial trace-class contraction obtained from the same atoms.  The
operator-norm estimate needed for the Kac root-open specialization is the
separate, proved statement (lem:root-open-sinfty of the paper); it is not built
into this definition and no replica factorization is assumed.  The later
allocation argument specifies
which carriers are left bare and proves the corresponding Euler bound;
no second copy of this majorant is introduced there.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.133942+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_e5bc523adf056d9ffeb113c97a81d7e542e8498e58ad3f632631e5a630f50c3a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. Let T_p be a random set, independent of X, containing each coordinate independently with probability p in [0, 1], and J(p) = E over T_p of Var(E[f | X_{T_p}]). Then J(p) = sum over nonempty S of p^|S| w_S = sum_{k=1}^n p^k W_k. Hence J^(k)(0) = k! W_k >= 0 for every k, J(0) = 0, J(1) = Var(f), and J is nondecreasing and convex on [0, 1].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Conclusion is constancy on the closure of U x [0,t_0] only","U must be connected","The maximum must be attained at a point with x_0 in U and t_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106923+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_e5db45cf444dc11d943ed80dd9009a1a1904ce853e38b9031ae8a4e06c9b3559","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a solution of the heat equation attains its maximum over $\\overline{U_T}$ at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)\\in U_T$, the conclusion is that $u$ is constant on $\\overline U\\times[0,t_0]$ -- the past of $t_0$ -- and nothing at all is claimed for $t>t_0$. Heat is not time-reversible, and the mean value property over heat balls only looks backwards. Counterexample: on $U=(0,\\pi)$, $T=2$, let $h(t)=1$ for $t\\le1$ and $h(t)=1-e^{-1/(t-1)}$ for $t>1$ (smooth, $h\\le1$, $h<1$ for $t>1$), and let $u$ be the solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with $u(\\cdot,0)\\equiv1$ and $u(0,t)=u(\\pi,t)=h(t)$. On $[0,1]$, $u\\equiv1$ by uniqueness; the weak maximum principle gives $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=1$, attained at the interior point $(\\pi/2,1)\\in U_T$; but for $t>1$, $u$ is not constant (its boundary values are $<1$ while, by continuity, $u$ stays near $1$ in the middle). So constancy holds exactly up to $t_0=1$ and fails afterwards. A second load-bearing hypothesis is connectedness of $U$: for $U=(0,1)\\cup(2,3)$ the solution equal to $1$ on the first component and to $e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\phi_1$ on the second attains its maximum at an interior point of the first component and is not constant on $U$. Finally, the interior maximum must be attained in $U_T$, i.e. at a point with $x_0\\in U$: a maximum on the lateral boundary says nothing about constancy (that is the Hopf lemma's domain, which asserts instead that the outward normal derivative is strictly positive there).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The counterexample uses H(p) = p^2 (smooth, uniformly convex) and zero data, so no exotic Hamiltonian is needed","'Solution a.e.' means Lipschitz plus the equation at points of differentiability","Uniqueness is restored by the viscosity property or, equivalently for convex superlinear H, by the semiconcavity bound of the Hopf-Lax solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418105+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_e6002f2b1fb67f105d5effe237759fa92f79220ba532358144c459114f6ad305","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in any uniqueness statement for u_t + H(Du) = 0 the solution must be a VISCOSITY solution (equivalently, for convex superlinear H, a Lipschitz a.e. solution satisfying the one-sided semiconcavity estimate). Satisfying the equation at almost every point plus the initial condition is far too weak. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = p^2, initial datum g ≡ 0. Both u ≡ 0 and v(x,t) := min(0, |x| - t) are Lipschitz on R × [0,∞), vanish at t = 0, and satisfy v_t + v_x^2 = 0 at every point of differentiability: for |x| < t one has v = |x| - t, v_t = -1, v_x = ±1; for |x| > t one has v ≡ 0. Only u ≡ 0 is the viscosity solution (it is also what the Hopf-Lax formula gives, since L(q) = q^2/4 and min_y ( |x-y|^2/(4t) ) = 0). Why v fails: at a point (0,t) with t > 0, v has a local minimum in x with a convex kink, so φ ≡ v(0,t) + c(t'-t) touches from below with φ_x = 0, φ_t = -1, and the supersolution inequality φ_t + φ_x^2 ≥ 0 reads -1 ≥ 0. Equivalently v violates semiconcavity: v(z,t) - 2v(0,t) + v(-z,t) = 2|z|, which is not O(|z|^2). Auditor's check: whenever a proof concludes 'u is the solution' from 'u is Lipschitz and solves the PDE a.e.', the argument is incomplete unless viscosity, semiconcavity, or a variational (Hopf-Lax) representation is verified.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496248+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6248aa0074ed65c0cb416759fb98cfbee64e1b86f405d7a62cdf77ef9f92b0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (First-break localization and tails) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level defined by
\[
        \Prob(K_d=k)=\pi_{d,k}\quad(1\le k\le d-1),
        \qquad
        \Prob(K_d=d)=\rho_d,
\]
where
\[
        \rho_d:=\prod_{r=1}^{d-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
\]
is the probability that no one-sided tie-break occurs before simultaneous completion.  Thus the value $K_d=d$ records this exceptional terminal event.  Then
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
In particular,
\[
        K_d\to\infty,
        \qquad
        \frac{K_d}{d}\to0
\]
in probability.  More precisely, for $k=o(d)$,
\[
        \prod_{r=1}^{k-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
        =\exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{d}+O\left(\frac{k^4}{d^3}\right)\right),
\]
and there are absolute constants $C,c>0$ such that, for every $R\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge R\sqrt{d\log d}}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C d^{-cR^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
More generally, for every $M\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge M\sqrt d}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C e^{-cM^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $R$ large enough the tail in
\eqref{eq:first-break-tail} is $o(d^{-1})$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149207+00:00","domain":"functional analysis for elliptic PDE","id":"claim_e668a967db6b2df1576259501b51767438bb0d124e237c2d8edd4b1aa48d5602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: there is beta > 0 with B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2 for every u in the Hilbert space H. Strict positivity (B[u,u] > 0 for u nonzero) is not enough, and neither is injectivity of the associated operator. Counterexample: H = l^2, B(u,v) = sum_k u_k v_k / k. This form is bounded (|B(u,v)| <= ||u|| ||v||), symmetric and strictly positive, but B(e_k, e_k) = 1/k tends to 0, so it is not coercive. The bounded functional F(v) = sum_k v_k / k is represented by the sequence (1/k) in l^2, yet B(u, .) = F forces u_k = 1 for all k, which is not in l^2: the equation has no solution. PDE instances of the same failure: (i) on H^1_0(Omega) the form B[u,v] = integral (grad u . grad v - lambda_1 u v) satisfies B[u,u] >= 0 with equality exactly on the first eigenfunction, and the Dirichlet problem for -Laplacian - lambda_1 is not solvable for general right-hand sides (the Fredholm orthogonality condition appears); (ii) on H^1(Omega) the Neumann form integral grad u . grad v annihilates constants, and integral f = 0 is necessary for solvability; (iii) on an unbounded Omega the Poincare inequality may fail, so integral (grad u . grad v) is not coercive for the full H^1 norm. Two further points a careful reader should keep straight: coercivity is sufficient but not necessary (for lambda strictly between two Dirichlet eigenvalues the form of -Laplacian - lambda is indefinite, yet the problem is uniquely solvable by the Fredholm alternative), and Lax-Milgram does not require B to be symmetric - symmetry only turns the solution into the minimizer of a quadratic energy (Riesz representation / Dirichlet principle).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6789d4681558e1453083424208786d0dc56c6880309cc2396d52ceae8d18ee8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 189 (error between $Q$ and $\tilde{Q}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as given by \eqref{e:qv.covar} and \eqref{e:tQ.notIs}. Then
	\[\Big|
	\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(1)\bigg\{
	\eta^2
	+
	\sum_{\rho\in\{\sigma,\tau\}}
	\bigg[
	\eta\bigg(
	\min\Big\{
	\Delta Q^\rho(q_d),
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^\rho(q_d)\Big\}
	\bigg)^{1/2}
	+ \Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg]
	\bigg\}\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$.
The same bound holds with $Q^\frozen$, $\tilde{Q}^\frozen$, $E^\frozen$
in place of $Q$, $\tilde{Q}$, $E$.

\begin{proof} Recall that $\vZ\equiv \vY-\vD$, so we can rewrite \eqref{e:qv.covar} as
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	= \bE \bigg[
		\Big( \Delta Y^\sigma(q_d)
			-\Delta D^\sigma(q_d)
			\Big)
		\Big(
		\Delta Y^\tau(q_d)
		-\Delta D^\tau(q_d)
		\Big)
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\,.
	\]
For simplicity of exposition, let us consider the case $\sigma=\tau=\RomI$.
Similarly to the argument for
Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep},
let $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$ denote the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} then tells us that $\Delta Y^\RomI(q_d)$ is within $2\eta$ of $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$, where
$a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from
$B$. Thus define $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ to be the process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^\RomI(q_d)
	\Big)^2
\,.
	\eeq
 It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	=\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	O(\eta)
	+\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2\,,\]
which allows us to bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg|
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta) 
	\bigg[\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^2\bigg]^{1/2}\\
	&\qquad\le
	O(1)\bigg\{ \eta^2+\eta 
		\Big( \Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}\bigg\}\,.
	
	\end{align}
This shows that increments of
$Q^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ are close. We can further bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	=\bigg| \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2
	- \frac{1}{|B|}\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^2\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	- 2
	\Big( \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)
	\bigg|\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	-2\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\bigg|\\
	&\qquad\le O(1)  
	\bigg\{
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2
	+ \eta\Big|\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| + \eta^2\bigg\}
	\le O(1)
	\max\bigg\{\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,\eta^2\bigg\}
	
	\,,\end{align}
having used the definition of $\bar{D}$ from \eqref{e:barD}, together with Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep}. Combining the bounds gives
	\[
	\Big|
	\Delta E^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le  O(1)
	\bigg\{ \eta^2 
	+\eta\Big( \Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Next note that \eqref{e:barQ.to.tildeQ} implies
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta \bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\,.\]
Meanwhile \eqref{e:Q.to.barQ} implies that either 
$\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$, in which case
$\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$ also,
or $\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)$ is much larger than $\eta^2$, in which case it is of the same order as
 $\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)$. It follows that
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.103264+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_e68f193186254c789712f4d9509a62ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle (i.e., a cylinder), but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle (product of two line segments) without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle (an even number of twists or an odd number of twists). The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group $H^{1}(S^{1},\\{+1,-1\\})$ which can be computed as isomorphic to the group $\\{+1,-1\\}$ where $+1$ corresponds to an even number of twists, and $-1$ to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(W, W') =d (W', W) on one probability space","normal and concentration bounds: E[W'|W] = (1 − a)W for some 0 < a ≤ 1 (an a-Stein pair); Theorem 3.7 also needs E[W²] = 1","Theorem 4.20: W non-negative integer valued and F a σ-field with σ(W) ⊆ F","Theorem 7.2: Var(W) < ∞, E[e^{θW}|W' − W|] < ∞ for all θ, and E[(W' − W)²|F]/(2a) ≤ BW + C"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T19:22:30+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e69a80727ebd2231790fcceb90b59cbd41f32829e67ebce07a251706532d55b9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD. Ross, Remark 3.3: if X_0, X_1, ... is a stationary Markov chain reversible with respect to the underlying measure, then W = W(X_0), W' = W(X_1) is an exchangeable pair, while the linearity condition must be verified separately. Theorem 3.7: if (W, W') is an a-Stein pair with E[W²] = 1 and Z is standard normal, then d_W(W, Z) ≤ √(Var(E[(W' − W)²|W]))/(√(2π) a) + E|W' − W|³/(3a). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.627841+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e69ac4b0d6805d654839bd0c715c6c9f4ab460cd1310b638e506a6fad318c3a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:upper_lower_general of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{X}$ belong to the domain of non-normal attraction of an $\alpha$-stable process $\bm{Z}$.\\

\[
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})
=\mathcal{O} ( G_2(t)^q)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.285897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e69ce9a9193dcd224bc7a66db7e2a67e23fd8a7e452dc938eec983f2b0dee69b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma KacRice of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[0,1]$ with a $2$-atom prefix
		$\{0,q\}$ for some $q\in(0,1)$, and let $\varepsilon\in(0,q/2)$.
		Let $\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)$ be the number of critical points $\mathbf{m}$ of
		$F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}$ such that
		\[
		\mathbf{m}\in \mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\frac1N F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\in(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon).
		\]
		For $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$, write $q_\mathbf{m}:=\frac1N\|\mathbf{m}\|^2$.
		
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item \textup{(Mixed case.)}
			Assume that for every $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ with
			$q_\mathbf{m}\in(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$, the Gaussian vector
			\[
			\bigl(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\bigr)
			\]
			is non-degenerate.  In particular, this holds for a genuine mixed
			$p$-spin Hamiltonian, i.e.\ when
			\[
			\xi(t)=\sum_{p\ge 2}\beta_p^2 t^p
			\]
			has at least two non-zero coefficients.
			Then
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=N\int_{[-1,1]^N}\int_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\,
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf'
				\right]
				\\
				\times
				\varphi_{(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))}(0,Nf')\,
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}\,\mathrm{d} f'.
			\end{multline}
			
			\item \textup{(Pure case.)}
			Assume that $\xi(t)=\beta_p^2 t^p$ is pure $p$-spin for some $p\ge2$.
			Recalling the notation~(equation eq:def-Rex-KR of the paper),
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=
				\int_{[-1,1]^N}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0
				\right]
				\varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				\\
				\times
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathbf{1}_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\!\left(\frac1N\mathcal R^{\rm ex}_\zeta(\mathbf{m})\right)
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}.
			\end{multline}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R^d)","the Plancherel transform is the L^2 extension of the L^1 transform"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264524+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_e6a7de372efdb69b5dda51fbcd54ebeef72e1430e1bd848aa9b086939563f833","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing distinction: for $f\\in L^1$ the transform is an honest absolutely convergent integral, bounded, continuous, defined at every $\\xi$; for $f\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$ it is defined only as the $L^2$-limit $\\hat f=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\widehat{f\\mathbf 1_{\\{|x|\\le R\\}}}$ (the unique continuous extension from the dense subspace $L^1\\cap L^2$), hence is an equivalence class defined only almost everywhere. Example: $f(x)=\\sin(\\pi x)/(\\pi x)\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$, whose Plancherel transform is $\\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ a.e.; the truncated integrals converge to $1$ for $|\\xi|<1/2$, to $0$ for $|\\xi|>1/2$ and to $1/2$ at $\\xi=\\pm1/2$, but no value at $\\pm1/2$ is meaningful for the $L^2$ transform. Consequences an auditor should check: (i) claims like '$\\hat f(\\xi_0)=0$' or '$\\hat f$ is continuous' are meaningless for $L^2$ data without naming a representative (the usual legitimate versions are 'a.e.' statements or support statements up to null sets); (ii) $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ is unavailable; (iii) that $\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\int_{-R}^Rf(x)e^{-2\\pi ix\\xi}dx$ exists for a.e. $\\xi$ when $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ is a deep result (the Fourier-integral form of Carleson's theorem), not a corollary of Plancherel, which only gives $L^2$ convergence and hence a.e. convergence along some subsequence of radii. On $L^1\\cap L^2$ the two definitions agree a.e., which is what makes the extension consistent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T12:08:18+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_e6ae446cd6fd7036517cf71cccaaa1cb4fa2b1cf94cd433f14ec3cf8acbcb1e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. Then the probability that all of them lie in a single open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin, equivalently the probability that the origin is not in their convex hull, equals $2^{-N+1}\\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\\binom{N-1}{k}$. In particular this probability is $1$ whenever $N \\le d$. Note that symmetry alone does not suffice: general position is needed, since for instance two points i.i.d. uniform on $\\{\\pm e_1\\} \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$ are symmetric (their joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin) but not in general position, and they lie in a common open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin with probability $1/2$ (exactly when the two points coincide; $e_1$ and $-e_1$ lie in no such halfspace, and the origin is in their convex hull), whereas the formula gives $2^{-1}\\left(\\binom{1}{0}+\\binom{1}{1}\\right)=1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.568178+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6ccd3bfb0bebac58eb198b65ce853be21569a59e5c13f54c485fca3321989c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Let $\psi$ denote a Lemari\'e-Meyer  wavelet  and $\varphi$ the associated scaling function. The hyperbolic wavelet basis is defined as the system $$\{\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2} :  \, (j_1, j_2) \in (\mathbb{N}\cup \{-1\})^2, \, (k_1, k_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\}$$
where
\begin{itemize}
\item if $j_1,j_2\geq 0$,
$$
\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1=-1$ and $j_2\geq 0$
$$
\psi_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1\ge 0$ and $j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{j_1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;,
$$
\item if $j_1=j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;.
$$
\end{itemize}
For any $f\in\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$, one then defines its hyperbolic wavelet coefficients by
\begin{eqnarray*}
c_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_1+j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1,j_2\geq 0\;,\\
c_{j_1,-1,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_1}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1\geq 0\mbox{ and }j_2=-1\;,\\
c_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=-1\mbox{ and }j_2\geq 0\;,\\
c_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}&=&<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=j_2=-1\;.
\end{eqnarray*}","status":"unverified"}

    a|y|^p+|z|^p+\frac m\gamma |y|^{p-2}\langle y,z\rangle \,,
\] and $\Delta_\alpha(t):=m_X(\mu_{X_t^J})-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)$. Hence, $ X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)=Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)\,,$
and
\[
    \mathrm d\hat Z_t^j
    =
    (-K_Z\hat Z_t^j-K_YY_t^j)\mathrm d t+\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}},
\]
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}
    :=
    \frac{\sigma}{m}
    \left[
        \left(1-\frac1J\right)
        S(Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^j
        -
        \frac1J\sum_{k\ne j}
        S(Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^k
    \right].
\end{equation}
The stochastic differential of \(L_p(t)\) is
\begin{align}
    \mathrm d L_p(t)
    &=
    \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
    \Bigg\{
    \left[
        \left(\frac{ap}{\gamma}-\frac m\gamma K_Y\right)|Y_t^j|^p
        -
        pK_Z|\hat Z_t^j|^p
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \left(
            ap-\frac m\gamma K_Z+\frac{m(p-1)}{\gamma^2}
        \right)
        |Y_t^j|^{p-2}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle
        -
        pK_Y|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}\langle \hat Z_t^j,Y_t^j\rangle
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}|\hat Z_t^j|^2
        +
        \frac{m(p-2)}{\gamma}
        |Y_t^j|^{p-4}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle^2
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)\,\mathrm d t
    +
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    \Bigg\},
    
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    :=
    p|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle \hat Z_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle
    +
    \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle Y_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle .
\end{equation}
We denote $ M_{p,t}:=\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J M_{p,t}^j$ as the local martingale part of \(L_p(t)\). The noise trace satisfies
\begin{align}
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)
    &=
    \frac12
    \operatorname{Tr}
    \left(
        \nabla^2(|\hat Z_t^j|^p)\,
        \mathrm d\langle M^{j,\mathrm{center}}\rangle_t
    \right)
    \notag\\
    &=
        \frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2}\left(1-\frac1J\right)^2 |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right] \notag \\
        &\quad
        +\frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2J^2}\sum_{k\ne j}|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right]\\
        & \leqslant
    \frac{p\sigma^2\chi_S}{2m^2}
    |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left(
        |Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
        +
        \frac1J\sum_{k=1}^J |Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
    \right).
    
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6f9e9d7ec2498c7cb28bfb52e107a4ef3ff20917a8c2f635ef00dcfe2ad1c75","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Conjecture conj:barcode_kernel_intro of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Around any macroscopic point $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ in the waterfall region $\mathcal{W}$, the
	random configuration of square lozenges
	on a horizontal slice
	converges to a
	determinantal \textbf{barcode process} on $\mathbb{Z}$ with the symmetric correlation kernel
	$\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)$.\footnote{In particular, 
	we conjecture that the limit (equation eq:K_barcode_intro of the paper) exists for all integers $s\ge t$.}
	The barcode process depends only on the parameters $q$ and $\kappa$,
	but not on the geometry of the hexagon or the macroscopic location $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$
	inside $\mathcal{W}$, as long as the waterfall phase is present, i.e., $\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$.
	
	The limiting kernel is $2\times 2$ block Toeplitz, that is,
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)& \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t+1)\\
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t+1)
		\end{pmatrix}
		=
			\begin{pmatrix}
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{00}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{01}(s-t)\\
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{10}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{11}(s-t)
			\end{pmatrix},
			\qquad s,t\in 2\mathbb{Z},
	\end{equation*}
	and satisfies
	$\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(0,0)=1-\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(1,1)$ 
	(the plot of this function
	in $q$ and $\kappa$ is given in (fig:density_rho_even_3d of the paper)).
	Consequently, the barcode process has global density $1/2$
	for every choice of $q$ and $\kappa$, and it is invariant
	under even but not odd shifts. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:06.325328+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e711218285039b69f8576bb9d8c47c1828db993c1e1254e4878e38192449df66","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Assume that for $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ the noisy system has a unique stationary measure $\mu^{\varepsilon}_{\s}$ and satisfies the trajectory Freidlin--Wentzell uniform LDP. Then for $m$-a.e. $\sigma\in\Sigma$, the upper large deviation bound
    \[
            \limsup_{\eps\to0}\eps\ln\mu^\eps_\sigma(F)
            \leq -\inf_{u\in F}E_{\Ac(\sigma)}(u)
    \]

    \[
            \liminf_{\eps\to0}\eps\ln\mu^\eps_\sigma(G)

        \ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$\kappa$-small $S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}}^\kappa,{\mathcal{D}}). 
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        It follows directly from the assumptions that restriction along ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ defines an equivalence $\ul{\textup{Fun}}_T^\text{fib $\kappa$-filt cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{\textup{Fun}}_T({\mathcal{C}}^\kappa,{\mathcal{D}})$. Moreover, ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ has fiberwise $\kappa$-small colimits, and applying [HTT]*{Example~5.3.6.8} pointwise, we see that a functor ${\mathcal{C}}\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$ preserves fiberwise colimits if and only if its restriction to ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ preserves fiberwise $\kappa$-small colimits. 

        As each of the left adjoints $s_!\colon{\mathcal{C}}(A)\to{\mathcal{C}}(B)$ preserves $\kappa$-compact objects (its right adjoint admits another right adjoint, so it is in particular $\kappa$-accessible), we see that each $s^*\colon{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(B)\to{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(A)$ for $s\colon A\to B$ in $S$ admits a left adjoint. We claim that also $s_!'\colon{\mathcal{C}}(X)\to{\mathcal{C}}(C)$ for $s'$ as in $((diag:pb-regular-card of the paper))$ restricts to ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(X)\to{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(C)$ (beware that the left-hand side is a priori different from ${\mathcal{C}}(X)^\kappa$); with this established the Beck--Chevalley condition for ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ will follow from the one for ${\mathcal{C}}$, i.e.~${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ will have $\kappa$-small $S$-colimits.

        To prove the claim, write $X\simeq\mathop{\textup{colim}}_iX_i$ as a $\kappa$-small colimit of representables in $\PSh(S)$, so that $s^*$ agrees up to equivalence with $(s_i^*)_{i\in I}\colon{\mathcal{C}}(C)\to\lim_{I^{\textup{op}}}{\mathcal{C}}(X_\bullet)$ for some cocone $(s_i)_{i\in I}$. By [descent-lim]*{Theorem~B}, this then admits a left adjoint given on objects by sending an object $(y_i)_{i\in I}\in\lim_{I^{\textup{op}}}{\mathcal{C}}(X_\bullet)$ to the colimit of a certain diagram $i\mapsto s_{i!}(y_i)$. If each $y_i$ is $\kappa$-compact, then so is each $s_{i!}(y_i)$ by the above, whence so is their colimit as $I$ is $\kappa$-small. This completes the proof of the claim, and hence of ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ having $\kappa$-small $S$-colimits.

        It only remains to show that a functor $F\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$ for $S$-cocomplete ${\mathcal{D}}$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition with respect to the maps $s\colon A\to B$ in $S$ if and only if this holds for the composite $Fi\colon{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$. This follows at once by observing that the collection of $X\in{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ such that $s_!FX\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;} Fs_!X$ is closed under ($\kappa$-filtered) colimits and contains ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(A)$, as ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition by construction of the left adjoints for ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.595219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77108d69273ab028a1744f0813b99f2291b438ccad572ffcfaf6dc41b2d0df7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:diffusion+jumpHKE of arXiv:2412.05030, 'Characterization of Subordinate Symmetric Markov Processes'] (Diffusion+jump type heat kernel estimates [CKW2020])
  

  For a regular Dirichlet form $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ of the diffusion+jump type, 
  we say HK$_{-}$($\phi_c,\phi_j$) holds if there exists heat kernel $p(t,x,y)$ of $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$
  and 
  there exist a properly exceptional set $\mathcal{N}$ and 
  constants $c_1 ,c_2,c_3,c_4 > 0$ such that
  for all $t > 0$ and $x,y \in M \backslash \mathcal{N}$
  \begin{equation}
    \begin{split}
        &c_1\left(\frac{1}{V(x,\phi^{-1}(t))} 1_{\{\phi(c_2 r) \le t\}} + \frac{t}{V(x,r)\phi_j(r)} 1_{\{\phi(c_2 r) > t\}}\right)\\
    &\le p(t,x,y)\\
    &\le c_3\left(\frac{1}{V(x,\phi^{-1}(t))} \wedge (p^{(c)}(c_4t,x,y) + p^{(j)}(t,x,y))\right).
    \end{split}
    
  \end{equation}
Here $p^{(c)}(t,x,y)$ defined in ((eq:diffusionHKE of the paper)) appears as the sub-Gaussian heat kernel and 
  $p^{(j)}(t,x,y)$ defined in ((eq:JumpHK of the paper)) appears as the stable-like heat kernel.
See Example (ex:diffusion+jump of the paper) for concrete examples of processes that enjoy ((eq:diffusion+jumpHKE of the paper)).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H real separable Hilbert, W isonormal Gaussian on H","the L^2 space is with respect to the sigma-algebra GENERATED BY W","f_n symmetric, and then unique"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77fa0481be857539e984e1e66a556b4287a9c335209411aaef62032c500226b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real separable Hilbert space and let W = { W(h) : h in H } be an ISONORMAL Gaussian process, that is a centred Gaussian family with E[ W(h) W(g) ] = <h, g>_H. For n >= 0 let the n-th WIENER CHAOS H_n be the closed linear span in L^2 of { He_n( W(h) ) : h in H, ||h||_H = 1 }, with H_0 the constants. Then the H_n are mutually ORTHOGONAL and L^2( Omega, sigma(W), P ) is their orthogonal direct sum. Equivalently, every square-integrable functional F of the Gaussian process has a unique expansion F = E[F] + sum_{n >= 1} I_n(f_n) with f_n a symmetric element of the n-fold symmetric tensor power of H, where I_n is the multiple Wiener-Ito integral, and the Ito isometry gives E[F^2] = E[F]^2 + sum_{n >= 1} n! ||f_n||^2. For H = L^2([0,T]) and W Brownian motion, I_n(f_n) is the n-fold iterated Ito integral of f_n and the expansion is the classical chaos expansion. The sigma-algebra must be the one GENERATED BY W: the decomposition describes L^2 of that sigma-algebra and says nothing about functionals involving independent randomness. [Wiener (1938), Ito (1951); see Nualart, The Malliavin Calculus and Related Topics, 2nd ed., Theorem 1.1.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0069-scaling-limit-of-critical-percolation-cluster-sizes-on-the-hypercube","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.043212+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e79112836e7be9ac2cb3fff34a4bbaf047ce7bf4d7f7033676f9bfe30b1fdf7b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare the exploration process of the hypercube with the Aldous exploration of the Erdos-Renyi graph. Result: Aldous's proof for G(n,p) uses that the exploration process is a random walk with drift theta - t and unit variance, up to depletion; on the hypercube the exploration of a cluster is a random walk whose step distribution depends on the local geometry (the number of unexplored neighbours of the current vertex is d minus the number of explored ones, and explored vertices are geometrically correlated). In the window the explored set has size V^{2/3} = 2^{2d/3}, which is a vanishing fraction of V, but the DEPLETION seen by a single vertex is not uniform: the explored vertices cluster geometrically, so the walk's drift correction is a functional of the geometry, not of the total explored mass as in G(n,p). This is exactly why the hypercube is harder than the Hamming graph (where the geometry is 'mean-field enough' and the scaling limit was obtained by Federico-van der Hofstad-den Hollander-Hulshof for the Hamming cube). A reduction: the scaling limit follows if the exploration's drift satisfies E[step | past] = theta 2^{-d/3} - (explored mass)/V + o(2^{-d/3}) uniformly over the window, i.e. if the local depletion is asymptotically equal to the global depletion; this is a 'non-backtracking randomness' statement about the geometry of critical hypercube clusters (that they are spread out like independent samples), which is the mean-field cluster geometry conjecture and is open. Obstruction: Local versus global depletion in the exploration walk; needs spread-out geometry of critical hypercube clusters.","status":"unverified"}

The same statement holds even more generally for all global fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163147+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7a259b569a3c7f2a1e314c50aded7834b8ddfdd61b4d51c243cce2d444ce673","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 24 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any fixed $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$, the function
    \beq
        
        (\bG,
        \tbmeta^{1:k},
        \bz^{1:k}
        )
        \mapsto F^{\riii}(k,\cB)\,,
    \eeq
restricted to domain $\cE_{\gd}$, is $O((kN)^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz. Consequently, for any $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$, there exists an $O((kN)^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function
    $\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$
    which agrees with the function \eqref{e:fp-Fii-kirszbraun-fn} on the set $\cE_{\gd}$. Moreover, we can choose the functions $\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ such that $\bbE \tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ is constant over all $\cB\in\scB(\lambda,\mu)$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall that $\bar{F}(\bG,\tbmeta^{1:k},\bz^{1:k},\by^{1:k},\cB)$ denotes the function appearing inside the supremum \eqref{e:F.iii}.
Since a supremum of Lipschitz functions remains Lipschitz, it
suffices to show that for any fixed $\by^{1:k} \in S_+(k)$, the function
    \[(\bG,\tbmeta^{1:k},
        \bz^{1:k})
        \mapsto
       \bar{F}
       (\bG,\tbmeta^{1:k},
        \bz^{1:k},\by^{1:k},\cB)\,,
    \]
restricted to domain $\cE_{\gd}$, is $O((kN)^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz. Let us abbreviate $\bar{F}_k$ for the above function, and note that it can be expressed as the sum of functions
$\bar{F}_{B,k}$, $F_{v,k}$, $\bar{F}_{U,k}$, and $F_{w,k}$, where for example $\bar{F}_{B,k}$ denotes the average of the function $\bar{F}_B$ from \eqref{e:bar.F.B} over $k$ orthogonal replicas. If $a\in B_j$, then we calculate
    \[
    \nabla_{\bg^a}
    F_{v,k}
    = \frac{2\hv_j}{kM}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    \frac{(\bg^a,\by^\ell)}{N}\by^\ell\,.
    \]
By the assumption that $\by^{1:k}\in S_+(k)$, we can bound
    \[
    \|\nabla_{\bg^a}F_{v,k}\|^2
    = \bigg(
    \frac{2\hv_j}{kM}\bigg)^2
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    \frac{(\bg^a,\by^\ell)^2}{N}
    \lesssim
    \frac{1}{k^2N^3}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    (\bg^a,\by^\ell)^2\,.
    \]
Summing over $a\in[M]$ gives
    \[\|\nabla_\bG F_{v,k}\|^2
    =\sum_{a=1}^M
    \|\nabla_{\bg^a}F_{v,k}\|^2
    \lesssim
    \frac{1}{k^2N^3}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    \|\bG\by^\ell\|^2
    \le \frac{(\|\bG\|_\op)^2 }{k N^2}
    \lesssim \frac{1}{kN}\,.
    \]
For $a\in B_j$, we also calculate
    \[
    \nabla_{\bg^a} \bar{F}_{U,k}
    = \frac{2\hU_j}{kMN|B_j|}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    \bigg(
                \sum_{b\in B_j} (\bz^\ell)_b \barbg^b, \by^\ell
            \bigg)
            (\bz^\ell)_a \by^\ell\,.
    \]
Again by the assumption $\by^{1:k}\in S_+(k)$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \|\nabla_{\bg^a} \bar{F}_{U,k}\|^2
    &= \bigg(
    \frac{2\hU_j}{kMN|B_j|}\bigg)^2
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    [\bz^\ell(B_j)\bG^{B_j}\by^\ell]^2
    ((\bz^\ell)_a)^2 N \\
    &\lesssim
    \frac{1}{k^2 N^5}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    (\|\bG\|_\op)^2 \|\bz^\ell\|^2 \|\by^\ell\|^2
    ((\bz^\ell)_a)^2
    \lesssim
    \frac{1}{k^2 N^2}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    ((\bz^\ell)_a)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Summing over $a\in[M]$ gives
    \[
    \|\nabla_\bG \bar{F}_{U,k}\|^2
    =\sum_{a=1}^M
    \|\nabla_{\bg^a} \bar{F}_{U,k}\|^2
    \lesssim
    \frac{1}{k^2 N^2}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^k
    \|\bz^\ell\|^2
    \lesssim\frac{1}{kN}\,.
    \]
The remaining two functions $\bar{F}_{B,k}$ and $F_{w,k}$ do not depend on $\bG$, so altogether this proves the desired bound on $\nabla_{\bG}\bar{F}_k$. We next turn to the derivative with respect to $\tbmeta^{1:k}$:
for $a\in B_j$,
    \[
    \nabla_{\tbmeta^{j,\ell}}
    \bar{F}_k
    =
    \nabla_{\tbmeta^{j,\ell}}
    \bar{F}_{B,k}
    =\frac{2\hB_j}{kMN}
    (\tbmeta^{j,\ell},\by^\ell)
    \by^\ell\,,
    \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.197113+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7a383e6e8a4882c83dceb16fa43d908c014c42efb8a516fc5d67ed46e77a32d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Distribution of the Stoppage Point.}

For $a\in \R$, let us note the $h_a(\mathrm{R})$ highest point in $\mathrm{R}$ above $a$:
\[h_{\mathrm{R}}(a):= \sup \{b: (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}\}.\]
In the last definition we can for instance adapt the convention that the supremum of an empty set is minus infinity.

Let $\landsc$ be a given random landscape.\\
Then, for $(x, y) \in \Half$ the stoppage point $X_{stop}(x, y)$ of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ has its CDF given by the following reformulation of events:
\[\{X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t\} =  \mathrm{below}([x, t],h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)})\cap \{t\leq\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}\} .\]

When $\landsc$ is a Poisson Building Process of intensity $\lambda$ and height distribution $\mathcal{L}$, Lemma \ref{dessous_diago} yields the following:
\[\p (X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t) = \exp \left(\int_{x}^{t} -\lambda \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\mathds{1}_{t \leq \max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} .\]
In other words, $X_{stop}(x, y)$ has its law equal to
\[g\times\Leb_{|[x,\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}]}+ \ \exp \left(-\lambda\bigintsss_{\hspace{-10pt}x}^{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} \hspace{-90pt} \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\delta_{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}},\]
where 
\[g: u\mapsto \lambda \mathcal{L}([h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(u), +\infty[)\exp\left(-\lambda \int_{x}^{u}\mathcal{L}(h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), +\infty[ \rm{d}a\right).\]

Moreover, conditioned on the stoppage point, the stoppage height is distributed according to $\mathcal{L}$ conditioned on being greater that $h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(X_{stop}(x, y))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499132+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e7b91c575adbfa0bce4ab714ce4186dd09394e0d520b2b9976c347c96e5089d7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and each is routinely dropped. (1) The cycle must be null-homologous in the domain where f is holomorphic (apart from the listed singularities). On the annulus U = {1 < |z| < 3} the function f(z) = 1/z is holomorphic with no singularity in U at all, yet the integral over the circle |z| = 2 equals 2πi, not 0: the circle winds once around 0, a point outside U. 'No singularities inside the contour' is not the hypothesis; 'winding number zero about every point off the domain' is. (2) Winding numbers multiply the residues. For the curve γ(t) = e^{2it}, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π (the unit circle traversed twice), the integral of 1/z is 4πi = 2πi times n(γ,0) Res, with n(γ,0) = 2. A figure-eight curve can even give cancellation, with winding numbers +1 and -1 about two poles. (3) The singularities must be isolated and f single-valued. f(z) = 1/sin(1/z) has poles at z = 1/(kπ) accumulating at 0, so 0 is not an isolated singularity, no residue is defined there, and the circle |z| = 1/2 encloses infinitely many poles: the residue theorem does not apply as stated (one must exhaust or use a different region). Similarly log z and sqrt(z) are not single-valued holomorphic functions on any punctured disk about 0, so they carry no residue at 0; a branch cut and a keyhole contour are required. Two further habits worth checking: a residue of 0 does not mean the singularity is removable (1/z^2 has residue 0), and when the contour is closed 'in the upper half-plane' the estimate showing the added arc's contribution tends to 0 (Jordan's lemma or an explicit bound) is part of the proof, not a formality.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378680+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e7c278a5c929afee616c48ad2dda5bb811314d807cba3f15b58d3461e5e114d4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A (deterministic, one-tape) Turing machine consists of: a finite set of states Q with a designated start state and designated halting states (for decision problems, an accept state and a reject state); a finite tape alphabet Gamma containing a blank symbol and an input alphabet Sigma not containing the blank; and a transition function delta mapping (non-halting state, tape symbol) pairs to (state, tape symbol, direction) triples with direction left or right. The machine operates on an infinite tape of cells each holding one symbol of Gamma, with a single head; initially the tape holds the input string from Sigma* followed by blanks, and the head is at the leftmost input cell. A configuration records the state, tape contents, and head position; each step applies delta to the current state and scanned symbol, rewriting the cell, changing state, and moving the head one cell. The machine halts upon entering a halting state; it may also run forever. It computes a partial function from strings to strings (output read off the tape at halting); it decides a language L if it halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings in L, and it recognizes (accepts) L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, possibly failing to halt off L. The Church-Turing thesis asserts that Turing machines capture exactly the effectively computable functions; the model is robust under adding tapes, two-way infinite tape, larger alphabets, or nondeterminism (for computability).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.819099+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, quasi-stationarity","id":"claim_e7eeccecd0f8bea88becac1ce1bab1f2c282eb12ad6ca9c19e907b3f5204364d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Pollett's Section 2 conjecture (ii) asks whether, for a lambda-transient irreducible countable transient class with almost sure absorption, every finite strictly positive limit of t^a e^{lambda t} p_t(i,j) must factor as A x_i m_j. Our result (id P0288, 2026-09-08): NO. Take the nearest-neighbour continuous-time walk on Z (rate 1 each side), killed at rate kappa everywhere plus an extra rate v at the origin. The class is lambda-transient with lambda = kappa, and t^{3/2} e^{kappa t} p_t(i,j) tends to [(|i| + 2/v)(|j| + 2/v) + i j] / (4 sqrt pi). The i j term makes the limit a rank-two form - its 2x2 minor on rows and columns {0,1} equals (2/v)^2/(16 pi) > 0 for every v - so no rank-one A x_i m_j factorisation exists; the reason is structural, a chain with two ends carries one degree of freedom per end. Verification as the source words it: the Feynman-Kac semigroup was solved directly at t = 100, 400, 1600, 6400, and against the claimed limits 0.141047, 0.282095, 0.705237, 0.423142 for (i,j) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,-1) at v = 2 the computed values converge monotonically to 0.141010, 0.282004, 0.705018, 0.422932, with the minor formed from the measured entries 0.019879 against the predicted 0.019894. PRIOR ART WARNING carried in the ledger row itself: Foley and McDonald published a discrete two-end construction from which the same continuous-time obstruction follows, so treat this as confirmed mathematics and probably known. continuous-time nearest-neighbour walk on Z at rate 1 each side killing rate kappa everywhere plus extra rate v at the origin lambda = kappa","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022562+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7f41a590668f96e971e280a5fd9dbfb77e47dd230eac59b266459a3f53e42ea","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Computational Distance]
Fix two distributions $\mu, \nu$ on a state space indexed by a size parameter $n$, and fix a degree parameter $d > 0$. We define
\be 
d_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mu,\nu) = d_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mu,\nu;n,d) \equiv  \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}_{n,d}} | \mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f]|,
\ee 

where $\mathcal{F}_{n,d}$ is the collection of real polynomials in the ambient coordinates of degree at most $d$ satisfying
\be 
\max(\Var_{\mu}(f),\Var_{\nu}(f)) = 1.
\ee","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a real-valued sequence, or for the approximate version a sequence with a controlled, typically o(n) or summable, subadditivity defect","the subadditive inequality a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n holding for all, or eventually all, pairs m, n","boundedness of a_n/n from below, or explicit acceptance that the limit may be -infinity, for the limit to be meaningful in context","for statistical-mechanics applications: correct identification of the quantity, such as a log partition function, as subadditive under the relevant combination operation, such as concatenation or union of volumes"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e80a55c79ea7ae42ed54422481e1478f6dc6886bfc54622384ee814fe9cfdb74","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). If a real sequence (a_n)_{n>=1} is subadditive, meaning a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m,n>=1, then lim_{n->infinity} a_n/n exists, possibly equal to -infinity, and equals inf_n a_n/n. This elementary but powerful lemma converts a one-directional combinatorial inequality into existence of a limit, and is the deterministic backbone behind results such as convergence of the free energy per site in statistical mechanics or the growth rate of a combinatorial quantity, for instance existence of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks, or existence of free energy limits in the Ising or Potts models under volume-doubling or concatenation subadditivity. An approximate or almost-subadditive version, a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n + e(m,n) with a controlled error term, such as e(m,n)=o(m+n) or a summable correction, still yields convergence of a_n/n to an infimum-type limit under mild additional conditions, a form often needed when exact subadditivity fails because of boundary effects. It does not give any rate of convergence, only existence of the limit, and it does not apply to sequences that are only superadditive or that fail monotonicity entirely without the appropriate sign flip; Kingman's theorem is the random, ergodic-theoretic generalization for stationary sequences and is not itself implied by Fekete's lemma. Typical failure: Verifying subadditivity only for a convenient special subsequence, such as powers of 2 or specific volume shapes like cubes, and then applying Fekete's lemma as though the inequality had been established for all m, n; the lemma genuinely requires the inequality for all pairs, or at least a cofinal family closed under addition, and skipping intermediate cases silently assumes exactly the regularity, such as shape-independence of the volume limit in statistical mechanics, that itself needs a separate van Hove or Fisher-type argument. Canonical reference: Fekete, 1923, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM, Chapter 1.","status":"unverified"}
