{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.674209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2ed3477afc3d07457bef4a154dbb7751193b6e2f0e726f426a90c07f78cebfd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 3 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional Finsler metric measure manifold. Then for $p>\frac{n}{2}$ and $K>0$, we have the following inequalities.
\ben
\item[{\rm (1)}] If $0< r\leq R\leq \frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{K}}$, then

\eeq

\item[{\rm (2)}] If $\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{K}}<r \leq R <\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{K}}$, then
\beq

&& \leq  \left(\frac{n-1}{(2 p-1)(2 p-n)}\right)^{\frac{p-1}{2p-1}}\left(\left\|{\rm Ric}_{\infty}^{K}\right\|_{p, R, \vartheta}(x_{0})\right)^{\frac{p}{2p-1}} \int_{r}^{R} \frac{1}{\sin^{2}(\sqrt{K} s)} ds.

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a martingale with respect to (F_n)","for the optional stopping consequence: tau an almost surely finite stopping time and the martingale uniformly integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3381e7ccdd3a3ab4f50fa4aa3f0083f4b6eac81113da66a80d044e9f35491f6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n)_{n >= 0} be a martingale for a filtration (F_n) and let F_infinity be the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the F_n. The following are equivalent: (i) the family {X_n} is uniformly integrable; (ii) X_n converges almost surely AND in L^1 to some X_infinity; (iii) there exists Y in L^1 with X_n = E[Y | F_n] almost surely for every n, that is the martingale is CLOSED. When these hold one may take Y = X_infinity, and X_infinity = E[Y | F_infinity]. Consequences: for a UI martingale, E[X_infinity] = E[X_0], and the optional stopping identity E[X_tau] = E[X_0] holds for EVERY almost surely finite stopping time tau, with no boundedness assumption on tau or on the martingale - this is a genuinely stronger conclusion than the standard three sufficient conditions (bounded tau, bounded martingale, or E[tau] finite with bounded increments). An L^1-bounded martingale need not be UI, and then only the almost sure half of (ii) survives. For p > 1, an L^p-bounded martingale is automatically UI by de la Vallee Poussin and converges in L^p as well; p = 1 is the exceptional case. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorems 13.3 and 14.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each f_n Riemann integrable on the compact interval [a,b]","uniform bound |f_n| <= M","pointwise convergence to f, AND f Riemann integrable - an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752811+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f36289c5312e1ca03cfca5ba87601f4ac8063f5554a56039a9f33e45b9a5702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be Riemann integrable, uniformly bounded (|f_n| <= M for all n), and suppose f_n -> f pointwise on [a,b] where f is ALSO Riemann integrable. Then integral_a^b f_n -> integral_a^b f. The Riemann integrability of the limit must be ASSUMED and does not follow: enumerate the rationals of [0,1] as q_1, q_2, ... and let f_n be the indicator of {q_1, ..., q_n}. Each f_n is Riemann integrable with integral 0, the family is bounded by 1, and f_n increases pointwise to the indicator of the rationals, which is not Riemann integrable. This is the essential defect that the Lebesgue integral repairs: the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem needs only measurability of the limit, which is automatic for a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Historically Arzela proved this in 1885 by a direct and rather delicate covering argument, before the Lebesgue theory existed. [Arzela (1885); see e.g. Luxemburg, 'Arzela's dominated convergence theorem for the Riemann integral', Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.361341+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f37bff03ece2c067d6056469a0ba4bb794ee80373ec4455c04f963ec5c1de767","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 49 (Trunk paths and vertices) of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Under $\q^m_n$, we have 
\[
X_j = m, \quad \text{for all } \bar{h} \le j \le \bar{h} + \lfloor c_0 n \rfloor.
\]
In other words, for each $j$ between $\bar{h}$ and $\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n\rfloor$, there are exactly $m$ vertices in $\cX_j$. These vertices belong to $m$ distinct ancestral lineages that remain separate at height $\bar{h}$. 
Let $\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_m$ be the $m$ coalescent subtrees at height $\bar{h}$.  
For $\bar{h}\le j \le \bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor$ and $1\le i\le m$, denote by 
\(z^j_i \in V(\mathsf{T}_i)\)
the unique vertex of $\mathsf{T}_i$ at height $j$. 
The sequence
\[
Z_i := \big(z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor}_i, z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor-1}_i, \ldots, z^{\bar{h}}_i\big)
\]
is called the trunk path of $\mathsf{T}_i$, and its elements are referred to as the trunk vertices of $\mathsf{T}_i$.  
The remaining $q_n(j)-m$ non-trunk vertices at height $j$ are denoted by $y^j_1, \ldots, y^j_{q_n(j)-m}$, where the subscripts are assigned arbitrary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.667215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3d0f4a43e1234f642677f9825b3630dc54cd55f6fb84c3189154d5d54f82428","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn eq:Ae-def of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Let $e=\{u,v\}$ be a bridge, where $u$ has label $1$ and $v$ has label $2$. 
Its original activation time and the lower bound recorded at activation are
\begin{align*}
 \gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \max\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u),\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\},\\
 L_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
The corresponding residual in the cumulative-hazard scale is
\begin{align*}
 R_e
 := H(\go_e)-H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) 
 = \go_e^\theta-(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta.
\end{align*}

For $q\geqslant\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the collision threshold
\begin{align*}
 L_e(q)
 :=
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
In particular, $L_e(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}})=L_e^{\mathrm{act}}$.

For $s\geqslant\mathfrak{a}_\ell\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the rescaled bridge age by
\begin{align}
 A_e(s)
 :=
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align}
Then $ L_e(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell)=\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}$.

The cumulative bridge hazard at rescaled time $s$ is
\begin{align}
 \gL_s
 &:= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}
 \left[ H\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}\right) - H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) \right]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}\left[\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell }\right)^\theta
 -(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta\right]
 \notag\\
 &=\int_0^s \frac{2\theta}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell ^\theta}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_q} A_e(q)^{\theta-1}\,\mathrm d q.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149599+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_f3f681977eb9ae940809b4e58a616eac3c6360d8024519e4cff1f440e2681399","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: an interior ball touching the boundary at the point x0 in question (and, for the strong maximum principle, the fact that such a ball can always be produced inside the open set where the solution is strictly below its maximum). Without it the conclusion 'the inward derivative at a boundary minimum is strictly positive' is false. Counterexample at a convex corner: in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with 0 < beta < pi and u(r, theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta). Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous on the closure, u > 0 inside and u = 0 on both straight edges, so 0 is a strict boundary minimum of u; but pi/beta > 1, so for every direction e pointing into Omega the difference quotient (u(te) - u(0))/t = O(t^{pi/beta - 1}) tends to 0: there is no Hopf gain at the vertex. No interior ball touches the vertex, exactly as the hypothesis requires. How far the hypothesis can be relaxed: the interior sphere condition may be replaced by an interior C^{1,Dini} (or interior paraboloid/cone-with-Dini) condition, but not by mere C^1 regularity of the boundary; there are C^1 domains where a positive harmonic function vanishing on the boundary has vanishing gradient at a boundary point - for instance the image of the upper half-plane near 0 under the conformal map z -> z log(1/z), whose boundary is C^1 but not Dini smooth at 0, and for which the inverse map has derivative tending to 0. Practical rule for an auditor: a proof that invokes Hopf's lemma (to get strict inequality, strict monotonicity, a sign of the normal derivative, simplicity of the first eigenvalue, or the strong maximum principle at the boundary) must say why the domain has the interior ball property at the relevant point; convex corners and cusps of the domain are where this silently breaks.","status":"unverified"}

\item There are $u,v\in K(C)$ with $K(u,v)=K(C)$ and $v^n=(u^2-b)/a$ for some $a,b\in K^\times$ if and only if $T_n\ne\emptyset$.

\begin{equation}
m\,p_t\,p_t''=(m-1)\,(p_t')^2 .

The coefficients of $m\,p_t\,p_t''-(m-1)(p_t')^2$ as a polynomial in $x$ are polynomials in $t$ over $K$, not all zero, and $T_n\cap K$ is the set of their common roots in $K$.

{"assumptions":["i.i.d., or otherwise well-structured, entries of the non-Hermitian matrix M with matching moment and normalization conditions, e.g. mean 0, variance 1/n","convergence, for almost every z or in an appropriately averaged sense, of the empirical singular-value distribution of M-zI, established via Hermitian random matrix methods","a uniform bound preventing the smallest singular values of M-zI from concentrating excess mass near 0, i.e. a least-singular-value or anti-concentration estimate","sufficient regularity to justify exchanging limits with the singular logarithm in the potential-theoretic identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997859+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4189aeabe1f62c5a51a59e2d74be239517995bf2c0f01ad54eb33b87fa93fe6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To study the empirical spectral distribution of a non-Hermitian random matrix M, such as an i.i.d.-entry matrix in the circular law problem, Girko's Hermitization method associates to each z in C the 2n x 2n Hermitian matrix H_z with off-diagonal blocks M-zI and (M-zI)^*, whose eigenvalues are plus and minus the singular values of M-zI. The identity log|det(M-zI)| = (1/2) sum_i log(s_i(M-zI)^2) relates the real part of the logarithmic potential of M's empirical spectral distribution at z to the empirical distribution of singular values of M-zI, a Hermitian and hence more tractable object accessible via Stieltjes transform and local law techniques from Hermitian random matrix theory. Establishing, first, convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI for almost every z, and second, a uniform bound preventing accumulation of small singular values near 0, needed because log is singular there, together imply, via potential-theoretic uniqueness, convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of M itself, for example to the circular law for i.i.d. entries. It does not work without the delicate small-singular-value control, typically the hardest and most technical part of the proof, requiring separate anti-concentration or least-singular-value estimates, and the method inherently gives information about the logarithmic potential, from which the actual distribution is recovered only via a separate potential-theoretic uniqueness argument. Typical failure: Establishing convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI and concluding convergence of the eigenvalue distribution of M without separately proving the required small-singular-value control; without a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value, which can be genuinely delicate for matrices with dependent or heavy-tailed entries, the logarithmic potential argument can fail even though the easier half of Girko's method has been verified, historically the main obstruction in proving circular-law universality under weak entry assumptions. Canonical reference: Girko, 1984, Theory of Probability and its Applications; Bai, 1997, Annals of Probability; Tao and Vu, 2010, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

# C019 v1: the averaged central peak is absent from each realized-label curve
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a local-window obstruction, not a global no-double-descent theorem.

## 1. Exact claim and dependencies
Use exactly C018's four stratified inputs, unit-norm single-index ReLU
teacher, fixed nu,kappa>0 (nu<=1), independent Gaussian hidden weights,
iid signed heads, both-layer GD step1/2 and sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(rho_e),
rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e). Unlike C018 retain the individual label realization:
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
All sixteen networks share initialization. For any fixed bounded interval
I=[A,B] with A<B, let J_e(I) be the integers k with
 b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e) in I.
Then
 lim_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P(each of the sixteen sequences (R_(e,m,xi)(k))_(k in J_e(I))
   is strictly monotone in one direction) = 1.             (1)
The direction may depend on xi and initialization. For small e, J has
many consecutive integers. In particular none of the sixteen individual
curves has decrease/rise/decrease witnesses entirely inside this window,
with probability tending to one in this iterated-limit sense.
C018's sixteen-trajectory average may nevertheless have such witnesses.
No single-realized-label theorem follows from that average. This claim
concerns only a bounded s window around (3/2)log(1/e)/b_s, not other times.

## 2. Exact unaveraged risk derivative
Write c_h=(1/4)sum_i h(i)xi_i for h=0,s,t,st, N_h=2sqrt(rho_e)c_h,
and U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e in the Gaussian width limit.
The frozen residual in mode h divided by alpha_e is
 q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h, q_h=exp(-b_h t).
Thus, with eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s, the derivative normalized by
2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st) is exactly
 D_(e,xi)(s)=sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
       {q_h N_h(N_h-U_(e,h))-q_h^2(U_(e,h)-N_h)^2},       (2)
at t=t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s.
C016/C017 give a joint Gaussian coupling, locally uniformly in s,
 e U_(e,s)->L_s=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1,
 b_t/(b_t+b_st), b_st/(b_t+b_st)->1/2, eta_e~e.
Let a=L_s^2 and B0=(L_t^2+1)/2; B0 is C017's B.
The constant-mode term is negligible faster than any power of e, even
with N_0=O(e^(-1/4)), because b_0 is bounded away from zero and
Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

## 3. Exhausting the sixteen sign patterns
The four-dimensional Walsh transform of a sign vector has just two types.
If xi has an odd number of + signs (eight patterns), all four c_h are
+/-1/2. If xi has an even number, xi is one of the eight signed Walsh
characters, so exactly one c_h equals +/-1 and the others vanish.
Consequently there are ten patterns with c_s!=0, four with c_s=0 and
one of c_t,c_st nonzero, and two with only c_0 nonzero.
This finite classification is verified exactly in the accompanying script;
it also follows by direct enumeration of the sixteen vectors.

For c_s!=0, (2) gives the locally uniform limit
 e^(3/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> -2sqrt(kappa)c_s L_s exp(-s).      (3)
Indeed q_s=e^(3/2)exp(-s), N_s=2sqrt(kappa)e^(-1/4)c_s,
U_s=e^(-1)(L_s+o(1)), and eta_e~e. The cross term
-q_s N_s U_s/eta_e has size e^(-3/4) and gives (3).
The terms q_s N_s^2/eta_e and q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e are O(1);
all remaining fast terms are smaller. Slow-mode terms are O(e^(-1/4))
and disappear after multiplication by e^(3/4). These estimates are
uniform on each fixed compact s interval.

If c_s=0 and either c_t or c_st is nonzero, the corresponding limit is
 e^(1/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> sqrt(kappa)(c_t L_t-c_st).         (4)
To check the slow terms without losing cancellations, rewrite their braces
in (2) as
 N_h U_h q_h(2q_h-1)-U_h^2 q_h^2+N_h^2 q_h(1-q_h).
Here q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)). After multiplication by e^(1/4), the
first term converges to 2sqrt(kappa)c_h times its U_h limit;
the second vanishes, and the third is O(e^(3/4)log(1/e)).
The weights tend to1/2. The fast contribution is only O(1) because N_s=0.
For these four patterns, exactly one of c_t,c_st is +/-1, so (4) is
nonzero unless L_t=0 in a t-pattern; that Gaussian event has probability0.

For the two constant patterns all nonconstant N_h vanish. Directly (2)
then gives, locally uniformly,
 D_(e,xi)(s) -> -a exp(-2s)-B0 <0.                       (5)
The constant-label term is again exponentially negligible.

Outside the null events L_s=0 and L_t=0, each of (3)-(5) has a strictly
nonzero, constant sign throughout any fixed compact interval. Uniform
convergence makes each frozen derivative have that sign for all sufficiently
small e. There are finitely many patterns, so this holds for all sixteen
simultaneously. Their integer-time frozen risks are therefore strictly
monotone throughout J_e(I). The Gaussian probability of this event tends
to one, by the coupling and bounded convergence.

## 4. Transfer of the LOCAL obstruction to actual nonlinear GD
For fixed e and finite integer horizon T, C018 Section3 proves joint weak
convergence of all actual risk values to their frozen Gaussian-width-limit
values. The proof works for each label pattern before averaging: prediction
transfer is uniform over the sixteen patterns, and squaring finitely many
prediction vectors is continuous. Choose T to include J_e(I).
The event that each of sixteen finite risk sequences is strictly monotone
in some direction is a finite union (over choices of direction) of finite
intersections of strict adjacent-value inequalities. It is therefore open
in this finite joint risk array. The open-set Portmanteau inequality gives
 liminf_m P(actual monotonicity event)>=P(frozen monotonicity event).
The right side tends to one as e decreases by Section3, proving (1).
Strict adjacent gaps need not have a uniform size in e: width is sent to
infinity at each fixed e first. No derivative of actual nonlinear GD is
introduced, and no uniform-width assertion is being made.

## 5. Consequence and exact scope
The dominant signed cross term in (3) disappears under noise averaging;
its sign is not controlled for a realized dataset. Slow signed cross terms
similarly survive in (4). C017/C018 obtain an averaged quadratic profile
only after these cancellations. Thus a high-probability peak in the mean
of sixteen trajectories is compatible with local monotonicity of every
constituent trajectory. Equation (1) is the exact obstruction to reusing
that proof as a single-dataset result. It does not rule out single-dataset
double descent in a DIFFERENT window or under another noise/initialization
scaling, nor for other input laws or feature-learning regimes.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018 are unaudited. Independent mathematical
and novelty review remain pending. The finite check certifies only the

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.488638+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f46b7ab8405d1fb823b2361e17c613458d59c8463a1caf3a8fd06d62636bcfe9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 1 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that $0<\alpha<1$ and $m\in L^\infty(\Omega)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[i)]

\eqref{Eq1} possesses a non-negative weak solution
$u_\lambda^+\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap C^{1,\gamma}(\overline{\Omega})$ for any
$\gamma\in(0,1)$, such that
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)<0,
\qquad
E_\lambda''(u_\lambda^+)>0.
\]
Moreover, the minimum energy level $(-\infty,\lambda^*)\ni\lambda
\longmapsto E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, and
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)\longrightarrow0

\]
\item[ii)]

\[

|\Omega^+\cup\Omega^0|>0.
\]
Then
$0<\lambda_{1,\Omega}<\lambda^*<+\infty$.
For every $\lambda\in(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)$, problem
\eqref{Eq1} possesses a non-negative weak solution
$u_\lambda^-\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap C^{1,\gamma}(\overline{\Omega})$ for any
$\gamma\in(0,1)$, such that
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)>0,
\qquad
E_\lambda''(u_\lambda^-)<0.
\]
Moreover, the corresponding minimum energy level $(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)\ni\lambda
\longmapsto E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, and
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)\longrightarrow+\infty
\qquad\text{as }\lambda\downarrow\lambda_{1,\Omega}.

If, in addition, condition
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{1,\Omega^0}>
\lambda_{1,\Omega^0\cup\Omega^+}

holds, then
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*.
\]
\end{itemize}

Then
\[
\lambda^*=\lambda_{1,\Omega^0},

without assuming condition {\rm (M)}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:23:37.815217+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f46f76cee63de6d808da09d1ff773eb71101280deb2d436a6f955821c90a012c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2609.03634, 'Joint Laws of Maximum Drawdown and Maximum Drawup for Spectrally Negative L\'{e}vy Process'] Fix $a<0<b$. Under $\mathbb{P}_{a,b}^{>}$, the pre-$H_S$ process, the intermediate process, and the post-$H_I$ process are independent and their laws are as follows;
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The pre-supremum process is the Doob transform of the spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process killed when it reaches $b$ before the exponential time $T$, with excessive function
\[
h^*(x)=\frac{\gamma}{\Phi(\gamma)}W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)
\frac{\left(W^{(\gamma)\prime}(b-a)\right)^2-W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)W^{(\gamma)\prime\prime}(b-a)}
{\left(W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)\right)^2},
\qquad a<x<b.
\]

\item The intermediate process is the Doob transform of the post-supremum process killed at $\tau_a$, with excessive function
\[
h^{**}(x)=\frac{\left(Z^{(\gamma)}(b-a)-1\right)
\left[
W^{(\gamma)\prime}(x-a)W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)
-
W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)W^{(\gamma)\prime}(b-a)
\right]}
{\left(W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)\right)^2},
\qquad a<x<b.
\]

\item The post-infimum process is the Doob transform of the spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process issued from $a$ and killed at $T\wedge\tau_b^+\wedge\tau_a^-$, with excessive function
\[
h^{***}(x)=1-Z^{(\gamma)}(x-a)
+\left(Z^{(\gamma)}(b-a)-1\right)
\frac{W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)}{W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)},
\qquad a<x<b.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.028487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4745d43e847bcbc7d0b5c612364593b7ae3449033d4447a268039029fb5e158","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ising-rpc of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Consider a tree with $L$ levels, rooted at $\varnothing$, in which every vertex before the last level has
		countably many children. We label the children of each vertex by $\mathbb{N}$, so a vertex at level $\ell$ is a sequence
		$(n_1,\ldots,n_\ell)\in\mathbb{N}^\ell$.
		
		For every $1\le\ell\le L$, attach to each vertex at level $\ell-1$ an independent Poisson point process on $\mathbb{R}$
		with intensity
		\[
		\theta_\ell e^{-\theta_\ell u}\,\mathrm{d} u.
		\]
		Order its points decreasingly and assign them in this order to the edges leading to its children. All these point
		processes are independent.
		
		For a leaf $\alpha=(n_1,\ldots,n_L)$, set $\alpha|0=\varnothing$ and
		$\alpha|\ell=(n_1,\ldots,n_\ell)$. Let $u_{\alpha|\ell}$ denote the label of the edge from
		$\alpha|_{\ell-1}$ to $\alpha|\ell$, and define
		\[
		u_\alpha:=\sum_{\ell=1}^L u_{\alpha|\ell}.
		\]
		For two leaves $\alpha^1$ and $\alpha^2$, let $\alpha^1\wedge\alpha^2$ be the largest
		$\ell\in\{0,\ldots,L\}$ for which $\alpha^1|\ell=\alpha^2|\ell$, and set
		\[
		s_{\alpha^1\wedge\alpha^2}:=q_{\alpha^1\wedge\alpha^2}.
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:01:15.318475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f47c8118beb4cd27c9aec88f0cfa46db152317e555f36c801a75868b8a939096","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Exact dynamic-kernel mismatch identity) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] Fix $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $x\in\mathcal X$. differentiable near every point
$\theta_s^{P,\lambda}+u\Delta_s^\lambda$ and

$\{\theta_t^{P,\lambda}+u\Delta_t^\lambda,
    \theta_t^{P,\lambda}+ud_t^\lambda\}$,
for $s,t\in[0,T]$ and $u\in[0,1]$.
Suppose, for $|h|$-almost every $z$ and every $s\in[0,T]$, that
$\theta\mapsto f_\theta(x_z)$ is differentiable at

 \mathcal K^{\rm ch,\lambda}(t,s;x,z)

    \int_{\X \times \MM} \E \left[\left( D_{(x,m_x)} F \right)^2\right] (\nu \otimes \QQ)(dx,dm_x) < \infty.
    \]
    For any point $x\in \X$, define a random variable $M_x$ independent of everything else, distributed according to $\QQ$.
    Then it holds that
    \[
    \mathbf{d}_W(F,N) \leq \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_0+ \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_2 + \hat{\gamma}_3
    \]
    and
    \[
    \mathbf{d}_K(F,N) \leq \hat{\gamma}_0 + \hat{\gamma}_1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \hat{\gamma}_2 + \hat{\gamma}_4 + \hat{\gamma}_5 + \hat{\gamma}_6,
    \]
    where
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\gamma}_0 &:= \E \left| 1- \Var(F) \right|\\
        \hat{\gamma}_1 &:= 2 \bigg(\int_\X \bigg(\int_\X \E \big[ |D_{(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/4} \cdot \E \big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/4} \nu(dy) \bigg)^2 \nu(dx) \bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_2 &:= 2  \bigg(\int_\X \bigg(\int_\X \E \big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \nu(dy) \bigg)^2 \nu(dx) \bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_3 &:= 2 \int_\X \E|D_{(y,M_y)}F|^3 \nu(dy)
    \end{align*}
    and
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\gamma}_4 &:= \bigg(4\int_\X \E|D_{(y,M_y)}F|^4 \nu(dy)\bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_5 &:= \bigg(8\int_\X\int_\X \E|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4 \nu(dy)\nu(dx)\bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_6 &:= \bigg(32\int_\X\int_\X \E\big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \cdot \E\big[|D_{(x,M_x)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \nu(dy)\nu(dx)\bigg)^{1/2}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^1 (Lipschitz flux suffices for the theory)","u ∈ L^∞; the test functions must be NONNEGATIVE, otherwise the inequality would force equality and lose all selection power","sgn is the usual signum, so the pair (|u-k|, sgn(u-k)(f(u)-f(k))) is the Kruzhkov entropy/entropy-flux pair"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417466+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_f4c7439626209bb4214a64c82f43190d941c048df2939c0d04fb206064491661","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^1(R;R^n) and u0 ∈ L^∞(R^n). A function u ∈ L^∞(R^n × (0,∞)) is a Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + div f(u) = 0, u(·,0) = u0, if for every k ∈ R and every φ ∈ C_c^∞(R^n × [0,∞)) with φ ≥ 0: ∫_0^∞ ∫_{R^n} ( |u - k| φ_t + sgn(u-k) ( f(u) - f(k) )·∇_x φ ) dx dt + ∫_{R^n} |u0(x) - k| φ(x,0) dx ≥ 0. Equivalently (for C^1 flux), η(u)_t + div q(u) ≤ 0 in the sense of distributions, with the initial datum taken in L^1_loc, for every convex entropy η ∈ C^1(R) with entropy flux q determined by q' = η' f'; the Kruzhkov family η_k(u) = |u-k| generates all convex entropies. Every entropy solution is a weak solution (take k larger than ||u||_∞ and k smaller than -||u||_∞ and combine the two resulting inequalities). The inequality has a sign: it expresses dissipation, and it is exactly the condition selected by the vanishing-viscosity limit u^ε_t + div f(u^ε) = ε Δ u^ε.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:32:29.005751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f50839e8583a8e7be60e84e95c5e077756857cecaefe6bfab498c202567bfe02","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem DL comp of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] {Duquesne_LeGall_06_Hausdorff}}]
  
  Let $(\mathcal{X}, d)$ be a boundedly-compact metric space.
  Fix $c > 1$ and fix a non-decreasing continuous function $g\colon [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$
  with $g(0) = 0$ and $g(2r) \leq c g(r)$ for all $r \geq 0$.
  Let $\mathcal{H}_g$ be the Hausdorff measure with gauge $g$.
  Then there exist constants $c', c'' \in (0,\infty)$, which depend only on $c$, 
  such that the following holds.
  Let $\nu$ be a Radon measure on $\mathcal{X}$ and let $A$ be a Borel subset of $\mathcal{X}$.
  Write $B(x,r) \coloneqq \{y \mid d(x,y) < r\}$ for each $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $r > 0$.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = \textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item 
    If $\displaystyle \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\nu(B(x, 2^{-n}))}{g(2^{-n})} \leq 1$ for every $x \in A$,
    then $\mathcal{H}_g(A) \geq c' \nu(A)$.

    \item 
    If $\displaystyle \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\nu(B(x, 2^{-n}))}{g(2^{-n})} \geq 1$ for every $x \in A$,
    then $\mathcal{H}_g(A) \leq c'' \nu(A)$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752684+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f508dc594a18c6b66feda84d09ec4e36e63f895880826437a51899385d203a1c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to X and let Y_n converge in probability to a CONSTANT c. Then (X_n, Y_n) converges in distribution to (X, c) jointly, and consequently X_n + Y_n converges in distribution to X + c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and if c is not 0 then X_n / Y_n converges in distribution to X / c. The constancy of the limit of Y_n is essential and is not a technical convenience: convergence in distribution alone gives no information about joint behaviour. Take X symmetric with X_n = X for all n and Y_n = -X for all n; then X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in distribution to X by symmetry, yet X_n + Y_n = 0 does not converge in distribution to X + X = 2X unless X is degenerate. Likewise convergence in probability of Y_n cannot be weakened to convergence in distribution even when the limit is constant, because for a constant limit those two modes coincide, which is precisely why the theorem can be stated with either for a constant target. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.591025+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f514f7e33cf77eb0b5c6b8670d4801b5b9b47f87f5626f82644194f36f851356","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.03750, '\\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D...'] We study the long-term distributional dynamics and small-noise asymptotics of two-dimensional nonautonomous stochastic primitive equations driven by Gaussian and multiplicative L\\'evy noise, together with moderate deviations for the purely jump model. A {\\em $\\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, \\mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\\left(C (\\Sigma \\times \\Lambda), \\mathcal{C}_{\\Sigma}\\right)$. For $i \\in \\Sigma$ we write $\\mathcal{L}_i(\\omega) = (\\mathcal{L}(\\omega))(i, \\cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\\mathcal{L}_i: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Lambda)$, which is $(\\mathcal{C}, \\mathcal{F})-$measurable. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215430+00:00","domain":"discrete geometry","id":"claim_f528a90663c3e15b8fac1b81c773ee78b7ca979ccfb7ac5f9bc09809c835ec77","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The phrase 'general position' carries two conventions in the theory of hyperplane arrangements, and they are incompatible. For a CENTRAL arrangement, where every hyperplane contains the origin, the useful condition is on the NORMAL vectors: every $d$ or fewer of them are linearly independent. This is the condition under which the central orthant count is exact. For an AFFINE arrangement, a widespread convention instead requires that any $p$ of the hyperplanes with $p$ greater than the ambient dimension have empty intersection. No central arrangement can ever satisfy the affine condition, because all of its hyperplanes share the origin. A central arrangement is therefore never in 'general position' in the affine sense, however generic its normals. Sources using the affine convention will appear to exclude exactly the case a central count is about, and citing one for the other is a live error.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.294524+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f52b7d5683614e53246433cb6a8171e35984fa17897dcd78ec0cf139427063bf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Lipschitz maps and Lipschitz model classes of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho_X)$ and $(Y,\rho_Y)$ be metric spaces, and let $L\ge0$.  A map
$f:X\to Y$ is called $L$-Lipschitz if
\[
    \rho_Y(f(x),f(y))
    \le
    L\,\rho_X(x,y)
\]
for every $x,y\in X$.  Its Lipschitz constant is
$
    \operatorname{Lip}(f)
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\neq y}
    \,
        \tfrac{\rho_Y(f(x),f(y))}{\rho_X(x,y)}
$.
When $h:X\to\mathbb R$ is real-valued, we also write $
    |\nabla h|(x)
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \limsup_{y\to x}
        \tfrac{|h(x)-h(y)|}{\rho(x,y)}
$ for its pointwise upper slope, with the convention that the value is $+\infty$ if the corresponding $\operatorname{limsup}$ is infinite.
\hfill\\
\noindent
For a metric space $(X,\rho)$, we define the unit Lipschitz model class
\[
    \mathcal F_1
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
    =
    \left\{
        f:X\to[-1,1]
        :
        |f(x)-f(y)|
        \le
        \rho(x,y)
        \text{ for all }x,y\in X
    \right\}.
\]
If $(X,\rho)$ has doubling dimension $0<d<\infty$, we abbreviate
$
    \mathcal F_{1:d}
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
$.
All such classes are equipped with the uniform norm
$
    \|f\|_\infty
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.396024+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f55c04608704ad20ac6944cc1b971270d7fd3596a2086e826d2859c2cd99bd49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Electrical networks}]
  Let $(V, E)$ be a connected, simple, undirected graph with finite or countably many vertices,
  where $V$ denotes the vertex set and $E$ denotes the edge set.
  (NB.\ A graph being simple means that it has no loops and no multiple edges.)
  For $x, y \in V$,
  we write $x \sim y$ if and only if $\{ x, y \} \in E$.
  Let $\{\mu(x, y)\}_{x, y \in V}$ be a family of non-negative real numbers such that 
  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y, x)$ for all $x, y \in V$,
  $\mu(x, y) > 0$ if and only if $x \sim y$,
  and
  \begin{equation}
    \mu(x) 
    \coloneqq 
    \sum_{y \in V} \mu(x, y) < \infty,
    \quad 
    \forall x \in V.
  \end{equation}
  We call $\mu(x,y)$ the \textit{conductance} on the edge $\{x,y\}$
  and $(V, E, \mu)$ an \textit{electrical network}.
  Note that the edge set $E$ is uniquely determined by conductances.
  We equip $V$ with the discrete topology 
  and define a Radon measure $\mu^{\#}$ as the \textit{counting measure} on $V$, 
  which is a Radon measure on $V$ given by 
  \begin{equation}
    \mu^{\#}(A) 
    \coloneqq 
    \# A
    = 
    \sum_{x \in V} \delta_{x}(A)
    \quad 
    A \subseteq V,
  \end{equation}
  where $\delta_{x}$ is the Dirac measure putting mass $1$ at $x$.
  Given an electrical network $G$,
  we write $V_{G}$, $E_{G}$, $\{\mu_{G}(x,y)\}_{x, y \in V_{G}}$, and $\mu^{\#}_{G}$
  for the vertex set, the edge set, the conductances, and the counting measure, respectively.
  When we say that $G$ is a \textit{rooted electrical network},

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.063036+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f561cc7d8ee062ff9eafbe2733a3246f7233b0e3a022f01b2ca3ccfd7b99ee81","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] Consider a sequence $\{f_n\}= \{f_n\}_{0 \leq n < T+1}$ of non-anticipative functions $f_n:\mathcal{S} \rightarrow [- \infty, \infty]$, $n\ge0$.

\vspace{.1in}\noindent $\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{supermartingale} sequence if
\begin{equation}  \nonumber 
\overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1} \leq f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{submartingale} if
\begin{equation} \nonumber 
f_j \leq \underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}~~a.e.\;\;0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{martingale} if
\begin{equation}\nonumber 
\underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= \overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["This is a reduction of candidates, not a classification or a numerical proof for every stable index."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f56a0e147e9085ca7af811dce58bae38fe443cd2f2e9f0fb5cdcc82ab3fb1945","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the remaining-problem reduction in the partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. A law lambda is freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal nu. The source's Theorem 1.4 shows that no nondelta law of finite variance (equivalently, in the free domain of attraction of the semicircle) is freely strongly unimodal. The record's proved Cauchy obstruction excludes every nondelta lambda in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law. The same closure argument shows, more generally, that a nondelta lambda is not freely strongly unimodal whenever it lies in the free domain of attraction of a free stable law that is itself not freely strongly unimodal. Problem 3.11 therefore reduces to two questions. (1) Is some free stable law of index alpha in (0,2), alpha != 1, freely strongly unimodal? (The index-1 case is settled by the Cauchy identity, and index 2 by the source's Lemma 3.1.) (2) Is some measure lying in no free domain of attraction freely strongly unimodal? Numerically, for the free stable laws lambda_alpha with K(w)=1/w - i(iw)^{alpha-1}, the unimodal witness nu = (1/10)U[0,0.05] + (9/10)U[0,16] gives lambda_alpha boxplus nu two interior maxima at alpha = 1.95, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7. This was computed by Belinschi-Bercovici subordination and calibrated against the exact Cauchy case at alpha=1. So those laws, and the laws attracted to them, are excluded numerically; only alpha=1 is a theorem. For alpha = 0.6 down to 0.3 the same nu, and three other one-sided uniform mixtures tried at alpha=0.5, give a single maximum. This is not evidence that those laws are freely strongly unimodal. The case alpha below about 0.65 remains open. This does not answer the existence question. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational in (0,1) with continued fraction [0; a_1, a_2, ...], a_i >= 1","p_n/q_n are the convergents given by the standard three-term recursions","eta_n = ||q_n alpha|| = |q_n alpha - p_n|, and ||t|| is the distance to the nearest integer","the rotation is R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle R/Z, and 'closest return' refers to the two-sided quantity ||q alpha||"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732376+00:00","domain":"continued fractions, circle rotations, renormalization","id":"claim_f57732cc5b24796cda6e07d98d78f7bf187cb2277e435a9b21d5d4dfa548e4b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let alpha in (0,1) be irrational with continued fraction alpha = [0; a_1, a_2, ...], all a_i >= 1, and let p_n / q_n be its convergents, defined by p_n = a_n p_{n-1} + p_{n-2}, q_n = a_n q_{n-1} + q_{n-2} with q_{-1} = 0, q_0 = 1, p_{-1} = 1, p_0 = 0. Put eta_n = |q_n alpha - p_n| and note the signs alternate: q_n alpha - p_n = (-1)^n eta_n. For n >= 1 one has eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} <= 1/2, so eta_n = ||q_n alpha||; at n = 0 this can fail (if a_1 = 1, i.e. alpha > 1/2, then eta_0 = alpha > 1/2 while ||alpha|| = 1 - alpha), so ALL statements below are for n >= 1. Write R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on T = R/Z. Then:

(a) BEST APPROXIMATION / CLOSEST RETURNS. For n >= 1 and every integer q with 1 <= q < q_{n+1} and q not equal to q_n one has ||q alpha|| > ||q_n alpha|| = eta_n. Consequently the denominators q_n are exactly the closest-return times of the orbit of 0 under R_alpha: q_{n+1} is the smallest integer q > q_n with ||q alpha|| < ||q_n alpha||, and the sequence of record-setting return times is precisely q_1 < q_2 < ....

(b) RECURSION AND SIZE. eta_{n-1} = a_{n+1} eta_n + eta_{n+1}; the eta_n strictly decrease to 0; 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n) < eta_n < 1/q_{n+1}; and the exact identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 holds for every n >= 1 (and also at n = 0 with the convention eta_{-1} = |q_{-1} alpha - p_{-1}| = 1).

(c) RENORMALIZATION INTO TWO ROKHLIN TOWERS. Let J_n be the arc of T whose endpoints are the two points q_{n-1} alpha - p_{n-1} and q_n alpha - p_n (of opposite signs), so J_n contains 0 and has length eta_{n-1} + eta_n; it is split by 0 into a piece of length eta_{n-1} and a piece of length eta_n. Then the first-return map of R_alpha to J_n is the exchange of these two subintervals: the return time is q_n on the piece of length eta_{n-1} and q_{n-1} on the piece of length eta_n. Equivalently the q_{n-1} + q_n sets R_alpha^i(base) -- i < q_n over the long piece and i < q_{n-1} over the short piece -- are pairwise disjoint and tile T, which is exactly the content of the identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 in (b). This is the standard renormalization scheme behind Ostrowski expansions and the three-distance theorem.

SHARP EDGES. (a) is a statement about the TWO-SIDED quantity ||q alpha||. The intermediate (mediant) denominators b q_n + q_{n-1} with 1 <= b < a_{n+1} are best ONE-SIDED approximations but in general do not minimize ||q alpha||, so they are NOT closest-return times -- confusing the two is the classic error here. The hypothesis that alpha is irrational is essential: for rational alpha the algorithm terminates, the orbit is finite and periodic, and the tower picture degenerates. Also note eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} is an inequality, not an asymptotic equality: eta_n and 1/q_{n+1} agree only up to a factor between 1/2 and 1, and a proof that needs the exact value must use eta_n = 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n * [0; a_{n+2}, a_{n+3}, ...]).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:01:56.346838+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f581c59cfadc59565da344104a1612cb4697c13802b8ff8f5c61da3d20962ca0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:UDS_ of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] \textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{P}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{P}_x$. Let $x>a$, and let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a).$ 
If $\tau \in (0,x-a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-a,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau+a-x$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(a) \&~(b).)

\textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{T}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{T}_x$. To do so, we will split into two cases: (i) if $(a+b)/2<
x< (3a-b)/2$, and (ii) $x \ge (3a-b)/2$. 
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=3em]
    \item[{\textbf{(i)}}] Assume that $(a+b)/2
< x< (3a-b)/2$, in which case we can only deposit on the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. Hence, let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,x-(a+b)/2)$, and deposit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(e).)
\item[{\textbf{(ii)}}] Let $x\ge (3a-b)/2$, and $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a)$. If $\tau \in (0,x-(3a-b)/2)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-(3a-b)/2,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau-(x-(3a-b)/2)$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(c) \&~(d).)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Algorithm:} When a trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ has been deposited on either $\mathcal{P}_x$ or $\mathcal{T}_x$, there will be two leftover strips. Conditional on the first deposition, the parking procedures on these two strips are defined to be independent copies of the $\mathcal{UDA}$, with the corresponding strip types and sizes. 
This procedure is continued recursively until there are no strips remaining which can fit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["weights nonnegative, not all zero","for the variance interpretation: i.i.d. observations with finite variance"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:17:06.630627+00:00","domain":"survey statistics / weighted estimation","id":"claim_f582d2971f91e2d79df8475b7b3a84e28609376a3e46cd4588963e2174f253ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For case weights $s_1, \\dots, s_n \\ge 0$ not all zero, the effective sample size is $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = (\\sum_i s_i)^2 / \\sum_i s_i^2$. It satisfies $1 \\le n_{\\mathrm{eff}} \\le n$, with $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = n$ if and only if all nonzero weights are equal and $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ if and only if a single weight is nonzero. The same factor governs every entry of a weighted sample covariance $\\sum_i s_i (x_i - \\bar x_s)(x_i - \\bar x_s)^T / \\sum_i s_i$ to leading order, so entrywise concentration bounds for the sample covariance transfer to the weighted one with $n$ replaced by $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-11-02T23:15:00.816560+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_f5876f03112732895ec534a8c063c90f07d46cd8426c60bca779c5bfd4692898","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The stationary law of the leftmost particles in Aldous's drift-jump process (2026). In Aldous's drift-jump process, k particles 0 < X_1 < ... < X_k move right with velocity equal to their position, and at the events of a rate-one space-time Poisson process the nearest particle to the right of the event jumps to it; Aldous (open problem, February 2018) asked for a fairly explicit description of the stationary distribution. The paper proves that the stationary distribution is unique and the law at time t converges to it in total variation from every start, and that in stationarity X_i = Gamma_{tau_i}, where Gamma_1 < Gamma_2 < ... is a rate-one Poisson process and, independently, tau_i is the first n at which the longest increasing subsequence of n independent uniforms reaches length i (a form of representation (42) in the 1993 notes of Aldous and Diaconis). Every joint survival probability P(X_{k_1} > s_1, ..., X_{k_r} > s_r) equals e^{-s_r} times a finite determinant with modified-Bessel-function entries, of size at most k(k-1) for the first k particles; for one particle it is Gessel's Toeplitz determinant. E(X_i - X_{i-1}) is the constant c(i) of Aldous and Diaconis (1999) for the i-th pile in patience sorting. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/drift-jump-leftmost-particles (commit c315f47b0278). Not refereed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:36.183309+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f5be7d68a02046f965686fb75e917eaf27357500baaeed761098b619fbebbfe2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let rows $w_1,\\dots,w_{m-1}$ be i.i.d. isotropic in $\\mathbb{R}^m$ ($m=\\dim\\mathrm{Sym}_d^0$ or $\\dim\\mathrm{Sym}_d$), let $c$ be the unit null vector of the design they span, and let $A$ be the unit-Frobenius symmetric matrix it encodes. By isotropy $\\sqrt d\\,A$ converges in moments to the semicircle law, so $d^{k-1}\\,\\mathbb{E}\\,\\mathrm{Tr}(A^{2k}) = C_k + b_k/d + O(1/d^2)$ with $C_k$ the Catalan numbers. The correction constant $b_k$ is NOT a function of the row's fourth moment alone. Evidence at $d=14$ over $\\sim10^5$ designs per row law: (i) rows with i.i.d. coordinates of kurtosis $\\kappa$ give $b_k$ a function of $\\kappa$ only, a three-point law and a Gaussian at $\\kappa=3$ agreeing to $0.2$--$0.5$ standard errors on $k=2,3,4,5$ while $\\kappa\\in[1,9]$ moves the excess by a factor $2.3$; (ii) but two constructions with the SAME typical-direction kurtosis and different dependence disagree by an order of magnitude --- a rank-one Veronese row (kurtosis $3+24/d$) and an i.i.d. row matched to that kurtosis give $k=2$ excess $0.462$ versus $0.041$, a factor $11$; (iii) interpolating with $z=(XX^\\top-rI)/\\sqrt{2r}$, a sum of $r$ independent rank-one forms, the excess falls roughly as $1/r$ ($0.46,0.23,0.13,0.085$ at $r=1,2,4,8$) while the kurtosis $3+12\\,\\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)/r \\to 3$. So within one dependence class the fourth moment tunes $b_k$, but across classes at fixed fourth moment $b_k$ varies by a factor of order ten; a derivation of $b_k$ for the Veronese row ($b_2\\approx7.7$, $b_3\\approx49$, $b_4\\approx248$, $b_5\\approx1148$) must use the rank-one dependence of $xx^\\top$, not a kurtosis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.169319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f5d7c9f7b71b6e2e22db71a5f7178d48fb7f017e0375cf0b81616f9e3752f137","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 68 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sxi}(\alpha,q_0)$. 

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\PRFTWOdefn \\
	\PRFTHRdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
Consider any controls
	\[(q_*=q_0, b, \sigma, w, p, \zeta=\delta_0, \zeta^\Ising) 
	\in \Adm^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\,.\]
	We will construct controls $(\tilde q_* = q_0, \tilde b, \tilde \sigma, \tilde w, \tilde p, \tilde \zeta = \delta_0, \tilde \zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\sxi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ so that the endpoint measures $\mu = \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$ and $\tilde\mu = \mu(\tilde q_*, \tilde b, \tilde \sigma, \tilde p, \tilde\zeta)$ coincide.
    This shows
    \[
        \Adm^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
        \subseteq 
        \Adm^{\sxi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
for all $L,\epsilon$, which implies the result by recalling Definition~\ref{d:measure.classes}. In fact, we will take \[(\tilde q_*, \tilde b, \tilde \sigma, \tilde p, \tilde\zeta) = (q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\,,\] so that $\mu = \tilde \mu$ is immediate.
    We will construct controls $(\tilde w, \tilde \zeta^\Ising)$, as well as $\tilde U' \sim \unif([0,1])$ and a Brownian motion $(\tilde W(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]}$, so that for $Y$ and $\tilde Y$ the processes defined by \eqref{e:formal.sde.ising} with (respectively) inputs 
    \begin{align*}
	&(q_*=q_0,w,\zeta^\Ising,
	(W(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]},U')\,,\\
	&(\tilde q_* = q_0,\tilde w,\tilde\zeta^\Ising,(\tilde W(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]},\tilde U')\,,\end{align*}
we have the equality of processes
    \beq
        
        (\tilde Y(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]}
        = (\xi \cdot Y(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]}\,,
    \eeq
    for a random variable $\xi \sim \unif(\{\pm 1\})$ independent of the process $(Y(t))_{t\in [q_0,1]}$. To this end, we construct $\tilde\zeta^\Ising$ as the symmetrization of $\zeta^\Ising$:
    \[ 
    \tilde{\zeta}^\Ising(A)
    \equiv
    \frac{\zeta^\Ising(A)
    +\zeta^\Ising(-A)}{2}
	\] 
for all measurable $A\subseteq \R$. We then sample $\tilde{Y}(q_0)\in\tilde{\zeta}^\Ising$, so that clearly $|\tilde{Y}(q_0)|$ is equidistributed as $|Y(q_0)|$. This symmetrization can be reversed, in the following sense. Define $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ to be the conditional probability of the event $\{Y(q_0)\geq 0\}$ conditional on $|Y(q_0)|$, i.e.,
    \[
        f(x) = \bbP\Big(Y(q_0) \ge 0
        	\,\Big| \,|Y(q_0)| =x\Big).
    \]
For $x,U'' \in [0,1]$ define
    \[g_f(x,U'') \equiv \begin{cases}
            x & U'' \le f(x), \\
            -x & U'' > f(x).
        \end{cases}
    \]
Having sampled $\tilde{Y}(q_0)\in\tilde{\zeta}^\Ising$, we next define
	\[\hat{Y}(q_0) 
	\equiv g_f(|\tilde Y(q_0)|,U'')\,.
	\]
We then verify that $\hat{Y}(q_0)$ is equidistributed as $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta$: for $x>0$,
	\begin{align*}
	&\P(\hat{Y}(q_0) \in dx)
	= \P(|\tilde{Y}(q_0)| \in dx)
		\bbP\Big(Y(q_0) \ge 0
        	\,\Big| \,|Y(q_0)| =x\Big)\\
	&\qquad=\P(|Y(q_0)| \in dx)
		\bbP\Big(Y(q_0) \ge 0
        	\,\Big| \,|Y(q_0)| =x\Big)
	=\P(Y(q_0) \in dx)\,,
	\end{align*}
and similarly for $x\le0$. It follows that we can set $Y(q_0) = \hat{Y}(q_0) \sim\zeta$. We then define
	\[
	\xi = \sign\Big(
		\tilde Y(q_0)Y(q_0)\Big)\,,
	\]
and we claim that $\xi$ is a symmetric random sign that is independent of $Y(q_0)$: for $x>0$,
	\begin{align*}
	&\P\Big(\xi = +1, Y(q_0) \in dx\Big)
	=\P(\tilde{Y}(q_0)\in dx)
	\P\Big(Y(q_0)\ge0 
	\,\Big|\ 
	|Y(q_0)|=x\Big)\\
	&\qquad= \frac{\P(|Y(q_0)|\in dx)}{2}
	\P\Big(Y(q_0)\ge0 
	\,\Big|\ 
	|Y(q_0)|=x\Big)

## Statement and experiment

and one S, with VC-d orientation class; N-2d remaining contexts are
known S. S has all K truths; each A has an independent uniform r-subset.
The factual source chooses contexts uniformly, then truths uniformly.
Training consists of actual iid factual context/candidate samples,
without partition tags. An independent verifier may supply ell true
candidates per variable context, uniformly without replacement, also
without orientation labels. Include those identities in the known
truth union C_x. Condition on ANY positive-probability data outcome
with sizes j_x=|C_x|<r in EVERY variable context. Counts and identities
may differ arbitrarily between siblings. Every orientation remains
compatible; compatible A supports contain C_A. The actual posterior
orientation probabilities need not be uniform.

Require exact source Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY compatible world, using
the uniform coarsening within exact g-probability bins. Allow all g.
Set h_i=min(j_left,j_right) for pair i and

 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N).

The proposed exact CONDITIONAL worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V(0)=sum_{i=1}^d (K-r)*b_{h_i}.                        (1)

An attainer has this risk in every actual compatible world. This is
not an assertion that all other generators have a pointwise lower
bound (C015's varying-count control disproves that). No unconditional
expected minimax value is inferred from (1).

For the same known truths with the partition additionally supplied,
the conditional worst-world oracle value is

 O_worst(0)=sum_i (K-r)*(r-h_i)/(Nr(K-h_i)).              (2)

Thus the exact worst-oracle estimation gap is

 V(0)-O_worst(0)
   =sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i)).                    (3)

The oracle in (2) takes a maximum over supplied orientations; it is
not the average actual-orientation oracle. Formula (3) weights the
conditional 1/N-per-pair classification error of the specified fair
completion of support-consistent ERM. No statistically optimal ERM
rate or general unweighted-error identity is claimed.

## Residual support variability forces one score level

Fix ANY robustly zero-calibrated generator g and its exact score
partition Pi. In every bin B, p_world(B)=g(B) for every compatible
world, hence its source mass is invariant under changing supports or
orientations. For a context x possibly A, let Q_x be its K-j_x
uncertified atoms. Since 1<=r-j_x<K-j_x, any two atoms of Q_x can be
swapped in a compatible A support while all other truth identities
remain fixed. If one were in B and the other outside, this swap would
change p(B) by 1/(Nr), contradicting invariance. Therefore each bin
contains either ALL or NONE of Q_x. Equivalently all Q_x atoms have
one common score; denote their unique bin B_x.

This argument FAILS if j_x=r, since there is then no residual truth
to swap. C016's neutral-bundle counterexample exploits exactly this
boundary, rather than contradicting the present strict hypothesis.

## Classifying each pair's invariant bins

Write s=j_L<=t=j_R<r for one pair; relabel siblings if necessary.
For a bin B let u_x=|B intersect C_x| and epsilon_x=1 if Q_x is in B,
else zero. The difference between its A-context and S-context source
contributions is

 delta_x(B)=(K-r)/(NrK)*(u_x-epsilon_x*j_x).

Independent flipping of this pair's orientation while holding all
other pairs fixed implies delta_L(B)=delta_R(B) for EVERY bin.

If B_L!=B_R, then in B_L the left delta is nonpositive and the right
delta nonnegative. Equality forces u_L=s,u_R=0. Similarly B_R has
u_R=t,u_L=0. Thus each context lies entirely in its own one score bin.

If B_L=B_R=B*, equality gives

 k=s-u_L=t-u_R, 0<=k<=s.

Outside B* every bin contains only known truths from these contexts
and contains the SAME number of known truths from each sibling.
Exactly k known truths from each sibling lie outside B*.

## Reduction to the balanced-count game

For each pair retain the smaller context's complete known set C_L.
In the larger context retain a subset C'_R of size s. If the residual
bins are different, choose any such subset. If they coincide in B*,
retain ALL k larger-context known truths outside B* and choose any
s-k additional known truths inside B*. This is possible since there
are t-k>=s-k such inside truths. The sets may depend on g; this is
a proof comparison, not the algorithm.

Expand the compatible world set by forgetting the t-s surplus truths
in the larger context. In the distinct-bin case both contexts had
one score, so every source bin mass and every false-atom count per
bin are unchanged under this expansion. In the common-bin case all
newly uncertified atoms lie in B*. Every other bin retains the same
known-true counts; in B* the A context always has r-k true atoms and
K-r false atoms, in either orientation and for every expanded support.
Thus again each source bin mass and each actual false-count-per-bin
vector is unchanged.

Do this independently for every pair. For the same fixed g,

* robust zero calibration holds on the EXPANDED balanced-count game;
* the set of possible false masses across its worlds equals the set
  across the original compatible worlds, orientation by orientation.

The expanded game has balanced known counts h_i and arbitrary known
identities. It need not preserve the original sample/verifier labels:
it is an enlarged source-world comparison, not a claimed posterior.
C015's general balanced-count lower bound at c=0 therefore yields
max_original H(g)=max_expanded H(g)>=sum_i(K-r)b_{h_i}.
Dependence of the selected balanced sets on g causes no problem:
the balanced theorem is uniform over all sets of the stated sizes.

## Balanced comparison lower bound, stated here for completeness

For the expanded known sets of balanced sizes h_i, average orientations
fairly and average compatible residual supports uniformly. This is an
artificial lower-bound distribution, not the actual posterior. Its
mean factual law mu gives density a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N) to known truths,
b_h to uncertified atoms in count-h pairs, and 1/(NK) to fixed S.
The false probability of each uncertified atom is tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)).
As h increases b_h decreases and tau_h increases; safe densities are
at least 1/(NK)>=b_h. For E_h the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, every inside density is <=every outside
density. Uniform coarsening in any bin transfers mass INTO E_h, so
mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h with T_h as in (6). Robust feasibility and
TV convexity imply TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c, hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+.
The artificial average false risk is exactly
tau_0*g(E_0)+sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h).
It is at least (6), and the maximum original risk equals the maximum
expanded risk and is at least this average. This proves the needed
balanced lower bound directly, for c=0 and throughout (4), without
requiring a prior-card theorem or any actual posterior identity.

## Attainment and oracle comparison

Select h_i known truths from each sibling before constructing g. Put
their two known-true groups at score (1/r+1/K)/(2N); put the remaining
2(K-h_i) pair atoms at b_{h_i}, and fixed S atoms at 1/(NK).
Each pair group has invariant p mass under all original worlds.
Exact-score mergers preserve invariance. This g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget, and each actual world's K-r false atoms per pair
all receive b_{h_i}. This proves the matching upper bound in (1).

If a supplied orientation chooses A at count j, the zero-budget oracle
has risk (K-r)*(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)), by the ordered known-A-group argument
of C009/C015. This quantity decreases with j, so its maximum over
independent orientations picks j=h_i in every pair, proving (2).
Subtracting gives (3) exactly.

This is a whole strict-unsaturation data region for arbitrary d,N,K,r,
not a theorem deduced from nine small finite partition searches. It
uses robust zero calibration critically and does not extend to c>0
by continuity alone. Saturated-context neutral bins are a real excluded

The reduction extends to EVERY budget

 0<=c<c_star=(K-r)/(2NrK).                               (4)

 TV(p_w,Pi,p_w',Pi)<=2c.                                (5)

If a context's uncertified atoms occupy two different score bins,
swap one true and one false uncertified atom in its A support. This
is possible since j_x<r<K. The coarsened source laws then differ

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:57:16.073393+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f625483b64e58598b6cfa8ed9a254c09274dc7f44a9bb180844f0a5bbdfc0aa3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Good blocks of arXiv:2507.00329, 'Oriented bond-site percolation in random environment and contact processes with periodic r'] At fixed scale $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we partition $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}$ into blocks of length $L_k$, that is,
    \[
    	I_{k,i} := [iL_k, (i+1)L_k), \quad i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0},
    \]
    so that each scale-\((k+1)\) block $I_{k+1,i}$ consist of $\lfloor L_{k}^{\gamma-1}\rfloor$ many scale-$k$ blocks, i.e., $\#\{m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0} \colon  I_{k,m}\cap I_{k+1,i}\neq\emptyset\} = \lfloor L_{k}^{\gamma-1}\rfloor$.
    On the initial scale, we call a block $I_{0,i}$ {\em good} if $I_{0,i}\cap X \neq \emptyset$. For general $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we call the scale-\(k\) block $I_{k,i}$ {\em good} if it either
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item contains no more than one bad scale-\((k-1)\) sub-block or      
        \item if it contains exactly two consecutive bad sub-blocks, i.e., there exists \(m\) such that \(I_{k-1,m}, I_{k-1,m+1}\subset I_{k,i}\) are bad but all other sub-blocks \(I_{k-1,n}\subset I_{k,i}\) are good themselves.   
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K and gcd(r,K-r)=1","Paired A/S VC-d family; uniform contexts then truths, uniform independent r-subsets in A, all K truths in S","Actual iid factual samples without tags and optional independent uniform partial verifier; known truth counts j_x<=r, no logically identified pairs","Robust exact-level source Mis_infinity<=c for EVERY compatible world,0<=c<1/(2NrK); arbitrary generators; conditional worst-world objective"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:04:06.350847+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; source-bin rigidity","id":"claim_f63d27667aecff51f3c3a2cde5580627be35364031ec5e239606e9551fea2ef5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Coprime alphabet/support sizes remove the saturation obstruction

T379-C019 v2: proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2. Arbitrary VC dimension and unequal known
truth counts, including saturation; conditional robust small-budget
game only. General noncoprime saturated mixtures and larger budgets
remain open here.

## Model and statement

Let d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K be integers with gcd(r,K-r)=1. There
are d unresolved A/S context pairs and N-2d fixed known S contexts.
Each S has all K truths; each A has an independent uniform r-subset.
The factual law chooses contexts uniformly then uniformly true within
context. Actual iid factual samples have no orientation tags. An
optional independent verifier supplies a uniform ell-subset of truths
in each variable context, including S, without orientation labels.
Let C_x be the distinct observed-plus-certified truth union. Condition
on ANY positive-probability data outcome with j_x=|C_x|<=r in every
variable context. Thus no orientation is logically excluded. Some
contexts may have j_x=r; sibling counts and sample repetitions may
differ arbitrarily. Actual orientation likelihoods need not be equal.

Write h_i=min(j_left,j_right) and D_h=#{i:h_i=h},0<=h<=r. Put

 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)), M_h=D_h*(2-h/r-h/K)/N,
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^r M_t.

For every 0<=c<1/(2NrK), the proposed exact all-generator conditional
worst-world frontier under source Mis_infinity<=c in EVERY compatible
world is

 V(c)=tau_0*(T_0-c)_+
       +sum_{h=1}^r(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+.          (1)

Source miscalibration is TV(g,p_Pi) using uniform coarsening of p in
exact g-probability bins. The same-data partition-supplied WORST-
ORIENTATION oracle has frontier

 O(c)=alpha_0*(Q_0-c)_+
       +sum_{h=1}^r(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+,       (2)

where alpha_h=2tau_h,A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr),Q_h=sum_{t=h}^r A_t.
In particular A_r=0: a saturated oracle group has zero residual mass,
so its risk-one coefficient must NOT be used to infer a nonzero slope.
The exact zero-budget estimation penalty is

 V(0)-O(0)=sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i)).              (3)

No exact endpoint, largest interval, actual-world-only calibration or
global expected minimax identity is claimed. This extends C017 to
saturation under the coprime arithmetic hypothesis, using a possibly
smaller interval. It does not contradict C016/C018's noncoprime cases.

## Discrete source-bin mass rigidity

Fix any robustly c-feasible generator g and its exact score partition
Pi. For every compatible world and every cell B, p(B) is an integer
multiple of 1/(NrK), since the original atom masses are 0,1/(Nr) or
1/(NK). This is a lattice statement about BIN MASSES; individual
coarsened atom probabilities have the additional bin-size divisor.
For two worlds w,w', uniformity within the SAME cells gives

 TV(p_w,Pi,p_w',Pi)=(1/2)*sum_B |p_w(B)-p_w'(B)|.

If any bin mass differs, the nonzero integer differences sum to zero,
so this TV is at least 1/(NrK). Triangle inequality and feasibility
instead give TV<=2c<1/(NrK). Therefore EVERY source bin mass is
world-invariant. This quantization argument itself needs no coprimality.

## Coprimality restores rigidity at a saturated sibling

For an unsaturated context j_x<r, swapping a residual true and false
candidate in a compatible A support shows that all uncertified atoms
occupy one score bin, as in C017. Consider an unequal pair with counts
s<t. The smaller context is unsaturated. If t<r both contexts already
have this property. If t=r, in any score bin let u_L be its known-L
count and epsilon_L indicate inclusion of all K-s uncertified L atoms;
let u_R be its known-R count and v_R its count outside C_R. Independent
orientation invariance gives

 (K-r)*(u_L-epsilon_L*s-u_R)=-r*v_R.

Hence (K-r)|r*v_R. Since gcd(r,K-r)=1, Bezout implies (K-r)|v_R.
Because 0<=v_R<=K-r, a cell contains either all or none of the
saturated context's outside atoms. Thus their score is also constant.
This is the step that fails for the noncoprime neutral bundles in C016.
The standard Bezout identity was returned in recall/walk004.txt,
card claim_63c5ddfd2e7e4d178b7628c572034232.

Both saturated counts r,r are already balanced; they need no expansion
and no assertion that their outside atoms occupy one score bin.

## Reduction to balanced minima

For each unequal pair both outside-known sets now occupy unique bins.
For any cell write u_x for its known-truth count and epsilon_x for
whether it contains the entire outside-known set. The A-minus-S source
contribution is (K-r)*(u_x-epsilon_x*j_x)/(NrK), so equality under the
orientation flip makes these expressions equal for the two siblings.

If the two outside-known bins differ, each contains an ENTIRE context
and none of the other context. If they coincide in B*, the number k
of known truths outside B* is equal in both siblings and at most s,
the smaller count. Retain all smaller-context truths. In the larger
context retain its k known truths outside B* and any s-k of its known
truths inside B*. Forget all other larger-context truths.

Expanding compatible supports by this forgetting preserves every source
bin mass: outside B* known counts are unchanged; in B* the A context
always has r-k truths. It also preserves each bin's false count for
each orientation: all K-r A false atoms remain in the same outside-
known bin. If entire contexts were separate bins, both facts follow
from fixed context mass 1/N and fixed false count K-r. Balanced pairs,
including r,r, are kept unchanged. This works independently across pairs.

Thus for the same g the enlarged balanced-minimum source game is still
robustly c-feasible and has exactly the same possible false masses.
The retained sets may depend on g, solely as a proof device. No claim
about their actual posterior or original sampling probability is made.

## Arbitrary-bin lower bound and construction

In the balanced comparison game average orientations fairly and
compatible supports uniformly. The mean factual law mu has density
(1/r+1/K)/(2N) on known truths, density
b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N) on uncertified atoms in count-h pairs,
and 1/(NK) in fixed S. Their artificial false probability is tau_h.
Increasing h decreases b_h and increases tau_h, including h=r.
Safe densities are >=1/(NK)>=b_h.

For the union E_h of uncertified groups at counts >=h, every inside
density is <=every outside density. In EACH cell, uniform averaging
therefore transfers mass into E_h: mu_Pi(E_h)>=T_h. Convexity of TV
over compatible worlds and robustness give TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c, so
g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+. The artificial average false risk is the layer-cake
sum tau_0*g(E_0)+sum_{h>0}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})g(E_h), which is at least
(1). The original worst risk equals the expanded worst risk and is
at least this average. Unequal actual posterior weights never enter.

For attainment select h_i known truths in each sibling, before seeing
any hidden orientation or residual support. Start at the balanced
comparison mean law; remove mass from uncertified groups in decreasing
h order, uniformly inside each count group, and transfer it to fixed S.
Each paired selected-known group and residual group has invariant p
mass under ALL original worlds. The generator is constant on each,
so exact-score mergers preserve invariance and Mis_infinity<=c.
Their false fractions are tau_h in EACH actual world; the false mass
is exactly (1) worldwise. The algorithm uses observed unions and model
parameters only, not hidden labels or future observations.

For a supplied orientation, ignoring its surplus A truths down to h_i
attains the min-count oracle bound. Conversely the compatible orientation
choosing the smaller-count sibling as A in every pair gives exactly
that oracle game. Ordered known-A residual density/risk tails yield (2),
including the zero-mass saturated group. This proves the worst-oracle
comparison. At c=0 subtracting the individual terms gives (3).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.327203+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f669b7380ef83b4fdac8c4a5ff8ca364ec3a81ad3f19c493c5d705e2aba9ef4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop smash-gl-left-Quillen of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The smash product of orthogonal spectra defines a left Quillen bifunctor 
    \[
        \cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}_\textup{$G$-global}\times\cat{$\bm{H}$-OrthSp}_\textup{$H$-global}\to
        \cat{$\bm{(G\times H)}$-OrthSp}_\textup{$(G\times H)$-global}.
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        To see that the pushout product axiom for cofibrations holds, it suffices to treat the case of generating cofibrations. Using that the enriched Yoneda embedding $\textbf{\textup{O}}^{\textup{op}}\to{\textbf{\textup{OrthSp}}}$ admits a strong symmetric monoidal structure, we then compute that the pushout product of $\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\smashp_{\varphi} G_+\smashp (\partial D^n\hookrightarrow D^n)$ with $\textbf{\textup{O}}(W,-)\smashp_\psi G_+\smashp (\partial D^m\hookrightarrow D^m)$ (where $\varphi\colon K\to G$ and $\psi\colon L\to H$ are homomorphisms) is given by
        \[
            \textbf{\textup{O}}(V\oplus W,-)\smashp_{\varphi\times\psi}(G\times H)_+\smashp\big((\partial D^n\hookrightarrow D^n)\mathbin{\raise.25pt\hbox{\scalebox{.67}{$\square$}}}(\partial D^m\hookrightarrow D^m)\big)_+,
        \]
        where we view $H\times K\subset {\textup{O}}(V)\times {\textup{O}}(W)$ as a subgroup of ${\textup{O}}(V\oplus W)$ via block sum. As $\textbf{\textup{Top}}$ is cartesian and $\cat{$\bm{(G\times H)}$-OrthSp}$ is topological, this is then indeed a cofibration, completing the proof of the pushout product axiom for cofibrations.

        Next, we will show that $i\mathbin{\raise.25pt\hbox{\scalebox{.67}{$\square$}}} f$ is a $(G\times H)$-global weak equivalence for any cofibration $i\colon A\to B$ between cofibrant objects and any $H$-global weak equivalence $f\colon X\to Y$ between cofibrant objects; this then in particular applies to the generating (acyclic) cofibrations, proving (up to exchanging the roles of $G$ and $H$) the remaining case for the pushout product axiom. For this we consider the defining pushout
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}
                A\smashp X\arrow[r,"i\smashp X"]\arrow[d,"A\smashp f"']\arrow[dr,phantom,"\ulcorner"{very near end}] & B\smashp X\arrow[d]\arrow[ddr, bend left=15pt,"B\smashp f"]\\
                A\smashp Y\arrow[r]\arrow[drr, bend right=15pt,"i\smashp Y"'] & P\arrow[dr,dashed,"i\mathbin{\raise.25pt\hbox{\scalebox{.67}{$\square$}}} f"{description}]\\
                && B\smashp Y\rlap.
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]
        By the previous proposition applied to ${\textup{triv}}_HA$ and ${\textup{triv}}_Gf$, the map $A\smashp f$ is a $(G\times H)$-global weak equivalence, and likewise for $B\smashp f$. Moreover, $i\smashp X$ is a cofibration by the previous step, so that $B\smashp X\to P$ is also a $(G\times H)$-global weak equivalence by left properness. We conclude from $2$-out-of-$3$ that also $P\to B\smashp Y$ is a $(G\times H)$-global weak equivalence, as claimed.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:34:20.707136+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f66eccff4d216fdf233f78b59bde6dd95dd28b44da63c559528c75ba7fda95cf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 (WKBC bridge-weighted regression and numerical consistency) of arXiv:2609.02196, 'Schr\"odinger Bridges on Lie Group Manifolds for Probabilistic Intrinsic Generation'] The population minimizer is \(\bm s^*=\nabla_{\bm\xi}\log h_t^{\beta^*}\), and
\begin{equation}
\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s)-\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s^*)
=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T
\int\norm{\bm s(t,x)-\bm s^*(t,x)}^2
P_t^{\rm SB}(\dd x)\,\dd t.
\end{equation}
Let \(P^{\bm s,\pi_0}\) denote the controlled law with normalized control
\(\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\bm s\) and initial law \(\pi_0\). If
\(P_0^{\rm SB}\ll\pi_0\) and the relevant Girsanov exponentials are true martingales, then
\begin{equation}
\KL(P^{\rm SB}\|P^{\bm s,\pi_0})
=\KL(P_0^{\rm SB}\|\pi_0)
+\gamma T\bigl[\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s)
-\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s^*)\bigr].
\end{equation}
In particular, when \(\pi_0=P_0^{\rm SB}\),
\begin{equation*}
d_{\rm BL}(P^{\rm SB},P^{\bm s,P_0^{\rm SB}})
\le
\sqrt{2\gamma T\bigl[\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s)
-\mathcal J_{\rm WKBC}^{\rm br}(\bm s^*)\bigr]}.
\end{equation*}
Thus the regression-to-path-law conversion has the explicit constant \(\gamma T\) and requires no auxiliary occupation-density-ratio constant.

For positive numerical factors \((f_{0,N},g_{T,N})\), the same reverse-KL argument applies to the corresponding numerical bridge and yields the path-space decomposition in Eq.~\eqref{eq:wkbc-total-error}. Under the approximation conditions in \cref{app:wkbc-implementation}, its numerical-bridge term tends to zero as the lattice, quadrature, Sinkhorn, interpolation, and initial-law approximations are refined, while its regression term vanishes with bridge-weighted risk consistency. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\Roman*)}]

 \begin{equation}

 \end{equation}
 This unitary gives the direct implication in
 \eqref{overview:eq:weak-closure}; collision-null replicas give the
 converse realization and the convergence of the finite contraction
 register.

 \item Put

 \end{equation}

 \begin{equation}

 \qquad G_C\indep A_*.
 
 \end{equation}

 factor $A_*$ need not be canonical.

 admits a sufficiently slow diagonal $J(n)\to\infty$ for which
 \begin{equation}

 and the finite-level characteristic-function error is bounded by a
